C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The 194 flames ignited for BRE significantly exceeds the 73 tests which were specified as 
required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  As such, more 
than 2.5 times as many flames were ignited than had been planned. 
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for 
all tests.  Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is done 
because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed 
per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some 
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  This 
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the 
project constraints. 
 
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland: 
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the 
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination. 
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for.  The ACME ops camera 
provides video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is 
too zoomed out.  [As a clarification, the ops camera has a fixed lens and its primary 
purpose is not flame measurements.]  The GigE camera has poor sensitivity in the 
blue, and after the ignition transient all our flames have been blue.  This camera only 
offers 1.4 megapixels of resolution and requires about 1 s exposures for blue flames, 
which is far too slow to be considered video.  The images provided by both cameras 
are, according to UMD marketing staff, at too low resolution to be used in press 
releases.  In round 2 we will increase the gain on the GigE camera, an option we were 
unaware of in round 1. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
See the discussion in III.D regarding fouling or degradation of the paint on the BRE 
burner’s heat flux sensors. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of such effects and it has thus far not been evaluated with 
available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  
Note that although the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is 
conducted, is equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) it was not utilized for 
BRE (or any ACME) testing because of the crew time needed to enable and disable the 
isolation before and after testing.

Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and BRE’s first round is considered to be successful despite the frequent 
saturation of the radiometer data discussed in section III.B.2.  Meanwhile, the second 
round is tentatively considered to be highly successful, where final assessment will 
depend on further review and analysis of the data. 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student 
Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker) 
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers, 
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering 
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design 
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).  
 
All of the round 1 and 2 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their 
original calibrations.  As presented below, the data is being processed to address the 
effect of the combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces. 
 
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from 
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass 
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated 
fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of 
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in 
an inert matrix).  Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real 
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.  Other than for a candle flame, this 
has not been shown before. 
 
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.   
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center (r = 9.5 mm). As the sensors 
are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion 
products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as the dew point 
for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature 
and can achieve temperatures over 100oC.  Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures 
below the dew point that lead to added heat to the sensor.  Above the dew point, the 
condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.  When the sensor is 
dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended.  
 
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the 
duplicative NASA BRE burner.  Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect 
in the ISS tests.  The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully 
evaporates.  More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect.  Fortunately, by 
the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.

Ambient temperature before ignition is applicable to all thermocouples that can be

Our analysis of the radiometer sensor data has indicated its consistent ability to measure 
the flame overall radiation heat loss fraction.  The method to determine the radiative heat 
flux component to the burner is more complex, and it is based on the geometrical details 
of the radiometers and burner surface relative distance and orientation.  Also, the burner 
surface will re-radiate heat that impinges the radiometer and it needs to be corrected.  
All of the available radiation data are processed for the first round of testing and an 
empirical radiation correlation with flame height was found.  
 
The video images of all the flames have been compiled and are being quantified in terms 
of flame shapes.  Also, a summary booklet of all of the key findings along with heat flux 
and surface temperature data for each test was compiled. 
 
Alexander Snegirev, our Russian partner, has attempted a numerical simulation of at least 
one of the ISS BRE tests.  That work is still in progress.  It should be remarked his student 
won the Student Prize for Best Presentation at the 9th International Seminar on Fire and 
Explosion Hazards held in St. Petersburg, Russia in April 2019 for simulating our 5-s BRE 
drop tests.  
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral 
student Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker) 
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat 
surface of 25 mm diameter.  Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have 
focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced 
wind for opposed flow spread.  We already knew that this would be possible from normal-
gravity research.  The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, 
has been shown to produce steady flames.  However, many droplet flames were found to 
extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame.  We see this as well in the extended 
ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal 
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia 
and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are 
all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft 
 
Figure 6 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred 
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a 
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done by using the arithmetic average 
of the center and offset heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux.

heat of combustion of about 24 kJ/g and a heat of gasification of about 3 kJ/g.  As such it 
could represent PMMA as a material solid.  This is a profound result indicating a common 
plastic could steadily burn under these NASA proposed atmospheric conditions.

content:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
127 
 
The experimental flammability maps are shown in Figures 15 and 16.  Both plots indicate 
a decreasing, inverse asymptotic-like curve that approaches zero, for heat of gasification 
with mass flux.  It is surprising that the data cluster about a nearly singular trend.  
However, both plots show that the heat of gasification is up to 20 % higher for the lower 
heat of combustion 23.6 kJ/g.  Our tests in the University of Maryland lab have shown, 
with the BRE in 1-g that similar results for propane-nitrogen mixtures have the opposite 
behavior with heats of gasification decreasing with heat of combustion for the same mass 
flux.  But again, the data mostly cluster about one trend line except for very low heats of 
combustion.  However, the corresponding 1-g heat of combustion data shift far to the 
right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 15 and 16.  For example, the 1-g 
data would indicate ( 𝑚̇”, 𝐿) points of about 30 g/m2s, 2 kJ/g and 10, 0.5.  Moreover, our 
previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with an apparent 
vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here.  Obviously, the current 
data at durations of minutes are more accurate than those limited to 5 s.  However, it has 
been shown that the ISS heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly 
steady.  Figures 15 and 16 include the heats of gasification derived from the self-
extinguished endpoint data as well.  Remarkably, the self-extinguished not-so-steady data 
follow the same trend as the steady data.  
 
Let us interpret Figures 15 and 16 in terms of the flammability of real materials in 
microgravity.  Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to 
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g.  Some 
selected literature values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are 
listed in Table 4.  The accuracy of the calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the 
two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic average of the two heat flux sensors data 
for obtaining the flammability map.  However, same results are shown considering the 
calorimeter data.  Figure 15 would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) 
would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s.  Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5 
g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.  
 
 
Round 2 tests were finished with 196 successful ignitions.  The measured heat flux by the 
transducers were used and the end point data of the long-duration tests (i.e., the tests in 
which the fuel flow was terminated as opposed to the tests that self-extinguished) were 
used to obtain heats of gasification.  The heats of gasification of these data from round 2 
testing as a function of fuel mixture mass flux are shown in Fig. 19.  One important fire

of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10

1 Feb. 2022 
130 
 
The imaging data from ops camera and ACME camera are used to create videos and image 
sequences for all of the tests.  Preliminary analysis on the first three days of the second 
round of ISS testing data was performed.  Pure methane was the fuel used for testing on 
the third day at 3 different nominal ambient conditions.  It was observed that methane 
was hard to ignite compared to ethylene and flames tend to self-extinguish faster even at 
a high oxygen concentration.  
 
A new method is used to examine the asymptotic behavior of the heat flux data.  The 
inverse of the burn-time was used as the abscissa and the transient data from the two 
heat flux sensors are shown in Figure 18 for one of the tests.  
 
Figure 28. Transient heat flux vs. inverse of the burn time for 20279B4 with XO2 = 37.95%, p = 
14.7 psia and mass flux of 2.46 g/m2s. 
 
Our preliminary analysis on the heat flux data led to the flammability map (heats of 
gasification, L, vs. fuel mixture mass flux) shown in Figure 19 which contains all of the 
round 2 tests with quasi-steady data [2].

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
141 
 
Appendix H. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 
This section is from Dennis Stocker’s log of ACME operations. 
 
BRE round 1, featuring tests with ethylene and the 25-mm burner  
 
2019 
Week 16: January 11-17 
David: On GMT 014, thank you for replacing the imaging modules in the CIR LLL-UV Imaging Package. Then 
on GMT 018, great job configuring the back of the CIR Optics Bench to support future ACME experiments. 
We appreciate all your hard work and diligence during the many intricate tasks! 
 
Week 18: January 25-31 
David: On GMT 031 & 032, great job configuring the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME 
experiment, BRE (Burning Rate Emulator). We appreciate your attention to detail during the many 
complicated tasks! We especially appreciate you taking all the closeout photos of the newly installed 
hardware. We will check out and calibrate the newly installed hardware next week and perform the first 
test points late next week. 
 
Week 19: February 1-7 
Oleg & Anne: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold & GC Bottles this week! We these new bottles installed, 
we look forward to starting the next ACME experiment, BRE (Burning Rate Emulator). 
 
Week 20: February 8-14 
On GMT 039, we performed our first ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points. Unlike the other 
ACME experiments, BRE is focused on improving spacecraft fire safety rather than practical terrestrial 
combustion. More specifically, BRE uses gaseous fuels to determine the flammability of liquids and solids 
in microgravity by selecting test conditions to match key parameters. We performed nine successful tests 
burning ethylene on the 25-mm diameter burner, where the burner’s embedded sensors measure the 
heat flux that would normally vaporize a liquid or solid fuel. The tests were conducted under a range of 
oxygen concentrations and pressures, including some atmospheres that could be used for future crew 
vehicles or habitats. 
 
Figure 1. Sequential Monochrome Images of the First BRE Flame Stabilized on the Cylindrical Burner 
 
Figure 1 shows a sequence of three images from BRE’s first on-orbit test. The first image shows that the 
flame grew to become nominally hemispherical (over the burner outlet, which can also be seen). The 
second image shows a hole in the top of the flame due to radiative heat loss. However, the third image

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
142 
 
shows that the flame recovered, where the hole closed. In this latter phase of the test, measurements of 
chemiluminescence (from OH*) clearly reveal that the flame was oscillating at approximately 1 Hz. These 
oscillations (the opening and closing of the flame’s top) were seen to grow in magnitude and are 
associated with the flame’s approach to extinction. In the first test, this lasted for an extended time, but 
in other tests at lower oxygen concentrations the oscillations sometimes lasted 10 seconds or less before 
the flame quenched. BRE seeks to understand the flame extinction and the conditions under which the 
flames become unsteady and finally extinguish. 
 
Week 21: February 15-21 
Testing for the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment resumed on GMT 051 following a revision of the 
ignition procedure.  Eight successful tests were conducted burning pure ethylene, which is naturally a 
sooty fuel because of its double bond, but the soot produced during ignition quickly vanished leaving a 
pale blue flame, where the flame temperatures were insufficient to generate soot.  These flames grow to 
be nominally hemispherical, then become quasi-steady although weakening, and finally become unsteady 
and extinguish when radiative heat losses become too great.  The experiment’s goal is to improve our 
understanding of material flammability in microgravity and thereby guide the selection of materials use 
in spacecraft.  
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
The video from test 19039G1 is typical of the BRE tests conducted thus far, where the flame grows 
to become nominally hemispherical, during which time the soot produced at ignition vanishes.  
The flame then becomes quasi-steady, e.g., in terms of the flame shape and size, although it can 
be seen that the flame weakens with time – becoming dimmer and more diffuse.  Oxygen 
transport to the flame is inhibited because it is blanketed by an ever-thickening cloud of carbon 
dioxide and water vapor.  Eventually, radiative heat loss leads the top of the flame (on the video’s 
left) to locally extinguish, leaving a hole in the flame.  But the fuel and oxygen, which are normally 
separated by the flame, mix and the flame quickly reestablishes, filling the hole.  A pattern of 
oscillation begins, which also features periodic lifting of the flame base from the cylindrical burner 
(on the right of the video).  The oscillations grow in strength, where the flame becomes 
momentarily just a ring.  At the end, before complete extinction, the flame also partially detaches 
from the burner, leaving a crack in the flame’s side extending from the base to its top. 
 
The durations of at least the quasi-steady and unsteady periods are strongly dependent on the 
atmosphere in the chamber, where both the oxygen concentration and pressure have been 
varied.  As one might expect, longer durations are observed at higher oxygen concentrations. 
 
Note that the brighter circle that can be seen in upper middle of the video is due to reflection from 
an optical sensor, which is not seen in the other three camera views. 
 
Week 22: February 22-28 
On GMT 056, we performed ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points with a 50% ethylene/50% 
nitrogen mixture. The flames with 50% ethylene may be steadier than the 100% ethylene flames, which 
require more oxygen at the same total flow rate. The 50% ethylene flames still exhibited flame growth, a 
quasi-steady period, and oscillations leading to extinction. The flames also quickly became soot free (i.e., 
all blue flame) after ignition.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
143 
 
 
Ignition, extinction, and the three main phases of the BRE flame’s life can be seen in this example plot of 
the OH* chemiluminescence measured by one of the three PhotoMultipiler Tube (PMT) modules on the 
ACME Chamber Insert. OH* is an excited molecule that loses energy by emitting a photon of light at a 
specific wavelength (in the ultraviolet). In combustion of most fuels, there is oxygen, hydrogen, and lots 
of energy making OH* measurements a good indicator of the flame. 
 
This data shows that the flame is weakening during the quasi-steady period when the flame size and shape 
is nominally constant. The OH* measurement also clearly shows the oscillations that precede extinction 
and their growing strength. The flame’s oscillations (e.g., with the opening and closing of the top) are at 
a nominally constant frequency that is a little less than 1 Hz. The huge OH* oscillations are the flame’s 
death throes when it splits open from bottom to top and partially detaches from the burner. 
 
Week 23: March 1-7 
On GMT 064, Oleg Kononenko replaced the CIR Manifold #2 Bottle that was consumed during test points 
on GMT 063. For these ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, we used higher fuel flow rates with 
the same fuel (50% ethylene/50% nitrogen) as the test points on GMT 056. We performed a total of six 
tests, where the first—in an atmosphere of 40% oxygen—was notable in that the flame didn’t extinguish 
during the five-minute test even though it was oscillating in the last three minutes. As expected, the flames 
in subsequent tests with higher flow rates grew to be significantly larger in size, and with their higher 
oxygen consumption, they extinguished in significantly shorter times. We observed dramatic oscillations 
with the large flames. Furthermore, these large oscillating flames became asymmetric; whereas, smaller 
BRE flames have been largely axisymmetric even when oscillating.

content:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
144 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
The test shown in this video is the first ACME test—of all the experiments thus far—to have such 
a high fuel flow rate. Initially, the flame behavior is similar to previous BRE tests. The flame is very 
sooty at ignition, due to ethylene’s double bond, where you can see the glowing soot particles 
pass through the flame. But the soot quickly fades away leaving a dim blue flame, where blue is 
the natural color of hydrocarbon flames. The flame expands to reach enough oxygen to consume 
the fuel. Meanwhile, the flame is blanketed by a thickening cloud of carbon dioxide and water 
vapor inhibiting the oxygen’s diffusion to the flame. With the poor oxygen transport, the flame 
weakens, and radiative heat loss leaves a hole in the flame. But oxygen then mixes with the fuel, 
causing the flame to quickly reestablish and the hole closes.  
 
With this flame’s large size, the edge of the flame opening can be seen to curve upward and 
outward—somewhat like a vase—where that is the fuel-lean rim of the flame edge. The opening 
and closing grows in strength as in previous tests, but the flame size is apparently so large that 
asymmetries begin. The flame eventually becomes mostly quenched with just a ring at the base 
and a highly dynamic spiral extending upward. As in previous tests, the flame partially detaches 
from the burner (right side of video), but in this case, the flame surprisingly persists for roughly 
20 seconds despite the large-scale detachment. While careful analysis will be challenging, this 
flame is visually dramatic with its swirling pulsations and powerful death throes. 
 
Week 24/01: March 8-14 
On GMT 072, Oleg Kononenko replaced the CIR Manifold #4 Bottle to support upcoming ACME BRE test 
points with pure ethylene fuel, and he installed the CIR Manifold #1 Bottle to support the upcoming CIR 
FOMA Calibration.  
 
On GMT 066 & 070, we performed the remaining ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points using 
diluted ethylene fuel (50% ethylene/50% nitrogen). These tests were conducted with low fuel flow rates 
under atmospheric conditions that could be used for future crew exploration vehicles (or habitats), i.e., 
with elevated oxygen concentrations (between 26% and 36%) and reduced pressures. Compared to prior 
tests, these flames were steady and didn’t extinguish during the allotted test durations.   
 
Even though these flames appeared steady, measurements of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence revealed 
that they were slowly weakening as each test progressed. Chemiluminescence occurs when excited 
molecules at a high energy state drop to a lower energy state by emitting a photon of a certain 
wavelength. CH* chemiluminescence is why hydrocarbon flames are blue; meanwhile the OH* 
chemiluminescence is in the ultraviolet. 
 
Although the flames were weakening, the thermal radiation from each flame slowly increased because of 
the lack of buoyancy, which, in gravity, removes the hot combustion gases from the vicinity of a flame. 
Instead, these flames became blanketed by a thickening cloud of hot and radiating combustion products, 
namely carbon dioxide and water vapor. This accumulation of products inhibited the transport of oxygen 
to the flame. Yet, with the low flow of diluted fuel, the oxygen diffusion was enough to maintain these 
flames during each test’s duration. If the test durations weren’t limited, these flames would have 
eventually gone out, but it could have taken many minutes for that to happen.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
146 
 
 
This plot illustrates the challenge faced in igniting some BRE tests. The plot is of OH* chemiluminescence, 
which is measured by a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) during the ignition period. Chemiluminescence occurs 
when a molecule drops from a higher to a lower energy level by emitting a photon of a specific 
wavelength. In this case, the excited OH* emits light in ultraviolet (at 310 nm). While this light is not 
visible, it is a good indicator of the flame’s strength or intensity. This plot shows how the flame repeatedly 
flashed across the burner. The flame didn’t stabilize until after the igniter was retracted. Unfortunately, 
by that time the igniter tip had already burned out. 
 
Week 5: April 5-11 
On GMT 094, the final test points were performed for the first round of testing for ACME BRE (Burning 
Rate Emulator). These were the first BRE test points to use very fine ceramic fibers in the flame to acquire 
temperature measurements from the color of the glowing fibers. During the past two months, over 60 
flames were ignited in this first round of testing to improve our understanding of microgravity 
flammability. 
 
This week, Christina Koch configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME experiment, 
Flame Design. Also to support Flame Design, Oleg Kononenko replaced the bottles on CIR Manifold #2, 
CIR Manifold #4, and the CIR GC Helium Manifold. Flame Design is focused on understanding the soot 
processes of flames. Test points will start in a few weeks.

Figure 1. Sample preliminary images from a BRE test, where both were processed from the same raw 
image file. Image (a) reveals the relative positions of the glowing ceramic fibers, while (b) is adjusted for 
determination of the temperature along the fibers. 
 
Figure 1 displays sample images, in which Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) was used to allow optical 
determination of the temperature along the ceramic fibers where they are hot enough to visibly glow. 
The harp-like array of 14-micron SiC fibers was translated throughout the flame allowing measurement of 
the entire temperature field. The temperature is determined by comparison of the red, blue, and green 
color planes of the images, which were taken with a digital camera characterized for quantitative 
measurements. The color of the fiber’s glow is indicative of the temperature, where yellow is hotter than 
orange, which in turn is hotter than red. (The blue in the flame results from the flame chemistry rather 
than the fibers’ broadband thermal radiation.)

2020

content:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
148 
 
Week 22: September 4-10 
On GMT 247, we began the second round of testing for ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) with 13 flames 
ignited using ethylene fuel. While the first round of testing only used the 25-mm diameter burner, this 
round of testing began with the 50-mm diameter burner to better understand the effect of burner size on 
flame behavior. Even though these flames burned for a long time, they were unsteady and extremely 
dynamic. Since BRE’s research focus is on quasi-steady flame behavior, the remaining tests will use the 
25-mm burner. 
 
In many of these 50-mm burner tests, heat loss caused the top of the flame to locally quench—creating a 
hole that allowed for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen. The flame was able to reestablish, closing 
the hole in its top. These oscillations occurred repeatedly and grew in strength such that the flame became 
a ring instead of a dome. Later in the burn, the flame often partially detached from the burner, creating a 
hole in the side of the flame that would also open and close repeatedly. In some cases, this behavior 
transitioned to a more constant hole, where the partial flame would swirl around the burner’s rim as if it 
were “chasing its tail.” 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This clip from a test point video shows the flame dynamics observed in the latter portion of the 
test. This test is burning 100% ethylene fuel in a combustion chamber environment of about 32% 
oxygen/68% nitrogen. The flame, which in microgravity would normally be dome-shaped, has 
largely quenched where only a portion is burning. In this phase of the burn, the flame appears to 
have mostly detached from the burner. The flame swirls around the burner’s rim, where the 
leading edge is bright because of the fuel/oxidizer mixing that occurs where the flame has 
quenched. While the nature of the oscillations changed over time, they made up about 70% of 
the flame’s life. In fact, this flame was still oscillating when the fuel flow was shut off (at a preset 
time), and the flame went out. 
 
Week 23: September 11 - 17 
In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Chris Cassidy replaced the burner, igniter 
arm and tip, and two mass flow controllers on the ACME Chamber Insert on GMT 258. This burner allows 
for steadier flames, and the mass flow controllers allow for slower nitrogen and fuel flow rates. 
 
Week 24: September 18 - 24 
On GMT 261, 13 ethylene flames were ignited for ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) with its primary 
burner, which has a 25-mm diameter outlet. Today’s flames were steadier than those with the 50-mm 
burner used on the previous test day. In fact, one of today’s tests appears to be the most stable BRE flame 
thus far, including the 62 BRE flames ignited in early 2019. The stability of flames in a no-breeze 
environment has important fire safety implications. The current approach to spacecraft fire is to stop 
ventilation so that the flames will quench, but the BRE results indicate that there are conditions under 
which flames will continue to burn in still air. 
 
On GMT 266, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4. An issue with 
the CIR Manifold #4 bottle valve delayed testing this week. From crew photos and video, we determined 
that the valve is already fully open, which we confirmed with powered ops on GMT 267. The CIR Bottle 
Valve Cover was cross-threaded when last installed, which caused it to bind on the valve. When rotating 
the valve cover to remove it, the valve also rotated. We will be able to resume test points next week!

ACME BRE Test Point Image 
 
This image of a dome-shaped flame is from late in a test in which the blue flame remained quasi-steady 
(i.e., changes are occurring at such a slow rate that the flame can be considered constant). The burner is 
illuminated from the left in red. The test was conducted in an atmosphere of about 30% oxygen (with a 
balance of nitrogen and gases resulting from preceding tests) with a reduced pressure of roughly 0.6 atm. 
Future crew exploration may feature vehicles and habitats at elevated oxygen concentrations and reduced 
pressures to facilitate ExtraVehicular Activity (EVA). BRE includes testing under such conditions because 
of the increased fire hazard with elevated oxygen concentrations. 
 
Week 25: September 25 - October 1 
In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the CIR GC Argon 
Bottle and opened the bottle valve at CIR Manifold #2 on GMT 272. He also took some very nice, detailed 
photos of the damaged CIR Bottle Valve Cover. 
 
Week 26: October 2 - 8 
On GMT 279, a record 21 flames were successfully ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) 
experiment using methane as the fuel, which was a first for this investigation. Methane is the primary 
component of natural gas and is a good contrast to ethylene, the fuel used in BRE’s preceding test days. 
Ethylene (C2H4) is naturally sooty in normal-gravity flames because of its C=C double bond; whereas, 
methane (CH4) has no carbon bonds. With a goal of improved spacecraft fire safety, BRE simulates the 
combustion of solid and liquid materials by matching key parameters in tests conducted with gaseous 
fuels. Testing with different gaseous fuels provides an understanding of flammability for a broader range 
of materials.

ACME BRE Test Point Image 
 
This preliminary false-colored image of a dome-shaped flame is from late in a test in which the blue flame 
remained quasi-steady through most of the test duration. Quasi-steady describes when changes are 
occurring at such a slow rate that the flame can be considered constant. This photo was taken shortly 
before the flame oscillated for a few seconds and then self-extinguished. While the flame’s top often 
locally quenches due to radiative heat loss, in this example the flame’s circular rim (at its base) has pulled 
away from the burner due to conductive heat loss. The curvature of the flame’s rim away from, rather 
than toward, the burner’s edge (which can be faintly seen on the left) is evidence of the flame-burner 
separation and the approach of the subsequent flame instability.

which is the primary component of natural gas, as the fuel. By innovatively matching key properties, BRE

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
151 
 
ACME BRE Test Point Image 
 
This preliminary false-colored image of a dome-shaped flame shows an array of 14-micron ceramic fibers 
making temperature measurements. The four visible fibers pass through or near the flame and glow 
because of the high temperature. This flame, which is non-premixed, is like a bubble in that the methane 
fuel is inside the bubble and the oxygen is outside the bubble. The flame shell, like the film of a bubble, is 
a thin sheet where the methane and oxygen come together and react, producing carbon dioxide, water 
vapor, light, and heat. The fibers are only visible where they are hot, near the flame shell, which is why 
the centers of the three lower fibers are not visible.   
 
The temperature profile along each fiber is optically determined from its varying hue through a technique 
known as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). In this image, the blue has been enhanced so that the soot-free 
flame is clearly visible along with the much brighter fibers, which naturally transition from red to orange 
to yellow as the temperature increases. 
 
Week 9: December 11 - 17  
On GMT 346, 12 flames were ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) experiment. To 
investigate the microgravity flammability of solid materials, these tests burned nitrogen-diluted ethylene 
fuel (50% ethylene/50% nitrogen). Generally, the flames continued to burn through their test duration, 
where some exhibited partial detachment from the burner’s rim or partial quenching—creating a hole in 
the flame top. Other flames were quasi-steady, which means changes were occurring at such a slow rate 
that the flame could be considered constant. The results from these tests may guide material selection 
for future spacecraft. 
 
On GMT 350, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to 
support upcoming ACME BRE test points using pure ethylene fuel.

test. Early in the test, the array of five ceramic fibers was translated into the flame to determine

the flame begins to locally quench due to radiative heat loss. The hole allows the fuel and oxygen, 
which are normally separated by the flame sheet, to mix. This mixing enhances flammability and 
causes the flame to reestablish and the hole to close. This oscillatory behavior occurs repeatedly 
at roughly 1 Hz while the opening in the flame becomes successively greater. This flame would 
have self-extinguished but was put out when the fuel was shut off at a preset time. 
 
Week 10: December 18 - 24  
On GMT 352, ten nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames were ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) 
experiment. Ethylene’s (C2H4) C=C double bond can create sooty flames. These tests were conducted in 
oxygen concentrations ranging between 32% to 40%. BRE’s goal is to improve our understanding of 
material flammability in microgravity and thereby guide the selection of materials used in spacecraft. 
 
On GMT 356, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #2 to continue supporting 
ACME BRE test points. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
Upon ignition, the ethylene flame in this video clip exhibits a lot of soot, which is bright whitish-
yellow in appearance. On Earth, soot is normally consumed as it passes through the flame sheet, 
but in this test point the soot particles are large enough to escape the flame. In microgravity, soot 
growth can be enhanced because it stays within the flame longer due to the absence of buoyancy. 
Despite this enhanced residence time, the soot fades away quickly as the burn continues. High 
temperatures are required to create the soot and microgravity conditions can lead to lower flame 
temperatures. There is no buoyancy to bring in fresh oxygen and the combustion products blanket 
these low-momentum flames. The carbon dioxide, water vapor, and soot contribute to radiative 
heat loss. This video clip ends as the flame becomes mostly blue and soot-free. 
 
Week 11: December 25 - 31  
On GMT 358, 17 ethylene flames were ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) experiment. 
These tests were conducted in oxygen concentrations ranging from 24% to 40%, and the ethylene fuel 
was generally diluted with nitrogen. At the higher oxygen concentrations, the flames were generally quasi-
steady and continued to burn until the fuel was shut off. In contrast, at the lower oxygen concentrations, 
the flames all self-extinguished. On GMT 364, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov replaced the gas bottle at CIR 
Manifold #2 to support continuation of ACME BRE test points.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
153 
 
ACME BRE Graph 
 
 
This graph shows as a function of time, the fuel flow (red) and three optical flame measurements from a 
test in which pure ethylene was burned. The optical flame measurements were made with 
Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules of OH* chemiluminescence (purple), CH* chemiluminescence (light 
blue), and broadband emissions in the visible and near UV spectrum (dark blue). OH* and CH* are 
transient molecules which, in the process of chemiluminescence, emit a photon at specific wavelengths 
when they drop to a lower energy level. The CH* chemiluminescence is the principal source of the blue 
seen in hydrocarbon flames, while OH* is in the ultraviolet and is used in ACME to indicate ignition and 
extinction. 
 
The initially sooty flame was ignited at 32 seconds, after which the hot-wire igniter was retracted. At about 
60 seconds, after the ceramic fiber array was inserted, the flame became quasi-steady. But the PMT 
signals weakened with time, where the low-momentum flame became increasingly blanketed by carbon 
dioxide and water vapor in the absence of buoyancy. 
        
At about 95 seconds, the increasing radiative loss caused the flame’s top to quench, creating a hole in the 
flame. This hole allowed the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, to directly mix. 
This mixing enhanced flammability, and the flame quickly reestablished and closed the hole, but then 
again, it locally quenched. This oscillatory behavior happened repeatedly at roughly 1 Hz with the flame 
opening growing with time until the flame became just a ring. We saw this phenomenon in the first round 
of BRE testing performed on ISS in 2019. A paper about computational modeling of it is now in press. 
 
At about 135 seconds, the flame began to partially detach from the rim of the burner and then reattach 
until it completely extinguished at 148 seconds.

154 
 
2021 
Week 14: January 15 - 21  
In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Victor Glover removed the broken fiber and 
replaced the igniter tip on the ACME Chamber Insert on GMT 018. On GMT 020, 15 ethylene flames were 
ignited for the ACME BRE experiment. The array of ceramic fibers (now with three instead of five 
functional fibers) was successfully used to determine the temperature distributions where the fibers were 
hot enough to visibly glow. Tests were conducted in atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft 
and habitats, where that included elevated oxygen concentrations and reduced pressures which can 
facilitate EVA preparation. At normal atmospheric conditions (e.g., ~21% oxygen by volume), the flames 
all self-extinguished. In contrast, three of the five tests conducted at 30-35% oxygen and 0.57 bar (i.e., 8.2 
psia) featured quasi-steady flames, which continued to burn through the test duration. While the oxygen 
concentration dominates the flame behavior, this day’s tests will enable a better understanding of the 
role of the atmospheric pressure on microgravity flammability. On GMT 021, Kate Rubins replaced the gas 
bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of ACME BRE test points. 
 
Week 15: January 22 - 28  
In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Kate Rubins replaced the burner in the ACME 
Chamber Insert on GMT 025. In contrast to the 25-mm burner that was removed, this burner is 50 mm in 
diameter and allows for larger flames. Tests are being conducted with this larger burner to investigate the 
dependence of the microgravity flammability on flame size. 
 
Week 16: January 29 – February 4  
On GMT 028, the final test points were performed for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) experiment 
led by researchers from the University of Maryland and Russia’s Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic 
University. In the study of microgravity flammability, 13 flames were ignited with the 50-mm diameter 
burner at oxygen concentrations from 40% to 23% in 1 atm. This larger burner allows for larger flames 
compared to the 25-mm burner that was used for previous tests. Generally, these larger flames tended 
to self-extinguish due to radiative heat loss, which scales with the flame size. In contrast, the smaller 
flames on the 25-mm burner were generally quasi-steady. BRE studies material flammability with the goal 
of improving spacecraft fire safety. 
 
On GMT 034, Kate Rubins and Victor Glover configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next 
ACME experiment, CLD Flame Part 3 (Coflow Laminar Diffusion). The general goal of CLD Flame is to 
extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted, especially under conditions where 
the flame is sooty or could become unstable. The results could lead to the improved design of practical 
combustion devices on Earth. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This clip from a test point video shows a flame’s oscillatory “death throes” leading ultimately to 
the flame’s extinction (not shown in the clip). Initially, radiative heat loss causes the top of the 
flame (on the video’s left) to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. That opening allows the 
fuel (from the burner) and oxygen (in the chamber) to directly mix, which increases the 
flammability and causes the flame to reestablish. But, due to heat loss, the flame partially 
quenches again, and the opening grows with each oscillation cycle. Later, the flame also begins to 
detach from the burner’s rim, leaving an opening at the flame’s base (on the video’s right). Here 
too the flame reestablishes but then opens again—the opening growing until it extends from the

to three weeks. The BRE experiment runs are focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically,

Appendix N. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The BRE data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments.  To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The BRE image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, typically used with a CH* filter (and likely always or nearly always for BRE) 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and 
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format.  In contrast, the analog video was 
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

University of Maryland graduate student Michael Bustamante was selected as a NASA Space

https://fpe.umd.edu/release/fire-protection-experts-available-to-the-media. 
 
For his work on BRE, Akshit Markan was awarded the University of Maryland Graduate School’s 
Outstanding Graduate Assistant Award for 2017.  Markan’s recognition for his outstanding work is 
further described at https://fpe.umd.edu/news/story/fpe-phd-candidate-wins-2017-outstanding-
graduate-assistant-award.  It explains, for example, that only the top 2% of Graduate Assistants were 
selected for this honor. 
 
In 2021, BRE Co-Investigator Peter Sunderland was inducted as a Fellow in the Combustion Institute 
for his “significant contributions to understanding laminar flame dynamics and soot formation and 
oxidation.”

including the BRE Science Requirements Document (SRD), are available for download from 
https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/downloads/.

Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018 
by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion 
Experiments.” 
 
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts 
of both genders, and the general public.   His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity (for which resources are available via  http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human 
spaceflight.  But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA 
and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL.  In this 
regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online.  For example, he 
regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Educators Conference 
(SEEC).   He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, four national Boy Scout conferences, 
the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree (which was held 
in the U.S.).  Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in these Scouting

content:
ABSTRACT 
 
 
 
 
Title of Dissertation: 
BURNING EMULATIONS OF CONDENSED 
PHASE FUELS ABOARD THE 
INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION   
 
 
 
Parham Dehghani, 
Doctor of Philosophy, 
2022 
 
 
Dissertation directed by: 
Professor Peter B. Sunderland,  
and Professor James G. Quintiere 
Department of Fire Protection Engineering 
 
 
Little is known about the fire hazards of solids and liquids in microgravity. Ground-based tests are 
too short to overcome ignition transients and testing dozens of condensed fuels in orbit is 
prohibitively expensive. Burning rate emulation is one way to address this gap. It involves 
emulating condensed fuels with gases using a porous burner with embedded heat flux gages. This 
is a study of microgravity burning rate emulation aboard the International Space Station. The 
burner had porous round surfaces with diameter of 25 mm. The fuel mixture was gaseous ethylene, 
and it was diluted with various amounts of nitrogen. The resulting heats of combustion were 15 – 
47.2 kJ/g. The flow rate, oxygen concentration in the ambient, and pressure were varied. Heat flux 
to the burner was measured with two embedded heat flux gages and a slug calorimeter. The 
effective heat of gasification was determined from the heat flux divided by the fuel flow rate. 
Radiometers provided the radiative loss fractions. A dimensional analysis based on radiation 
theory yielded a relationship for radiative loss fraction. RADCAL, a narrow-band radiation model,

yielded flame emissivities from the product concentrations, temperature, flame length, and 
pressure. Previously published analytical solutions to these flames allowed prediction of flame 
heights and radius, and when combined with the radiation empirical relationship led to corrections 
of total heat release rate from the flames due to radiative loss. Average convective and radiative 
heat flux were obtained from the analytical solution and a model based on the geometrical view 
factor of the burner surface with respect to the flame sheet, that were used to calculate heats of 
gasification. All flames burning in 21% by volume oxygen self-extinguished within 40 s. However, 
steady flames were observed at 26.5, 34, and 40% oxygen. The analytical solution was used to 
quantify flame steadiness just before extinction. The steadiest flames reached more than 94% of 
their steady-state heat fluxes and heights. A flammability map as a plot of heat of gasification 
versus heat of combustion was developed based on the measurement and theory for nominal 
ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4.

1. Introduction 
1.1 Motivation 
Human-crew space missions presented the possibility of many hazards, notably fires. A 
significant amount of research has been carried out on the characteristics of fire in normal gravity. 
However, it has been observed that the behavior of microgravity fires might be quite different. 
Some experiments have suggested that it might be easier to burn condensed phase fuels in 
microgravity. This highlights the need for an in-depth analysis of condensed fuel flames in 
quiescent artificial atmosphere in microgravity condition i.e., aboard the International Space 
Station (ISS). 
 
The recent urgency in fire control and safety is due to a fire on the Russian Mir space 
shuttle where an oxygen generator caused the blaze [1–3]. It was later found that the fire probably 
extinguished due to the depletion of oxygen supply. This sustained fire is a cause of concern, and 
the scenario calls for precautionary and preventive measures. To prevent a fire from starting in a 
spacecraft, it is necessary to study the conditions of flame development. The logical starting point 
is the case of a laminar diffusion flame in a quiescent environment. 
 
There are a number of variables that alter the way a fire spreads in a space vehicle. The 
effect of buoyancy is seen on Earth as the surrounding air is entrained in by convection which 
gives the flame an upward pointed shape. The negligible buoyancy in microgravity causes the 
flames to have a more hemispherical or bubble-like shape. The presence of forced convection, 
which aides in the spread of fire, comes from the ventilation in the spacecraft. The hemispherical 
shape of the diffusion flame also affects the soot behavior and the release of gases, which in turn 
affects the radiation losses from the flame.  
 
The flammability of various materials being transported into space is assessed through a 
series of normal gravity tests designed by NASA [4]. These tests aren’t sufficient to lay out the

characteristics of a flame in reduced gravity conditions [1]. The burning of numerous fuels has 
been tested in microgravity conditions and it is well documented [5–9]. The ideal scenario is to 
perform routine burn tests aboard the International Space Station (ISS) of potential materials, but 
this is not practical. 
 
In the proposed study, an innovative technique is suggested to study the burning of 
condensed phase fuels. A gaseous burner known as the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) has been 
developed to emulate the characteristics of a condensed fuel flame in a quiescent atmosphere. This 
emulation is theoretically achieved by matching four characteristic properties: heat of gasification, 
heat of combustion, surface temperature and smoke point for the same burner flow rate. BRE 
burner can provide a practical method to study the flammability of various materials aboard 
spacecraft. 
1.2 Literature Review 
Since the beginning of human aspirations for space flight, concerns and incidents have 
made the possibility of fire hazard a real concern [1–3]. Yet over the past decades, we still have 
limited knowledge of the full extent of fires in microgravity [4,10]. Extensive studies have been 
made on very small materials and burners, but these usually include flames with assisted ambient 
flows. We have long known that materials can burn in-place and spread by ambient flow with 
sufficient oxygen in all gravity conditions [6–9,11–30]. While spacecraft will have movement in 
its atmosphere, it is small and random. In microgravity, opposed flow flame spread provides its 
own flow in a quiescent atmosphere [18,26–28,31–33]. What has been deficient is the 
understanding of burning in-place on a surface in a quiescent atmosphere [10]. Anecdotal early 
Kimzey experiments showed that small items of plastics could burn, and controlled experiments 
of a candlewick flame could sustain burning for about an hour in microgravity [34,35]. Also, we 
have learned that liquid droplets can burn quasi-steadily, and steady burning theory is reasonably 
predictive although, the onset of cool flames can augment the burning[36–43].

Fire growth is a combination of three distinct processes: (1) ignition, (2) burning in-place, 
and (3) spread. In microgravity, we have a good understanding of opposed flow flame spread, and 
our knowledge of concurrent spread is also in good shape, as we have a good understanding of 
how items burn with a specified ambient flow. Ignition can also be adequately understood in 
microgravity given an insulting heat flux. In normal gravity, ignition time is reasonably predicted 
by theory that even neglects heat loss, so the process only depends on heat flux and material 
properties. The current study began based on the premise that material properties can be defined 
for fire growth computations, and they can be measured. Indeed, the NASA designated Test 2 is 
the Cone Calorimeter that allows for these property measurements. The NASA Test 1 [44], in 
regulatory use, considers the measure of upward spread in 1-g and at higher than normal oxygen 
mole fractions as the defining safety criterion for material use in spacecraft. Our work is aimed at 
employing Test 2 [45] with a procedure for measuring properties in conjunction with the 
theoretical prediction of burning in microgravity. 
 
The current study was begun some years ago to investigate efficiently the possible burning 
of simulated flat surfaces using a burner [10,46–49]. The burner gases allow ease of ignition and 
the setting of a steady flow rate. It has been also learned that even starting with a steady flow rate, 
the corresponding flame in microgravity grows for some time before an apparent steady state is 
perceived. Early drop facility microgravity experiments for 5-second duration suggested steady 
flame heat flux might occur within that time, but the flame continued to grow [10]. It was suspected 
that the blue flames seen would increase radiation loss as they grew and lead to radiation 
extinction.  
 
Our experiments in this document are all transient. But if a steady state is achieved, the 
data can be interpreted to represent a real material burning. The burner allows control of a fuel 
mixture that defines the heat of combustion per mixture mass (i.e., ethylene diluted with nitrogen 
can provide a range of heats of combustions up to 47.2 kJ/g which is the case of pure fuel). A 
measurement of the flame heat flux back to the burner allows computation of the heat of 
gasification, a key property appropriate to steady burning for an evaporative material. Even with

more complex pyrolysis and charring, an evaporative model leads to good estimates of time 
average burning in transient cases. The surface temperature of the burner relates to the material 
vaporization temperature, but this is a weak dependent parameter on the burning process, as it does 
not significantly affect ignition, and its associated radiative heat flux is usually relatively small 
compared to flame heat fluxes. We have hypothesized that the heats of combustion and 
gasification, both material properties, are key to defining flammability but as flame radiation is 
known to be significant in normal Earth gravity, we have added the smoke point. With these three 
parameters, our work has shown successful emulation of plastics and liquid pool fires of 25 and 
50-mm diameters [4,10,46–54]. In microgravity radiation from soot does not appear to be 
important, but the fuel’s products of water and carbon dioxide, as well as the fuel itself should be 
important for radiation. In short, the problem is to obtain the experimental flammability map (heats 
of gasification vs. fuel mixture mass flux, and eventually vs. heat of combustion) that allows 
obtaining the heat of combustion and heat of gasification to match with those of real materials 
[51,55,56].  
 
Numerical simulations for 5 tests conducted at normal atmosphere was able to successfully 
predict, heat flux, flame existence duration, flame size and radiative heat loss. All these tests led 
to some instabilities, flame oscillation before self-extinguishment. Description of the extinction 
process including instabilities, was another the key achievements of this study [50,57]. The steady 
growth of a flame with mass flux of 3.09 g/m2s (Xf = 1) ignited in atmospheric condition was 
numerically simulated and compared with experiments (DRM22 mechanism, time instants and 
peak temperatures are indicated) shown in Fig. 1.1. In the plots of each simulation, the color scale 
corresponds to the net radiative emission, and the lines were the iso-contours of the volumetric

Time increment between the frames (both experimental and numerical) is 3s. Spatial scale and

Xr. It will then be treated as lost energy and will be used to correct the heat of combustion used in 
the ellipsoidal model to analytically predict flame size, surface heat flux and steady state 
temperature. The other major finding was the flammability map that showed plastics can burn 
steadily in place in microgravity. The achievements of this study so far include analysis of the 
experimental results of round 1-ISS tests [50–52]. The major findings of this paper are correlation 
of radiative loss fraction with flame length, the flammability map and emulation of PMMA, and 
Nylon [51].  
 
The steady data will be used to assess the predictive modeling. The experimental conditions 
range over mass fluxes from 1 to 12 g/m2s, ethylene-nitrogen fuel mixtures of 15% and 100% 
ethylene, oxygen concentrations of 0.21 to 0.40, and pressures of 0.565 to 1 bar. The modeling is 
based on an analytic transient analysis developed with demonstrated numerical accuracy and good 
predictions with 5-s microgravity data. Here, that model will be modified by adjusting the heat of 
combustion, in that purely convective model, by its radiative heat loss. The flame radiative fraction 
is used to make this adjustment. It is shown that a model for the radiative fraction can be developed 
with dependence on an empirical constant. Given the radiative fraction, flame heat fluxes and 
flame temperature can be computed, while flame shape is independent of such. The flame 
temperature range of 1100 K to 1200 K with radiation loss will be used as a criterion for a stable 
flame or steady burning. The radiation code RADCAL is used to develop a model to predict flame 
emissivity and absorption coefficient. It is also shown that it is possible to predict the conditions 
for steady burning from known fuel properties, atmospheric conditions, and fuel diameter [52]. 
1.3 Objectives 
A circular porous burner with gaseous fuel, called the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), is 
developed to emulate the quiescent burning of condensed phase fuels. This  
burner is based on the previous emulators that were used for normal gravity and the drop tower 
experiments [4,10,46–48,55,56]. The premise of the BRE technique is that the emulation is 
achieved by matching four properties of a diffusion flame, i.e., heat of combustion, heat of 
gasification, surface temperature and smoke point. The former two properties are of primary

are as listed below. 
- 
Characterize the burners before data gathering experiments to insure having a good 
understanding of the measurement techniques used onboard the ISS. 
- 
Planning two rounds of microgravity tests to record data by changing different 
parameters, i.e., Fuel mixture mass flux, chamber ambient oxygen mole fraction, 
chamber pressure, fuel type and the burner size.  
- 
Correlate the experimental results by employing relevant steady-state theory and analyze 
the burner as a condensed fuel emulator in microgravity to obtain the flammability map.  
- 
Modify the slug calorimeter calibration constants [48] to account for the heat absorbed by 
the burner rim.  
- 
Examine the dependency of the BRE slug calorimeter on the burn time. 
- 
Convert all data recorded in each round of testing and analyze by segregation of data for 
identifying correlations. 
- 
Modify the radiative fraction correlation, found by dimensional analysis, to account for 
several more independent factors, i.e., Chamber pressure and oxygen mole fraction. It 
requires a working knowledge of RADCAL[58,59] by Grosshandler, a narrow band 
model used for radiation calculation. 
- 
Analyze flame temperature by utilizing ellipsoidal theory [49,60]  
- 
Analyze and estimate the average emissivity associated with each flame. 
- 
Obtaining a flammability map for microgravity condition to address fire safety of 
spacecrafts 
1.4 Roadmap and Timeline for Completion of Dissertation 
The first round of ISS tests preparation, data gathering, and data analysis led to publishing 
two journal papers and one other journal collaboration which are explained in sections 2-5.  
 
The second round of ISS tests provided valuable set of data to analyzed. The remaining 
time until graduation is dedicated to objectives introduced in section 1.3. The new results will be

2. Description of Experiments 
The BRE experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) were conducted in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) under the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity 
Experiments (ACME) program. Conducting the experiments required a collaboration between the 
UMD and NASA operations, and engineering team. The UMD team consisted of prominent faculty 
advisors (Dr. Quintiere, Dr. Sunderland, and Dr. de Ris), and students. The author of this thesis 
was the leading Ph. D. student for the BRE experiments aboard the ISS. Four undergraduate, and 
four graduate students collaborated with the analysis of this project under supervision of the faculty 
advisors and the leading student.  
The NASA team was responsible for providing the experimental apparatus, sending the 
equipment to the ISS, and installation of the hardware required for each experiment. The 
experiments were performed automatically by using a software developed by NASA team. Some 
tasks required human interaction on the space station such as, changing the fuel and oxygen gas 
bottles, installation of burners and specific hardware required for each experiment. NASA team 
also supported the UMD team by reviewing, revising and providing information as needed. 
The UMD team was responsible for: 
1. Preprocessing of the experiments:  
a. Calibration of the heat flux sensors, radiometers, and slug calorimeter. 
b. Identifying the working conditions of the sensors, mass flow meters and burners 
to ensure successful ignition and data recording on the test point days 
c. Identifying design parameters and develop a test matrix that could provide 
enough data for the objectives of this study 
d. Submitting the test parameters sheet (Appendix D) to NASA operations team 
two business days before each test point day. The total number of parameters 
were 69 that included, volumetric flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, ambient 
conditions for each test, camera settings, igniter position, etc. The parameter 
sheet was effectively the test matrix for each test point day, but with 
significantly more detail that helped NASA operations team to run the tests on 
the test day.

2.3 Fuel Mass Flux  
The fuel nitrogen mixture mass flux simulates condensed phase burning. If the flame is 
steady, the net average flame heat flux divided by this mass flux gives the theoretical heat of 
gasification of the condensed phase burning material. The fuel mixture volumetric flow rate is 
measured by a Hastings instrument HFM-300 with maximum flow rate of 0.2 and 0.5 slpm

3 Experimental Results of Round 1 Tests 
Burning experiments are analyzed for 59 successfully ignited tests using a gas burner 
(BRE) to emulate the steady burning of 25 mm diameter flat surface materials.  More than half of 
the tests resulted in long burns of at least 2 and as long as 5 minutes.  Mixtures of ethylene and 
nitrogen allow for 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g heats of combustion (LHV). Ambient conditions range from 
40 to 21 % oxygen and pressures of 1 to about 0.4 bar. NASA human habitat atmospheres have 
been used. Generally, it has been found that oxygen levels of 26 % and above can allow steady 
flames. The flames are thin blue in color and grow slowly over time for minutes. Some self-
extinguish, some had periodic oscillations, and others appear to have become steady and were shut 
down. Theoretical analyses show the shutdown flames were steady in growth, and all of the test 
endpoints were more than 94 % of steady state in flame heat flux. Flame heat flux for set mass 
flux allowed the estimation of heats of gasification to relate to steady solid materials that might 
burn in microgravity. Radiometers allowed the computation of flame radiative fraction that 
appeared to correlate well with the measured flame height. Results are shown for heat flux, flame 
height and base radius, radiative fraction as a function of fuel mixture mass flux, and various 
oxygen and pressure atmospheres. 
3.1 End Point Results 
Table 3.1 gives a summary of the end-point conditions found. The most useful data in this 
table are the apparent steady results where the duration of the test was long, appeared steady and 
the fuel flow rate was shut down. The issue of their steadiness will be theoretically examined to 
provide some justification for further examining these data as steady. The usefulness of these 
steady data is in the determination of the derived heat of gasification (heat flux divided by mass 
flux) to relate to real solid fuels that could burn steadily in microgravity at this scale.

3.2 Unsteady Results 
Unsteady results help in illustration of transient behavior of flames as well as distinguishing 
between steady and self-extinguished flames by observation of transient data and flame images. 
Data on the heat flux devices and four video cameras recorded the flame images over the time of 
a test after ignition. Although steady data is the main objective of this work, it is revealing to 
examine these transient data. For illustration three tests will be discussed here: 87B1, 51D1 and 
94K1 of Table 3.1. They have the same nominal atmospheres, 0.34 oxygen mole fraction and 0.56 
bar pressure. As the mass flux is increased: 1.78, 2.55 and 6.95 g/m2s, the flame grows taller and 
finally extinguishes at the highest flow rate. The self-extinguished flames occurred above 3 g/m2s 
and they all showed periodic growth and decay before final flame cessation. The video frame 
sequences are shown in Figure 3.1. They have been edited to give the best images, but in all cases, 
the color of the flames after early ignition effects, are blue. In some cases, apparent soot particles 
are disgorged through the flame (see Figure 3.1c at 6 s). In Figures 3.1a, and 3.1b, the flames grow 
and reach steady state before they were intentionally shutdown at about 3 minutes. This had to be 
done to conserve fuel and maintain reasonably constant atmospheres. The flame grows both 
radially and vertically in the images, and as the flow rate is increased the flame overhangs below 
the burner surface around the exposed burner copper edge and similar trend were observed by Ban 
et. al. General shape of the flames were also observed in ref [70] where the experiments took place 
in 1-g and their general shape were similar to those observed in current study. Figure 3.1c shows 
these effects more strongly, but now at 20 s the flame begins to partially extinguish. It periodically 
moves from full to partial in existence until complete elimination at 34 s.

The unsteady heat flux data are shown in the left plot of Figure 4, for the high flow rate, 
and the right plot of same figure, for the low flow rate case in Fig 3.1. The uncorrected transient 
calorimeter results are shown, as only the end points were corrected in Appendix A. These results 
reveal several unexpected characteristics. First, the center heat flux is higher than the “offset” 
sensor at 9.5 mm compared to the burner radius of 12.5 mm. One might expect the opposite based 
on the proximity of the flame to the surface; yet flame radiation from the product gases depends 
on on volume rather than distance. Second, the heat flux sensors and calorimeter net heat flux 
values all start very high and decrease to somewhat of an asymptote. In Figure 3.2 (Right), an 
effect prevalent in many tests, the two local gages drop sharply then gradually until an abrupt 
upward change occurs, followed by a smooth curve. This is believed to be due to early water 
condensation on the gages from the combustion products in contact with a relatively cool sensor. 
The small void space between the sensor and copper top can be a favorable condensation site. The 
liquid water acts as a barrier to conduction into the gage. The flame begins to evaporate water, 
further reducing the heat into the gage until it is dry. Then the dry gage suddenly senses the true 
flame heat flux. This effect was also demonstrated in our laboratory at 1-g. Third, after the water

Reexamining the flame behavior for an approximate constant mass flux, but with variations 
in the pressure, oxygen, and fuel concentration (or heat of combustion of the fuel mixture). 
According to Table 3.1 and by comparing Figures 3.3a, 3.3b and 3.4a, one could see the effect of 
nominal ambient oxygen mole fraction as it ranged from 0.4 to 0.265 with other parameters kept 
constant. In some tests that were shutdown, an apparent steady periodic behavior was 
demonstrated. This is shown in Figure 3.3b at 1 bar in which the periodic flame extinctions 
continue for nearly 1 minute before fuel shutdown, yet for the same of the conditions in Figure 
3.3b except with an atmospheric pressure of 0.56 bar there was no periodic behavior observed. 
Perhaps this is a pressure effect indicating the flames are more stable at the lower pressure.  
 
Finally, one could see the effect of fuel mole fraction by looking at Figures 3.3b and 6b. 
They show flames at nominal ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.34 and decreasing ethylene mole 
fraction from 1 to 0.5. All these image sequences suggest that higher oxygen, lower pressure, and 
lower heats of combustion tend to generate more stable flames that could reach steady state or last 
longer. Higher ambient oxygen concentration and lower pressure will result in higher flame 
temperature and higher radiative heat loss respectively, while fuel dilution with an inert (here we

Let us delineate the trends in the heat flux plots as a function of the mass flux, atmospheric 
oxygen and pressure, and fuel concentration in the fuel mixture stream. The latter represents the 
heat of combustion. First the local values will be examined. Center heat flux was about 50 % higher 
than offset located at r = 9.5 mm. Both heat fluxes decrease as the mass flux is increased. (This is 
associated with the flame located further from the surface). Heat fluxes increase nearly directly 
proportional to oxygen concentration. (But no steady data for 21 % oxygen). Heat fluxes increase 
as the heat of combustion decreases; nearly inversely related. (This is associated with flame 
height). Data at nominal 0.34 XO2, pure fuel, and fixed mass flux 2.55 g/m2s show a very slight 
increase in heat flux with pressure (This is insignificant and inconclusive). 
Let us now examine the average heat flux from the calorimeter. Figure 3.7 shows only the corrected 
data, and those data are less than the total collected because needed radiation information was not 
available for all the tests. The corrected data generally reduced the original data by up to a factor 
of 3 in a few cases, but the trend of the corrected data is now consistent with the local data to give 
us confidence that the correction is sound. The trends for the average heat flux are similar to the 
local data. Corrected average heat flux can be 20 to 70 % higher than the local center heat flux. 
Heat flux decreases with mass flux, increases with XO2 and decreases with fuel mole fraction. Also, 
data at nominal 0.34 XO2, pure fuel, and fixed mass flux 2.55 g/m2s show a very slight decrease in 
heat flux with pressure. (This is insignificant and inconclusive).

The flame is blue in all these tests as shown in Figs. 3.1, 3.3 and 3.4. This is common for 
microgravity burning with little or no soot. Therefore, the radiation comes from the gases above 
and below the blue flame. Figures 3.8a and3.8b show the “steady” and self-extinguished end-point 
data where radiation fraction could be determined from the radiometers. The trends of Figure 3.8a 
show that the fuel mole fraction (or heat of combustion) dominates over XO2 and pressure. The 
radiant fraction is nearly directly related to the heat of combustion with the pure fuel nearly twice 
as high as the diluted fuel mixture. It might appear that “steady” flames cannot have a radiant 
fraction above about 60%. Extinction of microgravity flames has been associated with radiation 
loss and subsequent flame temperature drop. For now, this relationship is not examined.  
 
It will be seen that flame height is also directly related to the heat of combustion. So, it 
suggests that radiant fraction might be more directly related to flame height. Moreover, there is a 
similarity between flame height and radius, so flame height might be a representation for volume 
and radiation losses from the aggregate of flame gases. Such a plot is presented in Figure 3.8b. 
Here a logarithmic correlation is given for the “steady” data only, but the figure includes the data 
just before extinction as well. The extinguished data somewhat follow the correlation, but we will 
interpret the correlation to hold for the “steady” end point flame, not for self-extinguished cases. 
The extinguished data range from about 0.5 – 0.8 for low XO2 (21 and 26.5%). While these are 
relatively high values of radiant loss fraction, there does not appear to be a critical value for 
extinction.

3.3.3 Flame Shape 
The flame shape nearly follows the previous theory of half oblate ellipse as demonstrated 
by Markan et. al.[49]. Both the height and radius grow with time as shown in Figures 3.9 and 3.10. 
The flame radius pulls in at the edge of the burner, distorting it from the theoretical ellipse. It may 
either standoff or extend a small distance below the burner face. Here we plot the flame height, 
the distance vertically from the center of the burner, and the radius, the radial distance along the 
face of the burner. Figures 3.9 and 3.10, show the results for the steady flames as a function of 
mass flux. As with the radiant fraction, the flame height and radius at “steady” state are primarily 
grouped by heat of combustion and increase with mass flux and heat of combustion. It is known 
from theory that the flame radius is a singular function of its length. In spite of not perfectly 
following the elliptical theory, this similarity is shown for the “steady” data in Figure 3.11.

3.4 Discussion of Results 
In the previous section the results have been presented and their trends have been discussed. 
The measurements have been used to compute the local and average net heat fluxes to the burner 
and derive the flame radiant fractions. The primary objective of this study is to determine if, and 
under what conditions, steady flames can occur in microgravity. We believe this is the first-time 
steady burning has been observed for a flat surface of 25 mm diameter in a quiescent atmosphere. 
Previously a tiny cylindrical candlewick has been observed to burn steadily [34,35]. The 
significance here for the burner is that steady burning can be related to condensed fuel properties 
through the theory of steady burning. Our hypothesis in this work has been to demonstrate that 
four fuel properties control steady condensed phase burning. This has been demonstrated in 1-g 
experiments by showing that burning rate, flame shape and color could be matched between real 
condensed phase fuels and a burner as discussed herein [46,55,56]. The four fuel properties 
required for matching in the 1-g experiments are heat of combustion, heat of gasification (L), fuel 
surface temperature and smoke point respectively. 
 
The burner steady endpoint surface temperatures ranged from 40 to 120 0C. These 
temperatures are relatively low for solid-phase fuels such as non-charring plastics that would apply 
directly here but, in the theory of steady burning the surface temperature is a relatively weak 
property compared to 1 and 2 above. In addition, the smoke point is likely irrelevant in 
microgravity, as it controls the radiation due to soot and that is not present in the microgravity 
flames seen. Consequently, the heat of combustion and the heat of gasification associated with the 
steady burner flames should represent the key solid fuel properties that can govern steadily burning 
in microgravity at 25 mm diameter. This has important safety implications. 
 
The heat of combustion in these experiments varies from 23.6 kJ/g for Xf = 0.5 and 47.2 
kJ/g for Xf = 1 based on ethylene. This is a range representative of many plastics. The question 
now is to evaluate the heat of gasification. Ideally the calorimeter net heat flux is the way to 
compute the heat of gasification, L. The theory of steady burning gives
