The results are shown in Figures 3.12 and 3.13. Both plots indicate a decreasing, somewhat 
inverse asymptotic-like curve, for heat of gasification with mass flux. It is surprising that the data 
cluster about a nearly singular trend. Also, both plots show the heat of gasification is up to 20 % 
higher for the lower heat of combustion 23.6 kJ/g. The results of Auth [55,56] who used the BRE 
in 1-g are added to Figures 3.12 and 3.13. The 1-g results for propane-nitrogen mixtures have the 
opposite behavior with heats of gasification decreasing with heat of combustion for the same mass 
flux. This could be due to the significance of soot radiation in the 1-g flames. But again, the data 
mostly cluster about one trend except for very low heat of combustion. The 1-g corresponding heat 
of combustion data shift far to the right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 3.12 and 
3.13. For example, the 1-g data would indicate (𝐿, 𝑚̇”) points of about 2 kJ/g, 30 g/m2s, and 0.5 
and 10. Moreover our previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with 
an apparent vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here. Obviously, the current 
data at durations of minutes over 5- s are more accurate. Moreover, it has been shown that the ISS 
heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly steady. Figures 3.12 and 3.13 include 
the heats of gasification derived from the self-extinguished endpoint data as well. Remarkably, the 
self-extinguished not data follow the same trend as the steady data. 
 
Let us interpret Figures 3.12 and 3.13 in terms of the flammability of real materials in 
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to 3 kJ/g, 
with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some selected literature

values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are listed in Table 3.1 [67,74]. 
Figures 3.12 and 3.13. would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) would burn 
in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5 g/m2s, and the 
phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s. These are very low values and if they 
occurred in 1-g they would be near the critical conditions for burning [75,76]. Indeed, Auth [55,56] 
finds that at 25 mm diameter, PMMA burns steadily at 19 g/m2s, and PE and PP both burn at about 
6 g/m2s. It is doubtful that the phenolic-glass composite could burn without extra external heating 
in 1-g. Yet, Figures 3.12 and 3.13 suggest it could burn in microgravity. The implication is that 
materials can burn more easily in microgravity than in normal gravity but with much lower burning 
rates.  
 
Fires on Earth in normal gravity become big, sustained fires because of heating from the 
fire’s surroundings. Fire on Earth is difficult generally to initiate in solids because of only 21 % 
oxygen in the atmosphere. In the current study it is seen that also in microgravity, this oxygen 
concentration did not favor ‘steady” burning. Can we expect fires to grow in microgravity so that 
as they heat their surroundings they can be reinforced as on the earth? The key to that answer is 
what controls the microgravity fire as it increases in size? Will flame radiation extinguish it? These 
questions need to be fully answered before fire safety in microgravity is understood. 
 
One important fire safety consideration, based on the findings of this study, is that solid 
materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from 
about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity. The NASA alternative flammability Test 2 using the 
Cone Calorimeter can measure these material properties [77,78]. As this study develops a more 
complete understanding, NASA may wish to put more emphasis into Test 2.

flames at atmospheres above 21 % oxygen. Theoretical analyses based on published work has 
corroborated that these long duration flames are nearly steady where it is shown that surface heat

flux tend to approach its steady value faster than flame size. Moreover, it is shown that lower fuel 
mole fractions (or heats of combustion) and higher ambient oxygen concentrations help flames 
burn for longer durations. Further analyses of the heat fluxes measured have allowed the estimation 
of the heat of gasification property associated with the steady tests. The findings suggest that solids 
of 25 mm diameter surfaces with heats of combustion from about 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g, and heats of 
gasification of 1 to 10 kJ/g can steadily burn in microgravity. Many commercial materials have 
these properties.  In microgravity, flames with lower heats of combustion, were closer to the burner 
surface which resulted in higher surface heat flux and larger heats of gasification accordingly 
which was a trend not seen in our 1-g experiments.  
 
Flame radiation fractions are obtained by radiative heat fluxes measured at endpoints for steady 
and at the peak of oscillating flames prior to self-extinction for self-extinguished flames. It is 
observed that all steady flames radiation fractions remained below 0.6. In addition, it has been 
found that the flame radiation fraction for the steady flames correlates well with the flame height. 
Future work will develop this relationship further to include other parameters and utilize it with 
previously published theoretical models to predict the steady outcome in general.  Hopefully, that 
analysis will give a more complete answer to the potential for fire growth in microgravity.

4. Analytical Transient Solution for Constant Mass Flux 
Burning experiments are analyzed for 29 steady burning flames using a gas burner (BRE) 
to emulate condensed phase burning of 25 mm diameter flat surface. Mixtures of ethylene and 
nitrogen allow for 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g heats of combustion (LHV). Ambient conditions range from 
21 to 40 % oxygen and pressures of 0.56 to 1 bar. The results are compared to predictions from 
analytic models developed to determine the flame radiation fraction, flame convective and 
radiative heat fluxes, flame shape, and heats of gasification for steady burning. Steady burning is 
theoretically decided by ensuring the flame temperature is above a critical value of 1100 K. Good 
agreement is achieved between experiment and predicted steady results. Further computations are 
made to determine the effect of ambient pressure and oxygen on burning for heats of combustion 
of 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g, diameters up to 100 mm, and vaporization temperatures of 80 and 350 ºC.  
It is found that for the range of analyzed conditions, heats of gasification of about 1 to 5 kJ/g, 
steady burning would result over a range of about 1 to 6 g/m2s.  Low pressure appears to yield 
more stable flames. The results have implications on how the fire safety of materials in 
microgravity should be determined. 
The complete solution for the unsteady purely diffusive burning of an oblate ellipsoidal 
surface with a uniform surface mass flux in time is given by Markan et al[49]. The results are 
summarized here because the formulas will be used throughout the paper as modified to include 
the heat of combustion reduced by a flame radiation loss fraction, Xr, the ratio of radiant energy 
lost by the flame to its combustion energy. The use of representing flame radiation effect by 
reducing the heat of combustion essentially assumes “a transparent flame” according to Jiang et al 
[79]. The original solution is based on thin flame theory with Schwab-Zeldovich variables giving 
the mixture fraction as given in Eq. (4.1)

4.5 Prediction of flame radiation fraction 
It was observed in the analysis of the data that the measured flame radiant fraction of the 
steady flames was a primary function of the flame height [51]. This prompted us to examine herein 
a theoretical basis for the radiant fraction cast in dimensionless terms. It will be shown that this 
exploration leads to a much more general correlation for the flame radiant fraction in terms of 
more variables than just flame height. Providing a prediction of Xr will then allow us to 
theoretically compute flame temperature at steady state, flame convective heat flux and model 
flame radiative heat flux from the initial information. This is how we will develop an approximant 
complete steady solution. 
 
4.6 Radiant fraction model formulation 
The radiation lost by the flame, with no visible soot, can be attributed to the products of 
combustion and their distributed temperature within a volume around the flame. The combustion 
products radiative heat flux is distributed through a surface area enclosing this volume. The rate 
of radiation lost by the flame can be represented in terms of a temperature, the gas emissivity, and

4.6.1 Model for emissivity and absorption coefficient 
A common way to evaluate emissivity for CO2 and H2O gases is to use Hottel’s charts 
[82,83]. In doing so, one must select a path length for a given partial pressure and temperature.

Planck value in the small limit. The Planck absorption coefficient for CO2 is about 10 (m-bar)-1 
and 2 (m-bar)-1 for H2O at 1400 K [74,83]. Note the absorption coefficient of Eq. (4.27) can be

Following encouraging estimations from the Hottel charts, we sought a more easily used 
computational method and used RADCAL [58,59] to calculate the gas mixture emissivity. 
RADCAL is a narrow-band model often used to estimate emissivity and absorption coefficient for 
these gases. The absorption coefficient of RADCAL is found by calculating the received intensity 
at a point located at a distance 𝑙 by taking into account the emission from the participating gas at 
temperature 𝑇+ with the surroundings at a fixed blackbody temperature of 300 K. The total 
emissivity calculated by RADCAL yields an also effective absorption coefficient defined in the 
same way as Eq. (4.27) for a given path length, l. 
RADCAL was run for partial pressures of water vapor and carbon dioxide from Eq. (4.26), 
ambient temperature (300 K), radiating gas temperature selected at 1400 K, no soot, and path 
length, l. Operating with the RADCAL code for the set of fuel and ambient pressure and oxygen 
conditions as our ISS experimental data, a general relationship is found for the absorption 
coefficient. Specifically, this was put in terms of 𝜅̃ as a function principally of path length. Here a 
modified absorption coefficient, 𝜅̃ is defined as

also needed to complete the theoretical determination of the heats of gasification that correspond

4.8 Flame temperature as a measure of extinction 
Given now the flame radiative fraction, the flame temperature can be computed from Eq. 
(4.15). This is key to determining if the flame can survive. The extinction of a diffusion flame is 
commonly governed by the Damkohler number, as the ratio of the time for diffusion divided by 
the time for the chemical reaction.  More completely it is controlled by the energy release of the 
chemical reaction and the heat loss from the system by both diffusion and radiation.  In all cases 
the flame temperature is most critical as it governs all of these processes. The flame temperature 
can be computed from Eq. (4.15). It is well known that the flame cannot survive below a critical 
temperature [67,75,76,85–91]. This has been examined in References [75,76] using the same type

extinction. The flame temperature becomes a surrogate for the Damkohler number, and in this case 
addresses both diffusive and radiative heat losses as described by Eq. (4.13). In normal gravity for 
buoyancy driven flames a critical temperature of 1600 K is accepted in the literature [67,75,76]. It 
is known that the critical flame temperature is a function of the local flame strain rate [85,90,91] 
where 1600 K corresponds to about a strain rate of 10 s-1, and 1100 K to a strain rate of 1 s-1. The 
former is used for purely buoyant flames in 1-g, and the latter is commonly used in microgravity 
as an extinction criterion [85–91]. Figure 4.7 shows the computed values of flame temperature for 
the ISS steady data [51] where the radiation fraction is predicted for all of the steady data (Figure 
4.6). The data points with lower heats of combustion have higher flame temperature because the 
flames radiation fraction varies inversely with the heat of combustion. We will examine these 
trends more carefully later using the predictive model in a more appropriate display. For now, it is 
clear from Figure 4.7 that all the steady results theoretically correspond to flame temperatures 
above 1100 K. This is now a straightforward predictive tool to assess whether steady burning in 
microgravity can occur.

The computation process proceeds as follows: 
1. The atmospheric conditions are specified for a given fuel-nitrogen mixture. This will fix 
the mass flux and heat of combustion. 
2. The flame height is computed, Eq. (4.18), then the absorption coefficient, Eqns. (4.35, 
4.36), non-dimensional radiation term “Ω” from Eq. (4.33) and the flame radiation fraction, 
Eq. (4.37). 
3. The flame temperature is then computed from Eq. (4.15).  If it is above 1100 K, then the 
flame is considered as a stable steady flame. 
4. The convective and radiative heat fluxes can then be computed by Eqn. (4.16 and 4.42).  
 
4.11 Flame Temperature 
Flame temperature is key, as it will theoretically indicate cases above 1100 K that are 
expected to be steady [85–91]. This allows a flammability mapping to be made to ultimately 
consider real solid fuel ranges for heat of combustion and heat of gasification properties that 
indicate the possibility of steady burning in microgravity at specific atmospheric conditions of 
oxygen concentration and pressure. (Of course, the solid fuel’s vaporization temperature needs to 
also be accounted for, but as its effect is relatively small, it will be fixed at a small value of 80 ºC, 
representative of the experiments.) Figure 12 shows the results. Actually, the flame radiative 
fraction must be computed first, before the flame temperature is computed. In doing so, all the 
values of radiation fraction are used in computing the flame temperature, but the results in Figure 
12 are terminated at 1100 K. In subsequent computations the results will reflect those conditions 
above 1100 K. 
 
It is striking in Figure 12 that the lower atmospheric pressure yields a wider range of 
burning conditions. This suggests that lower pressure favors burning. Some overall observations 
follow flame temperature, greater than 1100 K and indicates steady burning

4.17 Chapter Summary 
An analytical solution, based on classic diffusion flame theory, was used to analyze microgravity 
flames generated by a gaseous fuel-charged burner that emulates condensed-phase fuels burning. 
An empirical analysis based on flame radiation theory and measurements allowed us to correlate 
flame radiative loss fraction with a dimensionless parameter, Ω. The parameter includes the effects 
of ambient conditions (i.e., ambient pressure, oxygen mole fraction), fuel heat of combustion, 
surface temperature, and flame emissivity. (See Eqns. (4,18,32-36).)  Since BRE flames in 
microgravity do not contain soot, it is assumed that flame emissivity only depends on carbon 
dioxide and water vapor.  However, the empirical parameter Ω does depend on the fuel, and here 
only ethylene-nitrogen mixtures were examined.  RADCAL was used at a nominal flame 
temperature (1400 K) to determine the emissivity for a given path length taken as the center flame 
height. It was shown that if the RADCAL output absorption coefficients is divided by sum of the 
partial pressures of radiating component combustion products, all data will collapse on an 
empirical curve that suggests it only varies with path length. The path length is taken as the center 
flame height calculated analytically. Being able to calculate radiation fraction allows us to compute 
flame temperature in which 1100 K is taken as a criterion for flame extinction [10–14]. It also 
allows calculation of convective heat flux with a radiation correction on the heat of combustion. 
The radiation heat flux is computed based on geometrical view factor analysis along with Xr to 
give the available radiant heat flux that impinges on the surface. The net heat flux composed of 
the algebraic sum of convective, radiative and re-radiation from surface allows the heat of 
gasification to be computed for a specified fuel-mixture mass flux. The effect of burner size and 
surface temperature (350 ºC that represents real fuels burning) are also investigated. It is shown 
that as burner diameter is increased, flame radiant fraction is increased and heats of gasification 
are decreased in an asymptotic-like behavior. Surface temperature introduces substantial change 
in heat of gasification in which re-radiation heat loss decreases the burning rates, i.e., Figures 19

based fires, external radiation is the key to massive fire growth; it is likely this can be an issue in 
microgravity as well.  The analytical algorithm given in this paper has been shown to accurately 
predict steady conditions of burning for a surface of 25 mm diameter and has been examined for 
larger diameters. This analysis gives one a powerful analytical tool to predict the steady burning 
in microgravity as a function of fuel properties and ambient conditions.  
Let us examine the trends suggested by the theoretical results in terms of ambient conditions, fuel 
properties, and surface diameter.  Table 1 shows the increase (+) and decrease (-) trends for the 
key parameters of burning as a function of specified burning rate, pressure, oxygen atmosphere, 
and heat of combustion.  Ambient pressure effects are minor, and it affects the range of burning 
conditions, but not the overall burning rate. The effect of dropping the atmospheric pressure tends 
to expand the range of burning to higher burning rates. This is significant, as NASA seeks to 
provide habitable atmospheres of lower pressure and higher oxygen levels.  Such a move will 
enhance the burning conditions.   
 
The purpose of this burner emulation approach was to exploit an efficient way to study burning in 
a quiescent microgravity atmosphere.  We already knew that materials would burn with a directed 
oxygen flow, so an examination of quiescent conditions under pure diffusion flame conditions was 
thought to be essential. While steady burning might be thought as an ideal state, it is the end state 
for many material fires.  The key representative property of the steady state is the heat of 
gasification. This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions. 
In any case, the heat of gasification gives an indication of the energy needed to form a fuel gas for 
burning. In the burning emulation, the mass flux was specified, and the heat of gasification was 
derived, in the real problem, the heat of gasification is given and the question of burning arises. 
This question is resolved by use of the empirical flame extinction temperature. Indeed, the flame 
temperature is independent of the heat of gasification in the solution used herein but depends on 
the mass flux instead.

5. Analysis of the steadiness of the flames 
The likelihood of steady burning in microgravity is examined with Burning Rate Emulation 
(BRE) using a gas burner with a flat 25 mm diameter porous surface with two embedded heat flux 
sensors. The data are greatly expanded from a previous work. The fuel mixture used in this analysis 
are ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen resulting in a range of heats of combustion from 
12 to 47.2 kJ/g. An analytical solution of these flames was utilized to compute their steadiness, 
temperatures at flame sheet, and sizes. 103 flames were ignited in an ambient with nominal oxygen 
mole fractions of 0.21, 0.265, 0.34 and 0.40. 49 of those flames burned for the entire duration of 
the test before the fuel supply was terminated, while the remainder self-extinguished. The flames 
attained at least 90% of their asymptotic heights for all 49 fuel terminated flames. An estimated 
critical steady flame temperature ranging from 1100 to 1200 K was observed segregating the 
sustained and self-extinguished flames. Flame temperatures for the 49 terminated flames were 
above the critical temperature range indicating sustained steady burning, whereas below they self-
extinguished. The measured flame sizes, and radiative loss fractions are reported at the endpoint 
of the terminated tests. An empirical correlation of the radiative loss fraction with W, a 
dimensionless parameter, was obtained that allows prediction for real fuels at steady burning in 
microgravity. A flammability diagram, as a plot of the emulated fuel heat of gasification with its 
burning mass flux, for the range of steady data, is presented comparing how real fuels might burn 
steadily in normal and microgravity conditions. The results suggest that fuel mass flux burning 
rates would be about 3 to 4-times higher in 1-g. The heats of gasification and combustion of some 
real fuels are presented and compared against the burner flames. 
 
The steadiness of the flame heights is examined by utilizing the theoretical solution to these 
flames [49,51]. A critical flame temperature range of 1100 K to 1200 K was found to distinguish 
between the extinction and the 49 terminated flames becoming steady where the critical 
temperature in 1-g is 1600 K [75,85–88,91,91].

The theoretical solution to these flames is based on the classical diffusion flames theory and 
was used to estimate the steadiness of the flame heights [49,51,52]. The 49 fuel terminated flames 
reached 0.953 of their asymptotic height before fuel termination with standard deviation of 0.019 
[49,51,52]. The theoretical steady flame height is consistent with transient data extrapolated by 1/t 
~ 0. It should be noted that the prediction of flame height does not depend on radiation, but other 
parameters, such as the flame temperature, does depend on flame radiation [52]. In these 
calculations a specific heat of 1.23 kJ/kg K was used. 
 
5.2-Dimensional analysis of the Radiative loss fraction based on radiation theory 
A dimensional analysis of the radiation data of steady flames led to an empirical correlation 
flame radiation fraction, Xr with Ω, a dimensionless parameter [52]. Since the flames are blue and 
sootless, the dimensionless parameter depends on the partial pressures of CO2 and H2O for

flame temperature (see Eq. (5.3)).

coefficient of radiative gasses in the combustion products. Since the flames are sootless, and as

length, approaching the Planck limit at zero path length [74,83].

5.8 Chapter Summary 
The flammability of 25 mm diameter flat disk-shaped condensed-phase material is examined 
in microgravity for steady burning. The BRE using a gas fuel supplied burner with two embedded 
heat flux sensors is an efficient method to study burning in microgravity. The fuel mixture used in 
this study was ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen to give a range of heats of combustion 
per unit gram of the fuel mixture of about 12 to 47.2 kJ/g. An analytical solution to these flames 
was utilized to compute their steadiness, flame temperatures, and heights with good accuracy. 103 
flames were successfully ignited in a quiescent ambient with nominal oxygen mole fractions of 
0.21, 0.26, 0.34 and 0.40. 49 of those flames burned for the entire duration of the test before the 
fuel supply was terminated intentionally, while the remainder self-extinguished including all the 
flames burning in air (i.e., 0.21 nominal oxygen mole fraction). Elevated ambient oxygen 
concentrations above normal air enhances the flammability of materials while ambient pressure 
(not discussed here) had a negligible effect [21, 23]. The 49 terminated flames reached 95.3% of

their asymptotic value with a standard deviation of 1.9%. A steady critical flame temperature range 
of 1100 to 1200 K was observed that segregates the conditions of the steady and self-extinguished 
flames. Flame temperatures for the 49 terminated flames were above the critical flame temperature 
range indicating sustained burning. The flame size, and radiative loss fractions are reported at the 
endpoint of the tests. A dimensional analysis of the radiation data resulted in an empirical 
correlation of the radiative loss fraction, Xr with, W, a radiation dimensionless parameter. 
Arithmetic average of the two measured surface heat fluxes were used to compute the heats of 
gasification that resulted in a flammability diagram for microgravity data. The measured heats of 
gasification in normal gravity were added to the plot. A comparison between flammability of 
micro- and normal gravity showed that materials burn about 3 to 4 times faster on the ground. 
 
A theoretical methodology used herein could be applied to predict the burning rate of flat 
surfaces in microgravity. The effect of burning diameter and external radiation can be explored for 
various real fuels in steady burning under different ambient conditions. We recommend this be 
done.

6. Flammability Maps for Microgravity Flames on Top of a Flat Disk in 
a Quiescent Ambient 
 
The current criteria for material selection for use in spacecrafts is based on NASA test 1, an upward 
flame spread over a real material sample in a controlled environment in 1-g. However, there is no 
scientific basis to extrapolate the results of this test to microgravity condition. The induced flow 
because of buoyancy presence in normal gravity flames is in favor of steady flames, a condition 
that is not applicable to flames in µ-g. The inherent material properties that control flammability 
should not change with gravity field and this is essential for extrapolation of 1-g test results to µ-
g. BRE emulates condensed phase fuels by matching four material properties Dhc, L, ls, and Tb. 
The first two quantities are used for analysis of BRE results in microgravity[50–54,60]. The flames 
in this study are sootless and laminar smoke point is not applicable to µ-g results. 1-g emulations 
between the burner and real fuels were very good when matching L, Dhc, ls, with Tb not matched 
[4,10,46,47,55,56]. The Tb is the uncontrolled surface temperature Ts for BRE.  Our theory allows 
for including Tb in predictions [52]. This study provides a flammability map based on Dhc, and L 
for each nominal ambient XO2. These properties can be effectively measured by the Cone 
Calorimeter: NASA Test 2, not currently used to determine flammable hazard in space.  
 
Flammability maps are obtained for each XO2 used in this analysis (i.e., 0.4, 0.34, and 0.265). The 
extinction limits were obtained based on the criteria of setting a critical flame temperature range 
of 1100 K to 1200 K. The flammable zone will be the area where flames have flame temperatures 
above this range. Two extinction limits was obtained based on theory [52,60], radiative extinction, 
and small flame (convective) extinction limit.

increased. It explains the reason for the radiative heat flux becoming dominant over the surface as 
mass flux is increased. Accuracy of computation algorithm is supported by comparing the 
calculated, and measured heats of gasification, shown in Fig. (6.4).

predictions for the range of flammability for each heat of combustion. The criterial for identifying 
steady flames were like that shown in the previous chapters, using a critical temperature range of 
1100 to 1200 K. The radiative extinction limit shifts to the higher L, that is equivalent to lower 
mass burning rate, as heat of combustion is increased resulting in a slopped line shown on the 
flammability maps. The reason is that as heat of combustion is increased the flame size gets larger 
for the same mass burning rate. Therefore, the radiative extinction limit occurs at higher heats of 
gasification as heat of combustion is increased.

combustion). At low L as expected, the self-extinguished data points are observed until the first 
steady flames are observed at Xr of ~ 0.65 for XO2 of 0.4, ~ 0.6 for XO2 of 0.34 and ~ 0.55 for XO2

The flame temperatures at flame sheet, Tf ,assuming complete reaction are calculated [49,52] 
and shown on the bottom plots of Figs. 6.9  to 6.11. The trends shown by calculated Tf, are 
accompanied by more scatter that reveals the limitations of using a theoretical model that uses 
constant properties (i.e., cp and k for Nitrogen at 1400 K) to estimate flame properties. However, 
it gives valuable information of how flame temperature behaves by changing heats of combustion 
and heats of gasification, as the two key material properties used for burning emulations. 
Calculated Tf is increased by heat of combustion but first increases by heat of gasification until it 
reaches to its peak and then starts to decrease suggesting a parabolic shaped curves when plotted 
against heat of gasification. The reason for having a dome shaped curve is that there is a tradeoff 
between the sources of flame heat loss. For low heats of gasification, the flames are closer to their 
radiative extinction limit and cool down due to radiative heat loss compared to the small flames 
with higher heats of gasification, where heat loss to the fuel source is dominant and causes flame 
cooling down. At some point, the two sources of heat loss provide a situation in favor of Tf and 
thus, steady burning. The peak temperature moves to the right of the plots as heat of combustion 
is increased. By comparing the plots presented in the bottom of Figs. 6.9 to 6.11, one finds out that 
decreasing the ambient nominal XO2 decreases the steady flame temperature. Theoretical 
predictions shown by solid-colored lines confirm such a trend.

and pure convective extinction limits shown by slopped lines, it suggests that PMMA burns

In general, materials that fall in the flammable region identified in Figure 6.13, that have high ∆ℎ! 
and low L, such as PE and PP impose more risk to the fire-safety of spacecrafts because of higher 
heat release rate, and larger size that can better reach the surrounding and have more radiation 
emittance, an important factor for fire growth and spread. 
 
The radiative, small flame, and pure convective extinction limits are based on theory [52], and 
there are some steady flames in the extinction region. Also, the horizontal double solid line 
indicates the minimum ∆ℎ!,  required for ignition that was observed in the experiments. It shown 
that the minimum ∆ℎ!, required for ignition increases slightly from 10 to 12, and 13 when XO2 is 
decreased from 0.4, to 0.34, and 0.265, respectively. This limitation is due to the approximate 
nature of the calculated values, especially, average surface radiative heat flux. Also, the 𝑌9: are 
assumed to be constant and at their nominal values of 0.43, 27, and 29 compared to the actual 
experimental values that deviate up to 10% from their nominal value at the end of each test. This 
explains the inaccuracy observed in the flammability maps related to the extinction limits.

6.8 Critical heat release rate, and mass flux at extinction limits 
The critical heat release rate, 𝑚̇$$∆ℎ!,  corresponding to the critical flame temperatures (1100 K or 
1200K) used in this analysis is plotted against heat of combustion. It is observed that for the small 
flame extinction limit, the critical heat release rate corresponding to both critical temperatures 
approaches ~40 kW/m2. Critical HRR at extinction was also observed in [75,95]. However, for the 
radiative extinction limit the critical heat release rates increase significantly with XO2 (See Fig. 
6.16).  
Critical mass flux at the extinction limits is plotted and shown in Fig. 6.17. At the small 
flame extinction limit, the critical mass flux does not change with XO2 except that as XO2 is 
decreased the combustible range for heat of combustion decreases. In other words, higher oxygen 
concentration allows for materials with lower heats of combustion burn. Therefore, the critical 
mass flux as a function of ∆ℎ! for the small flame extinction limit can be defined with a single 
power-law fit as shown in the Fig. 6.17, similar to what was obtained in [75]. At the radiative 
extinction limit, the critical mass flux, increase with oxygen for a given  ∆ℎ!. Also, the flammable 
range of ∆ℎ! is increased with 𝑋9:.

6.9 Chapter summary 
A gas fuel supplied burner (BRE) was used to emulate burning of real solid and liquid fuels in 
microgravity to address the concerns regarding fire safety of spacecrafts. The burner had a porous 
surface that allowed gas mixture flowing which represents real material gasification. The gaseous 
fuel used in this study were ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen to generate a range of heat 
of combustion (LHV) from 10 kJ/g to 47.2 kJ/g. The BRE was installed inside a chamber that 
allowed ignition of flames in a controlled environment. The oxygen mole fraction and pressure 
were varied to study its effect on the flammability of the fuel mixture flow. The nominal ambient 
oxygen mole fractions used in this study were 0.4, 0.34, 0.265, 0.25, and 0.21 with ambient 
pressures of 1, 0.7, and 0.56 bar. Three of the atmospheres used were conditions that NASA is 
considering for human habitat in space crafts. Several cameras recorded still images and videos of 
the tests. Two heat flux sensors and two K-type thermocouples embedded to the burner surface 
were used to measure surface heat flux and temperature at the center and approximately 10 mm 
from the center of the burner. Several remote radiometers measured radiative heat flux from the 
flames that led to computation of radiative loss fractions, a quantity that was used to correct the

content:

heat of combustion in the analytical solution to the BRE flames. A critical temperature range of 
1100 to 1200 K, was chosen to distinguish between self-extinguished and steady flames. 146 
flames were ignited aboard the international space station. All flames that were ignited at nominal 
XO2 of 0.25, and 0.21 self-extinguished within 90 seconds. 46 flames burned for the entire duration, 
three minutes for most of the cases, before the fuel supply was terminated intentionally. These 
flames were close to their steady state value, and it was shown by the analytical solution, with their 
size being 94% of their steady state value on average and standard deviation of 1.9%. Average 
measured heat flux was used to obtain heats of gasification, a key parameter for fuel emulation. A 
dimensional analysis of the radiative loss fraction Xr based on radiation theory led to an empirical 
correlation. A geometrical model was used to estimate surface average radiative heat flux that 
resulted in computation of heat of gasification when added to the calculated convective and re-
radiative surface heat flux. The computed heats of gasification were compared with measured 
counterparts for the steady flames indicating good accuracy of the model used. Finally, a 
flammability map, as a plot of Dhc vs. L (the two key properties of materials that are used for 
emulation) was obtained for each nominal oxygen mole fraction, based on the experimental data 
and the theoretical predicted trends were shown for elaboration. Two extinction limits were 
introduced that identifies the flammability region. The radiative extinction limit was obtained 
empirically, by passing a line through a range that segregates self-extinguished and steady flames. 
The kinetic extinction limit was obtained theoretically for small flames, having small radiative 
heat loss. The properties of some of the real solids and liquids were shown on the flammability 
maps to study their flammability.

content:
137 
 
7. Conclusions 
Burning emulation in microgravity is investigated through a series of tests aboard the 
International Space Station to study flammability of condensed phase materials in quiescent 
atmosphere to improve safety of spacecrafts against fire hazard. Two sizes of the Burning Rate 
Emulator (BRE) were utilized to emulate burning of condensed phase materials with porous flat 
surfaces of 25 mm and 50 mm in diameter. Ethylene, and a diluted mixture of these fuels with 
nitrogen at different concentrations were used to achieve a range of heats of combustion of up 
to LHV of 50 kJ/g. The fuel mixture mass flux, ambient mixture and ambient pressure were among 
the design parameters. Radiation measurements were performed to obtain flame radiative loss 
fractions. A dimensional analysis of radiation fraction led to an empirical correlation. RADCAL, 
a narrow band radiation model, was utilized to obtain flame emissivity by executing the code with 
partial pressures of products, flame length, flame temperature and ambient pressure being input 
parameters. The correlation allowed correction of total heat release rate from the flames due to 
radiative loss and when combined with the analytical solution to these flames, allowed prediction 
of flame heights, radius, average convective and radiative heat flux that were used to calculate 
heats of gasification. In the burning emulation, the mass flux was specified, and the heat of 
gasification was derived, in the real problem, the heat of gasification is given and the question of 
burning arises. This question is resolved by assuming a flame extinction temperature. 
 
More than half of the tests resulted in long burns of at least 2 and as long as 5 minutes. 
Generally, it has been found that nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26 % and above can lead to 
steady flames which are thin blue in color and grow slowly over time for minutes. Theoretical 
analysis showed the shutdown flames were effectively steady in size, and all of the test endpoints 
were more than 94 % of steady state in flame heat flux based on theoretical estimation of flame 
steadiness. The key representative property of the steady state is the heat of gasification. This is 
exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions. Surface heat flux for 
set mass flux allowed the estimation of heats of gasification to relate to steady solid materials that 
might burn in microgravity. PMMA and POM were successfully emulated based on the 
flammability map achieved. Radiometers allowed the computation of flame radiative fraction that

content:
138 
 
appeared to correlate well with the measured flame height which led to a more accurate correlation 
based on dimensional analysis by also taking into account the effect of fuel and ambient mixture 
and ambient pressure. Heat flux, flame height and base radius, radiative fraction as a function of 
fuel mixture mass flux, and several ambient mixtures and pressures are presented as experimental 
findings.  
 
It is observed that for all steady flames, radiation fractions remained below 0.6 for the 
steady flames and correlate with the flame height. The dimensional analysis on the radiation 
parameter Ω confirms that it does depend on the fuel, and here only ethylene-nitrogen mixtures 
were examined. It is shown that if the RADCAL output absorption coefficients are divided by sum 
of partial pressures of water vapor and carbon dioxide, all data will collapse on an empirical curve 
that suggests it only depends on path length for a given hydrocarbon. Being able to calculate 
radiation fraction led to computation of flame temperature in which 1100 K is taken as a criterion 
for flame extinction. The radiation heat flux to the surface is computed based on a geometrical 
view factor analysis performed on calculated flame size along with the correlated Xr to calculate 
radiant heat flux to the surface. The net heat flux is composed of the algebraic sum of convective, 
radiative and re-radiation from surface which allows computation of heats of gasification. Burner 
size, surface temperature (350 ºC that represents real fuels burning) effects on the theoretical 
flammability map (L vs 𝑚̇>?@
$$
) are also investigated. It is shown that as burner diameter is 
increased, flame radiant fraction is increased, and heats of gasification are decreased. Surface 
temperature introduces substantial change in heat of gasification in which re-radiation heat loss 
decreases the burning rates. However, external radiation can offset this effect, and increase the 
mass flux. As in Earth-based fires, external radiation is the key to massive fire growth; it is likely 
this can be an issue in microgravity as well. The analytical algorithm given in this thesis has been 
shown to predict steady conditions of burning for a surface of 25 mm diameter and has been 
examined for larger diameters. This analysis gives one a powerful analytical tool to predict the 
steady burning in microgravity as a function of fuel properties and ambient conditions.

content:
139 
 
The trends suggested by the theoretical predictions in terms of ambient conditions, fuel 
properties, and surface diameter are presented in Table 6.1 that shows  
the increase (+) and decrease (-) trends for the key parameters of burning as a function of specified 
burning rate, pressure, oxygen concentration, and heat of combustion. The effect of dropping the 
atmospheric pressure tends to expand the range of burning to higher burning rates. As NASA seeks 
to provide habitable atmospheres of lower pressure and higher oxygen levels. Such a move will 
exacerbate the burning conditions. The steady flame temperature is independent of the heat of 
gasification as given herein but depends on the mass flux. The mass flux does depend on L, as well 
as the steady flame temperature, surface radiative and convective heat flux, re-radiation, and 
external radiant heat flux. Surface radiative heat flux is inversely proportional to the mass flux 
(and thus, flame size) but it is decreased at a higher rate compared to convection and re-radiation. 
Furthermore, it is the only heat flux component that is affected by ambient mixture and pressure 
as well as hydrocarbon properties. Hence, radiative heat transfer is responsible for determining 
extinction and in case of sustained burning, the mass flux. Therefore, the algorithm should be cast 
in terms of the ambient conditions, including external radiation, and hydrocarbon properties to 
determine if burning is possible and at what rate. The significant result of theoretical aspect of this 
study is presented herein as a flammability map that would give burning conditions for a given 
fuel in terms of its heat of combustion, heat of gasification and burning temperature.  
 
 
A flammability map as a plot of heat of gasification vs. heat of combustion was developed 
based on the measurement and theory for nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, 
and 0.4. The flammability maps were bounded by two extinction limits, radiative, and small flame

extinction limits. The extinction limits were theoretically obtained by applying critical flame 
temperature of 1100 K or 1200 K. The flammable zone consists of flames with temperatures higher 
than these values. Several real materials were emulated by matching their properties with the 
flammability maps. The development of flammability maps based on Dhc, and L, properties that 
can be effectively measured by the Cone Calorimeter, suggests NASA to use Test 2 to determine 
flammable hazard in space. Also, the effects of external radiation, and real material chemistry are 
suggested as subjects for future studies.

["Completing Burn Fraction on \"EventData\" Sheet"]
["This version of the ACME Chamber Calculator allows you to adjust the fraction of gas from a test point that is used in the ignition calculation.\n\nColumn AL (Burn Fraction) automatically populates with a \"1\" when Column B (Ignite) contains a \"Yes\". The \"Yes\" and \"No\" provided in Column B are based on the decision during operations. The calculator automatically assumes all fuel (or oxygen) from the test was consumed during the test point (Burn Fraction = 1).\n\nThe \"Burn Fraction\" can be updated for any test point even if Column B is marked \"No\". The equations will use the value in the \"Burn Fraction\" column and not the Yes/No designation.\nThe \"Burn Fraction\" value can be modified without unprotecting the sheet."]

["This version of the ACME Chamber Calculator allows you to adjust the fraction of gas from a test point that is used in the ignition calculation.\n\nColumn AL (Burn Fraction) automatically populates with a \"1\" when Column B (Ignite) contains a \"Yes\". The \"Yes\" and \"No\" provided in Column B are based on the decision during operations. The calculator automatically assumes all fuel (or oxygen) from the test was consumed during the test point (Burn Fraction = 1).\n\nThe \"Burn Fraction\" can be updated for any test point even if Column B is marked \"No\". The equations will use the value in the \"Burn Fraction\" column and not the Yes/No designation.\nThe \"Burn Fraction\" value can be modified without unprotecting the sheet."]

8. Output Files 
 
 
4. Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) 
*where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 
 
8.0 
Output FILES 
8.1 
Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc.  
The file contains a two-line header.  The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains.  The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data.  The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- 
A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 
11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
- 
25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in Table 2.  (The names of 
many of these values change depending on whether it is a BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) 
- 
Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board.  This is the E-Field control voltage. 
Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and DataRecordingStop commands at a 
rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Error! Reference source not found., defaulting to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling.

3 
 
8.2 
Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes.  The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category.  The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM-
DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory.  See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 
Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters.  Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received.  The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-
DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log.  The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s BRE experiment to facilitate its 
analysis.  The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the 
combustion gases.  For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging 
measurements.  Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational 
logs provide information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the BRE data begin by familiarizing themselves 
with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the BRE Final Report or the more 
comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document.  To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 19039A1_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D). 
Additional documents that may be important include:

2. BRE Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/BRE Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the 
science, preliminary results, and more.  It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in 
analyzing the BRE data. 
 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within 
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland.  The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), 
namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global, 
retired).  The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student 
in the Fire Protection Engineering department. 
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64.  
More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second-
round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021.  The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and 
the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner 
(although not together).

Report for ISS Increment 64 (which is included in the ACME/s-Flame Final Report).  A minor correction was 
made to Table 1 in which 19094 is now identified as April 4.  It had accidentally been identified as April 5 
in the 30-day reports, although the testing did extend past midnight in Cleveland, OH so the final tests

4 August 2022 
 
4 
 
 
were conducted on April 5.  Nonetheless, the BRE (and more generally ACME) test days and numbers are 
identified by the date on which the test day began, even if they occurred after midnight (whether on the 
ISS or in Cleveland).  
 
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45 
flames were ignited.  That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, when an 
additional 17 flames were ignited.  BRE’s second-round flame testing began in Sept. 2020, during 
Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited.  The second and final round of tests was 
completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames were ignited.  As a result, 
62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and second rounds of testing for a total 
of 194 flames. 
 
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI 
team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests 
to maximize its scientific outcome.  However, the break was longer than had been planned 
because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability.  As a result, BRE’s 
second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment, 
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), was completed, where that 
occurred in July 2020.  A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew 
launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches 
entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase. 
 
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene 
(C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out at a range of chamber 
pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in 
future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric 
conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.  
In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water 
vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.  An exception is tests conducted after the 
chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day.  But during tests 
days, the atmosphere was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests.  
Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 50 mm, 
and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  Therefore, the 
second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first 
round.  However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were carried out at 
roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary effect on flames.  Meanwhile, the tests in 
this round were carried out at various oxygen concentrations as in the first round but were more 
often conducted with ~40% oxygen, where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion.  
 
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently 
conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple 
hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary 
component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-
carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon

A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) data 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D).  The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number).  As such, the example, 19039A1 is test A1 conducted 
on the 39th day of 2019.  But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 40th) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 19039B1, 19039B2, and 19039B3) are 
typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or 
repeat.  Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0.  While initially used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient.  As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all.  The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically.  However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. 
 
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by 
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The first row is a header and provides a limited 
summary of the hardware and operational conditions.  The header is explained in Section 10.1 
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

These files can be analyzed with the INFICON’s EZ IQ software for its 3000 Micro GC (version 
3.3.2 SP2) which only works under Windows 7 or XP SP3 (with the NET Framework 3.0 and/or 
3.5).  INFICON has indicated that their newer software for the Micro GC Fusion will not work 
with 3000 Micro GC files.  However, it is possible that software developed by Agilent may be 
able to work with these files, where they apparently developed the EZ IQ software initially.  
 
NASA plans to analyze the files to determine species concentrations and make those results 
available, but the agency abandoned use of Windows 7 and earlier operating systems which 
has thus far prevented the planned analysis.  As a result, species concentration results are not 
yet available from the GCIP measurements, where the instrument was not used in the 
experiments preceding ACME.  It has furthermore only been used in a fraction of the ACME 
experiments, but BRE is one for which GCIP data was sometimes collected.  
 
4. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped 
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because 
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and 
installing alignment guides) on each test day.  However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis 
SAMS sensor head.  The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are 
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal 
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS). 
 
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn):  In 
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways 
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective 
of SAMS measurements from within the rack. 
 
Roadmap Spectrograms 
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can: 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap 
b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files) 
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice.  We refer to these PDFs as roadmap 
plots.  For SAMS, these are acceleration spectrograms, which for vibratory data are a 
good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency 
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot.  These spectrograms are mostly 
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale 
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension. 
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only 
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on 
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements. 
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science 
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some 
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under 
various conditions.

content:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
11 
 
 
 
Binary Data 
To download actual SAMS measurement data for use with your models or to correlate 
acceleration measurements with your science or support data, you can… 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad 
b. Navigate by GMT date, for example you can follow year, month and day links to end 
up at: https://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad/year2020/month06/day18/  where you see 
a list of SAMS sensor directories.  The sensor subdirectory of interest for CIR is 
samses_accel_es05. 
c. Once you click into that directory link, you will see data and header files listed for the 
CIR sensor. 
d. The instructions at the following link help you to read these data: 
http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/plots/user/mohan/how2read_pad_binary_files.html 
 
 
B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used 
for BRE or most of the current ACME experiments.  Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera 
was only used by the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study. 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera  
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera.  Its primary 
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is 
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.  It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/.  That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry 
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of

Soot temperatures can be determined from this camera’s images via techniques such as those 
described in the following references: 
a. S. De Iuliis, M. Barbini, S. Benecchi, F. Cignoli, and G. Zizak, Determination of the

https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-2180(97)00357-X

Angle Light Scattering and Spectrally Resolved Line-of-Sight Attenuation and Its 
Implication on Soot Color-Ratio Pyrometry, Applied Physics B 117 (2014) 287–303.  
https://doi.org/10.1007/s00340-014-5834-x 
c. B. Ma, S. Cao, D. Giassi, D. P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, B. A. V. Bennett, M. D. Smooke, 
and M. B. Long, An Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in a 
Coflow Jet Flame under Microgravity and Normal Gravity, Proceedings of the

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2014.05.064

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
13 
 
 
Particularly when making quantitative measurements, implementation of an Abel transform 
or similar is likely appropriate given the axisymmetry of the flames.  In fact, all six of the 
current ACME experiments feature axisymmetric or spherically symmetric flames.   
Approaches are compared in this paper: 
k. C. J. Dasch, One-Dimensional Tomography: A Comparison of Abel, Onion-Peeling, 
and Filtered Backprojection Methods, Applied Optics, 31 (1992) 1146–1152.  
https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.31.001146 
 
The a-k references above were taken from the following conference paper on early ACME 
results from the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment: 
Jesse Tinajero, Davide Giassi, Dennis Stocker, and Marshall Long. “Experimental Study on 
the Influence of Gravity on Highly Diluted and Sooting Coflow Flames,” 11th US National 
Combustion Meeting of the Combustion Institute, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019.   
 
Meanwhile, this paper on an ISS precursor to the CLD Flame experiment is an appropriate 
reference for determination of CH* concentration. 
D. Giassi, S. Cao, B.A. Bennett, D.P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, 
“Analysis of CH* Concentration and Flame Heat Release Rate in Laminar Coflow Diffusion 
Flames under Microgravity and Normal Gravity,” Combustion and Flame, Vol. 167, pp. 
198-206 (2016).  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2016.02.012 
 
Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often 
downlinked during a test day.  Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon 
object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing software.  
The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF format, 
where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following: 
• 
color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed)  
• 
dark frame subtraction 
• 
removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage)  
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employs a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is 
detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it 
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers.  The priority in the NASA conversion 
was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs. 
 
Most ACME investigators are processing the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software 
developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment.   The 
OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the 
latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.  A tutorial was prepared by Dr. 
Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found 
at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI.  It has also been broken up and posted 
in three parts in which the image resolution may be better: 
 
Part 1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdQHeQwokvY 
 
Part 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mua_8CfqhfM 
 
Part 3 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGRqgbIxZL4 
 
The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten by Tinajero as a Python function, where 
Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for MacOS, Linux,

and Windows operating systems.  The Python script to open the HOBJ files can be downloaded 
from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample. A tutorial for this function may be found at 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wbgWeJSilc. 
 
The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji 
variant, where both can be freely downloaded.  In either software package, the HOBJ files can 
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings: 
 
Image type 
16-bit unsigned 
 
Width 
1360 
 
Height 
1024 
 
Offset to first image 
6244 
However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as 
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented.  It 
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion.  As another option, 
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions. 
 
To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements, it is critical to avoid saturation, 
for example by using a camera gain of zero.  Another employed approach was to not use the 
camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 1.68, 
respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation.  Such multiplication can be 
done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the white 
balancing is accomplished with the commands: 
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68 
clip 4095 
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software 
because the color balancing was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the 
risk of saturation.  
 
However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD 
Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red) 
didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10%.  
This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication) 
for the green color plane. 
 
For Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP): “After rigorous testing, it was determined [by Tinajero and 
Long] that a modified version of the bilinear method could be used to optimize the conversion 
of raw fiber images to full resolution color images.  This modified version biases the linear 
interpolation along the length of the fiber.  This method combined with moderate use of 
defocusing was found to reduce artifacts created by standard demosaicing algorithms and 
was used in all of the fiber measurements described below.” 
Jesse Tinajero and Marshall Long. “Dilution Limits of Coflow Laminar Methane and 
Ethylene Flames in Microgravity Versus Normal Gravity,” 12th U.S. National Combustion 
Meeting, 24-26 May 2021. 
 
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format 
with 12-bit image data.  As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be 
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced.  Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are

susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit.  As a result, the images feature hot pixels which 
increase in number over the months and years in space.  As such, it will appear as if there is a 
star field within the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the images should ideally be processed 
to remove the bright outlying hot spots.  Radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera 
imaging. 
 
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure 
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  As a 
result, the framing rate was typically far less.  Different exposures are often selected for 
different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate 
may not be consistent.  Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating 
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under 
uncertain or varying flame intensities.  Bracketing can also used to simultaneously accomplish 
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP 
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. 
 
In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file 
which should be available for each successful flame test, e.g., to verify the exposure duration.  
These files are in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet 
software or alternately as a text file.  Column headings are found in the first row of such files.

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
16 
 
 
start) was nominally 10 fps rather than the 30 indicated by FrameRate.  It is furthermore 
important to understand that the exposure time (and thus actual framing rate) was often 
varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if bracketing was employed, i.e., 
where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different exposures.  
 
Unfortunately, it has been seen during bracketing that the reporting of exposure times in the 
metadata files is, or at least can be, offset.  Therefore, it is important to identify the brightest 
images, for example, in an image sequence to determine which had the longest of the 
bracketed exposure times.  
 
The parameter files, with names like ‘as run21028C1.txt,’ control the DataCam exposures and 
much more.  However, these files have not always saved as intended and were sometimes 
corrected after the fact.  In contrast, the text-file logs, with names such as 2021-01-28_12-
28_ACME.log, are a reliable source for the parameters which specified the imaging settings 
and much more.  There is a single file of this type for each test day (at least normally) and the 
parameters are a small fraction of the automated log content, but one can search for a test 
by its number.  Log files like this are discussed in section 4.C.5 of this document. 
 
Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright 
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward.  In 
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s 
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis.  This is contrary to an ACME 
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis 
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format.  In this regard, the science requirements were not 
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs. 
 
There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely 
reproducible.  Therefore, the scaling of the image data should ideally be established for each 
subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a test day.  The scaling can 
typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions.  
Meanwhile, the other cameras used in ACME testing had fixed lenses. 
 
3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera  
During ACME testing, this intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass 
filter and was generally archived at 23 fps. 
 
The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format and can be opened 
readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required. 
 
Note that this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially blocked by the arms of the fiber array 
for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to position the fibers across the flame. 
 
As with the ACME DataCam, it might be useful to check the metadata for the CFI intensified 
camera, which is in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet 
software or alternately as a text file.

4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s 
collimated illumination package.  The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet 
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for 
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction.  However, the camera’s red filter, 
corresponding to the red illumination, appears to be broad enough to permit significant soot 
incandescence to pass through the filter.  As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for 
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions.  After post-processing on the ground, 
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened.  The 
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps. 
 
It is important to understand that this camera’s images are of limited value for BRE because 
of the general lack of soot with exception of ignition.  But even considering that, the soot 
volume fraction can be computed using images from the ACME DataCam as discussed in that 
camera’s section.  
 
In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, this 
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera 
is nearly insensitive to blue.  The red filter was installed on 5 March 2018 and used throughout 
all subsequent ACME testing. 
 
 
C. Test Parameters and Other Files 
Files discussed in this section include the following: 
CIR chamber calculator file 
Test parameter file 
Notes 
Test timing 
Logs 
 
1. CIR chamber calculator file 
In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single file for each of BRE’s two rounds of 
testing:  
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2019-01-31 to 2019-04-09.xlsx 
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2020-07-22 to 2021-02-03.xlsx 
which provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after each 
BRE test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action 
involving gas flow into or out of the chamber.  As a result, this includes filling and venting 
operations, plus recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled 
with 13x molecular sieves. 
 
More specifically, the chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after 
each operation involving flow into or out of the chamber.  While the standard ACME data 
output files (discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test,
