burning, obtaining analytic solutions by the Pohlhausen integral method. Ahmad and Faeth [6, 7] examined both the 
laminar and turbulent cases following a similar theoretical approach. Investigators have conducted experiments that 
included the use of solid materials, ceramic plates saturated with liquid fuels, and burners to simulate real materials. 
Measurements on PMMA have been carried out by Ohtani et al [9] and Gollner et al [10].  More recently a direct 
numerical solution (DNS) of the full equations by Ali et al. [8] was obtained for a 1 cm plate at various orientations.  
The onset of instability from laminar flow over hot inclined plates has been reported by Lloyd and Sparrow [11] and 
Al-Arabi et al [12].  The current work was motivated by considering the use of burners to emulate the burning of 
real materials, in a non-Earth-gravity environment. 
This study follows the approach by Ahmad and Faeth [6, 7], extending their work to steady burning at multiple 
orientations. We use their experimental technique of porous ceramic plates soaked with liquid fuels of methanol and 
ethanol. We also adopt their theoretical integral modeling approach. In our model, however, we add an additional 
term describing the role of cross flow buoyancy normal to the plate. This term is the sole buoyancy term in the 
ceiling burning orientation of Orloff and de Ris [5]. Except for the DNS solution of Ali et al. [8], all previous 
boundary layer analyses ignored this effect and only considered the buoyancy component in the flow direction 
parallel to the plate. This parallel component does not differentiate between top and bottom burning for the same 
plate angle. 
EXPERIMENTAL 
The experiments used ceramic wicks, as shown in Fig. 1. They were soaked with methanol or ethanol. The pyrolysis 
region and surrounding border were constructed of 3.2 mm thick Kaowool PM and were backed with 12.7 mm thick 
Kaowool 3000 to minimize heat loss to the sides and rear of the fuel laden area. Sodium silicate was applied to the 
interface of the plate with the border to eliminate leakage of the liquid fuel. 
10 cm wide flat wicks of length 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 10 cm were constructed. Wicks were affixed to a stand capable 
of rotating 180° with respect to gravity. The mass of the wick was measured over time with a load cell, the mass-
loss rate or burning rate determined by the slope of the linear mass versus time curve. The flame standoff distance 
was recorded during steady burning using photographs recorded parallel to the plate. The photographs were 
analyzed to obtain instantaneous plots over the length of the plate. Additional details of these measurements can be 
found in Bustamante [13], along with heat flux results for 10×10 cm methanol soaked wicks with a 3 mm Schmidt-
Boelter sensor heat flux transducer located at the center of the plate. 
Flame Shape 
Figure 2 shows an array of instantaneous methanol flame images for the various burning orientations and plate 
lengths (with a fixed width of 10 cm). The images show that an increase in pyrolysis length increases fluctuations 
downstream of the leading edge beginning a transition to turbulence. Top burning plates show that buoyancy can 
cause separation of the boundary layer form the plate, resembling a plume-like flow. Beyond the plate, a wake 
plume occurs. For the pool fire case, the flame behavior changes from unsteady laminar flow to turbulent flow with 
increasing distance from the base and increased pyrolysis length. For the bottom ceiling fire case, the flame is blue 
and always laminar. Figure 3 shows these images in terms of digitized flame standoff locations at several instants of 
t me when “steady average p ate burn ng” occurred. The flame clearly begins to become unsteady at some locations.

These data can be analyzed in terms of a Grashof number (Gr) in order to generalize the departure from steady 
laminar flow. The Gr at which the unsteady flow begins is seen to increase from about 106 to 107 as the orientation 
of burning changes from the top to the bottom of the plate, as shown in Figure 5. Predominately steady laminar flow 
is observed for plates at –60 and –90 for lengths up to 10 cm. For these angles, the Grashof number for transition 
shall be greater than      . Some heat-transfer studies also found a decreasing Gr under which transition occurs 
when inclining heated surfaces of a plate from top to bottom [11, 12]. Their Gr for the end of the laminar region, 
however, are somewhat higher and follow a more extreme slope in comparison to this study, perhaps because they 
were not reacting flows which may induce an earlier transition due to large temperature gradients in the boundary 
layer. 
 
Average Burning Rate 
The average burning rate per unit area of the plate surface was determined for each plate length, orientation, and 
fuel. The steady values are reported, and contain some results where periodic unsteadiness occurs due to the onset of 
turbulence or plume-like flow. These data for all orientations and plate lengths of 1, 4, and 10 cm are shown in Fig. 
6a for methanol and Fig. 6b for ethanol. As the length of the plate decreases the burning rate increases, consistent 
with increasingly laminar flow for shorter lengths. At very small lengths (l = 1 cm in Figure 6), the heat transfer to 
the plate is predominant, and therefore fuel vaporization rates significantly increase as the flame anchors close to the 
fuel surface over a large portion of the short length.  
There is a distinct maximum at +30º (burning on the topside) for l = 1 cm, and this maximum diminishes with plate 
length. Blackshear and Murty [1], on the contrary, found a maximum at –50º (underside) for a plate of 15.9 cm.

There is little difference between the data for methanol and ethanol in this study. Figure 7 shows a more complete

ANALYSIS 
In order to explain the behavior of the data, the theoretical results of Ahmad and Faeth (A-F) [6, 7] are examined. As 
our flow is mostly laminar, with some unsteadiness, we use their laminar analytical solution. We also use their 
properties, as listed in Table 1. Their solution applies to boundary layer flows (-60º to +60º of our data), and 
accounts for the angle of inclination by the component of gravity along the plate using cosθ, but does not 
discriminate between top and bottom burning.

CONCLUSIONS 
Measurements of flame location and burning rate were recorded for flat plate wicks of methanol and ethanol, 
ranging in size from 1 to 10 cm, and oriented from 0º (vertical) to +/- 90º (top/bottom). The dimensionless laminar 
correlations of Ahmad and Faeth [6, 7] roughly support the data for flame location and burning flux, however the 
flame location is over predicted, and indicates no additional dependence on the angle. In contrast, the results for the 
burning rate indicate increasing rates with angle. In addition, there is a maximum burning rate at + 30º whose 
location with angle appears to decrease as the length of the plate increases. While the theory only considers laminar 
steady pure convection, issues related to the onset of turbulence and radiation is present. The inclusion of the cross 
flow, or normal pressure term, in the theory gives improved results, especially in predicting the differences in the top 
and bottom burning rate for the same plate orientation. Simple fits for mass burning rates and flame standoff, 
equations (2f) and (2g) were formed based on the theory which include dependence on the Grashof number, B 
number and angle.

8th U. S. National Combustion Meeting 
Organized by the Western States Section of the Combustion Institute 
 and hosted by the University of Utah 
May 19-22, 2013 
 
A Burning Rate Emulator for Study in Microgravity 
 
Y. Zhang, M.J. Bustamante,  P.B. Sunderland, J.G. Quintiere1  
 
 
P. Ferkul2 
 
1Dept. of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA 
2NCSER, Cleveland, OH 44135 
 
A gas-fueled burner with embedded heat flux gages has been used to emulate the burning characteristics of 
several liquid and solid fuels. Dubbed the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), it establishes the heat of gasification 
(L) in steady burning by measurements of surface temperature, incident flame heat flux, and flow rate of a 
gaseous fuel mixture. The mixture is selected with appropriate properties such as the heat of combustion and 
radiation character by the soot point. Results are shown to accurately emulate methanol, heptane, and PMMA 
pool fires of 50 mm in diameter. Used in a microgravity environment, a BRE can readily identify stable and 
steady burning conditions yielding relevant fuel properties: heat of gasification, surface temperature, heat of 
combustion, and smoke point. These properties identify a potential real condensed-phase fuel that can burn in 
microgravity. Repeated experiments identify a range of fuel conditions that can support microgravity burning. 
The flammability region is bounded by extinction values, and critical conditions needed for ignition can also 
be established. The plausibility of the BRE has been demonstrated for normal gravity conditions, and a burner 
without heat-flux sensors has achieved an appearance of steady burning in the NASA 2.2-s drop tower. 
Recent tests with a 50-mm-diameter burner including heat flux measurements conducted in a 5.18-s drop 
facility have indicated stable flames with ethylene.  
 
1. Introduction 
This study seeks to establish the burning conditions for condensed fuels in a quiescent environment. 
The burning conditions represent those of steady burning with the heat of gasification of the material 
as the principal fuel property. In addition, the heat of combustion controlling flame extent, surface 
re-radiation heat flux, and flame radiation properties will influence the burning rate. We seek to 
define the burning in terms of these properties by using an emulator having a controlled gaseous fuel 
supply to simulate steady burning of material with those properties. The burning rate emulator 
(BRE) can be operated to represent a range of real solid and liquid fuels, and can also simulate an 
applied external heat flux when considering an effective heat of gasification.  
Steady burning (rate per unit area or fuel flux) can be expressed as

The flame heat flux is controlled by diffusive and radiative components, and the surface re-radiation 
heat flux by the temperature of the vaporizing surface. In the case of the emulator burner (BRE), it is 
the burner surface temperature that gives the surface re-radiation. Heat flux gages in the surface 
record the flame heat flux distribution. With the measured gas flow rate of the burner, values of L, 
with and without an external heat source, can be determined from Eq. (1). By varying the gaseous 
fuel, the heat of combustion and the radiation character (notably the smoke point) can be varied. For 
a given configuration, a wide range of burning conditions can be readily established with the 
emulator (BRE). The long term goal is to use BRE to study the microgravity burning behavior of the 
condensed fuel. However, here we will mainly focus on establishing the feasibility of the emulator 
and sharing preliminary results in drop tower testing. 
2. Background 
Orloff (1971) and de Ris, de Ris et al. (1975) and Kim et al. (1971) pioneered the use of sintered 
metal burners for studying the burning of planar condensed-phase steady burning. As with the 
Brahmi et al. (2005) burner, the flow of the fuel is distributed uniformly over the burner. This 
uniform flow is in contrast to the actual flow velocity of the supplied vapor that is governed by the 
local heat transfer from the flame. As the flame shape changes, so does the vapor velocity. 
Nevertheless, de Ris and co-workers successfully simulated burning conditions for a wide range of B 
numbers. The B number is defined as

where Yox is the ambient oxygen mass fraction, Δhc is the heat of combustion, r is the stoichiometric 
oxygen to fuel ratio, cp is the specific heat of gas mixture, Tv is the surface vaporization temperature, 
and T∞ is the ambient temperature. 
For a given ambient condition, the B number is principally a function of the heat of gasification, L. 
The burning rate per unit area is also principally a function of the B number in purely diffusive or 
convective burning. Flame radiation and surface re-radiation perturb this simple dependence. 
However, the relatively simple dependence could be emulated by the de Ris burner, and is shown to 
follow laminar flame theory. Thus, despite the imperfection of a uniform burner velocity, the results 
yielded theoretically supported results for burning and flame shape. 
In the de Ris burner, the heat of gasification was determined by Eq. (1) with no external radiation 
and negligible re-radiation. The latter was accomplished by flowing water through the burner’s 
sintered metal matrix. An energy balance on the water, after considerable time to achieve thermal 
equilibrium of the burner, allowed an average flame heat flux to be determined. Nitrogen addition to 
the gaseous fuel also allowed for variations in the supplied fuel mixture mass flux.

3 
Another proof of burner emulation was demonstrated by Bustamante et al. (2012) by comparing the 
flame standoff distance in the laminar region for burning of inclined flat plates. A pure methane 
flame was used in a porous plate burner and compared to a methanol flame on a fuel-soaked wick 
plate. Results showed the similarity in the flame shape along the surface oriented at different angles 
from a ceiling fire, to a vertical wall fire, to a pool fire. Also the onset of transition to turbulent flow 
was matched. The paper noted a difference of fire size in the turbulent over-fire region due to a 
mismatch between the heats combustion of methane and methanol. 
3. Experimental Method 
A BRE burner has been designed and constructed, inspired by the de Ris burner. Its size has been 
selected based on our flight and drop tower tests, and the burner size used by Brahmi et al (2005). 
The BRE burner has a face of 50 mm in diameter. Owing to the anticipated heat flux variation over 
the surface while burning in microgravity or normal gravity, two sensors are used. An appropriate 
averaging of the two heat fluxes provides the needed average heat flux for computing the heat of 
gasification. The thermocouples at the operating face record the surface temperature, allowing the 
re-radiation heat flux to be estimated. Glass beads provide a porous matrix for fuel flow, ensuring a 
uniform fuel flux, and porous brass screen serves as its face and internal layers. Figure 1 shows the 
BRE burner with heat flux sensors at the center and near the edge.  
 
Validation in 1-g. A series of tests were performed to assess burner’s ability to emulate condensed-
fuel combustion. It was reasoned that fuel properties that control the burning rate are (1) the heat of 
combustion, especially controlling flame height; (2) the heat of gasification, an approximation to 
evaporative condensed-phase fuels; (3) the surface temperature or corresponding re-radiation; and 
(4) the smoke point, which determines flame radiation. These properties must reasonably match 
those of the condensed fuel of interest.  
The burning rate of the condensed fuel is determined by a load-cell measurement of a pool fire. Then 
literature values are established for the four fuel properties as described above. Two of the four 
properties – heat of combustion and smoke point – are matched by selecting the proper gaseous fuel. 
 
 
Figure 1. BRE burner with 50 mm diameter surface.

4 
The other two properties – heat of gasification and surface temperature – indicate the burning 
condition. We wish to match these properties with a gaseous fuel mixture having the same mixture 
flow rate as the pool fire to evaluate the concept of BRE.  
We tested the BRE to see if it could emulate a 50 mm pool of methanol burning steadily. The mass 
loss rate of methanol was measured and the flame was photographed. To match the methanol with 
the BRE we would need to use a gaseous fuel with the same flow rate. To match the flame height 
and consequently the heat flux, the fuel must have the same heat of combustion. In addition, 
consideration of the sooting tendency led to the choice of methane as the gaseous fuel. Nitrogen was 
added to the fuel stream to match the heat of combustion of methanol, 19.1 kJ/g (Tewarson, 2002). 
The gas burner BRE used a fuel mixture of 52% (volume) methane with 48% nitrogen. The flow rate 
of the mixture was 33 cc/s to match the burning rate of the methanol, 11g/m2-s.  
If the BRE concept is correct, the two flames should be nearly identical in appearance and heat flux 
distribution. The measured heat fluxes in the BRE are 5.5 and 21.3 kW/m2 for the heat flux gages 
located at the center and at 1.5 cm from the center, respectively. A weighted average over their area 
segments gives an average value of 15.6 kW/m2. Corresponding surface temperature measurements 
yield an average temperature of 160 ºC (141 – 170 ºC). Assuming an emissivity of unity for the 
oxidized porous brass surface, the re-radiative heat flux is 2 kW/m2. Consequently, the heat of 
gasification associated with the BRE is computed from Eq. (1) as L = (15.6 – 2 kW/m2) / (11g/m2-s) 
= 1.24 kJ/g. The literature value for methanol is 1.20 kJ/g (Quintiere, 2006). Besides the 
approximations in the calculations, the slight difference possibly arises because the BRE surface is 
hotter than the boiling point of methanol, 64 ºC. The visual confirmation of the BRE to emulate the 
methanol pool fire at 50 mm diameter is shown in Fig. 2a and 2b, in which the flames are compared 
when the slightly oscillating images are similar. 
 
We sought to evaluate whether the burner could also emulate other burning conditions. We 
considered a 50-mm-diameter burning pool of heptane and PMMA. The choice of the gaseous fuels 
was similar to that of methanol. Ethylene was selected be used as the burner gas to simulate heptane.

4. Applications of the BRE 
Having demonstrated the BRE’s capability to emulate the combustion of various fuels in normal 
gravity, extensions of its use can be considered. In addition to steady burning, the conditions of 
ignition and extinction can be examined relative to condensed-phase fuels. By the determination of 
these conditions, a mapping of the properties that allow burning with boundaries of ignition and 
extinction can be produced. This conceivably can be done in normal as well as microgravity. 
Moreover the conditions of burning can be efficiently established in microgravity using the BRE. 
Some preliminary results in this regard are examined below. 
Conditions at ignition or extinction. Mass-loss flux at ignition and extinction limits are important 
properties of fires. Yet their evaluation for materials is difficult to capture with current experimental 
methods. Materials experience a sudden jump in mass-loss rate when ignited or when they suddenly 
extinguish. Such transients are difficult to accurately measure. By using the BRE, the mass-loss rate 
could be clearly identified by increasing the flow rate of fuel gradually until the establishment of the 
flame is observed, or decreasing it after a flame is sustained.  
A theoretical analysis for extinction can be put forth based on the relationship for steady burning, 
and its ability to exceed a critical flame temperature for the flame to survive. A critical temperature 
needed for the survival of a diffusion flame can be taken as 1300 ºC (Quintiere and Rangwala, 
2004). This temperature is a reasonable criterion for the extinction of a laminar flame under its 
environmental conditions, including gravity effects. Following B-number theory for pure convective 
burning, and considering a small B number as would occur near extinction, we write:

6. Conclusions 
1. We are able to match the burning rate and flame characteristic of a condensed-phase fuel by 
matching the heat of combustion and smoke point of the condensed fuel with a gaseous fuel and 
inert in the BRE. This has been demonstrated for pool fires of methanol, heptane and PMMA. 
2. By adjusting the fuel flow rate to match the burning rate of the pool fire with the selected gas 
mixture, the BRE flame yields similar burning conditions as the pool fire of 50 mm diameter, not 
only in the fuel property (heat of gasification), but also in the flame appearance. Although the 
surface temperature was not perfectly matched, the results were reasonable. 
3. Extinction and ignition conditions for the burning of condensed-phase fuels can be studied much 
more easily and accurately with the BRE. 
4. The success in validating the emulation ability of BRE burner would justify its usage in studying 
the burning behavior of condensed fuels of interest by using a simulation gaseous fuel. We hope 
to use this to explore microgravity fires. 
5. Preliminary drop test results using a 50 mm BRE appears to yield nearly steady burning 
conditions. While these conditions may not all correspond to real condensed-phase fuels, they 
contribute to a flammability mapping of possible fuels that can burn. 
  
7. Acknowledgments 
The authors would like to thank M. Willnauer, E. Muller and P. Klaess for their contributions. This 
work was funded by NASA Grant NNX10AD98G for which Dennis Stocker is the technical contact 
and provided important support. Eric Neumann and his staff at NASA’s Zero-Gravity Research 
Facility were instrumental in the successful conduct of the drop tests.

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 21 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-001 Disposition  
RFA # 01 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
One of the criteria for PDR is a preliminary limited 
life items list. Just because other experiments may 
not have such a list does not mean ACME should not 
have such a list. ACME presents a unique situation 
where experiments will occur in the same chamber 
as the Cube is located as well as tubing, wiring, 
cooling lines, etc. The project should to start 
identifying their materials lists from the Computer-
Aided Design (CAD) drawings so that compatibility 
issues/soft goods shelf life/limited life items can be 
identified early in the design cycle. Maybe testing 
would also be needed as well for materials with 
unknown compatibility? 
 
Identify the material 
compatibility and shelf life limits 
for the soft goods used in 
ACME and CIR 
 
It has been determined by the 
project that a materials analysis 
would not be done for PDR due to 
funding and resource limitations.  
The plan is to have this analysis 
and MIUL completed at CDR. 
  
Although the analysis was not 
complete at PDR, the ACME 
project is aware of potential issues 
with the Data Cube and other 
electronics and their compatibility 
with the gaseous fuels.  These 
issues are currently being tracked 
in the Risk Management 
Implementation Tool database.

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 22 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-002 Disposition  
RFA # 02 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
In many of the presentations, the presenters 
indicated CIR heritage for a choice of hardware. It 
seemed as though CIR was treated as a ‘black box’ 
that ACME hooks into. ACME fuels need to be 
compatible with CIR and also cause no issues to 
CIR. 
The following items need to be investigated further to 
assess compatibility: 
• ACME Venting compatibility with CIR hardware 
• Are the gases/liquids compatible with CIR 
hardware, particularly with the soft goods in the 
solenoid valves? The board was told the solenoid 
valves contained FKM o-ring. For the ACME 
gases, NBr is the recommended rubber for most of 
the gases, if not all. 
• What are the limited life items for CIR? Do any of 
the items need be replaced prior to ACME use? 
An assessment of the venting 
compatibility has been addressed 
and was deemed acceptable. 
 
As the project matures, CIR will 
assess compatibility of materials in 
their system with ACME gasses, 
products of combustion and any 
other applicable interactions. 
 
ACME anticipates this will be 
completed by CDR.

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 23 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-003 Disposition  
RFA # 03 
Originator: Al Linne 
Originator Concurrence:  7 November 2013 
Statement of 
Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
There are no warnings to 
eliminate damage to the 
test hardware 
To minimize the likelihood of 
hardware damage, the flight & 
ground software designs 
should incorporate software 
requirements to identify invalid 
commands and command 
parameters that are outside of 
allowable limits and to alert 
operations personnel that 
invalid commands were 
entered. 
 
A complete software command list for the ACME hardware has 
been derived from operational requirements for the ACME 
system.  Operational limits have been defined for each 
command and incorporated into the software requirement set.  
The software requirements are documented in the Software 
section of the ACME Engineering Requirements Document 
(ERD) ACME-REQ-001.   
This list of signals is also documented in the ACME Data 
Dictionary Document (ACME-DOC-008).   
These documents will be available for NASA review and 
comment during the CDR.   
The approved operational limitations will be built into the 
ACME ground command station software at the TSC.  Every 
command sent by an operator will be checked against these 
established limits.  Commands that violate safe ranges will be 
rejected (on the ground) and the operator will receive an error 
message.  This ground software will be verified, as part of the 
overall ACME test and verification  campaign, to ensure no 
command can ever reach the ACME hardware that is outside 
of these safely established limits.

RFA # 04

Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
A detonation analysis has 
not been completed. 
Perform a detonation analysis on the 
expected ACME gas mixtures. This 
should be done prior to the ACME Phase 
0/1 Flight Safety Review, since it may 
inform some of the hazard analysis. Also, 
the results of this analysis could drive the 
consumables usage and could limit the 
amount of science performed. 
An ACME detonation analysis has been performed 
for the Inverse Flame Experiment, which is the the 
worst case hazard.  It was chosen because of the 
possible oxygen interaction with ACME CIA 
hardware (i.e. materials compatibility).  The 
analysis validated that the present configuration 
could safely meet requirements.  The analysis has 
not impacted the design. 
 
A full detonation analysis of all experiments will be 
completed prior to the Phase 2 Flight Safety 
Review.

(CIR & ACME hardware) to ensure system 
meets the intent of CIR hazard analyses.

completed with the participation of the CIR 
Team.  An Integrated Safety Data Package

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 27 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-007 Disposition  
RFA # 07 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME project plan did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
planning. There was no evidence of a 
bottoms up cost estimate or a bottoms 
up schedule. Both of these are vital in 
ensuring the project has been thought 
through and that sufficient resources are 
available to successfully complete the 
project. The only budget shown was the 
program budget, and it may not be 
adequate complete the current scope of 
the ACME project. 
The ACME Systems Engineering 
Management Plan also did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
technical management. It provided 
details through PDR/CDR, but not the 
project lifecycle. 
Update the Project Plan. Complete a 
bottoms up cost estimate and a 
bottoms up end-to-end schedule. 
Consider performing a parametric cost 
estimate. To be of value, these should 
be performed within 6 months of the 
PDR.

Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-008 Disposition  
RFA # 08 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME Engineering requirements 
document is incomplete. While it appears 
that the Science requirements have been 
thoroughly addressed, carrier 
requirements (both CIR & ISS) and 
safety and mission assurance have not 
been addressed in the ACME ERD. It is 
important to thoroughly identify all 
requirements which are imposed on the 
system and subsequently must be 
verified. A related concern is the number 
of requirements that must be verified. 
There are a large number of 
requirements on the system and the 
verification program could be extensive. 
Complete the ERD. This should be 
done within 6 months of the PDR to 
ensure the CDR design meets all 
requirements that are levied on the 
system. Environmental testing 
requirements should be included as 
part of this, waivers for fragile 
equipment should be identified early. 
When developing the verification 
program look for ways to combine & 
streamline the verification process. 
The document FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME 
addresses carrier requirements (both CIR 
and ISS).  ACME-REQ-001 points there. 
 
Safety and Mission Assurance 
requirements will be detailed in the ACME 
Hazards and Integrated CIR-ACME 
hazard reports.  Following the Phase 0/1 
Flight Safety Review, where these Hazard 
Reports are approved, the requirements 
will be incorporated into ACME-REQ-001. 
 
The verification process will group 
requirements by discipline identified to 
facilitate verification and validation.

The project has done a good job of 
writing operational requirements, but they

requirements that the GRC science and 
engineering teams were not aware of.

RDR-004 RFA which has not been 
closed out as of the PDR. 
It is imperative that: 1) the currently 
documented operational requirements 
are vetted with each of the PIs; 2) the 
engineering team talks with each of the 
PIs. This will ensure that both parties 
fullly understand what is meant by 
each of the requirements, and also 
give the engineering team a chance to 
uncover additional operational 
requirements.

vetted the operations requirements 
documented in ACME-SRD-001 with the 
respective Pis.  Dennis has also 
discussed the Ops requirements with the 
ACME engineering team to be sure they 
are well understood.

with the operations requirements has 
been completed and released. 
 
This information should be sufficient to 
close RFA ACME-RDR-004.

ACME Testing Plan 
•
As Engineering Model sub-systems are built, they will be 
functionally tested to validate performance at that level

Camera and CIA to validate performance at the system level

validating carrier interfaces 
•
Since the EM is built to flight drawings, it will then undergo Qual 
testing: Vibration, EMI and thermal 
•
When the Flight Unit is complete the Flight AVP, CIA and Data 
Camera will undergo flight level environmental testing: Vibe, EMI 
and offgas 
•
The remainder of flight verification testing will then occur after 
the flight environmental testing

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 62 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
Spherical Burner
 
Spherical Burner 
The upper part of the spherical burner will be supplied by Princeton 
University under the following conditions: 
 
1) Princeton University: Fabricate a 1/4”, 3/8”, and 1/2” spherical burner head with supply tube per ACME 
ISRD 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 1.2.5, and 1.2.6.  
2) Princeton University: Perform preliminary tests on the above spherical burner heads following ACME 
ISRD 1.2.3 as a guide and conferring with NASA ACME Project Scientist.  
3) Princeton University: Deliver accepted spherical burner heads to NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC).  
4) NASA GRC performs additional acceptance tests as necessary (microgravity).  
5) NASA GRC deliver acceptable spherical burner heads to ZIN Technologies Inc. as government furnished 
equipment (GFE.) via C727.  
6) Zin Technologies Inc.: Accept and serialize spherical burner heads from NASA GRC.  
7) Zin Technologies Inc.: Perform additional fabrication on S1101MFA1218, S1101MFA1223, and 
S1101MFA1228 per ACME ISRD 1.2.4, 1.2.6, and 1.2.7. This fabrication will produce the following top level 
assemblies: S1101MFA1216: 1/4” spherical burner assembly, S1101MFA1220: 3/8” spherical burner 
assembly, S1101MFA1225: 1/2” spherical burner assembly  
8) Zin Technologies Inc.: Deliver S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 to NASA GRC via 
a DD1149.  
9) NASA GRC: Test and verify S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 per ACME ISRD 
1.2.3.  
10) NASA GRC: Deliver verified spherical burner assemblies along with verification certification documents 
to Zin Technologies Inc. as GFE via C727.

Glenn Research Center

AVP Command and Control 
94 
ACME Single Board Computer will coordinate CIR diagnostic hardware and 
control ACME hardware: 
•Intel Core 2 Duo Processor 1066 MHz 
•1GB DDR3 RAM onboard 
• Ethernet Ports 
•1 port receives commands and transmits telemetry from and to the 
CIR Input Output Processor (IOP) 
•1 port sends control signals  and receives data acquisition packets 
from data acquisition “Cube” located in ACME Chamber Insert 
Assembly. 
• 1 port receives video from digital camera package.  
•RS 232 Ports 
•Transmits commands to ACME Chamber insert Color camera.  
•Controls Motion Control Boards/Stepper Motors. 
•RS 422 Port  
• Communicates to Mass Flow Controllers – monitoring 
operation/functionality.

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 95 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
AVP Control and Data 
 Management 
95 
 
 
 
 
 
•
Two 4 Axis Motor Control Boards coordinate actuation of ACME motors to 
perform input/output functions: 
• Insert and retract position of igniter and Thin Film Pyrometry (TFM) 
• Digital camera zoom, iris, focus control and filter insertion 
•
Cube Analog input (differential inputs) and outputs (single ended) 
collect experiment telemetry and provide hardware control. 
•
 Analog Outputs 
• D/A Cube +5 – 0 outputs to relay boards provide the discrete I/O 
channels to chamber – on/off, enable/disable to MFCs, valves, 
igniters, both stepper drives, illumination, High Voltage and a 
variable output to control MFC, High Voltage, Photomultiplier gains. 
•
 Analog Inputs 
• Collects Radiometer, Photomultiplier, Gas flow rates, Multiple 
Temperature points data, Ion Current and High Voltage Grid 
measurements.

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 151 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
Depress / Repress 
• Unless part of a pressurized system, all volumes are designed to 
adequately vent due to station / vehicle depressurization 
• Vented Containers will be verified by the stored energy method (SDP 
STD-ACME-1 17.a) where the volume has a stored energy < 3,063 ft-
lbs.  Volumes with a stored energy > 3,063 ft-lbs will have a depress 
rate calculated. 
 
• Depress rates are calculated* for each volume to show that the 
volume’s depress rate is greater than maximum station / vehicle 
depress rate so no pressure load is generated 
• Maximum depress rate is defined in section 3.1.1.2.1.5 part B of SSP-
50835 Rev C as 13.3kPa/s (1.93psi/sec) 
 
 
 
*AIAA Journal, October 1986, Vol. 24, No. 10, pg 1709-1711, “Formulas for Venting or Charging 
Gas from a Single Volume”, H.T. Yang

Combustion Chamber Atmosphere 
Mixing 
The oxidant MFC can provide up to 30 slpm (based on nitrogen (N2)) 
flow. The oxygen gas concentration is a function of the gas bottle size, 
as listed below.  
•
2.25 liter bottle provides a maximum of 50% O2, balance diluent at 
2000 psia. 
•
3.8 liter bottle provides a maximum of 30% O2, balance diluent at 
2000 psia. 
  
A Nitrogen manifold can supply inert gas types such as N2, He, and 
CO2, as well as oxidant blends below 30% oxygen, to the chamber. In 
addition, this manifold provides the interface for the utilization of the ISS 
supplied N2. This manifold also can directly route the pressurized gas to 
the chamber, by-passing the regulator. The N2 MFC can provide up to 
30 slpm (based on nitrogen (N2)) flow.

ACME Risk Summary 
•
Risk ID: ACME-014 
•
Risk Title: IPSU to IOP image transfer rates take too long 
•
Risk Statement: Given that the current data transfer rates from the IPSU 
to the IOP is severely limited, transfer of ACME data may take an 
unacceptable amount of time and may reduce obtainable science for the 
allotted operational time on board ISS. 
•
Likelihood: 4 
•
Consequence: 3 
•
Approach: Watch. Need to keep an eye on this and follow up  
with the CIR team to keep updated on transfer improvements. 
•
Latest Status: 09/17/13 - The IPSU-G is going to have their  
PDR September 26th 2013. The IPSU-G will eliminate  
the need to transfer image data from an IPSU to the IOP for downlink  
because the IPSU-G will be able to directly downlink image data to  
the ground. A trigger for this risk would be the cancellation of the  
IPSU-G project that would require ACME to mitigate, accept, etc...

Title: High Oxygen Concentration Results in Fire 
 
Description: Fire resulting from material incompatibility with high 
oxygen concentrations. Note: Current Science Requirements specify 
an 85% oxygen bottle for Inverse Flame experiments. 
 
Controls:  
1.All CIA materials will be analyzed and selected for compatibility with 
up to 40% oxygen. 
2.To compensate for the lack of flammability test data of some 
materials over 30% oxygen levels, non-metallics used inside the

Title: Release of Adsorber Cartridge Contents into Habitable Volume 
Description: Generation of (toxicity hazard level = 0, see HMST) 
particles due to launch loads and subsequent release into habitable 
volume during Adsorber Cartridge replacement results in injury to 
crew  
Controls:  
1.
The Adsorber Cartridge is designed with a 40 micron sintered 
metal filter, which is smaller than the grain size (1680 microns) 
of chemicals, located at both the inlet and outlet ports, to keep 
particles from escaping. 
2.
The Adsorber Cartridge is designed so that each end of the 
Adsorber Cartridge has redundant seals QDs and a manual 
valve which seals the Adsorber Cartridge for removal. 
3.
Constituents of Adsorber Cartridge are limited to Silica Gel or 
Molecular Sieve for ACME. 
FCF-ACME-01

Glenn Research Center

Title: Exposure of Crew to Toxic Byproducts During Chamber Operations 
Description: Carcinogenic soot particles from the combustion chamber 
contaminate the habitable atmosphere causing crew illness if inhaled or 
floating particles could cause injury to the eyes.  
Controls:  
1.
The soot production for ACME experiments will be below the SMAC limit 
and does not exceed Tox 0. 
2.
The chamber air will be circulated through a tested Adsorber Cartridge 
for 15 minutes until free floating soot is removed, prior to venting.  
3.
The chemicals selected for the Adsorber Cartridge will remove the soot 
and combustion by-products. 
4.
Each Adsorber Cartridge shall have a content label and serial number. 
5.
Approved crew procedures shall be used for installation and removal of 
an Adsorber Cartridge. (TBR) (This control is also covered in CIR Hazard 
Report, FCF-C05 Inadvertent Release of Toxic Fuels and Combustion By-products 
and CIR Hazard Report, FCF-C28 Inadvertent Venting of High Oxygen, Pre-mixed 
Gases or Fuel through ISS Vent) 
 
FCF-ACME-02

content:
ACME Critical Design Review– 240 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
Integrated Phase II Hazard 
Reports  
FCF-ACME-04 
Title: Adiabatic Combustion Ruptures CIR Combustion Chamber or CIR Exhaust 
Vent Package during ACME experiments (except for the Inverse Flame Experiment) 
Description: Rapid overpressurization during the combustion of ACME gaseous 
fuel and oxidizer/diluent exceeds the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber and/or 
exhaust vent package resulting in damage to CIR or ISS hardware or injury to the 
crew. 
Note (on hazard report):   
1.
This hazard report works in conjunction with CIR hazard report FCF-C07, “Adiabatic Combustion 
ruptures the chamber walls, causing damage to station and/or injury to crew.“  Overpressurization due 
to combustion will be controlled by limiting the fuel volume in each gas bottle.  The CIR Valve Timers 
will be placed in the fuel mode.  The chamber will be pre-filled with gaseous oxidizer and gaseous fuel 
will flow through the ACME burner. 
2.
CIR is responsible for filling the experiment gas bottles.  The ACME detonation analyses determine the 
limits on fuel volumes in each bottle.  The fuel gas volumes will be chosen such that even if the entire 
contents of a bottle were to be released into the CIR Combustion Chamber, any adiabatic combustion 
would result in a pressure less than the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber.  The MDP of the CIR 
chamber is 135 psia. 
3.
The CIR bottle leakage hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C08 
Leakage of Pressurized System. 
4.
The CIR system rupture hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C10 
Rupture of Pressurized Systems.

The BRE data is organized in PSI by burner and fuel composition. Raw data, Video and Images Data, and Experiment Documents are available on the “Scientific Data and Information Tab” of each of the four “Experiment Data” records:
1. 25-mm burner, 50% ethylene (balance nitrogen)
2. 25-mm burner, 100% ethylene
3. 25-mm burner, 100% methane
4. 50-mm burner, 100% ethylene

Within each “Experiment Data” record, “Raw Data”, “Images” and “Audio/Video Files” are available on the “Scientific Data and Information” tab. Test names are formatted YYDDDX# where YY identifies year, DDD identifies day of year (GMT), X identifies a letter and # identifies a number – where the different numbers can be for repeats but are typically variants. Record naming and listings are based on the detailed information in the test conditions table below (page 2). 
Test specific raw data files are located on the “Raw Data and Information” tab of the “Raw & Analyzed Data” record. The first row of the .csv files provides information about the test configuration. 
Associated Images are located on the “Image Data and Information” tab of the “Videos & Images” record. Videos can be found of the “Video Data and Information” tab as well. 

There are other supporting reports available on the other tabs of the “Investigations” record.

content:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
13 
3.0 
EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION INTERFACES 
ACME commands originate from the ACME Ground Software (AGS) CSCI on a ground 
workstation at the Telescience Center (TSC) at Glenn Research Center (GRC).  These commands 
are then forwarded through a variety of systems until they eventually end up at the CIR on the 
ISS.   
 
Figure 1  ACME System Diagram 
 
 
3.1 
CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) Interface 
Commands sent through the CIR IOP (Input Output Processor) are in the format required by 
FCF-ICD-0076A.  See section A.1, FCF Command Protocol for a listing of the required 
command formats, including all required headers.  All commands from the ground go to the IOP 
with the FCF Command Header and User Data filled in.  Commands from ACME to the IPSUs 
and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the 
packet to the IOP for routing.

3.1.1 
ACME Commands 
Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of 
commands. 
Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a 
string is less than the available length then a terminating zero character needs to be used.  The ground command software will make 
this transparent to the normal user. 
The Common Group is so-named because it is implemented in code shared between payloads.

3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
moduleIdentifier 
2 
Uint16 
Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2) 
Command parameters 
80 
Area for module command-dependent parameters. 
 
3.1.2.3 
GoToIdle 
The GoToIdle command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the IDLE state. 
Command ID: 0xC003 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_IDLE 
 
3.1.2.4 
GoToExp 
The GoToExp command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the EXPERIMENT state. 
Command ID: 0xC004 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_EXPERIMENT

SetRegistryItem 
The SetRegistryItem command selects an item in the registry file, 
/payload/app/config/AcmeConfig.ini, for modification by the SetRegistryValue command. The 
full path including group is required.  In Table 32, AcmeConfig.ini Contents, the full path is 
/Group/Key. 
Command ID: 0xC008

# Bytes 
Type 
Description

3.1.2.9 
SetRegistryValue 
The SetRegistryValue command selects the key set via the SetRegistryItem command and 
modifies it with the supplied value.  All software sub-systems are notified of the change and 
apply it used in the sub-system.  This is just a temporary change. It must be saved with the 
SaveRegistry command to become permanent in the AcmeConfig.ini file.  See Table 32. 
Command ID: 0xC009 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_REGISTRY_SET_VALUE

3.1.2.21 
FtpSendFile 
The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine. 
Command ID: 0xC015 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_FILE 
 
3.1.2.22 
FtpSendDirectory 
The FtpSendDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpLocalDirectory command 
and the FtpRemoteDirectory command to copy a directory recursively from the local machine to 
the remote machine.  
Command ID: 0xC016 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_DIRECTORY 
 
3.1.2.23 
FtpGetFile 
The FtpGetFile command uses the information set via the FtpRemoteFile and 
FtpRemoteDirectory commands and the FtpLocalDirectory command. If an absolute path is 
provided in the FtpRemoteFile command the result of the FtpRemoteDirectory command is 
ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC017 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_FILE 
 
3.1.2.24 
FtpGetDirectory 
The FtpGetDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpRemoteDirectory 
command and FtpLocalDirectory commands to copy a directory recursively from the remote 
machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC018 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_DIRECTORY

MoveFiles 
The MoveFiles (linux ‘mv SRC DIR’) command moves SRC(s) to DIR. Source directory is set 
via the SetSource command and the destination directory is set via the SetDestination command. 
Wildcards * (any number of unknown characters) and ? (one unknown character) may be used in 
the filter. A blank filter or a filter consisting of a single * is interpreted as all files. If a single file 
move is desired, give filenames in the source and destination. A better solution is to use the 
RenameFile command. If moving an entire directory tree is desired, use the RenameDirectory 
command.  
Command ID: 0xC01D

SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

3.1.3.3 
SystemCloseTestPoint 
The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE 
3.1.3.4 
SystemResetMotionController 
The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER 
 
3.1.3.5 
SystemCirFlowState 
The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
} 
 
 
Command ID: 0xC107 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_CIR_FLOW_STATE

IntensifiedCameraSafe 
The IntensifiedCameraSafe command  places the intensified camera in a state that is safe for 
turning on lights without harming the camera by sending commands to the IPSUG.  The filter is 
commanded to home position and a fixed delay occurs to allow this to finish (without checking 
that it is finished).  Then the filter is sent to a safe position with another fixed delay.  The gain is 
set to 2048 (reporting back 2500).  Gate type is set to pulsed and gate width is set to zero 
(reporting back 20).  The delays and safe parameters are defined in the Intensifier group in 
AcmeConfig.ini.

ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter.

3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

ACME Flow Group Command Details 
For flow group commands refer to the latest revision of drawing S1101MFS004, “ACME/CIR 
Integrated Pneumatic Schematic” to see how flow devices are connected to each other.  A screen 
shot of the ACME CIA portion of this drawing (Rev A) is shown below.  Gas from the CIR 
comes in at the bottom of the diagram; fuel through QD11, nitrogen bypass through QD12, and 
static mixer through QD13.

3.1.6.1 
FlowEnableMfcs 
The FlowEnableMfcs command turns the mass flow controllers on or off.  Initially they are all 
turned on as soon as the cube boots.  After this first power-on the MFCs are queried for their 
configuration, including full scale flow which appears in telemetry.  Subsequent commanded 
power-ons do not cause a query of configuration.

3.1.6.5 
FlowMfcSerialCommand 
The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is 
specified by the registry value: Flow/MfcSerialCommandTimeoutMsec.  See Table 32.

FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing ramping

The FlowRampedWave command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or 
not at all, at a specified ramp rate A for a specified duration A, waits a specified hold duration

3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

3.1.7.11 
PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)

The ExtinctionDetectionConfigure command defines the limits, averaging duration, and method 
of extinction detection.  Detection of extinction using this configuration does not begin until the

averaged over the specified duration.  These averages are compared to the specified limts.  The 
numberOfInstruments parameter is used to indicate how many instrument averages must go

ACME E-Field Group Command Details 
3.1.8.1 
EFieldEnable 
The EFieldEnable command enables or disables the high voltage supply that powers the electric 
field mesh.  This command also effectively performs a EFieldSetVoltage command with voltage 
parameter equal to zero prior to an enable and after a disable.  Any waveforms are stopped by a 
disable. 
 
This command controls the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-6 (HV2_EN) signal.  See Table 18. 
 
The high voltage supply is an Ultravolt part number 20A12-N4-Y6-C. 
 
Command ID: 0xC601 
Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_ENABLE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description 
state 
1 
Uint8 
0 = Disable 
1 = Enable 
Disable sets HV_EN to 0V.  Enable sets 
HV_EN to 5V. 
 
3.1.8.2 
EFieldSetVoltage 
The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
stepVoltage < 0 starts at maxVoltage and steps to minVoltage (and back up if cycles 
> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

3.1.8.5 
EFieldRectangularWave 
The EFieldRectangularWave command is an EFieldSteppedSignal command but there is a 
second step with its own size and duration.  The two step sizes can be the same or opposite 
polarity. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
If (stepAVoltage + stepBVoltage) < 0 the sequence starts at maxVoltage. 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single step sequence between min and max voltage. 
- 
stepAVoltage = -1 * stepBVoltage produces a square wave between minVoltage and 
minVoltage + stepAVoltage.

This analog input layer in the UEI PowerDNA Cube has 16 differential input channels with an input range of +/-10 Volts and 18-bit

* MFCA1_FULL_SCALE.  Device is Teledyne Hastings HFC-D-302.

IPSU Status 
Value 
State 
Description 
0 
None 
No test point-related commands have been sent to the IPSU or IPSU-G yet. 
1 
Command Sent 
Command has been sent to IPSU or IPSU-G. 
2 
Command Failed 
Last command to IPSU or IPSU-G failed.  For an IPSU this means a -1 in the subCommand field of the 
returned command.  For an IPSU-G this means that the fcfSource in the returned command was not 
CMD_complete = 0x81. 
3 
Command Successful 
Last command to IPSU or IPSU-G was successful.  For an IPSU this means not a -1 in the subCommand 
field of the returned command.  For an IPSU-G this means that the fcfSource in the returned command was 
CMD_complete = 0x81. 
4 
Command Timed Out 
The IPSU or IPSU-G did not respond to the last command sent before the timeout period was up.  Timeout 
period is registry value Ipsu/IpsuPhaseTimerPeriodMsec.  See  Table 32. 
5 
Inactive 
This is an inactive IPSU as determined by the SystemDefineSetup command.

content:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
122 
7.2 
AcmeLogging.ini 
This file located in /payload/app/config allows filter levels to be configured so that more or less 
information shows up in the telemetry and file message logs.  In the message log each message 
contains a logging category, for example “acme.diag” or “zt.fcf”.  To turn off a category make a 
rule in AcmeLogging.ini.  For example, “acme.diag=false” turns off any message with the 
acme.diag category.  Comments in the file indicate available categories. 
7.3 
Motion_ACME.ini 
This file located in /payload/app/config contains configuration for motion control of the camera 
package when ACME is controlling the camera motion instead of IPSU-G.  It specifies the 
camera serial port (serialPortNumber=3 means use /dev/ttyS3) and parameters for each axis. 
While no longer used it may still be included to show what IPSU-G should have for this file. 
7.4 
Script Files 
Script files are used to conduct automated operations using the commands: SetScriptDirectory, 
LoadScript, RunScript, AbortScript, PauseScript, ResumeScript, and ChangeScriptParameter.  
They are named with a .js extension (for java script) and are typically stored in the 
/payload/app/scripts/ directory or any sub-directory of /payload/app/scripts, but can be anywhere 
as long as the SetScriptDirectory and/or LoadScript commands specify the location. 
The language used to write script files is technically ECMAScript-262 ( http://www.ecma-
international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/Ecma-262.pdf).   A brief summary can be 
currently found at https://wiki.qt.io/JavaScript.  
Many ACME functions and variables have been made visible to the scripts.  All commands and 
their parameters can be used.  All current telemetry is available.  Public methods in controllers 
derived from XSystemController can be called.  Any other objects passed to the QT macro 
Q_DECLARE_METATYPE(object) in the ACME source code can be used. 
Several helper functions are preloaded to the script engine and can also be used.  print(message) 
logs a message.  sendCommand(command) sends the specified command to the command 
handler.  uSleep(time) pauses script execution for the specified number of milliseconds. 
More helper functions are loaded from the script file “/payload/app/scripts/helpers.js” if it exists. 
Here is an example of a basic ACME script: 
// BasicScript.js 
 
// When RunScript command is received this says to execute the run function below 
AcmeAvionicsController.runScript.connect(run); 
 
//This variable must be named parameters so the ground and flight software can manipulate the 
values. 
var parameters = { parameter1:1.0, parameter2:4, parameter3:true }; 
 
// from helpers.js.  This tells the ground software the parameters and values so they can be 
// displayed and modified using the ChangeScriptParameter command 
printParams();

content:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
124 
8.0 
OUTPUT FILES 
8.1 
Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file 
named and stored at /payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where 
testpointName is the parameter received in the SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is 
optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc.  
The file contains a two-line header.  The first line has the date and time, documentation of the 
setup received in a SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains.  The second line has the 
column headings for the subsequent rows of data.  The text of the column headings is defined by 
the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on whether 
the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column 
headings should match the data which is the following: 
- 
A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 
11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in 
Table 16. 
- 
25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in 
Table 17.  (The names of many of these values change depending on whether it is a 
BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) 
- 
Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board.  This is the E-Field control 
voltage. 
Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and 
DataRecordingStop commands at a rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry 
entry, see Table 32, defaulting to 8 msec for 125 Hz sampling. 
8.2 
Mass Flow Controller Setpoint File 
If the registry value Flow/WriteMfcSetpointsToFile is true when the SystemOpenTestPoint 
command is executed then a file of MFC setpoints is created alongside the data output file.  The 
name of the file will be /payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_mfcSetpoints.csv.  The 
first row of text contains the same header as the data output file.  The second row contains the 
headers, “Time,MFCA1Setpoint(V),MFCA2Setpoint(V),MFCA3Setpoint(V)”.  Subsequent 
rows are written whenever one of the three MFCs change setpoints and includes the changed 
setpoint and the current setpoints of the other two MFCs, and a timestamp with millisecond 
resolution.  The file is close when the SystemCloseTestPoint command is executed. 
8.3 
Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-
mmACME.log, where YYYY is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is 
minutes.  The date in the name is when the log file is created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category.  The timestamp is 
of the format YYYY-MM-DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is 
milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory.  See section 1.1 for information about the logging 
category and how to filter them out if desired.

8.4 
Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.3, includes messages showing commands received and their 
parameters.  Command log files contain only the details of each command received.  The files 
are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log.  The 
format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the command name 
followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, 
including header information. 
9.0 
DIRECTORY STRUCTURE 
The files described in the previous two sections are stored on the solid state drive in the 
following locations. 
Table 33  Directory Structure 
Directory Strucure 
Path 
Contents 
/payload 
Root directory for ACME files.  The script, startup.sh, looks here 
during each software startup to see if there is new software in a tar 
file to install.  
/payload/app 
Root directory for ACME application files. 
/payload/app/bin 
AcmeMp and FcfCommunications executables are located here. 
/payload/app/config 
Configurations files: 
     AcmeConfig.ini 
     AcmeLogging.ini 
/payload/app/scripts 
Science Qt script files including the automatically loaded helpers.js 
script. 
/payload/app/scripts/shell 
System bash scripts for startup, software updates, and directory 
listings. 
/payload/logs 
Message log files and command log files. 
/payload/sci 
Root directory for ACME science files. 
/payload/sci/YYDDDtt 
Data output files and Mass Flow Controller Setpoint files.  The 
names of the directories are what is specified in the TestPointOpen 
commands, tentatively to follow the convention of YY=year (ie. 17 
for 2017), DDD=GMT day (001-365), and tt=test points of the day 
(ie. A1, A2, B1, …).

Type K Thermocouple Conversion 
Input to this conversion is thermocouple output in millivolts and cold junction temperature in 
Celcius. First convert cold junction temperature (C), cjTemp, to millivolts in regard to a type K 
thermocouple: 
𝑐𝑗𝑀𝑣= −0.176004136860E −01 + 0.389212049750E −01 ∗cjTemp
+ 0.185587700320E −04 ∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝2 −0.994575928740E −07
∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝3 + 0.318409457190E −09 ∗ 𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝4 −0.560728448890E
−12 ∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝5 + 0.560750590590E −15 ∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝6
−0.320207200030E −18 ∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝7 + 0.971511471520E −22
∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝8 −0.121047212750E −25 ∗𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝9 + 𝑎0 ∗𝑒𝑎1(𝑐𝑗𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝−𝑎2)2 
 
         
,where 
            
 
a0 = 0.118597600000E+00 
             
 
a1 = -0.118343200000E-03 
             
 
a2 = 0.126968600000E+03 
             
Next add cjMv to thermocouple output:    totalMv = cjMv + tcMv 
If totalMv is between 0 and 20.644 mV 
𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 (𝐶)
= 25.08355 ∗totalMv + 0.07860106 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣2 −0.2503131 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣3
+ 0.08315270 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣4 −0.01228034 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣5 + 0.0009804036
∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣6 −0.00004413030 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣7 + 0.000001057734 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣8
−0.00000001052755 ∗ 𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣9 
             
If totalMv is between 20.644 and 54.886 mV     
𝑇𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 (𝐶)
= −131.8058 + 48.30222 ∗totalMv −1.646031 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣2
+ 0.05464731 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣3 −0.0009650715 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣4
+ 0.000008802193 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣5 −0.00000003110810 ∗𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑀𝑣6
