content:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
2 
 
1. Introduction 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ 
section of the following conference paper. 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in 
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States 
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
 
While the paper was written for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the BRE investigation.  The figure 
referenced in this excerpt is not included herein.  Clarifications and additional information, not in the 
conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity has 
included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to 
make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a 
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As an extreme example, there were crew 
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME 
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two 
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the 
initial use of the same coflow burner.  Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks 
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
BRE has its own unique burners and it was the first ACME experiment conducted with large flames, as 
compared to those in the CLD Flame and E-FIELD Flames investigations.  That required changes to some 
optical elements for BRE as well as subsequent ACME experiments.  BRE was also the first experiment to 
use the CIR facility’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).  As a result, the initial BRE set-
up included 9 days of crew activity, mostly by Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques, although that 
includes 4 days in which hardware was either gathered or stowed. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing.  The CIR 
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the 
ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  Two shifts of personnel are 
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many 
pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried 
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are 
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per 
two weeks.  On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles.  Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and 
that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity.  As 
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A team of four carry 
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically 
exceed 50 pages on days including testing.

content:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
3 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real 
time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that 
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters.  That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA 
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory 
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In 
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep 
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can be 
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the 
analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center.  
Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for BRE, have been conducted in an automated manner 
using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low 
rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is 
downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images are often downlinked 
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically 
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The review helps to verify parameters 
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter 
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion 
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay 
Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with 
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 
minutes. 
 
About eight flames were ignited per test day in BRE’s first round, neglecting the day in which no tests were 
conducted because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of the preceding test day.  The nominal 
durations were typically planned for 2 or 3 minutes but some tests were 5 minutes long.  Meanwhile the 
second round of BRE had roughly 15 tests conducted per day, but the durations were nominally 2 minutes 
at most. 
 
Unlike E-FIELD Flames, the BRE experiment also made use of the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentational Package (GCIP) to measure species concentrations of the atmosphere in the combustion 
chamber.  There is no sampling probe and measurements are only made before, between, or after tests 
when the chamber atmosphere was ‘stirred’ through use of a fan.  The GC measurements were made on 
roughly 60% of the test days with flames in the first round, specifically on 19039, 19063, 19066, 19070, 
19087, and 19094.  In the second round, such data was acquired on less than half of the test days, 
specifically on 20247, 20261, 20279, and 20352.

content:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
4 
 
Like E-FIELD Flames, BRE made periodic use of the adsorber cartridge, for example between atmospheres 
and after GC measurements, if any, were made. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis.  
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment 
is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split 
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results 
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round.  This paper reports on early results 
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas 
bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s 
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010.  At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, the general target was 50 tests per 
experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used 
to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair 
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers 
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by 
venting the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively 
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For 
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
The 999-second limit on the valve safety timers has thus far been common for all ACME testing.  However, 
the timers can be reset to 999 by nearly completely venting the chamber.  Sufficient time and gas resources 
are needed to vent and refill the chamber and still conduct tests afterward, but this was done on most BRE 
test days.  The only exceptions were 19039, 19063, and 19091 where in the last case no flames were ignited 
because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of the prior test day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as 
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the research, NASA 
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  But as discussed, the ACME 
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned 
durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.  
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and 
downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select 
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  Nonetheless, the limit sometimes 
forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  …

2. Test Sequence and Parameters 
All BRE tests conducted on the ISS were carried out using automated software which had its roots in 
ACME’s Integrated Science Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations 
Requirements Documents (SORD, Rev. A).  The BRE Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course 
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering team 
in developing the control software. 
 
The major phases of the test sequence are graphically displayed in Figure 1, which incorporates the 
optional pre-flow first implemented on BRE’s third test day.  The lines appearing in the figure represent 
the nitrogen flow rate, the fuel flow rate, the igniter position and power.  The lines that are more lightly 
shaded represent some optional changes to flow rates, for example the pre-flow.  However, the flow 
variations in the darkly shaded lines are also optional.  The phases are described in detail at the bottom 
of the schematic, where the nomenclature generally corresponds to the script parameter names.

20 May 2022

With the exception of the first two test days in which the script didn’t feature the pre-flow option shown 
in Figure 1, the BRE script used 69 parameters.  The early script revision added the four parameters found 
at the end of this list, which includes example values from the final BRE test, 21028G5.  The parameters 
are briefly explained, where many of them are common to all ACME experiments because of their use of 
the same set of modular hardware.  The lines separate general types of parameters, e.g., those 
corresponding to imaging, ignition, the fiber array, gas flow, etc.  
 
 
testpointName:21028G5, 
 
test point name that will be used by the IPSUs and ACME Data File (in the image and data file 
names and directories) 
preIgnitionDataTimeSec:0, 
 
time (in seconds) ACME Data File records data before IPSUs open test point and start archiving 
images 
postFlameDataTimeSec:15, 
 
time (in seconds) ACME Data File records data after the postFlameImagingTimeSec has elapsed 
which occurs after command sent to close manifolds (i.e., stop gas flow) 
useIPSUs:true, 
 
indicates if IPSUs will be used (images archived) for the test point 
ipsuTimeoutSec:40, 
 
time (in seconds) to wait for command responses from IPSUs and IPSUG when opening and 
starting test points 
useAcmeCamera:true, 
 
indicates if the ACME Camera will be used for the test point 
useIntensifiedCamera:true, 
 
indicates if the CIR Intensified Camera will be used for the test point  
ipsu1ArchiveRate:2, 
 
indicates that every nth HiBMS Camera (IPSU1) image is saved (archived) (e.g., 10 indicates every 
10th image) 
dataCameraPreIgnitionExposureUs:1000000, 
exposure (in microseconds) of the ACME Camera prior to ignition and igniter retraction (set for 
imaging the igniter and ignition event) 
dataCameraTestExposureUs:50000, 
 
exposure (in microseconds) of the ACME Camera after igniter retraction (set for imaging the 
flame) 
analogCameraPreIgnitionShutter:2, 
 
shutter speed of the ACME Chamber Insert Camera (ops camera - no IPSU data recorded for this 
camera) prior to ignition and igniter retraction (set for imaging the igniter and ignition event) 
analogCameraTestShutter:2, 
shutter speed of the ACME Chamber Insert Camera (ops camera - no IPSU data recorded for this 
camera) after igniter retraction (set for imaging the flame) 
intensifierGainAmplitude:50000, 
 
CIR Intensified Camera intensifier gain setting; commanded to this value after turning off chamber 
LED lights; this is the actual gain value; the script will convert to counts when sending the 
command 
preIgnitionImageTimeSec:0, 
 
time (in seconds) IPSUs record images before the CIR fuel manifold is commanded open

ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
11 
 
3. BRE Script 
For a deeper understanding of the experimental procedure, the final version of the JavaScript used to 
control the BRE tests is presented here.  Neglecting the first two days of testing, it was largely unchanged 
throughout the two rounds of BRE operations.  The minor changes included: 
~2020-03-17 
flow ramp hold was fixed so that the hold values were achieved exactly  
~2020-12-18 
ignition detection was disabled prior to igniter arm retraction so that the 
retraction wasn’t interrupted  
The first change was implemented between the first and second rounds of testing, while the second was 
made during the second round. 
 
The significant early change in the script was related to the comparatively large internal volume of the 
BRE burners which led to concern about understanding the composition of the gas initially flowing from 
the burner.  Therefore, on the second BRE test day (20 Feb. 2019, i.e., 19051), a no-flame ‘test’ was run 
before each flame test in which the burner was flushed with nitrogen.  A shortcoming of this measure was 
that the time between the nitrogen flushing and the start of the fuel flow was not precisely controlled.  
Therefore, the script was revised to allow specification of a ‘pre-flow’ with a specified wait time between 
the pre-flow and the start of the gas flow for the flame.  The revised version, which added four new 
parameters, was implemented on BRE’s third test day (25 Feb. 2019, 19056) and eliminated the need for 
the no-flame ‘test’ to flush the burner with nitrogen. 
 
With the addition of the scripted pre-low and wait time, the basic non-imaging data was captured during 
both the pre-flow and in the flame test, but not during the intervening wait period.  Therefore, one should 
pay close attention to the time stamp when reviewing BRE data prior to the start of the fuel flow because 
the listed time abruptly jumps. 
 
Note that the early portion of the script includes an example set of parameter values which are 
overwritten by values specified for each test. 
 
 
/** 
 * BRETest.js 
 * Script which executes a BRE test point. 
 *  
 * Assumptions: 
 *    - Cameras are configured except that data camera exposure and analog camera shutter 
 *      are set in this script, and the intensified camera gate and gain are set here. 
 *    - ACME Camera lens and filter is configured. Intensified Camera filter is configured. 
 *    - IPSUs being used, as specified in SystemDefineSetup command, are ready 
 *    - Mass flow controllers are enabled and zeroed 
 *    - PMTs are enabled 
 *    - ExtinctionDetectionConfigure and one of the ExinctionDetectionSet Action commands 
 *       has been issued and ExtinctinctionDetectionSetState(Disabled) 
 *    - Ignition detection parameters are set as desired using the IgnitionDetectionConfigure command. 
 */ 
 
//Hook up to the runScript signal to show where to start execution 
AcmeAvionicsController.runScript.connect(run);

4. Test Matrices 
For all ACME experiments, including BRE, the test planning was refined in multiple steps as described in 
this section.  Despite refinement, the experiments were always expected to address the science objectives 
approved in the ACME ISRD. 
 
A. Test Matrices: Years in Advance 
The test matrices found in section 5 of the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) were the basis for planning the equipment and resources, such as gas 
bottles, needed to carry out each of the NASA-selected ACME experiments.  For BRE, the test 
matrices are found in section 5.5.  The investigators were each directed to define matrices with 
required testing which included at most one burner configuration and no more than nominally 50 
flames ignited.  Regarding these constraints specified by Project Scientist Dennis Stocker, the 
intent was to conduct focused rather than comprehensive research given the considerable 
resources required for testing on the International Space Station.    Meanwhile, there were no 
limits put on desired or highly desired tests because of NASA’s plan to only carry out tests 
designated as required.  
 
NASA Glenn’s ISS Control Board later decided to limit ACME testing to nominally 4 months of ISS 
testing per experiment which with preparatory operations, minor delays, repeat testing due to 
science loss, etc. were expected to typically occur in a total of 5 months.  This decision was made 
with the expectation that the required testing, e.g., as specified in the ISRD, could at least mostly 
be accomplished in that time period assuming the availability of crew and other needed 
resources. 
 
As part of his planning, Stocker instigated an alternating sequence of experiment testing, wherein 
investigators would get a break in their testing in order to analyze early results in depth and with 
that knowledge achieve higher science outcomes in their second round of testing.  As a result, 
each experiment was expected to get 2 months of testing per round, which meant nominally 8 
test days per round of testing.  Within that time constraint and available resources, experiments 
were ultimately permitted to plan for and conduct more tests than had been specified as required 
in the ISRD, despite the initial planning which ignored desired and highly desired testing. 
 
B. Test Matrices: Months in Advance 
At least a few months in advance of testing, ACME investigators were directed to submit a refined 
test matrix for the upcoming round corresponding to available hardware, gas bottles, and the 
agreed number of test days.  The refinement could be based on what is learned from 
experimental, analytical, or computational efforts which followed the 2013 ISRD.  Generally, this 
planning was done in detail comparable to that found in the ISRD, with the important exception

controllers (and thus specification of the flow ranges) and gas bottles so that overall experiment 
operations, including crew activity, could be adequately planned.  In this regard, it had to establish 
general operational plans for the chamber atmosphere on each day of testing including filling, 
scrubbing (via circulation through the adsorber cartridge), venting (whether partial or complete), 
and measurements, if any, with the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). 
 
C. Test Matrices: Days in Advance 
Soon after BRE’s start, the investigators were required to submit their test parameters for all 
planned tests by noon Eastern at least three business days in advance of each scheduled test day.  
Those submissions included all of the test parameters within the script and additional ones 
outside of the script.  Most of the latter dealt with the camera settings which don’t change during 
a test, for example the filters used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames 
Investigation (CFI) intensified camera.  Outside of the script, the investigators were again required 
to specify the chamber atmosphere(s) and when GCIP measurements, if any, are planned.  It was 
expected that those correspond to the plan submitted months earlier, but some allowances were 
made for changes.  The script parameters, e.g., specifications of flow rates, didn’t need to 
correspond to those previously specified, but they normally had to correspond to the hardware 
and gas bottles planned months earlier and generally the chamber atmospheres as well by 
extension.

Within constraints, the ACME tests conducted could use different parameter values than those 
specified in advance.  While the planning is critically important, the plans themselves are not 
particularly useful for interpreting the data.  This is because most tests were conducted with 
parameter values that differed in at least a few ways from those planned days earlier.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME- REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014 
Page ii of vii 
 
PREFACE  
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is a next generation mini-
facility designed to support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of 
advanced gaseous combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the 
Fluids and Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the 
International Space Station in the US Lab Module. 
The ACME mission is to perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame 
extinguishment investigations using the Combustion Integrated Rack.  The ACME will allow 
investigation using pure fuels and mixtures of fuels at various chamber atmosphere pressures, 
compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity environment allows for 
measurement and observation of flame formation and extinguishment processes that cannot be 
made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of the ACME allows for flexibility in 
configuring for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  This hardware 
will provide the apparatus for dispensing, deploying and igniting fuel.  When new experiments 
are proposed the additional experiment specific hardware will be provided.  This requirements 
document reflects such a case, including only the new requirements of the ACME investigation.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION   
1.1 
Purpose 
This document will define the engineering requirements necessary to successfully complete 
science and safety requirements.  This document will be used by the ACME design engineers to 
develop the systems necessary for ACME.  Interface and carrier requirements levied on ACME 
will be documented in the ACME ICD, FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME.  ACME will use the existing 
Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) hardware and software platform design 
already developed as a baseline for meeting the requirements found in this document where 
applicable.  Due to the reuse of the MDCA platform design, ACME operational safety concerns 
will be addressed in existing MDCA documents where applicable.  Requirements in this 
document levied on the ACME carrier, the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), will be 
communicated to the ACME-CIR Interface / Sustaining Engineering Team 
1.2 
Scope 
This Engineering Requirements Document assesses the system requirements and lessons learned 
of the existing Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) and Flame Extinguishment 
Experiment requirements needed to successfully build the hardware and develop avionics 
software and how these requirements are implemented.  The Engineering Requirements 
Document (ERD) will provide information regarding the ACME experiment and ensure that 
requirements are quantifiable, verifiable and specific.  The ACME ERD consists of six sets of 
requirements:  Science Requirements, Operational Requirements, FCF/CIR Integration 
Requirements, Derived Requirements, Software Requirements and Safety Requirements.

changes to requirements.  This document along with the ZIN Requirements Management 
Procedure (P04005) is meant to facilitate this process.  Other project documentation supports this 
effort and their completion is also required.  A project shall use the following documents and 
procedures during the requirements development process: 
 ZIN Requirements Management Procedure P04005 
 SpaceDOC II Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP) or a Project SEMP as 
necessary  T04001 
 ZIN Requirements Database T04003 
 Project Concept of Operations (ConOps)  T04002 
 Project Engineering Requirements Document (ERD)  
3.1.1 Stakeholder Analysis 
An understanding of a customer’s needs and goals for a project is paramount to the requirements 
development process.  Ultimately, it is the customer who will be using the hardware built to the 
specifications laid out by the requirements a project develops.  A customer’s satisfaction with the 
performance of the developed hardware and the benefits the hardware’s operation provides to 
stakeholders is the ultimate measurement of a projects success.  Therefore, a project shall 
perform a stakeholder analysis in the early phases (Pre-phase A or Phase A) of the project life 
cycle. 
3.1.1.1 
Identify Stakeholders 
Project requirements are elicited from Project Stakeholders. A stakeholder is any entity with a 
legitimate interest in the project.  They are any person or organization that is actively involved in 
a project, or whose interests may be positively or negatively affected by execution or completion 
of the project. Some stakes an entity may have in your project are: Interest, rights, ownership, 
knowledge, impact or influence, contribution, etc. Examples of stakeholders can include: 
 ZIN Technologies (further broken into Project Manager, QA Manager, Resource 
Manager, etc.) 
 Principal Investigators and Project Scientists 
 Customer 
 NASA (further broken into GRC, JSC, ISS, etc.) 
 Product users 
 Product integrator 
Stakeholders shall be identified and documented in a Project SEMP using the Project SEMP 
template T04001.

3.1.1.2 
Identify Level 0 Stakeholder Requirements 
To initiate the requirements elicitation process a project should discuss and develop a short list of 
the main goals and products of the project. Ideally there would be less than 10 and around 4 or 5 
main Level 0 requirements. This step should immediately follow the identification of the Project 
Stakeholders. 
3.2 
Obtaining Requirements 
Once the preparations for developing requirements have been made early in the life cycle of a 
project, the engineering team can begin to develop a set of requirements that will guide the 
design and development of the systems necessary to fulfill the Project Stakeholder’s needs.  
These “build-to” or engineering requirements begin to take shape typically in Phase A of a 
project life cycle and continue to be developed throughout the design phase of the project. 
3.2.1 Identifying All Stakeholder Requirements 
After the initial, Level 0, stakeholder requirements have formed a foundation for discussion, a 
project can initiate the collection of all stakeholder requirements. Inputs for identifying more 
detailed stakeholder requirements will include: Source documents, stakeholder needs and project 
constraints such as cost, schedule and hardware/software solution restrictions. Stakeholder 
requirements can also be found in interface documents, concept documents developed by the 
project, ZIN organizational and industry standards, test results and design maturation 
discussions, stakeholder meetings, etc. At this point in the project trade studies are ongoing and 
specific hardware and software solutions are beginning to be formulated. 
Requirements shall be properly documented with traceability and captured in a Requirements 
Development Matrix Database using the ZIN template T04003. Traceability shall include (as 
appropriate): 
 The source document identity 
 The paragraph title 
 The sentence number  
The requirements will then further be documented using this template as the project’s 
Engineering Requirements Document, which is generated from the database. 
Figure 1 shows the various sources of project requirements in a block flow diagram.  This 
section should also make apparent what requirements are housed and maintained by the project 
engineering team and which are external requirements that are not included in this document but 
must also be considered during the design process.  Note the color coded differentiation between 
internal project documents and external documents.

3.3.1 Requirement Quality 
Requirement statements shall be clear and concise and decomposed to such a level that there is 
only one requirement in each requirement statement. Requirements shall use the word “shall” to 
clearly identify the demand upon the project team. Some tips to identify poor requirement 
statements are: 
 Use of superlatives such as best, most 
 Subjective language such as “user friendly”, “easy to use” 
 Vague pronouns 
 Ambiguous adverbs and adjectives such as “almost always”, “significant”, “real-time”, 
“various”, “few”, “many”, “appropriately” 
 Open-ended, non-verifiable terms such as “provide support”, “as a minimum”, “but not 
limited to” 
 Comparative phrases like “better than” or “higher quality” 
 Loopholes such as “if possible”, “as appropriate” 
 Other indefinites such as “etc.”, “to be determined (TBD)” 
At the time a requirement is identified, a verification method shall also be identified and 
documented in the Requirements Database. Verification methods include test, inspection, 
demonstration and analysis. This will encourage the writers of the requirement to evaluate 
whether they have written a verifiable requirement and provide an instant check of the 
requirement’s value. This step shall be done early in the project, typically in Phase B of the 
project life cycle. 
3.3.2 Requirement Validation 
As mentioned above, understanding stakeholders’ needs and goals is an important step in 
forming requirements.  Ensuring that your requirements are written in a way that fulfills these 
expectations is the next step.  Along with understanding the manner in which the requirement 
will be verified it is also important to analyze whether or not the requirements and the solutions 
they offer align themselves with stakeholders initial operational and programmatic goals. 
Requirement validation requires forethought as to whether or not the hardware that the 
engineering requirements will produce can perform in a manner that fulfills the stakeholders 
goals.  Simplified, validation becomes the question: Are you building the right hardware?  For 
example, have your requirements properly captured the precision and accuracy needs of a 
particular measurement device?  All project requirements shall be validated against stakeholder’s 
requirements.  This includes any transition or derived requirements.   
3.4 
Approving Requirements 
The approval of the ERD serves as an official method of communication between the 
engineering team and the NASA Project Manager.  Communication between the engineering 
team and NASA stakeholders will have invariably been occurring throughout the requirements 
formulation process.  However, the ERD approval is where these requirements are formally 
agreed upon and baselined.

3.5 
Maintaining Requirements 
Maintenance of requirements is one of the most essential steps to a project’s requirements 
development effort.  Even after the ERD has been baselined there could be many instances when 
it would need to be updated. A new stakeholder could be identified, maturation of the product 
design could bring about new derived requirements from within the engineering team, and of 
course frequent review of the requirements could result in finding flaws in the requirement 
statements that can be fixed.  
Following the logic of this process it is easy to see how many of the project’s fundamental 
documents are affected by the requirements. Therefore, when a requirement is modified or 
added, each document discussed in this process is also subject to change. 
This step shall happen regularly in the Project Life-Cycle to constantly ensure the integrity of the 
end product. Requirements documents, the Requirements Development Matrix and associated 
project documents shall be updated prior to major project gateway reviews at a minimum.

5.0 
ACME HARDWARE PRODUCT DESCRIPTION 
The ACME investigation will be using the MDCA hardware and software concepts and design 
when appropriate. The ACME hardware consists of three hardware system domains, the 
Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System, the Avionics Package (AVP) System and the ACME 
Imaging Packages (IMAG) System.   
The CIA provides the mechanism for the combustion event.  The ACME CIA Flow subsystem, 
which interfaces with the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA), provides gas 
mixing and flow control.  The AVP is the center of control and power distribution for ACME.  
And, the IMAG provides imaging of the combustion event including that provided by the carrier 
(CIR).

Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) numbering for traceability across the ACME Project

5.1 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System 
The ACME CIA System provides all the necessary hardware and interfaces to perform science 
on one platform.  The available interfaces are the CIR Water Thermal Cooling System (WTCS), 
and the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA).  Most experimental functions occur 
within the CIA structure and many associated subsystems are found on the CIA.  The CIA 
consists of the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) which is the functional hardware and 
upon which the various subsystems are structurally based.  Other subsystems found on and 
around the CIA include the Gas Flow System (FLOW), Exchangeable Gas Burner System 
(Burner), Ignition System (IGN), Engineering Analog Camera System (OpsCam), Diagnostics 
System (DIAG), Measurement System (MEAS), E-Field System (E-FIELD). 
 
 
FIGURE 3. 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) Design 
5.2 
Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) System 
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA and acts as the primary mechanical interface 
with the CIR combustion chamber.  It consists of two endplates, support structure, and extraction 
handles.

5.3 
Cooling Plate System 
ACME will use two cold plates mounted to the Experiment Mounting Structure interfacing with 
the CIR Water Thermal Control System (WTCS).  One cooling plate can be attached to each end 
plate.  The hardware to accommodate this is identical to that used on MDCA System.  The 
cooling plates are plumbed together using rigid tubing, and attached to the IRR WTCS interfaces 
with flexible hoses and quick disconnects. 
5.4 
Gas Flow System (FLOW) 
There is a reconfigurable flow system on the CIA that is auxiliary to the CIR FOMA.  Gases are 
received from FOMA via quick disconnects on the Interface Resource Ring (IRR).  The gases 
are directed through interchangeable Mass Flow Controllers, which are replaced as experiments 
require.    Gases are then directed through a series of switching and isolation valves to the burner 
or directly vented into the chamber for chamber fills. 
5.5 
Gas Burner System (Burner) 
The burner system consists of three different types of exchangeable burners made from varying 
inner and outer diameter stainless steel tubing supported by an electrically insulating ceramic 
base.  There are 4 types of burners:  Spherical (3), Gas Jet (7), Co-flow (1) and Burning Rate 
Emulator (2).  Each burner tip is smooth and without burs or sharp edges to aid in the gas 
deployment.  The burners are mounted with a coupling that allows exchangeability of the burners 
and maintains the precise alignment of the system.  Spherical and Gas-Jet burners also include 
burner temperature thermocouples. 
5.6 
Ignition System (IGN) 
The Ignition System will reuse the design of the MDCA System igniter, with a different 
deployment scheme. 
The ignition system consists of a hot wire igniter subassembly mounted to a deployment arm.  A 
Haydon-Kerk linear actuator motor and driver board controls the position of the deployment arm.  
The igniter tip is mounted to an insulating ceramic structure attached to the end of the arm.  The 
entire top assembly is removed from the arm and replaced on an experiment basis to maintain the 
precise geometry necessary for igniter functionality and to reposition the igniter tip based on the 
burner tip’s position. 
5.7 
Analog Camera System (OpsCam) 
The Analog Camera System will be provided, internal to the combustion chamber, primarily as a 
near real-time visual aid to engineering for hardware operation monitoring and troubleshooting.  
In addition, this view will provide a near real-time “look” into the chamber for science 
throughout the flame combustion event. 
5.8 
Illumination System (OpsCam) 
The Illumination System consists of an array of high intensity, white light LEDs that receive 
power from the relay board hardware and are controlled by the Data Acquisition Unit.  The

illumination system intensity will be variable to avoid saturation of diagnostics.  This 
illumination system is provided to support the Analog Camera System. 
5.9 
Diagnostic System (DIAG) 
Two of the diagnostic systems the Radiometers, the Photomultiplier Tube Modules (PMTs), and 
the Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array are located on the Insert.  This hardware supports 
Diagnostic Analysis of the Flames. 
5.10 Radiometer System 
The Radiometers will provide relative measure of flame radiation and emissions, over the 
wavelength range of 0.2 m – 11 m, throughout the combustion event.  The Radiometer System 
will be mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Data from the 
Radiometers will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power 
via the Relay Board to the Radiometer System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 
3.4.2). 
5.11 Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) System 
The Photomultiplier Tube Package will provide high-sensitivity relative measurements of flame 
radiation and chemiluminescent emissions of electromagnetic energy over a wide range of 
frequencies and intensity levels throughout the combustion event as well as flame detection and 
extinction determination.  The PMT System consists of three Hamamatsu PMT modules, 
mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Additional filters will be 
required for the 2 PMT modules used for narrowband emissions.  Data from the PMT modules 
will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power via the Relay 
Board to the PMT System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 3.4.2). 
5.12 Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array System 
A Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array arm mounted to a translating motor to move the array into 
and out of the flame.  The translating motor will be an Ultramotion brand linear stepper motor 
and encoder, similar to that used by MDCA System for its igniter.  The Array will be stowed out 
of the combustion area during E-Field testing, or when the Array is not required, but will not be 
removed from the chamber.  The array can be aligned with either the HiBMs-2 or ACME data 
color camera. 
5.13 Measurement System (MEAS) 
The ACME measurement system encompasses the measurement subsystems involved in 
detection and measurement of the experiments with the exception of diagnostic systems 
mentioned above in section 3.4.1.6 and CIR provided diagnostics.  The following sensors are a 
part of the Measurement System:  Far Field Thermocouple Array, Pressure Transducers for 
differential pressure measurement, and heat flux sensors for the BRE burners. 
5.14 E-Field System (E-FIELD) 
The E-Field system consists of two High Voltage (HV) sources (one negative and one positive 
polarity), a passive network, an insulated mesh electrode and an insulated burner electrically 
connected to the returns of the HV supplies.

The Avionics Package System (AVP) provides power conditioning and power distribution,

The Avionics Package will house the main electronics and data storage for the ACME hardware

A main computer processor is responsible for controlling CIA hardware, imaging hardware to 
execute test points as well as acquiring, storing, and downlinking experiment data.  Experiment 
control and sequencing will be uplinked from the ACME Ground System (AGS) software, at the 
TSC, to the ACME Main Processor (AMP) System software that is resident on the main 
processor in a PC/104 stack configuration.  The main processor communicates with the CIR

5.16.2 Color Camera Data Store (CDS) System 
The ACME Color Camera data is stored on a hard drive in the AVP.  The hard drive is 
removable and replaceable on orbit. 
5.16.3 Power Distribution System (PDS)  
The AVP Power & Distribution System provides power to the equipment in within the AVP and 
the CIA via four 28VDC, 8 amp circuits from the CIR’s Electrical Power Control Unit (EPCU).  
In the AVP, the power is converted to the necessary voltages, regulated and filtered.  Power 
distribution and control within the Chamber is handled by a data acquisition unit and a pair of 
custom designed relay boards.  These devices handle all of the communications with the AVP as 
well as the activation of various components of the CIA. 
5.17 ACME Imaging Package System (IMAG) 
The ACME Imaging (IMAG) System provides all optical imaging and non-optical imaging 
information for acquisition and storage concerning each of the ACME experiments. 
5.18 Data Color Camera Imaging System (DataCam) 
The ACME Data Color Camera Package (see Figure 4) will provide a view of the combustion 
event.  The current Color Camera Package concept consists of an Allied Vision (formerly 
Prosilica) GC1380CH (30fps) camera.  The camera is external to the chamber mounted at a 
UML Location on the Optics Bench.  Power to the Data Color Camera Package is supplied via 
the UML location. 
5.19 CIR Imaging Subsystems 
ACME will utilize the CIR LLL-UV, HiBMS-1, and HiBMS-2 Packages.

6.1 
Internal Interfaces 
The internal interfaces between ACME and CIR are listed below and the requirements for these 
interfaces will be defined in ACME Interface Control Document for the Fluids and Combustion 
Facility, FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME. 
 Structural/Mechanical and Stowage 
 Electrical Power 
 Command and Data Handling 
 Payload and Diagnostics 
 Thermal Control 
 Exhaust Vent 
 FOMA Gas Delivery 
 Environmental 
 
6.2 
External Interfaces 
6.2.1 Launch Configuration Interfaces 
ACME provided hardware is non-operational in whatever launch vehicle is chosen to get it on-
orbit.  ACME hardware will be stowed in standard containers provided by ACME and will only 
have physical and structural interfaces with the containers. 
6.2.2 On-orbit External Interfaces 
ACME has no direct external interfaces on-orbit.  All interfaces with the FCF, US LAB, ISS and 
the ground are provided indirectly through CIR.

7.0 
ACME ENGINEERING REQUIREMENTS 
Engineering requirements are ACME’s build-to requirement response to science requirements 
levied by NASA.  This section is drawn from the information filled into the ZIN Requirements 
Development Matrix (T04003) using the Requirements Management Procedure (P04005.)  
ACME’s requirements are organized according to the project’s PBS.  This helps to keep the 
reader and reviewer thinking in terms of the whole system. 
The SSC_ID column is for useful organization and sorting of the system requirements in the 
Requirements Tracking Matrix (RTM) into categories by system, subsystem, or other traits for 
measurements and metrics that may be of interest.  The SSC (System/Subsystem Classification) 
is a three digit number which relates to the Product Breakdown Structure (PBS) which in turn is 
a subset of the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).  The first digit of the SSC relates the 
requirement to the system assignment.  The second digit of the SSC relates the requirement to 
the subsystem assignment.  The third digit of the SSC is used to relate the requirement to the 
product classification or type:  flight hardware product (0), flight software product (1), or ground 
software product (2), in which they affect.  The SSC is followed by an underscore as a delineator 
and then a unique four digit identification number.  The underscore, versus the dash, is used to 
keep the SSC and ID married as one object in the database.  Requirements with like qualities of 
interest may be grouped together by ID number for ease of sorting.

System

MEAS 
570_0010 
2.1.1 
Chamber Pressure – Accuracy 
ACME shall ensure the absolute chamber 
pressure is measured with an accuracy of ± 1% of 
reading. 
MEAS 
570_0020 
2.1.2 
Chamber Pressure – Range 
ACME shall ensure the pressure measurement 
range is 0.1 to 4 bar absolute. 
MEAS 
570_0030 
2.1.3 
Chamber Pressure – Sampling Frequency 
ACME shall ensure the chamber pressure is 
measured at 1 sample per second or faster with a 
response time of 0.5 second or less. 
  
  
2.3 
Gas Flow Rate 
FLOW 
520_0760 
2.3.1 
Gas Flow Rate – Accuracy 
ACME shall provide each gas flow rate 
measurement with an accuracy of ± 5% of the 
reading or better.   
  
  
2.4 
Burner Pressure Differential 
MEAS 
570_0060 
2.4.1 
Burner Pressure Differential Accuracy 
ACME shall provide the pressure differential 
between the BRE and spherical burner supply 
tube inlet and the chamber with accuracy of ± 2 % 
of the reading. 
MEAS 
570_0070 
2.4.1 
Burner Pressure Differential – Orientation 
ACME shall provide the pressure differential for 
the BRE and spherical burner measured 
downstream of any valves. 
MEAS 
570_0080 
2.4.2 
Burner Pressure Differential – Range 
ACME shall provide a pressure differential 
measurement range for the spherical burner that 
is from 0.1 to 1.5 times the pressure drop across 
the spherical burner at a flow rate of 5 slpm, on a 
N2 basis, in cold flow testing (i.e., with no flame). 
  
  
  2.5 
Electric Potential 
E-FIELD 
580_0380 
 2.5.1,  2.5.4 
Electric Potential – Accuracy 
ACME shall provide electric potential 
measurement between the mesh electrode and 
the high voltage (HV) ground terminal to an 
accuracy of within the larger of 20 VDC or ± 1% of 
the reading. 
E-FIELD 
580_0390 
2.5.2 
Electric Potential – Range 
ACME shall provide an electric potential 
measurement range of ± 10 kilovolts. 
  
  
3.1 
ACME Analog Camera 
OpsCam 
550_0010 
3.1.1 
Analog Camera – Wavelength Response 
ACME shall provide a wavelength response of 
400 to 700 nanometers. 
OpsCam 
550_0020 
3.1.2 
Analog Camera – Focusing 
ACME shall focus the analog camera on the CIR 
chamber axis where the Field of View (FOV) 
plane includes the CIR chamber axis.

ACME shall provide a data camera with a 
wavelength response of 400 to 700 nanometers.

ACME shall provide a data camera with a 
sensitivity, especially to dim blue light at 431 
nanometers, matching or exceeding cameras 
equipped with a Sony ICX285 2/3” Progressive 
scan CCD.

each imaging system centered on and 
perpendicular to a CIR window axis.

adjust the exposure time settings between tests 
prior to ignition via uplink control.

ACME shall provide the data color imaging

Burner Temperature Measurement 
MEAS 
570_0120 
3.4.1.1 
Spherical Temperature – Location 
ACME shall provide spherical burner surface 
temperature measurement at a location between 
20 degrees and 90 degrees of the burner tube. 
MEAS 
570_0130 
3.4.1.1 
Spherical Temperature – Probe Non-Visible  
The ACME burner design shall ensure the probe 
is not visible during mission science in at least 
one view of the data color imaging. 
MEAS 
570_0150 
3.4.1.2 
Gas-Jet Surface Temperature – Location 
ACME shall provide a gas-jet burner surface 
temperature measurements on the exterior 
surface of the burner as close as possible to its 
outlet tip where the measurement device does not 
disturb the axisymmetric of the flow and flame. 
MEAS 
570_0170

ACME shall provide temperature measurements 
of all burner types such that, if a probe used, it is 
smaller than 250 microns in thickness.

570_0180

Burner Temperature – Accuracy 
ACME shall provide temperature measurements, 
of all burner types, with a precision of ± 2 degrees 
Celsius and an accuracy of ± 5 degrees Celsius.

3.4.1.6 
Gas-Jet Temperature – Range 
ACME shall provide a temperature measurement 
with a range of 0 to 300 degrees Celsius for the 
gas-jet burner. 
MEAS 
570_0200 
3.4.1.7 
Spherical Temperature – Range 
ACME shall provide a spherical burner surface 
temperature measurement range of 0 to 700 
degrees Celsius.

ACME shall provide an additional BRE burner

ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
3 
 
1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of 
used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that is sufficient for 
informed interpretation of the experimental results.  In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to 
review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects 
may be briefly addressed. 
 
The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station (ISS) in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and 
ethylene.  In addition to the fuel state, the current ACME experiments use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., 
diffusion) flames for their studies.  To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric 
or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. 
 
Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in 
spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space 
(CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). 
 
The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was 
used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.  The facility was reconfigured and set 
up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 25 astronauts from 
Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s 
research.  As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that 
began in Nov. 2017.    It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the 
CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. 
 
The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various 
documents, such as those listed below.  These are listed in reverse chronological order, where the oldest 
predate the facility’s completion and have become outdated in some regards.  References 1, 2 and 4 also 
discuss ACME, but were all prepared prior to the completion of ACME’s spaceflight hardware. 
1. Suleyman A. Gokoglu, Daniel L. Dietrich, Dennis P. Stocker, Paul V. Ferkul, Sandy L. Olson, Michael 
C. Hicks, Amelia Rai (editor), Neesha Hosein (editor), and Cory Duke (designer), “Combustion 
Science: A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station,” NASA Publication NP-2015-10-034-
JSC (2015). 
2. J.M. Hickman, D.L. Dietrich, M.C. Hicks, V. Nayagam, V., and D. Stocker, “FLEX: A Decisive Step 
Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program,” 1st Annual International Space Station 
Research and Development Conference, Denver, Colorado 26-28 June (2012). 
3. “Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity: NASA Glenn Provides the Keys with the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility,” NASA fact sheet FS-2011-06-035-GRC, PS-00538-0611 (2011). 
4. T.F. O'Malley, W.A. Sheredy, and D.P. Stocker, “Combustion Research on the International Space 
Station,” 59th International Astronautical Congress, Vol. 2, pp. 756-766 (2008). 
5. Terence F. O’Malley, Karen J. Weiland, Craig A. Myhre, Frank G. Gati, Myron E. Hill, and John H. 
Snead, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility and First Payloads: The Multi-User Droplet 
Combustion Apparatus and the Light Microscopy Module: Enabling Research on the ISS,” 57th 
International Astronautical Congress,  IAC-06-A2.1.07, 2-6 Oct. 2006, Valencia, Spain (2006). 
6. T. O’Malley and C. Myrhe, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility Combustion Integrated Rack and 
the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus: Microgravity Combustion Science Using Modular

TM--2002-210981, AIAA-2001-4927, September 2002. 
8. Robert L. Zurawski and Nora G. Bozzolo, “ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility: Combustion 
Integrated Rack: Payload Accommodations - Principal Investigator’s Guide,” NASA report, 
September 2000. 
 
The CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia.  
In 1997, the combustion research facility was within Spacelab on the STS-83 and STS-94 (Microgravity 
Science Laboratory) missions.  It was subsequently reconfigured and flew in 2003 within SPACEHAB, again in 
the shuttle’s payload bay, in the STS-107 mission.  The Combustion Module investigations included Laminar 
Soot Processes (LSP), Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL), and the Water-Mist Fire 
Suppression Experiment (Mist).  Although all three experiments burned gaseous fuel, each had its own 
chamber insert, whereas ACME features a single modular chamber insert to accomplish multiple 
investigations.  A significant difference between the CIR and its shuttle precursor is that the ISS tests are 
remotely commanded from the ground without crew involvement, which wasn’t the case with the 
Combustion Module research.  But in all cases the crew are required to configure the necessary hardware. 
 
While extensive, this report is far from exhaustive but there are other reports which provide additional 
detail useful for interpreting ACME’s experimental results.  Some key examples include the following:

Abbreviations are addressed at the end of this report, but ERD stands for Engineering Requirements 
Document and many of the engineering requirements were directly derived from ACME’s science 
requirements.  Meanwhile, key hardware dimensions, for example of the burners, and other details are 
confirmed in the Inspection Verification Report.  Also note that the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Cool 
Flames radiometer reports are specific to certain ACME experiments, whereas the other reports are 
general to all of ACME.

with questions about the ACME project.

2. Engineering Overview 
 
A. General Description 
This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ 
section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017.  As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards.   Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description.  As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

content:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
6 
 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.  
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests.  The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.  However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing.  The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.  
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy.  The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow,

content:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
7 
 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.  Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.  Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit.  Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm.  ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.  
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space.  The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center.  Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.   
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.  The clear “filter” is

content:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
8 
 
of fused silica.  Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination.  Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high 
definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.   
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).   
 
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.   
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band.  This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers.  The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.  During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements.  For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:   
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.  
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.  
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position.  Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and 
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate.

content:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
9 
 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, 
but not all, of ACME’s operations.  In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used 
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera 
is very insensitive to blue.  Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.  Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently 
broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for 
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described 
in the following papers: 
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties 
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty-Eighth 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972.  
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z.-G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of 
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524.  
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522. 
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images. 
 
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations.  And because operations are constrained by the data limits, 
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing.  And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment.   This was a design 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments. 
 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging.  Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests.   This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was 
generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s-Flame testing with 
particularly dim flames.  Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed 
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame.  More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-
4600. 
 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs).  There is a crew-exchangeable

ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
10 
 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of 
experiments.  The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other 
instrumentation.  One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrow-
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4.  The narrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful.  The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 
from the burner.  It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource 
available to other ACME experiments.  Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the 
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.   
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner.

content:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
28 March 2021 
11 
 
A third radiometer array was developed for the CFI-G experiment, where it is important to 
understand that only a single radiometer array can be used at a time. 
 
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they 
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure.   
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the 
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor.  Figures representing the measured FOVs 
of the as-built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of this document.   
 
Unfortunately, the radiometers in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE 
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round.  However, those radiometers similarly 
saturated in many of round 2 tests.  In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers 
have a fixed gain.  Meanwhile, each sensor in the radiometer array developed for the CFI-G 
investigation has two fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain.   
 
For more information about the standard radiometer array used for most ACME testing, see the 
Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).  Meanwhile, you can learn about the other 
radiometer arrays from the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-012) and the 
Cool Flames Radiometer Characterization Report (CIR-RPT-4600).    
 
An additional wide-view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned 
downstream of the burner and flame at 30o from the chamber axis.  This detector is primarily 
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the 
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays.   Like the radiometers on the two linear 
arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 micron and its field of view will be 
established by an appropriately selected aperture. 
 
The FOV of the off-set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F.  Learn more about this sensor from 
the Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).   
 
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three 
PMTs.  Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, 
and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is 
aligned with most of the other instrumentation.  The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, 
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have 
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM).  The pair of detectors will enable 
measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively.  The third PMT will be equipped with a 
neutral density filter to prevent saturation.  Like many other components, the PMT array can be 
removed from the chamber insert by the crew. 
 
Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain.  However, the PMT signals 
sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high.  See the PMT Characterization Report 
(ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs).   
 
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of 
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments.  They are of limited utility for other 
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip.  Therefore, they will
