3.0 
REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT 
3.1 
Preparation for Requirements 
The preparation for developing proper project requirements is an important first step.  Preparing 
in this sense means establishing procedures for identifying, approving, allocating and managing 
changes to requirements.  This document along with the ZIN Requirements Management 
Procedure (P04005) is meant to facilitate this process.  Other project documentation supports this 
effort and their completion is also required.  A project shall use the following documents and 
procedures during the requirements development process: 
 ZIN Requirements Management Procedure P04005 
 SpaceDOC II Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP) or a Project SEMP as 
necessary  T04001 
 ZIN Requirements Database T04003 
 Project Concept of Operations (ConOps)  T04002 
 Project Engineering Requirements Document (ERD)  
3.1.1 Stakeholder Analysis 
An understanding of a customer’s needs and goals for a project is paramount to the requirements 
development process.  Ultimately, it is the customer who will be using the hardware built to the 
specifications laid out by the requirements a project develops.  A customer’s satisfaction with the 
performance of the developed hardware and the benefits the hardware’s operation provides to 
stakeholders is the ultimate measurement of a projects success.  Therefore, a project shall 
perform a stakeholder analysis in the early phases (Pre-phase A or Phase A) of the project life 
cycle. 
3.1.1.1 
Identify Stakeholders 
Project requirements are elicited from Project Stakeholders. A stakeholder is any entity with a 
legitimate interest in the project.  They are any person or organization that is actively involved in 
a project, or whose interests may be positively or negatively affected by execution or completion 
of the project. Some stakes an entity may have in your project are: Interest, rights, ownership, 
knowledge, impact or influence, contribution, etc. Examples of stakeholders can include: 
 ZIN Technologies (further broken into Project Manager, QA Manager, Resource 
Manager, etc.) 
 Principal Investigators and Project Scientists 
 Customer 
 NASA (further broken into GRC, JSC, ISS, etc.) 
 Product users 
 Product integrator 
Stakeholders shall be identified and documented in a Project SEMP using the Project SEMP 
template T04001.

3.1.1.2 
Identify Level 0 Stakeholder Requirements 
To initiate the requirements elicitation process a project should discuss and develop a short list of 
the main goals and products of the project. Ideally there would be less than 10 and around 4 or 5 
main Level 0 requirements. This step should immediately follow the identification of the Project 
Stakeholders. 
3.2 
Obtaining Requirements 
Once the preparations for developing requirements have been made early in the life cycle of a 
project, the engineering team can begin to develop a set of requirements that will guide the 
design and development of the systems necessary to fulfill the Project Stakeholder’s needs.  
These “build-to” or engineering requirements begin to take shape typically in Phase A of a 
project life cycle and continue to be developed throughout the design phase of the project. 
3.2.1 Identifying All Stakeholder Requirements 
After the initial, Level 0, stakeholder requirements have formed a foundation for discussion, a 
project can initiate the collection of all stakeholder requirements. Inputs for identifying more 
detailed stakeholder requirements will include: Source documents, stakeholder needs and project 
constraints such as cost, schedule and hardware/software solution restrictions. Stakeholder 
requirements can also be found in interface documents, concept documents developed by the 
project, ZIN organizational and industry standards, test results and design maturation 
discussions, stakeholder meetings, etc. At this point in the project trade studies are ongoing and 
specific hardware and software solutions are beginning to be formulated. 
Requirements shall be properly documented with traceability and captured in a Requirements 
Development Matrix Database using the ZIN template T04003. Traceability shall include (as 
appropriate): 
 The source document identity 
 The paragraph title 
 The sentence number  
The requirements will then further be documented using this template as the project’s 
Engineering Requirements Document, which is generated from the database. 
Figure 1 shows the various sources of project requirements in a block flow diagram.  This 
section should also make apparent what requirements are housed and maintained by the project 
engineering team and which are external requirements that are not included in this document but 
must also be considered during the design process.  Note the color coded differentiation between 
internal project documents and external documents.

content:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 7 of 117 
 
 
3.3.1 Requirement Quality 
Requirement statements shall be clear and concise and decomposed to such a level that there is 
only one requirement in each requirement statement. Requirements shall use the word “shall” to 
clearly identify the demand upon the project team. Some tips to identify poor requirement 
statements are: 
 Use of superlatives such as best, most 
 Subjective language such as “user friendly”, “easy to use” 
 Vague pronouns 
 Ambiguous adverbs and adjectives such as “almost always”, “significant”, “real-time”, 
“various”, “few”, “many”, “appropriately” 
 Open-ended, non-verifiable terms such as “provide support”, “as a minimum”, “but not 
limited to” 
 Comparative phrases like “better than” or “higher quality” 
 Loopholes such as “if possible”, “as appropriate” 
 Other indefinites such as “etc.”, “to be determined (TBD)” 
At the time a requirement is identified, a verification method shall also be identified and 
documented in the Requirements Database. Verification methods include test, inspection, 
demonstration and analysis. This will encourage the writers of the requirement to evaluate 
whether they have written a verifiable requirement and provide an instant check of the 
requirement’s value. This step shall be done early in the project, typically in Phase B of the 
project life cycle. 
3.3.2 Requirement Validation 
As mentioned above, understanding stakeholders’ needs and goals is an important step in 
forming requirements.  Ensuring that your requirements are written in a way that fulfills these 
expectations is the next step.  Along with understanding the manner in which the requirement 
will be verified it is also important to analyze whether or not the requirements and the solutions 
they offer align themselves with stakeholders initial operational and programmatic goals. 
Requirement validation requires forethought as to whether or not the hardware that the 
engineering requirements will produce can perform in a manner that fulfills the stakeholders 
goals.  Simplified, validation becomes the question: Are you building the right hardware?  For 
example, have your requirements properly captured the precision and accuracy needs of a 
particular measurement device?  All project requirements shall be validated against stakeholder’s 
requirements.  This includes any transition or derived requirements.   
3.4 
Approving Requirements 
The approval of the ERD serves as an official method of communication between the 
engineering team and the NASA Project Manager.  Communication between the engineering 
team and NASA stakeholders will have invariably been occurring throughout the requirements 
formulation process.  However, the ERD approval is where these requirements are formally 
agreed upon and baselined.

3.5 
Maintaining Requirements 
Maintenance of requirements is one of the most essential steps to a project’s requirements 
development effort.  Even after the ERD has been baselined there could be many instances when 
it would need to be updated. A new stakeholder could be identified, maturation of the product 
design could bring about new derived requirements from within the engineering team, and of 
course frequent review of the requirements could result in finding flaws in the requirement 
statements that can be fixed.  
Following the logic of this process it is easy to see how many of the project’s fundamental 
documents are affected by the requirements. Therefore, when a requirement is modified or 
added, each document discussed in this process is also subject to change. 
This step shall happen regularly in the Project Life-Cycle to constantly ensure the integrity of the 
end product. Requirements documents, the Requirements Development Matrix and associated 
project documents shall be updated prior to major project gateway reviews at a minimum.

5.0 
ACME HARDWARE PRODUCT DESCRIPTION 
The ACME investigation will be using the MDCA hardware and software concepts and design 
when appropriate. The ACME hardware consists of three hardware system domains, the 
Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System, the Avionics Package (AVP) System and the ACME 
Imaging Packages (IMAG) System.   
The CIA provides the mechanism for the combustion event.  The ACME CIA Flow subsystem, 
which interfaces with the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA), provides gas 
mixing and flow control.  The AVP is the center of control and power distribution for ACME.  
And, the IMAG provides imaging of the combustion event including that provided by the carrier 
(CIR).

Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) numbering for traceability across the ACME Project 
Lifecycle.  The number convention utilizes a SSC (System/Subsystem Classification) followed 
by an underscore and the uniquely allocated four digit requirement identification number.

5.1 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System 
The ACME CIA System provides all the necessary hardware and interfaces to perform science 
on one platform.  The available interfaces are the CIR Water Thermal Cooling System (WTCS), 
and the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA).  Most experimental functions occur 
within the CIA structure and many associated subsystems are found on the CIA.  The CIA 
consists of the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) which is the functional hardware and 
upon which the various subsystems are structurally based.  Other subsystems found on and 
around the CIA include the Gas Flow System (FLOW), Exchangeable Gas Burner System 
(Burner), Ignition System (IGN), Engineering Analog Camera System (OpsCam), Diagnostics 
System (DIAG), Measurement System (MEAS), E-Field System (E-FIELD). 
 
 
FIGURE 3. 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) Design 
5.2 
Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) System 
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA and acts as the primary mechanical interface 
with the CIR combustion chamber.  It consists of two endplates, support structure, and extraction 
handles.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 12 of 117 
 
 
 
5.3 
Cooling Plate System 
ACME will use two cold plates mounted to the Experiment Mounting Structure interfacing with 
the CIR Water Thermal Control System (WTCS).  One cooling plate can be attached to each end 
plate.  The hardware to accommodate this is identical to that used on MDCA System.  The 
cooling plates are plumbed together using rigid tubing, and attached to the IRR WTCS interfaces 
with flexible hoses and quick disconnects. 
5.4 
Gas Flow System (FLOW) 
There is a reconfigurable flow system on the CIA that is auxiliary to the CIR FOMA.  Gases are 
received from FOMA via quick disconnects on the Interface Resource Ring (IRR).  The gases 
are directed through interchangeable Mass Flow Controllers, which are replaced as experiments 
require.    Gases are then directed through a series of switching and isolation valves to the burner 
or directly vented into the chamber for chamber fills. 
5.5 
Gas Burner System (Burner) 
The burner system consists of three different types of exchangeable burners made from varying 
inner and outer diameter stainless steel tubing supported by an electrically insulating ceramic 
base.  There are 4 types of burners:  Spherical (3), Gas Jet (7), Co-flow (1) and Burning Rate 
Emulator (2).  Each burner tip is smooth and without burs or sharp edges to aid in the gas 
deployment.  The burners are mounted with a coupling that allows exchangeability of the burners 
and maintains the precise alignment of the system.  Spherical and Gas-Jet burners also include 
burner temperature thermocouples. 
5.6 
Ignition System (IGN) 
The Ignition System will reuse the design of the MDCA System igniter, with a different 
deployment scheme. 
The ignition system consists of a hot wire igniter subassembly mounted to a deployment arm.  A 
Haydon-Kerk linear actuator motor and driver board controls the position of the deployment arm.  
The igniter tip is mounted to an insulating ceramic structure attached to the end of the arm.  The 
entire top assembly is removed from the arm and replaced on an experiment basis to maintain the 
precise geometry necessary for igniter functionality and to reposition the igniter tip based on the 
burner tip’s position. 
5.7 
Analog Camera System (OpsCam) 
The Analog Camera System will be provided, internal to the combustion chamber, primarily as a 
near real-time visual aid to engineering for hardware operation monitoring and troubleshooting.  
In addition, this view will provide a near real-time “look” into the chamber for science 
throughout the flame combustion event. 
5.8 
Illumination System (OpsCam) 
The Illumination System consists of an array of high intensity, white light LEDs that receive 
power from the relay board hardware and are controlled by the Data Acquisition Unit.  The

ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 13 of 117 
 
 
illumination system intensity will be variable to avoid saturation of diagnostics.  This 
illumination system is provided to support the Analog Camera System. 
5.9 
Diagnostic System (DIAG) 
Two of the diagnostic systems the Radiometers, the Photomultiplier Tube Modules (PMTs), and 
the Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array are located on the Insert.  This hardware supports 
Diagnostic Analysis of the Flames. 
5.10 Radiometer System 
The Radiometers will provide relative measure of flame radiation and emissions, over the 
wavelength range of 0.2 m – 11 m, throughout the combustion event.  The Radiometer System 
will be mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Data from the 
Radiometers will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power 
via the Relay Board to the Radiometer System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 
3.4.2). 
5.11 Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) System 
The Photomultiplier Tube Package will provide high-sensitivity relative measurements of flame 
radiation and chemiluminescent emissions of electromagnetic energy over a wide range of 
frequencies and intensity levels throughout the combustion event as well as flame detection and 
extinction determination.  The PMT System consists of three Hamamatsu PMT modules, 
mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Additional filters will be 
required for the 2 PMT modules used for narrowband emissions.  Data from the PMT modules 
will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power via the Relay 
Board to the PMT System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 3.4.2). 
5.12 Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array System 
A Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array arm mounted to a translating motor to move the array into 
and out of the flame.  The translating motor will be an Ultramotion brand linear stepper motor 
and encoder, similar to that used by MDCA System for its igniter.  The Array will be stowed out 
of the combustion area during E-Field testing, or when the Array is not required, but will not be 
removed from the chamber.  The array can be aligned with either the HiBMs-2 or ACME data 
color camera. 
5.13 Measurement System (MEAS) 
The ACME measurement system encompasses the measurement subsystems involved in 
detection and measurement of the experiments with the exception of diagnostic systems 
mentioned above in section 3.4.1.6 and CIR provided diagnostics.  The following sensors are a 
part of the Measurement System:  Far Field Thermocouple Array, Pressure Transducers for 
differential pressure measurement, and heat flux sensors for the BRE burners. 
5.14 E-Field System (E-FIELD) 
The E-Field system consists of two High Voltage (HV) sources (one negative and one positive 
polarity), a passive network, an insulated mesh electrode and an insulated burner electrically 
connected to the returns of the HV supplies.

5.15 ACME Avionics Package System (AVP) 
The Avionics Package System (AVP) provides power conditioning and power distribution, 
system control, data acquisition and CIR and ground interface for the ACME insert.  The AVP 
will house the main electronics for the ACME hardware and will be mounted on the CIR Optics 
Bench.

5.16 Avionics Package (AVP) 
The Avionics Package will house the main electronics and data storage for the ACME hardware 
and will be mounted at the CIR PIL (PI location), using the standard Optics Bench interfaces.   
5.16.1 Main Computer System (MCS) – Control and Data Management 
A main computer processor is responsible for controlling CIA hardware, imaging hardware to 
execute test points as well as acquiring, storing, and downlinking experiment data.  Experiment 
control and sequencing will be uplinked from the ACME Ground System (AGS) software, at the 
TSC, to the ACME Main Processor (AMP) System software that is resident on the main 
processor in a PC/104 stack configuration.  The main processor communicates with the CIR

commands, downlinked data and images, through the International Space Station (ISS)

5.16.2 Color Camera Data Store (CDS) System 
The ACME Color Camera data is stored on a hard drive in the AVP.  The hard drive is 
removable and replaceable on orbit. 
5.16.3 Power Distribution System (PDS)  
The AVP Power & Distribution System provides power to the equipment in within the AVP and 
the CIA via four 28VDC, 8 amp circuits from the CIR’s Electrical Power Control Unit (EPCU).  
In the AVP, the power is converted to the necessary voltages, regulated and filtered.  Power 
distribution and control within the Chamber is handled by a data acquisition unit and a pair of 
custom designed relay boards.  These devices handle all of the communications with the AVP as 
well as the activation of various components of the CIA. 
5.17 ACME Imaging Package System (IMAG) 
The ACME Imaging (IMAG) System provides all optical imaging and non-optical imaging 
information for acquisition and storage concerning each of the ACME experiments. 
5.18 Data Color Camera Imaging System (DataCam) 
The ACME Data Color Camera Package (see Figure 4) will provide a view of the combustion 
event.  The current Color Camera Package concept consists of an Allied Vision (formerly 
Prosilica) GC1380CH (30fps) camera.  The camera is external to the chamber mounted at a 
UML Location on the Optics Bench.  Power to the Data Color Camera Package is supplied via 
the UML location. 
5.19 CIR Imaging Subsystems 
ACME will utilize the CIR LLL-UV, HiBMS-1, and HiBMS-2 Packages.

6.1 
Internal Interfaces 
The internal interfaces between ACME and CIR are listed below and the requirements for these 
interfaces will be defined in ACME Interface Control Document for the Fluids and Combustion 
Facility, FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME. 
 Structural/Mechanical and Stowage 
 Electrical Power 
 Command and Data Handling 
 Payload and Diagnostics 
 Thermal Control 
 Exhaust Vent 
 FOMA Gas Delivery 
 Environmental 
 
6.2 
External Interfaces 
6.2.1 Launch Configuration Interfaces 
ACME provided hardware is non-operational in whatever launch vehicle is chosen to get it on-
orbit.  ACME hardware will be stowed in standard containers provided by ACME and will only 
have physical and structural interfaces with the containers. 
6.2.2 On-orbit External Interfaces 
ACME has no direct external interfaces on-orbit.  All interfaces with the FCF, US LAB, ISS and 
the ground are provided indirectly through CIR.

7.0 
ACME ENGINEERING REQUIREMENTS 
Engineering requirements are ACME’s build-to requirement response to science requirements 
levied by NASA.  This section is drawn from the information filled into the ZIN Requirements 
Development Matrix (T04003) using the Requirements Management Procedure (P04005.)  
ACME’s requirements are organized according to the project’s PBS.  This helps to keep the 
reader and reviewer thinking in terms of the whole system. 
The SSC_ID column is for useful organization and sorting of the system requirements in the 
Requirements Tracking Matrix (RTM) into categories by system, subsystem, or other traits for 
measurements and metrics that may be of interest.  The SSC (System/Subsystem Classification) 
is a three digit number which relates to the Product Breakdown Structure (PBS) which in turn is 
a subset of the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).  The first digit of the SSC relates the 
requirement to the system assignment.  The second digit of the SSC relates the requirement to 
the subsystem assignment.  The third digit of the SSC is used to relate the requirement to the 
product classification or type:  flight hardware product (0), flight software product (1), or ground 
software product (2), in which they affect.  The SSC is followed by an underscore as a delineator 
and then a unique four digit identification number.  The underscore, versus the dash, is used to 
keep the SSC and ID married as one object in the database.  Requirements with like qualities of 
interest may be grouped together by ID number for ease of sorting.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 63 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
DataCam 
310_0080 
3.2.7 
3.2.10 
Data Camera – FOV Spherical Flames 
ACME shall provide a data camera with a FOV of 
at least 90mm in diameter for the spherical and 
BRE flames. 
DataCam 
310_0090 
3.2.8 
3.2.10 
Data Camera – FOV Gas-Jet & Coflow Flames 
ACME shall provide a data camera with a FOV of 
35mm along the chamber axis and at least 20mm 
orthogonal to the CIR chamber axis for the gas-jet 
and coflow flames. 
DataCam 
310_100 
3.2.9 
3.2.10 
Data Camera FOV – Rectangular FOV 
ACME shall provide a data camera with the long 
dimension of the FOV aligned with the chamber 
axis, if the FOV is rectangular. 
DataCam 
310_0120 
3.2.11 
Data Camera – Filter Option 
ACME shall provide the capability to utilize an 
optical filter with data color imaging system. 
DataCam 
310_0140 
3.2.11 
Data Camera – BG7 Filter  
ACME shall provide a BG7 Schott glass filter with 
a transmittance from 400-700 nm matching within 
± 5% of 1mm thickness for the data color camera. 
DataCam 
310_0141 
3.2.11 
Data Camera - Band Pass Filter 1 
ACME shall provide a 430 nm band pass filter 
with transmission curves that match within ± 5% 
of transmittance data for a 10nm full width at half 
maximum transmission. 
DataCam 
310_0142 
3.2.11 
Data Camera - Band Pass Filter 2 
ACME shall provide a 450 nm band pass filter 
with transmission curves that match within ± 5% 
of Thorlab transmittance data for a 10nm  full 
width at half maximum transmission (FWHM.) 
DataCam 
310_0143 
3.2.11 
Data Camera - Filter Position 
ACME shall provide a filter barrel with filter 
positions 0-3 as empty, BG7, 430nm, and 450nm. 
DataCam 
310_0150 
3.2.12 
Data Camera – Frame Rate 
ACME data camera shall provide 20 frames/s or 
faster when imaging the full sensor at a bit depth 
of at least 3x12. 
DataCam 
310_0160 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings Bit Depth 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the bit depth settings of the data camera 
between tests prior to ignition. 
DataCam 
310_0190 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings, Gain 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the gain settings between tests prior to 
ignition via uplink control. 
DataCam 
310_0220 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings Iris 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the iris settings between tests prior to 
ignition via uplink control. 
DataCam 
310_0250 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings, Exposure 
Time 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the exposure time settings between tests 
prior to ignition via uplink control.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 64 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
DataCam 
310_0280 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings, Framing 
Rate 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the framing rate settings between tests 
prior to ignition via uplink control. 
DataCam 
310_0310 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings, Binning 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the binning settings between tests prior to 
ignition via uplink control. 
DataCam 
310_0340 
3.2.13 
Data Camera – Adjustable Settings, Region Of 
Interest (ROI) 
ACME data camera shall provide the ability to 
adjust the Region Of Interest (ROI) settings 
between tests prior to ignition via uplink control. 
DataCam 
310_0470 
3.2.15 
Data Color Imaging – ORU 
ACME shall provide the data color imaging 
system(s) as an ORU and removable from the 
Optics Bench UML during spaceflight. 
  
  
3.4 
Burner Temperature Measurement 
MEAS 
570_0120 
3.4.1.1 
Spherical Temperature – Location 
ACME shall provide spherical burner surface 
temperature measurement at a location between 
20 degrees and 90 degrees of the burner tube. 
MEAS 
570_0130 
3.4.1.1 
Spherical Temperature – Probe Non-Visible  
The ACME burner design shall ensure the probe 
is not visible during mission science in at least 
one view of the data color imaging. 
MEAS 
570_0150 
3.4.1.2 
Gas-Jet Surface Temperature – Location 
ACME shall provide a gas-jet burner surface 
temperature measurements on the exterior 
surface of the burner as close as possible to its 
outlet tip where the measurement device does not 
disturb the axisymmetric of the flow and flame. 
MEAS 
570_0170 
3.4.1.4 
Burner Temperature – Probe Size 
ACME shall provide temperature measurements 
of all burner types such that, if a probe used, it is 
smaller than 250 microns in thickness. 
MEAS 
570_0180 
3.4.1.5 
Burner Temperature – Accuracy 
ACME shall provide temperature measurements, 
of all burner types, with a precision of ± 2 degrees 
Celsius and an accuracy of ± 5 degrees Celsius. 
MEAS 
570_0190 
3.4.1.6 
Gas-Jet Temperature – Range 
ACME shall provide a temperature measurement 
with a range of 0 to 300 degrees Celsius for the 
gas-jet burner. 
MEAS 
570_0200 
3.4.1.7 
Spherical Temperature – Range 
ACME shall provide a spherical burner surface 
temperature measurement range of 0 to 700 
degrees Celsius.

content:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 65 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
MEAS 
570_0201 
3.4.1.9 
BRE Temperature Measurements - Heat Flux 
Location 
ACME shall provide a BRE burner outlet surface 
temperature measurements at both heat flux 
measurement locations. 
MEAS 
570_0202 
3.4.1.9 
BRE Temperature Measurements - Additional 
Locations - 25mm Burner 
ACME shall provide an additional BRE burner 
outlet surface temperature measurements not in 
an outlet hole and at 180 degrees from the offset 
heat flux sensor at radial positions of 5 ± 0.5mm 
and 10 ± 0.5mm for the 25mm burner. 
MEAS 
570_0203 
3.4.1.9 
BRE Temperature Measurements - Additional 
Locations - 50mm Burner 
ACME shall provide an additional BRE burner 
outlet surface temperature measurements not in 
an outlet hole and at 180 degrees from the offset 
heat flux sensor at radial positions of 5 ± 0.5mm 
and 15 ± 0.5mm for the 50mm burner. 
MEAS 
570_0204 
3.4.1.10 
BRE Temperature Measurements - Probe 
ACME shall provide temperature measurement 
probes that are .3mm in diameter or less that are 
thermally bonded to the burner outlet plate. 
MEAS 
570_0205 
3.4.1.11 
BRE - Temperature Range 
ACME shall provide a BRE burner surface 
temperature measurement range of 0 to 500 
degrees Celsius.    
  
  
3.4.3 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature 
DIAG 
560_0010 
3.4.3.2 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature 
ACME shall provide hot soot-free region 
temperature measurements made simultaneously 
on 5 or more lines spaced 5mm ± 0.5mm apart 
from neighboring lines. 
DIAG 
560_0020 
3.4.3.3 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – TFP 
Reposition Between tests 
ACME shall provide hot soot-free region 
temperature measurements with the ability to 
reposition the measurement lines or fibers 
between tests to uplinked positions. 
DIAG 
560_0030 
3.4.3.3 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – TFP 
Reposition During Tests 
ACME shall provide hot soot-free region 
temperature measurements with the ability to 
reposition the measurement lines, or fibers, 
during tests to uplinked positions. 
DIAG 
560_0060 
3.4.3.3 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – Axial 
Position 
ACME shall provide the ability to move the axial 
position along its length of a TFP fiber relative to 
the burner as a function of time within ± 1mm.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 66 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
DIAG 
560_0090 
3.4.3.4 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – Fiber 
Retractable 
ACME shall provide hot soot-free region 
temperature measurements where the fibers, if 
used, shall be retractable with minimal 
disturbance to beyond 100mm from the burner. 
DIAG 
560_0110 
3.4.3.4 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – Fiber 
Removable 
ACME shall provide the TFP fiber array fully 
removable for replacement. 
DIAG 
560_0130 
3.4.3.9 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – Fiber 
Orientation 1 
ACME shall provide fiber orientation such that 
they intersect with and are orthogonal to the CIR 
chamber axis. 
DIAG 
560_0150 
3.4.3.9 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – Fiber 
Orientation 2 
ACME shall provide fiber orientation such that 
they are orthogonal, with a tolerance of ± 25 
degrees, to the line of sight of the corresponding 
imaging system. 
DIAG 
560_0160 
3.4.3.13 
Hot Soot-Free Region Temperature – TFP 
Fibers as ORU 
ACME shall provide the fibers mounted within 
ORU(s) and removable from the ACME CIA 
during spaceflight, if the hot soot-free region 
temperature measurement is made by TFP. 
  
  
  3.4.4 
Far-Field Temperature Measurement 
MEAS 
570_0230 
3.4.4.1, 
3.4.4.2 
Far-Field Temperature – Avoidance Region 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements along unobstructed lines passing 
through the intersection of the CIR chamber 
window axes that avoid the region within 20 
degrees of the burner supply tube. 
MEAS 
570_0240 
3.4.4.3 
Far-Field Temperature – Near Radial Array 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements from at least the following radial 
locations measured in mm from the intersection of 
the CIR chamber window axes: 13, 25, 50, 100, 
200, and 200 in a direction orthogonal to the other 
200mm position (when the intersection of the CIR 
window axes is considered the origin of the two 
rays.)

content:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 67 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
MEAS 
570_0250 
3.4.4.4 
Far-Field Temperature – Distant Radial Array 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements from at least the following radial 
locations measured in mm from the intersection of 
the CIR chamber window axes:  45, 60, 100, 100 
(in a direction orthogonal to the other like-
distance position, when the intersection of the 
CIR window axes is considered the origin of the 
two rays), 200, 200 (in a direction orthogonal to 
the other like-distance position, when the 
intersection of the CIR window axes is considered 
the origin of the two rays.) 
MEAS 
570_0260 
3.4.4.5 
Far-Field Temperature – Positioning Accuracy 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements with each position known in three 
dimensions to within ± 3mm or less. 
MEAS 
570_0270 
3.4.4.6 
Far-Field Temperature – Range Inside 40-mm 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements in the range of 700-1700 degrees 
Celsius for the "near" radial array for positions 
inside 40mm from the intersection of the CIR 
chamber window axes:  13 and 25mm. 
MEAS 
570_0280 
3.4.4.6 
Far-Field Temperature – Range Outside 40-
mm 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements in the range of 0-1250 degrees 
Celsius for each radial array for positions outside 
of 40mm from the intersection of the CIR 
chamber window axes:  45, 60, 100, and 200mm. 
MEAS 
570_0290 
3.4.4.7 
Far-Field Temperature – Sensor Precision 
Inside 40-mm 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements such that the temperature sensors 
have precisions for each radial array of ± 1.2C for 
the positions inside 40mm from the intersection of 
the CIR chamber window axes:  13 and 25mm. 
MEAS 
570_0300 
3.4.4.7 
Far-Field Temperature – Sensor Precision 
Outside 40-mm 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements such that the temperature sensors 
have precisions for each radial array of ± 1.2C for 
the positions outside 40mm from the intersection 
of the CIR chamber window axes:  45, 50, 60, 
100, and 200mm.   
MEAS 
570_0330 
3.4.4.9 
Far-Field Temperature Measurement – ZOE 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements with a cylindrical zone of 
exclusion with a diameter of 50mm and 
maximized extending from the intersection of the 
CIR chamber window axes to 10mm beyond each 
temperature measurement position.

content:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 68 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
MEAS 
570_0350 
3.4.4.10 
Far-Field Temperature Measurement – TC 
Probe Parallel  
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements such that if thermocouples are 
used, each probe (including the junction) shall be 
within 10 degrees of parallel to a ray from the 
intersection of the CIR chamber window axes to 
the temperature measurement position to a 
distance of at least 100mm from the intersection 
of the CIR chamber windows. 
MEAS 
570_0360 
3.4.4.11 
Far-Field Temperature Measurement – TC 
Probe OD 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements such that each probe within a 
radial distance of 100mm shall have an outer 
diameter limit of the following or smaller:  0.2mm 
within 5mm of the measurement position; 2mm 
within 20mm of the measurement position; 3.5mm 
within 50mm of the measurement position. 
MEAS 
570_0370 
3.4.4.12 
Far-Field Temperature Measurement – ORU 
ACME shall provide far-field temperature 
measurements such that the sensors within 
100mm of the intersection of the CIR chamber 
window axes that are ORU's 
  
  
3.6 
Radiant Emission Measurement 
DIAG 
560_0180 
3.6.2 
Radiant Emission – Minimum FOV 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements such that the minimum region for 
each measurement is at least a 120-mm diameter 
FOV at the intersection of the CIR chamber 
window axes. 
DIAG 
560_0190 
3.6.3 
Radiant Emission – Orthogonal FOV Array 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements with a linear array of five 
measurements made where the view from each 
detector is equidistant from and orthogonal to the 
CIR chamber axis within ± 3 degrees. 
DIAG 
560_0200 
3.6.3 
Radiant Emission – Orthogonal Centered FOV 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements with one of five's FOV is centered 
on the intersection of the CIR chamber window 
axes. 
DIAG 
560_0210 
3.6.3 
Radiant Emission – Orthogonal Uniform FOVs 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements where four of five FOVs are  
positioned uniformly, with equal spacing of no 
more than 30mm ± 1mm, across a span of at 
least 60mm ± 1mm in each direction.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 69 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
DIAG 
560_0220 
3.6.4 
Radiant Emission – Non-Orthogonal, 
Additional FOV 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements where one additional FOV is also 
made at angle(s) other than orthogonal to the CIR 
chamber axis for a FOV centered on the 
intersection of the CIR chamber window axes. 
DIAG 
560_0230 
3.6.4 
Radiant Emission – Non-Orthogonal, 
Additional FOV Downstream 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements where the additional 
measurement, non-orthogonal to the chamber 
axis, are uniformly spaced in an angle relative to 
the orthogonal direction, and cover a span from 
orthogonal to at least 60 degrees ± 2 degrees 
downstream, of the burners. 
DIAG 
560_0240 
3.6.5 
Radiant Emission – Spectral Range 
ACME shall provide flame radiant emissions 
measurements where the detector has a spectral 
range of 0.2 to 11 microns and an irradiance 
range of 0.0001-0.1 W/cm2. 
DIAG 
560_0241 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emissions - BRE 
ACME shall provide one primary and two or more 
secondary radiant flame emissions for BRE 
burner tests. 
DIAG 
560_0242 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission - BRE FOV Size 
ACME shall provide a field of view for the BRE 
radiant emission measurements that fully includes 
a cylindrical zone downstream of the burner 
surface that is 50mm in diameter by 50mm in 
length. 
DIAG 
560_0243 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission - BRE FOV Position 
ACME shall provide a cylindrical field of view for 
BRE radiant emission measurements that is 
aligned with the chamber and BRE burner axis. 
DIAG 
560_0244 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission - BRE FOV Shape 
ACME shall provide a conical field of view for 
each radiant emission measurement that have 
the same angle between the field of view edges 
and a plane passing through each measurements 
center axis. 
DIAG 
560_0510 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission -BRE Burner Exclusion 
From Primary 
ACME shall provide a primary radiant emission 
measurement that blocks the BRE burner from 
the FOV with a blocked thickness of the 
cylindrical zone of less than 5mm when measured 
parallel with the burner axis. 
DIAG 
560_0520 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission - BRE Burner Exclusion of 
Lense 
ACME shall not use lenses on the radiant 
emission measurements to form the field of view.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 70 of 117 
 
 
System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description 
DIAG 
560_0530 
3.6.8 
Radiant Emission - BRE Burner Identical 
ACME shall use identical sensors for all radiant 
emission measurements. 
  
  
  3.7 
Chemiluminescent Emission Measurement 
DIAG 
560_0290 
3.7.2 
Chemiluminescent Emission – Simultaneous 
ACME shall provide simultaneous 
chemiluminescent emissions measurements at 
310 and 431 nanometers with a 10 nanometer or 
larger FWHM, and broadband from 300 to 600 
nanometers.  
DIAG 
560_0300 
3.7.3 
Chemiluminescent Emission – Minimum FOV 
ACME shall provide chemiluminescent emissions 
measurements with a 120mm diameter FOV, 
centered on the intersection of the CIR chamber 
window axes.   
DIAG 
560_0310 
3.7.4 
Chemiluminescent Emission – Sensitivity 
ACME shall provide chemiluminescent emissions 
measurements with a typical Radiant Sensitivity 
of at least 40 mA/W (as measured at the peak 
sensitivity wavelength.) 
DIAG 
560_0340 
3.7.6 
Chemiluminescent Emission – ORU 
ACME shall provide chemiluminescent emissions 
sensors as ORU(s) and removable from the 
ACME CIA during spaceflight. 
  
  
3.8 
Ion Current Measurement 
E-FIELD 
580_0430 
3.8.1, 3.8.2, 3.8.3 
Ion Current Range 
ACME shall provide measurements of ion current 
produced between the burner and mesh electrode 
where it's amplitude is over a range of at least 0 
to 25 micro amps with an error of no more than 
the larger of ± 5% of the reading or ± 0.05 micro 
amps. 
MEAS 
  
3.1 
Heat Flux (BRE burner tests only) 
MEAS 
570_1050 
3.10.1 
1.13.12 
Heat Flux - Sensor  
ACME shall provide heat flux measurements at 
the outlet of the BRE burner using a Schmidt-
Boelter thermopile type heat flux transducer. 
MEAS 
570_1060 
3.10.2 
1.13.12 
Heat Flux - 25mm Burner Center 
ACME shall take a heat flux measurement at the 
center ± 0.1mm of the 25mm BRE burner. 
MEAS 
570_1070 
3.10.2 
1.13.12 
Heat Flux - 50mm Burner Center 
ACME shall take a heat flux measurement at the 
center ± 0.1mm of the 50mm BRE burner. 
MEAS 
570_1080 
3.10.2 
1.13.12 
Heat Flux 25mm Burner Offset 
ACME shall take a heat flux measurement at a 
position with an offset radius of 10mm ± 0.1mm 
for the 25mm BRE burner. 
MEAS 
570_1090 
3.10.2 
1.13.12 
Heat Flux 50mm Burner Offset 
ACME shall take a heat flux measurement at a 
position with an offset radius of 15mm ± 0.1mm 
for the 50mm BRE burner.

System 
SSC_ID 
ISRD 
Trace 
ERD REQ Title/Description

3.10.3 
Heat Flux - Relative Size 
ACME shall provide heat flux sensors that have a 
diameter of less than 10% of the BRE burner's 
outlet surface. 
MEAS 
570_1210 
3.10.4 
Heat Flux - Orientation 
ACME shall provide downstream facing heat flux 
sensors that are flush with the BRE burner outlet 
surface ± 0.05mm. 
MEAS 
570_1220 
3.10.4 
Heat Flux - Flush Mount 
ACME shall provide heat flux sensors that are 
flush with the BRE burner outlet surface ± 
0.05mm. 
MEAS 
570_1230 
3.10.5 
Heat Flux - FOV 
ACME shall provide heat flux sensors that have 
no restrictions to their fields of view, geometrically 
by the burner. 
MEAS 
570_1240 
3.10.6 
Heat Flux - Emissivity 
ACME shall provide heat flux sensors whose 
surface has an emissivity of .93 for a range of 
0.6-15 microns. 
MEAS 
570_1250 
3.10.7 
Heat Flux - Range 
ACME shall provide a heat flux measurement 
range of 0-50 kW/m2. 
MEAS 
570_1260 
3.10.8 
Heat Flux - Precision 
ACME shall provide heat flux measurements with 
a precision of ± 1%. 
MEAS 
570_1270 
3.10.8 
Heat Flux - Accuracy 
ACME shall provide heat flux measurements with 
an accuracy of ± 5% of full scale. 
MEAS 
570_1340 
3.10.9 
3.10.7 
Heat Flux - Measurement 
ACME shall provide a BRE burner where the heat 
flux measurements remain within 0-50 kW/m2.

8.0

free area within 0.5 second after igniter off.

[CIR] Chamber Atmosphere

500_0010

Chamber Atmosphere – Composition CIR Support 
The ACME flow system shall provide the capability to vary 
the gas composition within the CIR chamber with an 
accuracy of ±0.005 mole fraction of each concentration.

Chamber Atmosphere – Dry Gases CIR Support 
The ACME flow system shall provide dry chamber gas.

The ACME flow system shall maintain a dry chamber 
atmosphere.

500_0030

Support 
The ACME flow system shall provide chamber gas 
containing less than a mole fraction of 0.01 of 
contaminants H2O and CO2. 
CIA 
500_0040 
1.11.2 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Mixed CIR Support 
The ACME flow system shall provide a well mixed 
chamber atmosphere such that the chamber fan moves 
100 times the gas volume in the chamber. 
CIA 
500_0050 
1.11.3 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Quiescence 
ACME shall provide quiescent conditions of the chamber 
atmosphere achieved with a hold period of at least 300 
seconds prior to ignition, following filling, venting or 
actuator motion.   
CIA 
500_0060 
1.11.3 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Convective Disturbances 
ACME shall provide chamber atmospheric conditions such 
that convective disturbances during a test point are limited 
to those caused by burner gas flow, combustion, the 
igniter, and the motion of the mesh electrode and any 
diagnostics.  
CIA 
500_0070 
1.11.3 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Quiescence Data Sampling 
ACME shall provide quiescent conditions extending 
through the entire duration of the data collection. 
CIA 
500_0080 
1.11.4 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Initial Pressure Range 
ACME shall provide the capability to vary the initial, pre-
test chamber pressure in the range 0.1 to 3 bar absolute.  
CIA 
500_0090 
1.11.5 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Initial Temperature Range 
ACME shall provide the initial, pre-test ambient 
temperature of 290 to 310 degrees Kelvin. 
CIA 
500_0100 
1.11.5 
  
Chamber Atmosphere – Initial Temperature Uniformity 
ACME shall provide the initial, pre-test ambient 
temperature that is uniform within ± 5 degrees Kelvin.

Experimental Objectives
Understand flame ion production and use ions to control 
diffusion flames by modifying local convection (via the ion 
wind) and local species transport (via direct ion drift)
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and 
chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the 
amount of inert in the fuel.

and ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of 
total fuel flow rate and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
C) Evaluate and control sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction 
and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field 
voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate 
and amount of inert added to the fuel stream
and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied 
voltage to characterize and control combustion behavior.

content:
ACME CLD burner hot wire anemometry measurements - 12/26/16 
 
This report summarizes the results of the hot wire anemometry measurements performed on the revised 
version of the flight unit of the ACME CLD burner to assess the symmetry of the flow profiles. 
• A cold flow of air was employed for the coflow, and a cold flow of nitrogen was used for the fuel flow. 
• With respect to the following figure, the arrows identify the scanning directions followed to probe the 
velocity profiles on the burner. With reference to the plots in the following pages, the scanning 
directions are labeled and colored as follows. 
• Direction “A” 
• Direction “B” 
• Direction “C” 
• Direction “D” 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ACME CLD burner top view and hot wire scanning directions. 
 
• The flow velocity was measured with a TSI 1212-T.15 90° probe. 
• The teal arrow identifies the camera viewing direction. 
 
The measurements were performed in accordance to the Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD), and listed in the following. 
 
1.4.9: The burner shall have a uniform flow profile that is axisymmetric, i.e., where the velocity is 
independent of the angular position, especially (at radial positions) near the burner center. For the coflow 
burner, axisymmetric flow means that the variation in axial velocity with angular position (e.g., as measured 
in 1.4.11) shall be less than 10% of the (mean) velocity, where this shall hold for all radial positions from 0 to 
10 mm.  
•   verified 
1.4.11: The burner’s flow profile, across a plane orthogonal to the burner axis and within 0.5 mm 
downstream of the inner tube outlet, shall be well documented. The spatial uniformity shall be verified by 1g 
measurement of the velocity field using a cold flow (i.e., with no flame) simultaneously through both the 
annulus and the inner tube. The axial velocity shall be measured across a diameter of 30 mm at increments 
of no greater than 5 mm, especially within 5 mm of the burner axis where the increments shall be no greater 
than 1 mm. Unless otherwise specified, measurement across one diameter is sufficient. 
•   verified 
• The increments used were 0.25 mm, for both coflow and fuel tube regions. 
• Three heights above the burner outlet were scanned: 0.5 mm, 5 mm, and 10 mm.

while the red and green curves are the left and right velocity profiles, respectively (defined with respect 
to the burner centerline). The flow rates have been set based on a nominal coflow I.D. of 25.4 mm, and a 
fuel tube I.D. of 2.16 mm and O.D. of 2.41 mm. The black dashed lines identify the boundaries of the fuel

1.4.9: The burner gas shall be ejected parallel to the chamber axis and without either swirl (i.e., helically 
rotating flow) or turbulence (i.e., eddies). To be without turbulence, the axial velocity at any position 0.5 mm 
downstream of the burner (e.g., as measured in 1.4.11) shall be constant with time within 3% (i.e., of the 
time-averaged value). 
•   measured 
• Each data point has been evaluated as a one second average (sampling @4000 Hz). 
• Only one scanning direction was considered (direction “A”). 
• Scanning intervals were equal to 1 mm. 
• The error bars, in the “flow velocity" plots, are equal to ±. 
• The noise, and therefore the deviation from the time averaged value, was seen to be inherent in 
the measuring device, and not dependent on the flow (see 0 cm/s measurement). 
• The "percent deviation" plots display the relative difference of the absolute value of  with respect

content:
Experimental apparatus and hot wire calibration  
The air and nitrogen used for the coflow and fuel flows were set using the following mass flow 
controllers: 
• Coflow: Sierra Instrument Smart Trak, maximum flow rate of 20 slpm of air. 
• Fuel tube: Unit Instruments Inc., maximum flow rate of 300 sccm of N2. 
The nitrogen controller was calibrated daily, before any measurement, with a manual bubble flow meter. 
The calibration of the air controller (which was known to be stable and repeatable) was verified twice, 
once before any measurement, and once at the end, with a mechanical flow meter calibrator. 
The hot wire system used was a TSI IFA-100 coupled to a TSI 1212-T.15 90° wire probe (tungsten 
platinum coated filament with a 3.8 m diameter). The settings implemented for the electronics were: 
• Cable resistance: 0.413 ohm 
• Operative resistance: 10.56 ohm 
• Bridge compensation: 35 
• Gain: 20 
• Offset: 1 
The following plot shows the result of the calibration performed on the hot wire probe (using a TSI 
112700 calibrator), as well as the interpolating curve used to evaluate the flow velocity from the hot wire 
voltage readings. 
 
For the burner scan, the hot wire probe was mounted on a horizontal translation stage driven by a 
Velmex stepper motor; the height of the probe was varied with the help of a second manual translation 
stage. The software OMA was used to control the stepper motor, as well as to record the hot wire voltage 
signals through a LabJack U12.

content:
Electric field, ions and flames 
Background and motivation 
•  Hydrocarbon flame’s inherent electrical 
property was reported more than two 
centuries ago. 
•  Most of the theories with regard to the 
electrical charge carriers and ionization 
process were not extensively elaborated 
until after the 1950s. 
•  The book, written by Lawton and Weinberg, 
on the electrical aspects of combustion 
integrated the knowledge at the time (1969) 
of a flame’s systematic ion generation as 
well as electrical control of flames based on 
laboratory tests and observations. 
•  Pederson and Brown (among others) 
identified chemi-ionization mechanisms in 
hydrocarbon flames in 1993. 
Why microgravity?

Electric field, ions and flames 
Background and motivation 
•  The dominant ion, H3O+,  
from the hydrocarbon 
flame zone is found 
experimentally and 
numerically. 
•  CHO+ + H2O à H3O+ + CO 
•  Chemi-ion driven wind is 
the result of the ion drift.  
•  The ion transport is 
dominated by the 
electrokinetic drift while 
the ion convection and 
diffusion are relatively 
small. 
•  Ion drift velocity: the 
positive ion accelerates 
between each collision with 
neutral gas molecules. 
•  Induced drift velocity: each 
collision transfers the newly 
acquired kinetic energy to 
the neutral gas.

force on earth.

content:
Electric field, ions, and flames 
Background and motivation 
•  Hydrocarbon flame’s inherent electrical property 
was reported more than two centuries ago. 
•  Most of the theories with regard to the electrical 
charge carriers and ionization process were not 
extensively elaborated until after the 1950s. 
•  The book, written by Lawton and Weinberg, on 
the electrical aspects of combustion integrated 
the knowledge at the time (1969) of a flame’s 
systematic ion generation as well as electrical 
control of flames based on laboratory tests and 
observations. 
•  Pederson and Brown (among others) identified 
chemi-ionization mechanisms in hydrocarbon 
flames in 1993. 
Why microgravity?

Electric field, ions and flames 
Background and motivation 
•  The dominant ion, H3O+,  
from the hydrocarbon 
flame zone is found 
experimentally and 
numerically. 
•  CHO+ + H2O à H3O+ + CO 
•  The ion transport is 
dominated by the 
electrokinetic drift while 
the ion convection and 
diffusion are relatively 
small. 
•  Chemi-ion driven wind is 
the result of the ion drift.  
•  Ion drift velocity: the 
positive ion accelerates 
between each collision with 
neutral gas molecules. 
•  Induced drift velocity: each 
collision transfers the newly 
acquired kinetic energy to 
the neutral gas.   
•  ​𝐹↓±  =​𝑗 ⁄​𝐾↓±   
F: body force 
J: current density 
K: mobility 
•  Electric body force usually 
around 1-10 times the  
buoyant force on earth.

content:
Electric Field Effects
Ion reactions make up a small subset of 
combustion kinetics.
Microscopic electric field effects:
• Charge separation
•Acceleration prevented by                     collisions 
with neutrals
• ~100 m/s ion drift velocity
Macroscopic field effects:
• Ion-driven wind (~1 m/s)
• Reshaping of the reaction zone
• Change in flame luminosity
• Altered stability
• Forced extinction
Starik and Titova, 2002

• Flame oscillations are present for a variety of applied field strengths.

• Luminous oscillations (~30 - 40Hz region)

ionization.

content:
Main Flame characteristics
•
Flame height was shown to not be affected by a change in gravity field.
•
Flame width was affected by producing a thinner plume as it was expected. 
•
Detachment with the burner tip was observed numerically and it might be 
attributed to the numerical challenge of these boundary conditions.
•
The new combination of chemical kinetic model proposed containing excited 
species and ions has shown to predict important characteristics of the non-
premixed methane laminar jet flame.
CH* chemiluminescence
•
CH* profiles showed a brighter flame while going to higher gravity 
environments (hypergravity conditions).
Ions
•
High concentration of H3O+ produced and transported far away from the 
flame.
•
Higher concentration of naturally produced ions has been observed under 
hypergravity conditions. The electric field effect could be increased under 
strong gravity environments.
Summary

content:
•
The extruded burner geometry shows an I-V curve similar to the one obtained in the experiments in a 1g 
environment. Changes in the boundary condition have to still be performed.
•
The saturation point in the I-V curve obtained using the flush burner geometry simulation is aligning with 
the one obtained experimentally. The peak of positive charges (H3O+) that reach the upper electrode (anode) 
is displaced from the center, aligning with the experimental observations. However, simulations at sub-
saturation regimes show that higher e-fields are needed in the simulation in order to get the same ion 
currents (z-direction) than the ones obtained experimentally. This might be caused by the interaction 
between burner (positive electrode) and reaction zone. More investigation has to be performed in order to 
clarify this phenomena.
Next steps:
•
Define why sub-saturation flush burner geometry simulations show that higher electric fields are needed to 
achieve the ion currents obtained experimentally.
•
Proceed by simulating jet geometry burner flames at 1g.
•
Proceed by simulating the three burner geometries at 0g.

content:
Final remarks and future work
Final remarks
• We have built a chemical kinetic model that contains the minor species CH*, OH*, H3O+
and HCO+ and trust-worthily predicts non-premixed flame behavior at steady state. 
Comparison between experimental and numerical results validated the reduced model.
• Speed up in the simulations without e-field in comparison with detailed model was 
obtained (> x2).
• The size of the reduced model should be small enough to handle e-field 2D simulations.
Near-future goals
Validation of the model
• Change the burner geometry and repeat the simulation, comparing it to experiments.
• Check how the methane flame responds to an external applied e-field, comparing it to
experiments (at 1g and µg).
Others
• Repeat the mechanism reduction process with an C2H4 detailed model.

Chemi-ions:
Ions naturally produced within the combustion reaction of hydrocarbon
ﬂames.
How do external electric ﬁeld eﬀects produce observed ﬂame reactions?

joule heating increasing ﬂame temperatures.

highly energized electrons enhancing reaction rates.
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
mechanical drag on bulk gas by migrating ions.

Discussion
What is the source of the super-saturation ion currents?
Possible sources:
1. Electrical breakdown
▶global breakdown - unlikely
(since ﬁeld strengths ≪25kV/cm)
▶local breakdown - likely
(corona discharge, thermal ionization)
2. Electron Avalanche
▶more likely to occur with negative ﬁeld strengths.
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
▶enhancement to gas ﬂow dynamics enhancing local mixing leading to
enhanced chemi-ionization reaction rates.

2011 7th US National Combustion Meeting  
Organized by the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute  
and Hosted by the Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 
March 20-23, 2011 
Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion  
K. Swenson1, S. Karnani2, D. Dunn-Rankin2, F. Takahashi3, D. Stocker1, and        
Z-G. Guang3 
1NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135 
2Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of California at Irvine, 
Irvine, California 92617, USA 
3National Center for Space Exploration Research on Fluids and Combustion, Cleveland, Ohio 
92617, USA 
This paper describes measurements aimed at understanding the influence of electric fields on 
flames where buoyancy has been removed. Given that buoyancy and an electric field can have a 
similar influence on flames, buoyancy can obscure the contribution of an electric field in a normal 
gravity (1g) environment. Experiments were performed in the microgravity conditions of NASA’s 
2.2 Second Drop Tower on a simple jet diffusion flame to isolate the influence of an electric field. 
Results show similarities between the ion current response of a methane flame in an electric field 
in both 1g and microgravity (μg). Under some coflow velocities and electric fields strengths, it is 
possible to modify the flame shape so that it resembles a flame in 1g.  
1. Introduction 
 
When oxidized, hydrocarbon fuels produce a number of intermediate species, a small 
subset of which are charged. Hence, an electrostatic field applied across the flame zone creates a 
charge separation; opposites attract and ions move toward their respective opposite electrode. 
Acceleration of the ions is limited as momentum is transferred through collisions with neutral 
molecules. These repeated collisions induce a wind of companion neutral gas, which can 
potentially affect flame stability [1, 2], induce convection [3], and simulate microgravity [4-6]. 
 
In a 1g environment, the plume of hot gases from a flame naturally induces, through mass 
continuity, a convective flow to the neighboring cooler environment, giving rise to the flame’s 
characteristic teardrop shape. In a microgravity environment, buoyant convection, which in 1g is 
responsible for the transport of fresh oxidizer to a flame, is removed, leaving forced convection 
to dominate the flow field while species transport is a function of both that and molecular 
diffusion[7]. A number of experiments [8-10] have studied electric fields applied to flames in 
microgravity environments to measure mobility, its influence on burning rate constants, and the 
feasibility of inducing forced convection in a buoyancy free environment.  
 
The comparable influence of buoyant convection makes studying ion wind effects on 
flames in a 1g environment difficult. By removing buoyancy, the ion wind becomes a dominant 
force capable of creating similar flame shapes in a non-buoyant environment. This paper’s 
objective is to explore the different ion current regimes of a small diffusion flame when affected 
by an electric field in 1g and μg using the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.

2. Experimental  
The experimental drop rig (Figure 1) includes a cylindrical test chamber (24.6 cm i.d., 53.3 cm 
length), flow system, and data acquisition/control hardware. The burner is a stainless-steel fuel 
tube (2.1 mm i.d., 2.4 mm o.d.), coaxially positioned inside the cylindrical test chamber. For 
conditions requiring a coflowing annulus of gas, the stainless-steel fuel tube is coaxially 
positioned inside a Pyrex® converging nozzle (27.3 mm exit i.d.), through which air flows. Gas 
flow was controlled with a fixed orifice and upstream pressure. A hot-wire igniter (coiled 29-
gauge Kanthal, 11 cm length), which can be positioned over the burner by a rotary solenoid is 
used to ignite the fuel (CH4, 99.97%). Data signals from thermocouples, pressure transducers, 
radiometer (Dexter, ST150 Amplified), and a tri-axis accelerometer (Crossbow, CXL02TG3-S) 
are digitized and recorded at 20 Hz. The flame is observed by a CCD color camera (Hitachi HV-
D30), transmitted through a tethered optical fiber, and recorded using a digital video recorder 
placed atop the Drop Tower.  
 
To establish a steady flow through the flow orifice, fuel is introduced to the burner 8 seconds 
prior to the drop event (t = 0). Following ignition and igniter retraction, a selected high voltage is 
applied to the mesh electrode relative to the burner. The mesh screen was located 5 cm above the 
nozzle tip. The average strength of the electric field is approximated as:

3. Results and Discussion 
Flame response is presented in the following graphs by plotting the measured ion current as a 
function of the applied field. It should be noted that the burner is always grounded and electrical 
potentials are applied at the electrode. The polarity of the field is considered positive when the 
mesh electrode has a positive potential with respect to the burner electrode. All data points, 
except where noted, are averaged between t = 1.6 s to t = 2.1 s of the drop to avoid measuring the 
flame’s transient response. Data points were only included in the data set if a flame was present. 
Error bars represent the standard deviation of the shunt voltage in this same time period.  
Figure 3 shows the relationship between ion current and electric field strength for a 24 cm/s 
methane velocity in μg and 1g. Both conditions, regardless of polarity, show a sub-saturation 
region characterized by a near quadratic increase in ion current with voltage and a saturation 
region where ion current remains constant with increasing voltage. The ion current response 
exhibits minor differences in magnitude when changing gravity levels with a negative potential 
mesh in the sub-saturation and early saturation regions. At larger field strengths, initial transients 
from the voltage step can extinguish the flame.  Points that involve extinguishment are measured 
over different time periods and should not be considered accurate; however, the values are 
plotted for completeness and to show that extinguished flames have a clearly discernable 
behavior. For a positive potential mesh applied in μg, the ion driven wind forces the flame 
against the burner tube. The flames are partially quenched on the burner tube, reducing the

as a function of applied electric field strength and coflow velocity. The pink vertical line 
corresponds to the base location of a 1g flame without an applied field. The graphs show that a

produce a flame with a similar area and flame base location as the unforced 1g flame. 
 
4. Conclusion 
The ion current response is nearly identical in μg and 1g environments, with the exception of the 
positive saturation plateau. This is expected considering that ion production is a global measure 
of flame behavior that is dependent on the flow field regardless of the driving mechanism. At 
electric field strengths greater than 1.8 kV/cm in μg, the flame begins to oscillate and the ion 
current jumps up significantly. At this point a faint corona glow is observed from the nozzle tip. 
At electric field strengths more negative than -1.6 kV/cm, the flame is unable to adjust to the 
abrupt change in flow conditions and extinguishes. Future research will include intermediate 
voltage steps or a ramp for testing at higher field strengths. Within the respective uncertainties, 
the surface area and flame base location of the images presented in Figure 4 are equal; where a    
-0.6 kV/cm electric field or a 24 cm/s coflow acting on a μg flame can produce a flame shape 
similar to that of a 1g flame without these influences.  The flames at these conditions are shown 
in Figure 4. A deeper understanding of how electric fields effect flames may lead to future 
applications such as soot control and applications where efficiency and stability can be actively 
controlled with electric fields.

2 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fun-
damental understanding of chemi-ionization and ion-driven convection in flames.  It also 
uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and 
stability limits in the absence of buoyancy.  This work is based on prior foundation stud-
ies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an 
earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics.  The cur-
rent SRD proposes to use the extended-duration microgravity environment to further de-
velop an understanding of electric fields in combustion processes and their potential ap-
plications.   
The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created 
through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in 
microgravity environments.  For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric 
fields have demonstrated powerful influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning 
velocity, extinction, and stability.  The source of these influences resides in ion wind ef-
fects.  In microgravity, where there are no density-driven buoyant effects to contend with, 
ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to 
manipulate combustion systems.  This project includes both academic study of electric 
field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion proc-
esses.   
Our prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be 
used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in 
order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because 
flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near-limit conditions; 
(b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this proc-
ess can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to 
affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are 
shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and 
(d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between 
flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at satu-
ration.   
In 1-g, the above-mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interactions 
that cannot be unraveled.  Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following 
experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the 
relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel 
flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of 
the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid changes in electric fields; (C) 
determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate 
the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields. 
The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-flow burner.  
The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nominally non-
sooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame 
strength.  The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21% 
O2 and 79% N2.  The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber

3 
and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner 
mouth.  The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a 
steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine 
the flame’s steady state response and time response.  The data to be recorded include the 
applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH* luminosity, 
flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric 
potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field.  In addition, a 
desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field 
as a function of the electric field conditions.   
The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of 
flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electri-
cally control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits 
and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind.  For example, a 
lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor 
point.  Therefore, electric fields acting on near-limit flames can exert a large influence 
because they can affect the local mixing behavior.  The role of electric fields on soot 
formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influ-
ence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects are found im-
portant) in sooting flames.   
Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those 
driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth grav-
ity.  In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the 
response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy ef-
fect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy.  
In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and 
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under 
all conditions.  Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales 
of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) are dominated by convec-
tion (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot studies require high 
quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop towers.  In ad-
dition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames requires ex-
periments lasting tens of seconds. 
Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior 
and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames 
can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct 
chemical or local convective influences).  Electric field effects on flames have been 
documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influ-
ences that affect ion generation behavior.  For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant 
influences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using 
electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames.  The proposed study removes this 
confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric 
field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames.

1 INTRODUCTION 
 
The first subsection provides the fundamentals that link chemi-ionization in flames with 
convective flows created when electric fields act on the ions generated.  Later subsections 
describe the variety of 1-g laboratory experiments exemplifying the scientific data we 
have found valuable in linking flames to their electrical properties.  For the purposes of 
this SRD, the details of this introductory section are less important than the examples of 
our preliminary results which inform our proposed selection of objectives and science 
data end products.  To focus on the proposed flight experiment, it is possible to skip di-
rectly to Section 1.4 and then refer to background information as needed.  
 
1.1 Background and Overview of Ion Driven Winds in Flames 
 
In addition to being a major liberator of chemical energy, hydrocarbon flames naturally 
produce charged intermediate species (ions and electrons) during the chemical-to-thermal 
energy conversion.  Generally speaking, chemi-ions and their associated species in hy-
drocarbon flames do not participate substantially in the major heat release reaction path-
ways.  Hence, the chemical kinetics of ion species in hydrocarbon flames has not been 
studied as extensively as for those species or reaction mechanisms associated with igni-
tion/extinction phenomena and pollutant formation.  Nevertheless, many of the chemical 
kinetic pathways are fairly well

lease reactions.  For example, the most populous cations (positive ions) are present in 
peak concentrations on the order of 1010/cc, or with mole fractions in the range of 10 ppb. 
 
The concentration of electrons (which 
make up the majority of the negative 
charge carriers) is even lower than the 
concentration of positive ions because 
electron mobility is very high so that 
relatively few electrons are needed to 
balance the charge flux carried by the 
more massive and more populous 
positive charge carriers.  Nevertheless, 
the free charges in the flame make the 
reaction zone a very good conductor 
(similar to that of a conductive metal).  
More importantly, if an electric field is 
applied across the flame, the charges 
can be separated into unipolar regions, as shown in Figure 1.2.  In the case where the an-
ode (higher potential electrode) is close to the flame, the electrons can then easily exit the 
gas phase system, leaving the positive ions to collide with neutral molecules as they mi-
grate through the unipolar space between the flame and the cathode (lower potential elec-
trode).  During this migration process, the ions impart momentum to the neutral gas 
equivalent to the acceleration they have achieved in the electric field between mean-free-
path collisions.  The collisions are so frequent, that the ions quickly establish a drift ve-
locity governed by their mobility.  The collisions thereby link the ionization processes to 
the neutral gas flow.  This phenomenon is referred to as a Chattock wind, an ion-wind, or 
more accurately an ion-driven wind, and is described in some detail by Lawton and 
Weinberg [7].   
 
In all of the applications involving electrical generation of convection, a unidirectional 
gas flow is induced by using a large electric field to act on the charges of a unipolar ion 
cloud in the region between the ion source and a second, usually earthed, electrode, or set 
of electrodes.  In these cases, the body force on a unit volume of the gas is equal to that 
on the charges it contains, provided that they have a constant mobility and do not acceler-
ate.  In atmospheric pressure systems, the latter condition on acceleration is met easily, 
but in regions of high temperature gradients or changes in chemical composition, the con-
stant mobility condition is not.  Fortunately, these regions are often of limited spatial ex-
tent and so the effects of variable mobility are usually ignored.  As described, for exam-
ple in references [8,9] isothermal ion driven flow (with constant mobility) is described 
generally by the coupled equations of fluid continuity and momentum along with an elec-
trical model, including, Poisson’s equation governing the electric field,

where e and q represent fundamental charge and number density of charges, respec-
tively, and the sign in the subscript denotes the polarity.  This unipolar condition applies 
so long as the field at the target electrode(s) does not reach magnitudes large enough to 
cause secondary ionization and electrical breakdown of the neutral gas there.  Beyond 
breakdown, F decreases because the secondary ions counterflow and neutralize those 
driving the process.  The space charge causes E to grow in the inter-electrode region and 
the consequent eventual electrical breakdown generally determines the maximum effects 
that can be achieved.  Extending the unidimensional concept suggests that the distribution 
of body force and consequent pressure gradients results in gas flow which can be tailored 
by appropriate design of the electrode geometry.  Under ideal circumstances, forces can 
be achieved that are hundreds of times those of buoyancy [10], but in typical combustion 
situations, the ion driven wind will be on the order of a few m/s and the force achieved 
will be a few times that of buoyancy.  Although this may not seem substantial, ion driven 
winds have been used to extinguish flames [11].   
 
The above equations show that an electric field applied to the flame can create a direct 
body force, or force per unit volume, on the system just as buoyancy does in a gravita-
tional field.  Because buoyancy can be a dominant characteristic of terrestrial combustion 
processes, it may seem less than obvious why physics regards gravity as a “weak force.”  
However, if we consider a small magnet picking up a metal object with the entire earth 
pulling in the opposite direction, it becomes obvious how much stronger the electromag-
netic forces are.  It is hardly surprising, therefore, that electrical forces acting on charge 
carriers can effectively substitute for gravitational influences or, more generally, provide 
for vigorous combustion control in its absence (i.e., in microgravity).  It is the opportu-
nity for exploiting the electric force in flames that motivates this research activity.  Al-
ready, electric fields have demonstrated powerful influences on combustion processes 
that include flame shape [12,13], sooting behavior [14-16], burning velocity [17,18], ex-
tinction [11,19], and stability [20,21].  The foundation of many of these results, as dis-
cussed in Lawton and Weinberg [7], reside in ion wind effects.  In microgravity, where 
there are no density driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an im-
portant (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion 
systems.  Hence, the zero gravity environment provides a unique opportunity to probe 
and exploit the electrical aspects of flames [22].
