allowing for determination of soot volume fraction through an extinction technique previously 
employed in microgravity research [21-23].  Unfortunately, because of trade-offs demanded by 
limited chamber volume and large number of instruments and components, the collimated light 
is obstructed substantially by the electrode mesh mount, limiting the utility of this camera for the 
E-FIELD Flames experiment. 
 
B. Additional Details 
The preceding section described the hardware was used in the first round of E-FIELD Flames 
testing, where that was conducted with the coflow burner.  The second round was conducted 
with the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner, which was built with the same tubing as the coflow burner’s inner 
tube.  However, it is important to note that the nominal inner diameter (ID) in both cases was 
2.16 mm, i.e., approximately 2.2 mm rather than 2.1 mm.  While potentially confusing, this met 
the tolerance requirement for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner.  Meanwhile, the nominal outer 
diameter (OD) was 2.41 mm, again for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner and the inner tube of the coflow 
burner.  It is also important to understand that the gas-jet burner was slightly taller than the 
coflow burner, where the electrode mesh was nominally 35 and 37 mm downstream of the gas-
jet and coflow burners, respectively (based on the outlet of the inner tube in the case of the 
coflow burner). 
 
It is expected that a separate supporting document will be created in the future to describe the 
ACME hardware in greater detail.  Meanwhile, it can be helpful to consult the ISRD, relevant 
drawings, and various reports.  Some important reports include the characterization reports for 
the data camera (see ACME-RPT-010), radiometers (ACME-RPT-011), and Photomultiplier Tubes 
(PMTs, ACME-RPT-013).  Key hardware dimensions and more are confirmed in the inspection 
report (ACME-VER-001 Rev. A), while many science requirements are addressed in the ACME ERD 
Verification Report (ACME-VER-002).  In this regard, ERD stands for Engineering Requirements 
Document and many of those requirements were directly derived from the science requirements.  
Contact ACME’s Project Scientist Dennis Stocker (216-433-2166, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov) with 
questions or for more information. 
 
C. Hardware Shortcomings 
As previously discussed, the slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies 
(recommended in the ISRD) did not meet the requirements necessary to achieve the requested 
time response performance, and as such inhibited determination of the flame’s response time to 
rapid changes in the electric field strength. 
 
The negative and positive high-voltage power supplies were to have been coupled, as described 
for example in Appendix C of the ISRD.  However, switching between the two high-voltage power 
supplies led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) so the power supplies were 
completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time.  As such, testing was limited to a 
single polarity at a time. 
 
The imaging for soot volume fraction via light extinction was largely blocked by the bracket 
holding the electrode mesh, where this was a design trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s 
large number of cameras and other optical instruments.  However, Prof. Marshall Long (Yale

10 April 2021 
16 
 
University), who is also an ACME investigator, has an alternate technique for determining the soot 
volume fraction from ACME’s data camera (DataCam) imaging. 
 
The DataCam is unfortunately not as sensitive as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames.  
Therefore, the imaging with that camera has typically been at a long exposure time, e.g., 0.65 s, 
even though it is a video camera capable of 30 frames per second (fps).   The principal exception 
has been when making soot pyrometry or Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. 
 
Between its thickness and the anti-reflection coating, the DataCam’s blue-green filter excessively 
attenuates the red light making its use undesirable.  The filter’s purpose intended was to balance 
the intensity of the three colors in flame imaging to facilitate pyrometry.  The accuracy of the 
pyrometric temperature measurements was diminished as result of this shortcoming. 
 
It is expected that lesser shortcomings will be addressed in the envisioned document describing 
the ACME hardware in greater detail than presented here. 
 
4. Preliminary Results  
A. Changed Test Plans 
To limit their scope, ACME investigations were limited to a single burner type and the E-FIELD 
Flames tests identified as required in the ISRD were with a gas-jet burner.  However, during the 
hardware development (and thus prior to spaceflight operations) it was determined that the slow 
response of the high-voltage power supplies (suggested in the ISRD) inhibited determination of 
the response time of the flame to the electric field, i.e., objective B.  To make up for that science 
loss, the experiment was permitted to conduct a portion of its tests with ACME’s coflow burner, 
where such tests had been identified as desired in the ISRD.  The gas-jet burner used for the E-
FIELD Flames investigation matched the inner tube of the coflow burner.  Therefore, the tests 
conducted allowed assessment of both the coflow and jet entrainment, where tests with the 
coflow burner were carried out with and without a coflow. 
 
It had also been conceived that some tests would be conducted in which the polarity of the 
electric field was varied.  However, the switching between the two high-voltage power supplies 
led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI).  Therefore, the electrical design was altered 
such that the power supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time.  
This avoided the excessive EMI but prevented changes of polarity within a test, as had been 
planned for the step response procedure described in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD.  It also led to the 
need for crew to swap the power supplies to enable testing at each polarity. 
 
To be clear, these significant changes to the experiment were made prior to the spaceflight 
operations where the decisions were made by the project management to manage the budget 
and schedule.  
 
In addition to the above hardware-driven changes to the test matrix, a series of other smaller 
changes ensued as choices for more consistent scientific outcomes were sought.  All adjustments 
were based on finding more effective ways to utilize the space time experiments.  The change 
history included the following.

10 April 2021 
17 
 
Fall 2016: Removed the 1.3-mm jet burner from the test plan - The original concept was to 
compare results from two jet burner sizes, but a single jet burner with the co-flow burner was 
clearly the better combination once the use of two burner types was allowed. 
 
September 2017: Changed tests with 30% CH4 to 40% CH4 - This change occurred because ground 
testing with the coflow burner indicated that the more dilute methane flames were not stable at 
similar conditions.  Therefore, to ensure stable starting conditions, the slightly higher fuel 
concentration was chosen. 
 
January 2018:   Changed tests with 80% CH4 to 70% CH4 - This modification was made in order to 
better span the dilution range; we decided that changes of 30% dilution in two steps (i.e., 40%, 
70%, 100%) was more consistent. 
 
December 2017: Added parameters to the draft script (i.e., software) - Parameters were added 
to make it convenient to adjust the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) gains and thus maintain useful 
PMT signal strengths over the wide range of flame conditions.  Parameters were also added to 
provide more flexibility in the step response script, where independent specification of on and off 
step durations was implemented so that testing wasn’t restricted to square waves.  
 
Before operation in 2018: Added script parameters for the initialize voltage and duration - The 
parameters were helpful in clearly defining the starting point for the electric field strength. 
 
During operation in 2018: Took actions to improve gas flow performance - A nitrogen (N2) 
priming time was added to the script to allow the flow to stabilize.  Mass Flow Controller (MFC) 
performance was improved by remote adjustment of the cracking and Proportional, Integral, and 
Derivative (PID) settings.  
 
During operation in 2018: Implemented improved control of the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
settings - More detailed camera settings were added to the script.  This importantly included 
specification for camera bracketing to allow photography with a set of exposure times.  All of 
these changes gave more control over the camera and improved the data quality; the changes to 
camera settings were designed to help get images over a wide dynamic range (where part of the 
flame was bright with soot and other parts were dim).  The bracketing was only partly successful 
as the hardware was unable to maintain reliable shutter times when the request was shorter than 
the maximum framing rate of the camera, but the brackets were effective when long exposures 
were used.   
 
During operation in 2018: Did not use open loop and step response script - During testing we 
discovered that the standard sweep and ramp scripts could be used to provide the kind of 
information that would have been possible with the open loop and step scripts because of the 
hardware limitations on the power supplies described earlier.  That is, the time response and 
single polarity features of the power supplies meant that a creative sweep design could mimic 
what would be obtained for a single target voltage with fixed step duration. 
 
(a) Setting the electric field to a zero voltage in the step response procedure deactivated the 
High-Voltage Power Supply (HVPS) between steps.  The recovery time of the HVPS between 
two steps during shut offs is more than two seconds, while there is limited fuel flow time (999 
seconds without resetting it by evacuating the chamber).  Hence, testing the flame response

B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations 
The narrative description of the operations is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the 
following conference paper: 
 Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report.  As a minor note, 
the size of some figures was adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity 
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the 
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the 
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the 
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may 
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As 
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure 
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the 
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.  
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed 
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the 
testing.  The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer 
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they 
typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are 
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., 
from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours 
of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks.  On intervening 
weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.  
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and 
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors 
and that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 
activity.  As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A 
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in 
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements 
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the 
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s 
planned parameters.  That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in 
communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately 
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In advance of the test day, the

10 April 2021 
20 
 
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies 
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  It is also 
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can 
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, 
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images 
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for 
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The 
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the 
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is 
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  Midway through a day’s E-FIELD 
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with 
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, 
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and 
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic 
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite 
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a 
daily basis.  The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame 
spread and material flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, 
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional 
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from 
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of 
their second round.  This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the 
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and 
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established 
in 2010.  At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of 
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, 
the general target was 50 tests per experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas 
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is 
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the 
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow 
in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion 
chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to 
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For E-FIELD 
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, 
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the

10 April 2021 
21 
 
research, NASA does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is 
almost always limited to the planned durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount 
of data.  More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-
shift transfer and downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where 
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in 
comparison.  It is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow 
of ‘air’ which also fills the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow.  A test 
includes starting the gas flows to prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, 
retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame to steady slightly before energizing the electric field 
to its initial value.  The flame is again allowed to steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a 
specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified voltage changes and durations.  The 
sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps.  After each test, a duplicate field 
sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the ion current through 
the flame. 
 
The first phase tests in E-FIELD Flames employ the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, 
with the fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface.  The results shown in this paper 
are for tests conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of 
synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa.  The mesh 
is held at a negative potential relative to the burner in these tests.  The sweeps shown in this 
paper extend to at least -7 kV, where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 
1-2 seconds.  The details of the voltage changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
23 
 
C. Summary of Preliminary Results 
The following text is the abstract from a 2019 conference paper on early results from the first 
round of testing: 
Y.-C., Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, D., U. Hegde, U. and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Ion Current and 
Flame Changes with Electric Fields in Microgravity,” 11th U.S. National Combustion Meeting 
2019, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019. 
 
This work presents changes in reaction zone shape and location, as well as ion currents obtained 
after applying an electric field onto a diffusion flame with fuel dilution in the International Space 
Station (ISS). As one of the projects of Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
(ACME), the E-FIELD Flames experiments were initiated in March and completed in November of 
2018 with a series of flame studies on the coflow burner and the jet burner within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR). The coflow burner, presented in this paper, consists of a small central fuel 
jet and a concentric outer ring flowing with synthetic air. The research examines fundamental 
hydrocarbon flame behaviors driven by the chemi-ion response during the combustion process. 
The experiment is conducted by applying high voltage onto a copper mesh situated 37 mm above 
the burner tip, where measurements include images and ion currents over a range of electric field 
strengths and time histories depending on the region of interest (e.g., near the saturation 
transition). This paper specially investigates the flame behavior while flowing different 
methane/nitrogen mixture compositions. Among other effects, the results show that the electric 
field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when 
there is no coflowing air. 
 
The preliminary results are discussed in greater detail in sections based on the burner 
configuration (coflow burner and jet burner), fuel (methane and ethylene), and dilution levels 
tested.  First presented are the results from the methane flames with the coflow burner and then 
with the jet burner.  Then, the ethylene flame results are presented.  Before providing the results, 
it is important to clarify the terminology of polarity and field direction adopted for this system. 
 
Field direction and polarities 
The electric field is established between the two electrodes, burner and mesh, which are 
connected separately with positive and negative polarity, as the test requires.  Because this 
research has no gravitationally relevant direction, any orientation can serve as the spatial 
reference coordinate.  The vast majority of research in electric field related combustion study is 
conducted at earth gravity, where the buoyancy is one of the key properties considered and 
repeatedly discussed.  In microgravity, a facing upright burner is equivalent to one facing upside 
down (or even sideways) scientifically because the buoyancy/gravitation force is zero.  To 
maintain the concept where the nominal field strength coincides with the direction of an ion 
driven wind that results from positive ions flowing from high to low potential, the positive field 
direction aligns with the fluid flow direction (where the jet flows) from burner to mesh, as positive 
ions repel from the burner (Enominal= -V/d); a negative electric field is the opposite direction from 
mesh to burner, and the positive ions move toward the burner, as indicated in Figure 7.

Figure 9: Ion current as a function of field strength and fuel velocity with no coflow. 
(a) 15 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
The first set of results show the voltage-current (V-I) curve for flames in microgravity.  The curves 
are qualitatively similar, with a parabolic increase in ion current with increasing nominal field 
strength, up to a peak.  Following the peak, increasing the voltage creates a distinct decrease in 
ion current, towards a saturation plateau, where the ion current remains constant with increasing 
field strength.  Although the plateau is not apparent in Figure 8, it is clearly seen in all cases when 
a sufficient field strength is applied (e.g., Fig. 9), where the sufficient field strength depends on 
the fuel flow rate and coflow.  In all the curves, the jagged features are spikes following a voltage 
step change that are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when rapid 
steps are requested.  These overshoots notwithstanding, the V-I curves follow smooth and 
reproducible trajectories. 
 
For comparison, the equivalent V-I curves for 1-g flames with the same burner configuration with 
no coflow are shown Figure 10 [J. Tinajero, dissertation, 2015].  The results are too recent to allow 
a detailed analysis and discussion, but some significant observations from these results and the 
comparison follow. 
 
1. The ion current peaks at approximately the same field strength for both velocities in 1-g while 
in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity occurs at a lower field strength, 
where the field strength at the peak current seems to scale linearly with the fuel velocity. 
   
2. In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it show a 
gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results.  Instead, there is a distinct 
peak in the ion current with a severe decrease to a saturation condition.  That is, the microgravity 
saturation is not the maximum ion current observed.  This difference is more dramatic when there 
is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment plays an important role whether caused by 
buoyancy or a forced coflow.

To help clarify some of the ion current behaviors, Figures 11-12 show representative flame images 
from the color digital camera at different field strengths for the four cases presented.  The flame 
geometry changes very little in the presence of a weak electric field.  With a weak coflow, these 
low-momentum microgravity flames form nominally spherical shapes with a weak (or no) electric 
field, as seen in the leftmost images.  But in the absence of the coflow, the flame broadens to 
reach more oxygen and lifts from the burner. 
 
From the middle three images, we can see that as the electric field increases, the ion driven wind 
pulls upwards on the flame and entrains oxidizer into it.  This increases the intensity of the 
reaction producing more ions per unit surface area and increasing the overall ion current.  At field 
strengths greater than that resulting in the peak ion current, voltage increases cause an expansion 
of the flame and a decrease in reaction intensity, which drops the overall ion current.  This does 
not happen in normal gravity because the buoyancy dominates the flame shape.  The cause for 
the expansion in the flame size at higher voltage is not yet clearly understood, though it may be 
that there is a stronger radial ion flux at higher voltages.  Regardless, the behavior of a peak ion 
current is different than that seen at normal gravity.

shown in Fig. 13 and 14, respectively.  The images are taken with different shutter speeds based 
on the flame luminosity and where the average of several background images is subtracted.  There 
is no coflow in the outer concentric region to enhance the air/fuel mixing, and hence the flame is

the start, a weak electric field is applied to help maintain the dim jet flame, demonstrated as the 
very first image of each condition (e.g., at 0.05 kV/cm).  The flame quickly responds to this weak

steady initial condition.  We call this the initial voltage, which is applied before the voltage sweep.  
During the initial voltage period, the electric field is held for at least two seconds and typically 
four seconds where the flame is nominally hemispherical (as shown in the figure) as it gradually 
lifts away from the burner tip. As shown in Figures 13 and 14, for both positive and negative field 
strengths, the ion current peaks when the flame is the most compact; specifically at field strengths

For the positive field, the voltage-current (V-I) curve in microgravity shows a very similar trend as 
is observed from the very first sets of results presented in the 2018 Spring meeting of the Central 
States Section with the 100% methane fuel condition but with additional results from over a larger 
range of voltage.  The ion current increases parabolically with the nominal field strength and then 
reaches a peak.  With a further increase in voltage, the current undergoes another parabolic-like 
decrease and slowly increases back up again.  This is shown for 70% methane in Fig. 15(a).  Similar 
increasing parabolic behavior is seen for 40% methane (Fig. 15(b)) but with a less steep 
development with the field strength.  The second increase of the ion current is not complete due 
to the low fuel concentration, power supply limits, and the fixed distance of the mesh electrode.

The results in this paragraph are for flow rates of 24 and 19 cm/s methane jet. The image data 
and ion current plots presented are preliminary results without any further polishing or detailed 
processing. The experimental test points with NASA data format and figure numbers are

Images of a methane jet flame at 19 cm/s for positive and negative field strengths, are shown in 
Fig. 17 and Fig. 19, respectively. The very first image of each condition, e.g., 0.05 kV/cm, 
demonstrates the initial voltage stage before the voltage sweep experiment.  The jet flames are 
relatively more stable initially and less stable under high voltage than the previously reported jet 
flames using a coflow burner with no coflow.  As the positive field is applied to the jet, the flame 
becomes compact in width and height. The immediate change observed is the bright soot 
aggregating around the flame tip.  With an increase of electric field strength, the flame shrinks 
and the soot is less distributed at the tip.  The voltage is swept at 350 volts per step and held at 
each voltage for two seconds. The ion current is sampled at 125 Hz (like the rest of the non-
imaging data) and the monitored current fluctuation at the same voltage step is shown in the 
graph.  The ion current to electric field strength (V-I) graph is plotted for 24 and 19 cm/s flow 
velocity in Fig. 18, and the current is initially increasing parabolically with the voltage applied.  The 
ion current corresponds to the flame appearance in that the current increases and reaches a peak 
at the most compact flame, e.g. 1.28 kV/cm for 19 cm/s (Fig. 18b) where the soot is almost gone 
(Fig. 17).  The flame base starts rising slightly around the current peak 1.28 kV/cm and lifts higher, 
with one side of the reaction wing attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further.  The 
flame is not always lifted at the same side/edge of the burner tube, therefore, the attached 
reaction wing sometimes rotates along the tube edge with approximately the same lift angle 
under the same electric field strength but even the lifted edge flame remains relatively stable.  
With further electric field increase, the flame starts fluctuating and a distinct dancing 
phenomenon can be seen from the I-V curve where the ion current oscillates widely at the same 
field strength; the fluctuation is crossing more than 3.5 A  (between ~ 1.2 to 5 A) and reaching 
5.0 A for 24 cm/s.  Similarly, this oscillation at the same voltage is observed for 19 cm/s with the 
ion current spanning around 2.5 A (~ 1.4 to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; the flame images are 
shown as 1.76 and 2.04 kV/cm in Fig. 17. These very high peak values may represent an incipient 
corona or discharge event.  The combustion extinguishes with the oscillation at 1.84 kV/cm for 24 
cm/s and 2.04 kV/cm for 19 cm/s.

Under the negative field, the methane jet flame encounters the downward ion wind (around the 
flame) and is not sustained after 1.76 kV/cm for 24 cm/s, being blown out by the electric field.  
The 19 cm/s flame lasts until 1.93 kV/cm.  When the flame experiences a negative field, its height 
decreases and the full flame is moved onto the tube, similar to a downward pointing jet flame in 
1g [Papac et al., Ann. N. Y. Acad. Sci., 2006, 1077, 585-601]. The change of the flame width is not 
as clear or obvious as with a positive field but it still changes, shown in Fig. 19 for 0.05, 0.14, and 
0.23 kV/cm.  The ion current (V-I curve, Fig. 20) also increases with the field strength but 
differently than with the positive field without a clear curved slope.  Instead, it decreases 
parabolically after reaching the current peak.  The current peak corresponds to the most compact 
flame at 0.32 kV/cm for 19 cm/s and 0.41 kV/cm for 24 cm/s.  The peak ion current is 0.53 and 
0.55 A, as shown in Fig. 20(b) and 20(a) respectively.  Soot also appears at the flame tip but with 
a wider distribution along the reaction sheet.  The soot reduces with increasing negative field 
strength, and it disappears at 0.80 kV/cm (Fig. 19) along the parabolic decay line after passing the 
ion current peak.  The flame width and height also expand after the most compact flame (at the 
peak current).  This trend is demonstrated in the images in Fig. 19 of 0.51 kV/cm and higher 
nominal field strength.  The flame is pushed down around the jet burner so that it glows red.  
Notice also that there are several sparkler-like soot particles at 1.18 and 1.93 kV/cm.  Further 
evaluation of this soot sparking is underway.

The experiment results reported above involve two types of burner and configurations using 
methane as fuel at different dilution percentage, but this section of the research is focused on the 
science of how the chemi-ions react during combustion of multi-carbon content fuel, ethylene 
(C2H4), under the influence of an electric field in a microgravity environment. Only the more 
highly diluted ethylene results are included here because the higher concentrations produce so 
much soot that the electric field effects on the flame are secondary to those effects on the soot 
directly.  In some cases, we found soot buildup on the burner and the mesh.  The lower ethylene 
concentration cases did not suffer from these complications.  Positive and negative electric fields 
are applied onto the planar mesh oriented orthogonally and around 37 mm above the fuel jet 
exit.

D. Surprises and New Discoveries 
We expect many more discoveries to arise as we sort through the detailed data sets, but the initial 
surprises and discoveries include: 
 
(1) The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, 
where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the 
flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.  These 
results show that buoyancy driven flows are an important influence on 1-g flames even when an 
electric field is applied. 
 
(2) When soot is present in a flame, electric fields create a wide range of unpredictable behaviors 
that include elimination of the soot through what appears to be enhanced mixing for combustion, 
showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable 
dancing flames.  Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar 
conditions with 1-g flames. 
 
(3) There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current.  
The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even 
though the flame is most compact. 
 
(4) The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric 
fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench.  This stabilizing feature of 
electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may 
be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity. 
 
(5) Jet flames under the influence of the electric field were unstable at high field strengths, and 
these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration 
near the jet burner tip.  The flame behavior was dramatic but difficult to characterize, suggesting 
a spatially- and time-varying field/flame interaction.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021

E. Accomplishment of Approved Objectives 
All major science objectives were accomplished.  As identified below, objectives A, B, C, and D, 
were completed with differing degrees of success. 
 
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. 
This was accomplished through the collection of V-I curves at all experiment conditions.  This 
objective was completed with great success. 
 
B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to 
large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and 
amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
Although the power supplies were not capable of rapid downward voltage changes, the upward 
steps were sufficiently fast to permit the time response evaluation.  In microgravity, the 
preliminary results suggest that the time response is faster than is seen in 1-g suggesting that the 
changes in the buoyancy driven flows play a role in the time response of these flames on earth.  
The scientific understanding associated with this objective was sufficient. 
 
C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total 
fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
This objective was only partially completed because the key soot volume fraction instrument was 
unavailable to the experiment because of the obscuration of the High-Bitdepth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera by the bracket holding the electrode mesh.  The location of the luminous soot 
was identifiable, however, so the qualitative results were completed.  There is, however, the 
potential to use additional calibration of the ACME color camera and the associated pyrometry 
and total luminosity to provide the temperature and soot volume fraction from the images that 
were collected.  This objective was met sufficiently. 
 
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the 
combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to 
stabilize or reattach these flames. 
Both aspects of flames mentioned in the objective were determined.  As mentioned above, the 
electric field was definitely successful in stabilizing flames that would otherwise quench after 
ignition or not burn stably.  There was not an opportunity to produce true near-limit lifted flames, 
but the effect of the ion-driven wind for generating more intense combustion and compact flames 
was clearly demonstrated.  This objective was met sufficiently.  
 
The formal success criteria were presented in Section 2.D.  As can be seen from the science 
objectives completed, the project definitely met the high success criteria and partially met the 
complete success criteria.  Complete success was only missed because, as described under the 
objectives, only some time response data was obtained, and there were specific cases where the 
ion-driven wind helped stabilize flames that would otherwise be difficult to achieve a sustained 
ignition.  The electric field was also able to blow out flames under some conditions.  The response 
time of the power supplies, and the inability to switch polarity during a single experiment

(different power supplies were needed) made it impossible to fully test the open loop control of 
the flame. 
 
We also had a desired objective of imaging the thermal field around the flame.  This information 
would be very valuable for providing direct imaging of the ion-driven hot gas plume.  Schlieren or 
shadowgraph imaging was not available to the ISS experiment.  One alternative would be to run 
a limited number of long-duration drop tests using a schlieren rig and an equivalent electric field 
burner, but the path to this outcome is not yet formally defined. 
 
F. Additional Objectives Achieved 
As we became more familiar with the conditions that provided the most impactful data, we 
reconstructed some test cases to provide more comprehensive matching of fundamental 
conditions.  For example, it is known that flames of similar character (i.e., temperature and 
intensity) have saturation ion currents that scale with the input carbon to the flame.  This is 
because the dominant chemical pathway to the key ion species includes HCO+.  Hence, to examine 
this feature of flames under electric field influence, we ran additional conditions with matching 
input carbon content. 
 
Matching carbon content with higher or lower flow rates: In addition to the core objectives 
achieved, experiments were run to match the carbon content of flames as a test for the role of 
fuel carbon in the ion-current peak production.  Classical theory shows that ion current scales with 
carbon content for premixed flames, and some 1-g data shows similar trends for diffusion flames, 
but no one had determined if the concept held for zero-g flames. 
 
Flame response hysteresis: We also obtained data for flames where the electric field was ramped 
up and down to determine any effects of hysteresis in the ion current or flame response.  This 
was an additional objective achieved.   
 
G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a unique data set 
of chemi-ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models 
and theories can be evaluated against the results.  As an example, the very distinctive shape of 
the V-I curve in microgravity, when matched in models, will give a very good indication that the 
feedback between ion driven wind and changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then 
further change the ion current is captured accurately. 
 
These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects 
on flames.  
 
The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated 
with combustion behavior) or actuator (ion-driven wind changes the flame shape and 
characteristics).  This work, as was originally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the 
sensing and response potential of electric fields in combustion.  The applications can include the 
control of flames.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
40 
 
Follow-On Experiments  
We hope to have a third round of testing so that we can concentrate on flames in the coflow 
burner configuration that we found to be the more useful and symmetric than those with the jet 
burner.  It is likely that the more uniform electric field is responsible for this observation.  
 
As noted above, useful results regarding the flame response time were obtained despite the slow 
response time of the power supply time through tests with fast upward voltage steps in some 
configurations.  The step response is not as comprehensive as we would like, however, to confirm 
the links between the ion driven wind as actuator and sensor. 
 
For objective D, we obtained very interesting information about flame stabilization and 
destabilization using electric fields but not in the manner we expected.  Rather the destabilizing 
influence of the field producing fluctuations in the flame was more pronounced a phenomenon 
than we had seen when buoyancy was also part of the body force involved.  We did not get to 
limit flames except that we showed clearly how in microgravity a flame can be stabilized with a 
small field rather than simply expanding and extinguishing.  So that is some information again at 
the limit.  We can discover more by concentrating on very low field strengths. 
 
The outcomes of the first two rounds justify further testing because the results were so successful.  
The success showed how perfectly the E-FIELD Flames experiment fits the capabilities and 
limitations of the CIR.  It is a configuration that can use the imaging capabilities at their current 
performance effectively.  The experiments manipulate flames between quasi-steady behaviors in 
microgravity rather than passively observing non-steady flames evolving.  The first rounds of 
testing spanned the experimental configuration space in terms of gases, flow rates, field ranges, 
and burner types.  These spanning experiments mapped the phenomena but did not allow a deep 
dive into the conditions that showed the most dramatic changes of flame character with changes 
in electric field strength.  In addition, excessive amounts of soot made unraveling some of the gas 
phase ion chemistry more complicated in the pure fuel cases, so we can now concentrate on 
moderate sooting cases.  In general, the bonus tests let us go back to the known "best case" 
situations and resolve the processes (e.g., flame shape, luminosity, soot formation and 
disappearance, ion current).  That is the matrix we proposed.  
 
It is not within the scope of the current work, but we continue to advocate for a Schlieren imaging 
capability in zero-g combustion systems.  The ability to image hot gas flows would benefit a range 
of experiments and would be particularly useful for the flames in electric field situations because 
alternative methods for determining flows would not be possible in the high field environments.  
It may be that the 5-second drop facility is appropriate for many of these companion tests.

Appendix B. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report for ISS 
Increments 55 and 56 
 
15 Nov. 2018 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report  
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 55 and 56 
 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
E-FIELD Flames 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): 
Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA 
PI project scientist: 
 
Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, University of California, Irvine, CA 
Lead collaborator: 
Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia 
NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
PS team member: 
Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, 
OH 
 
 
 
I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing 
through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and 
stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of 
ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

content:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
44 
 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.  
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests are conducted with 
methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-
producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They are conducted with both a 
simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a 
coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to 
assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provides a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), 
where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is 
measured.  The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

10 April 2021 
45 
 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone.  Length scales are 
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  Momentum-
dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low 
velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to 
their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames 
because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity 
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The 
absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability 
behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity testing 
can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application.  Chemi-ion species, electronically 
excited chemiluminescent species are very low concentration in typical flames, making the 
reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog 
ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
46 
 
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 142 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment during Increments 
55 and 56.  The first round of testing occurred from March to May 2018, which was 
followed by a second round, which began in September 2018 and was still underway at 
the beginning of Increment 57.  The first round of tests resulted in 120 ignited flames 
conducted with the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD 
Flame) experiment, where CLD Flame’s second round occurred between the two rounds 
of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results 
in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific 
outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for E-FIELD Flames, where all of the ISS 
results are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all 
currently planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the E-FIELD Flames ignited for E-FIELD Flames during Increments 55 and 
56, including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 
1.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
The primary hard drive for the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit - for 
Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on April 27, 2018 (18117).  For ACME 
experiments, the IPSU-G is used for two key cameras, the ACME color digital ‘data’ 
camera (i.e., DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, 
which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH* 
chemiluminesence.  Use of the IPSU-G was recovered by astronaut Scott Tingle on 
May 7 (18127) by the removal of that primary drive.  The removed drive was 
reinstalled on Aug. 14 (18226) by astronaut Ricky Arnold during the second round of 
CLD Flame testing.  Although the hard drive was installed in the secondary position, 
the IPSU-G surprisingly again became unusable.  Therefore, it was removed on Aug. 
22 (18234) by astronaut Alex Gerst, returning it to use, albeit without the intended 
storage capacity.

content:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
48 
 
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable in mid-Sept. 2018 and was not operable at the start of E-
FIELD Flames’ second round.  Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD 
Flames, where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for 
the mesh electrode.  Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269) and Oct. 1 (18274) were 
conducted without HiBMs imaging or the CIR illumination.  It was later determined to 
be an issue with a cable connection, which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on 
Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other ACME tasks. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are infrequent, 
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment).  It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame.  As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and 
has taken place during CLD Flame operations on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 
18022, 18038, 18046, 18143, and 18241.  In this regard, there are an assortment of 
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC tuning

10 April 2021 
49 
 
has been beneficial in some cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was 
seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was 
implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame 
measurements.  That approach has been partially successful and was introduced 
during E-FIELD Flames’ first round.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to 
each test was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round.  A replacement 
MFC for the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round 
of CLD Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.  
 
The final day of testing during E-FIELD Flame’s first round was conducted with highly 
sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, which tends to push the flame 
down toward the burner.  A significant amount of soot deposited on the burner, both 
on the inner tube from which the fuel issues as well as the honeycomb in the burner 
annulus from which the air flows.  The extent of the soot wasn’t appreciated until 
flame testing for CLD Flame’s second round began on May 25 (18145).  Additional 
evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the decision was made to 
have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was clear that the gas flow 
from the burner was affected by the soot buildup.  A cleaning procedure was 
developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on June 19 (18170).  
The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 (18172), but the 
evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue.  The cable mating 
was corrected by Arnold on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing of the cleaned 
burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177).  Regular flame testing 
in CLD Flame’s second round finally commenced on July 5 (18186), six weeks after the 
soot accumulation was identified as an issue.  However, useful scientific results were 
obtained on the June 26 evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led to a 1- 
month delay. 
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply.  Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required.  In contrast, 120 flames were ignited in the experiment’s first 
round, i.e., first half.  In that round, roughly 200% more flames were ignited than had 
been planned.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package.  Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use.

10 April 2021 
50 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful. 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the E-FIELD Flames experiments includes video recordings from the operations 
camera for general flame behavior, the ACME data camera for high resolution images at 
various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera 
images and non-imaging data at 100 Hz.  The non-imaging data is extracted using Matlab 
scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to show trends of ion 
current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters 
(fuel, flowrate, burner type).  Image data is processed using the OMA software (also 
developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).   
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day, the data 
has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At this stage, 
with operations ongoing, the analysis is comparative and qualitative, just to show the 
major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Results from the early E-FIELD Flame experiments have demonstrated clear differences 
between normal-gravity and microgravity flame behaviors.  A few examples include the 
distinct maximum of ion current for co-flow burner flames in microgravity, where the 1-g 
flames more smoothly reach a saturation condition.  The results also show that the 
electric body force can produce flame oscillations similar to those driven by buoyancy in 
normal gravity, and microgravity flame shapes with an electric field can mimic normal-

with a 3.1 cm/s coflow. (a) 15 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function 
of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve.  This curve provides information 
on the flames ability to produce chemi-ions based on its saturation ion current, and it 
provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of 
carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process.  More 
compact, higher temperature flames produce more chemi-ions than do larger more 
diffuse reaction zones of lower overall temperature for the same fuel flow.  The first effect 
(i.e., the relationship between carbon influx and peak ion current) can be seen in Figure 
2, where the flow of 15 cm/s methane produces slightly above 2 microamps of ion current 
at the peak (1.5 kV/cm) and the flow of 19 cm/s methane has a peak of 2.75 microamps.  
While the ratio is not exact, the peak ion current is nearly proportional to the flow

velocity.  Another interesting feature of these curves is the peak value.  Traditional 
electrical aspects of flames studies look for a saturation ion current plateau, where the 
ion current remains fixed despite an increase in applied electric field.  For these 
microgravity flames, there is a pronounced peak in the ion current at saturation and then 
a gradual decrease to a global saturation plateau.  This is a strikingly different behavior 
than is seen in 1-g, and the behavior is even more pronounced for the case where there 
is zero coflow. 
 
 
Figure 2. Ion current as a function of the field strength and fuel velocity with a 3.1 cm/s 
coflow. (a) 15 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
As can be seen in Figure 3, which is the same V-I curve result in microgravity for the case 
where there is no coflowing air, and Figure 4 shows the flame images.  These figures again 
show a reasonably linear scaling of peak ion current with fuel flow velocity, but they 
demonstrate a very pronounced peak ion current with a rapid drop to a global saturation 
ion current plateau.  Since these are diffusion flames, essentially all of the fuel is being 
burned independent of the flame’s shape and the applied electric field, but it seems clear 
that the electric field is affecting the chemi-ion production capability of the flame.  As is 
apparent from the flame images, the flame is most compact at the voltage consistent with 
the peak ion current.  With increasing voltage, the flame becomes less compact and the 
ion current decreases.  We presume that the flame remains at saturation throughout this 
period (that is, the flame is producing as many ions as it can, and those ions are being 
removed from the reaction zone as soon as they are created) so the decrease in ion 
current results from a change in combustion intensity.  We can explore this hypothesis 
further using the PMT data collected in the experiments.

54 
 
 
(1) The ion current reaches a peak at approximately the same field strength for both 
velocities in 1-g while in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity 
occurs at a lower field strength.  The field strength at the peak current seems to scale 
linearly with the fuel velocity. 
 
 
Figure 5. Ion current as a function of field strength and fuel velocity with no coflow in 
normal gravity. (a) 16 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane. 
 
(2) In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it 
show a gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results.  
Instead, in microgravity there is a distinct peak in the ion current with a severe 
decrease throughout the saturation condition, with a final saturation plateau 
observed at voltages substantially above the voltage at peak ion current.  That is, the 
microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed.  This 
difference is more dramatic when there is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment 
plays an important role whether caused by buoyancy or a forced coflow.  
 
(3) The peak ion current is higher for microgravity than comparison 1-g flames.  The 
reason is not obvious at this point but may result from a more focused upward flow 
from the electric body force and ion-driven wind as compared to the combined effects 
of the ion wind and buoyancy. 
 
(4) The peak ion current is approximately proportional to fuel flow velocity, which, as 
described in prior studies, reflects the relationship between ion production and the 
carbon flux into the system.  The peak ion current also increases with the coflow which 
suggests that healthier oxidizer transport helps increase the ion production.

Appendix C. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report for ISS 
Increments 57 and 58 
 
1 June 2019 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report  
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 57 and 58 
 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
E-FIELD Flames 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The investigation was carried out in two rounds of 
tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with 
a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57.  As a result, there is nothing 
to be reported for Increment 58. 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): 
Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA 
PI project scientist: 
 
Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, University of California, Irvine, CA 
Lead collaborator: 
Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia 
NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
PS team member: 
Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH 
 
 
 
I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was 
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current 
passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the

10 April 2021 
59 
 
analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the 
development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.  
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests were conducted 
with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of 
soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They were carried out with both 
a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without 
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner 
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provided a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the 
burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field 
strength was measured.  The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead 
smoothly ramped.
