content:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
60 
 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  For example, chemi-ion species, 
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, 
making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.  
With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex 
nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion 
application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console 
commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed 
in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

10 April 2021

III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58.  Note that the investigation’s 
testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 
58.  The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and 
September-November 2018.  The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited 
flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively.  The coflow burner was 
developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD 
Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned 
years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the E-FIELD Flames ignited for E-FIELD Flames during Increments 55-57, 
including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 1.

electrode.  Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269), Oct. 1 (18274), Oct. 9 (18282), 
Oct. 12 (18285), and Oct. 17 (18290) were conducted without HiBMs imaging or the 
CIR illumination.  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, which 
was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other 
ACME tasks.  As a result, the subsequent E-FIELD Flames tests were carried out using 
the HiBMs camera and illumination package. 
 
4. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling 
software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the 
igniter.  As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   
The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These 
are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment).  It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame.  As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This ACME activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame 
tests, and has taken place on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 
18046, 18143, 18241, 19059, and 19112.  In this regard, there are an assortment of 
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC 
adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It 
was seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow

was implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame 
measurements.  That approach was partially successful and was introduced during E-
FIELD Flames’ first round.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test 
was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round.  A replacement MFC for 
the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD 
Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.  
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply.  Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required.  In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly 
three times as many flames were ignited than required.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package.  Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use. 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful.

content:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
65 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings 
from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the 
ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame 
luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz.  The non-imaging 
data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame 
researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function 
of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type).  The PMT data 
is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations.  Image data is processed using 
the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).   
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day.  All of 
the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At 
this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can 
be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), 
fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high 
dilution) and fuel flow velocity.  The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were 
sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant.  At this stage, the 
analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior 
in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy 
modifies the electrical response of the flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gas-
jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner.  For example, 
the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in 
microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames 
with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report).  The parabolic behavior is evident 
even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise.  This rising trend is not 
observed with the coflow burner.   
 
The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high 
field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit 
or collect free charges.  Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the 
ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk 
flow.  These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, 
hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it 
accumulates.  More work is needed to sort through these elements. 
 
Positive electric field for 100% methane fuel with jet burner  
The preliminary findings for the gas-jet burner in this section highlight the representative 
information of electric fields applied to a small hydrocarbon flame in the 0-g condition.  
The ISS tests covered a wide range of conditions which allowed the flame to settle as its

luminosity and the ion current were also recorded in all cases.  Figure 1 shows example 
flame images representative of the jet tests conducted with methane as fuel.  The voltage 
is indicated as the nominal field strength (kV/cm).  Since the physical spacing from the 
burner to the mesh is 35 mm, 1.16 kV/cm represents nominal potential of around 4000 V 
across the flame.  It is important to note that with the sharp-edged jet burner, there is an 
electric field concentration near the burner tip, so the field in that region will be stronger 
than is indicated by the nominal field strength and stronger than would be seen for the 
coflow burner where the coflow portion of the burner acts as a planar electrode to 
mitigate the field concentration at the jet burner’s tip. 
 
 
Figure 1. Flame images observed from the data camera at 19 cm/s methane jet with 
positive field applied. (Unit: kV/cm) 
 
The very first image of each condition, e.g., at 0.05 kV/cm, demonstrates the initial 
voltage stage before the voltage sweep test commences.  The jet flames are relatively 
more stable initially and less stable under high voltage than the previously reported 
flames using a coflow burner with no coflow [Chien et al., Ion Current and Flame Changes 
with Electric Fields in Microgravity, WSSCI Pasadena 2019].  As the positive field is applied 
to the jet, the flame becomes both narrower and shorter.  An immediate change is the 
appearance of bright soot at the flame tip.  With an increase of electric field strength, the 
soot region diminishes as the flame shrinks. 
 
The voltage was increased 350 volts per step and held at each voltage for two seconds. 
The ion current data rate was 125 Hz and the monitored current fluctuation at the same 
voltage step is shown in the graph.  The ion current to electric field strength (i.e., i-v) graph 
is plotted for 24 and 19 cm/s flow velocity in Figure 2, where the current initially increases 
parabolically with the applied voltage.  The ion current corresponds to the flame 
appearance in that the current increases and reaches a peak at the most compact flame, 
e.g., at a field strength of 1.36 kV/cm for a 19 cm/s burner flow (as seen in Figure 2b).  At

that maximum, the soot is almost gone (as seen in Figure 1).  The flame base starts rising 
slightly around the current peak and lifts higher, with one side of the reaction wing 
attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further.  The flame is not always lifted 
at the same edge of the burner tube; therefore, the attached reaction wing sometimes 
rotates along the tube edge with approximately the same lift angle under the same 
electric field strength.  Otherwise, the lifted edge flame remains relatively stable.  With 
further increases in the electric field strength, the flame starts fluctuating and a distinct 
dancing phenomenon can be seen from the i-v curve where the ion current oscillates 
strongly at the same field strength.  The fluctuation crosses more than 3.5 A (between 
~1.2 to 5 A) and reaches 5.0 A for the 24 cm/s case.  Similarly, this oscillation at the 
same voltage is observed for 19 cm/s with the ion current spanning around 2.5 A (~1.4 
to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; corresponding flame images are shown as 1.86 and 2.16 
kV/cm in Figure 1.  These very high peak values may represent an incipient corona or 
discharge event.  The combustion extinguishes with the oscillations at 1.95 kV/cm for 24 
cm/s and 2.16 kV/cm for 19 cm/s.  
 
The flame geometries and soot distribution under the electric field influence clearly differ 
when comparing the gas-jet burner results with those from the earlier coflow burner tests 
without a coflow (i.e., with the same jet flow for each), where the annulus of the coflow 
burner acted as a planar electrode.  But the maximum amount of ions produced within 
the flame (as evidenced by the ion current reaching the plateau) is similar for the case 
where the fuel flow velocity matches at 19 cm/s.  The current also peaks around the same 
field strength per unit distance.  Moreover, the oscillation behavior only exists in the jet 
burner experiment and furthermore influences the ion current monitoring due to the 
unstable flame behavior responding to the high field strength.

this sparking is underway.

In all of the i-v curves, the ion current data points at each field strength stretch across 
~0.1 A for each step, which are the jagged features from the spikes following a voltage 
step change that are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when 
a rapid voltage step is requested.  These overshoots notwithstanding, the i-v curves follow 
smooth and reproducible trajectories. The wide range of the ion current after the 
saturation plateau is due instead to the flame oscillation.  
 
This report shows the initial results of the E-FIELD Flames experiment using the gas-jet 
burner in the International Space Station (ISS).  The positive field allows the soot to 
concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source.  The 
flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field 
strength.  This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow 
burner from the first round, with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 
30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between 
electric field effects, ions, and charged soot. The negative field allows the flame to 
maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity. The yellow soot appears for both of 
the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing 
field strength after reaching the current peak.  The role of soot in the i-v behavior of these 
flames requires further investigation. 
 
Early E-FIELD Flame results from the ISS testing were presented in following oral and 
poster presentations:

Diffusion Flames,” 11th Multi-Agency Coordinating Committee for Combustion 
Research (MACCCR) Annual Fuel and Combustion Research Review, Livermore, 
CA, 9-11 April 2018. (oral presentation)

Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” Central

April 2018. (conference paper and oral presentation) 
3. Chien, Y.-C., Tinajero, J., Stocker, D., Hegde, U. and Dunn-Rankin, D. “Small 
Diffusion Flames under the influences of Electric-Field: Microgravity and Gravity,” 
37th International Symposium on Combustion, Dublin, Ireland, 29 July to 3 Aug. 
2018.  (Work-in-Progress poster) 
4. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, Jesse Tinajero, Dennis Stocker, Uday Hegde, Derek Dunn-
Rankin, “Microgravity Experiments of Electric Field Effects on Laminar

Appendix D. Operational Timeline 
All dates are in 2018, when the E-FIELD Flames operations were conducted.  The following text was taken 
from the ‘ACME Activity Log (selected)’ section of the informal “ACME Operations (Ops) Log” prepared by 
Dennis Stocker.  The only addition is the identification of the investigation’s two rounds and intervening 
second round of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  The red text indicates the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
77 
 
Appendix F. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 
This text is from the ‘ACME Ops per the Payload Weekly Science Summary’ section of the informal “ACME 
Operations (Ops) Log” prepared by Dennis Stocker.  The only addition is the identification of the 
investigation’s two rounds and intervening second round of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD 
Flame) experiment.    As a minor note, the sizes of some figures were adjusted in this report, but none were 
cropped. 
 
Increment 55-56 (with round 1 featuring the coflow burner and the start of round 
2 featuring the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner) 
Week 02: March 2-8 
Nemo: Excellent job replacing the imaging module in the CIR HiBMS Imaging Package on GMT 064! Thank 
you for all your hard work and diligence during the many intricate tasks. You replaced this imaging module 
in support of the next ACME experiment, E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames). 
 
Maker: Great job installing the ACME Mesh and replacing the ACME Bypass Controller on GMT 067! Thank 
you for all your hard work and attention to detail. You performed these tasks in support of the next ACME 
experiment, E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames). 
 
E-FIELD Flames studies how electric fields at different voltages influence flames. An electric field can 
strongly influence the motion of the ions produced by a combustion reaction. The resulting ion-driven 
wind impacts flame stability and soot production and reduces pollutant emissions. The results will lead to 
a better understanding of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
Week 03: March 9-15 
On GMT 073, we performed the first ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points. This first day was very successful with ten flames ignited for studying the effects of 
an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show that the high-voltage electric field 
created forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot 
production. The ability to control flames with an electric field may have practical applications on Earth. 
For example, an electric field could be used to stabilize a flame in fuel-lean conditions, which would lead 
to reduced pollutant emissions compared to a typical combustor. 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
While the light is still on at the beginning of this video, you can see the copper mesh, which is 
used to create the electric field. Before the electric field is activated, the flame is dim and 
spherical. However, as the negatively-charged copper mesh is energized at a steadily increasing 
potential, the flame becomes brighter and narrower—transforming into a shape similar to that of 
flames in normal gravity. The bright yellow tip is caused by soot. Near the end of the test, the 
flame suddenly becomes dim and spherical again when the electric field is deactivated. (This video 
is at 2x normal speed.) 
 
Week 04: March 16-22 
Anton & Maker: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottles this week! The new Manifold #2 bottle allows 
us to continue performing test points in a combustion chamber environment of air, and the new Manifold 
#4 bottle allows us to perform test points with diluted methane instead of pure methane.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
78 
 
On GMT 078 and 080, we continued performing ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames) test points to study the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. All tests 
so far have used pure and nitrogen-diluted methane, the dominant component of natural gas. 
 
 
Figure 1. Composite Image of E-FIELD Flames at Increasingly Negative Electric-field Potential (100% 
Methane) 
 
Following ignition, the copper electrode mesh (downstream of the burner) is energized at a relatively low 
voltage and is then gradually stepped up to several kilovolts. In the current testing, the mesh is negatively 
charged relative to the burner. As a result, the electric field enhances the upward motion of the transient 
positive ions within the flame, inducing an “ion wind,” which affects the overall gas motion. 
 
Figure 1 shows how an increasingly negative electric-field potential affects a flame during a single test 
point. The resultant “ion wind” dramatically affects the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production (the 
bright flame tip is caused by soot). This flame used 100% methane fuel; whereas, the tests conducted with 
40% methane were soot-free under all conditions tested. 
 
(Note that this is a preliminary image, where the apparent flame luminosity is not consistent from flame 
to flame.) 
 
Week 05: March 23-29 
Anton: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new bottle allows us to perform test 
points with ethylene fuel instead of methane. 
 
On GMT 087, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) test 
points using pure ethylene fuel. 
 
Week 06: March 30 - April 5 
Anton: Thank you for replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle on GMT 089. The new bottle allows us to perform 
test points with diluted ethylene fuel instead of pure ethylene. 
 
Maker: On GMT 093, great job installing the ACME Mesh Pos Power Supply and replacing the ACME igniter 
tip! You removed the negative power supply and installed the positive one to allow us to perform test 
points using a positively charged electric field to influence the flame. You replaced the igniter tip for 
preventative maintenance. We returned to performing test points later in the week. 
 
On GMT 092, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) test 
points using diluted ethylene fuel. Our first test points using ethylene fuel instead of methane were 
performed on GMT 087. These used pure ethylene. Ethylene produces a lot of soot when it burns, and we 
are investigating how an electric field influences this soot production.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
79 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This video shows two test points side-by-side to compare the burning characteristics of 100% and 
30% ethylene. The 100% ethylene flame is much bigger and brighter than the 30% flame (the 
copper mesh is illuminated by the brightness). The yellow color is caused by soot with the 30% 
flame having only a yellow tip. As the negatively charged copper mesh is energized at a steadily 
increasing potential, both flames become narrower in shape and bluer in color. The changes in 
the 100% flame are visually more dramatic. 
 
When the electric field is deactivated near the end of the tests, the flames suddenly become 
broader and brighter again. The yellow tip of the 30% flame returns as well as the soot “horns” of 
the 100% flame. These soot “horns” are caused by heavy soot production just within the flame. 
Looking closely at the video, you can see where soot escaping from the 100% flame forms a 
discolored ring on the copper mesh. This soot escaped because of the sudden end to the 
intensified combustion created by the electric field. 
 
Week 07: April 6-12 
Anton: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottles this week! The new Manifold #2 bottle allows us to 
continue performing test points in a combustion chamber environment of air. The new Manifold #4 bottle 
allows us to again perform test points with diluted methane but this time with a positively charged electric 
field. 
 
On GMT 095, we performed our first ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points with a positively charged electrode mesh. These tests demonstrated the ability of the 
electric field to control the soot characteristics of a flame. We observed that the flames (30% ethylene) 
became soot-free at high electric-field potentials. While soot can be advantageous for some combustion 
processes, e.g., to enhance radiant heating, it is a health concern and often unwanted. Today’s tests 
demonstrated the potential for the practical application of electric fields to control soot within flames. 
One of the goals of E-FIELD Flames is to gain a fundamental understanding of this capability, which could 
lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
At the start of this test, before the positively charged electric field is activated, the top half of the 
flame is yellow because of the glowing soot. As the voltage is increased—ultimately to 10 
kilovolts—the soot fades away (so the flame is all blue), the flame shifts toward the burner, and 
the base dramatically broadens. The effect of the electric field on the flame can truly be seen 
when the electric field is deactivated near the end of the test, and the flame quickly returns to its 
natural state.    
 
Week 08: April 13-19 
Drew: Thank you for replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle on GMT 108. The new bottle will allow us to again 
perform test points with pure methane but this time with a positively charged electric field. 
 
On GMT 102 and 106, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points using diluted methane fuel. The first set of E-FIELD Flames tests uses a burner that can 
simultaneously flow air and a gaseous fuel mixture.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
80 
 
 
Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with (left) and without (right) a Simultaneous Flow of Air 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
The “red” flame in Figure 1 benefited from the oxygen supplied by the simultaneous flow of air from the 
burner; in contrast, the “blue” flame relied on entrainment and diffusion for its oxygen supply. Although 
the fuel velocity is the same in both tests, the small “red” flame is attached to the burner, while the “blue” 
oxygen-starved flame is much wider and is lifted from the burner. These characteristics help the “blue” 
flame get the oxygen required to consume the fuel. Meanwhile, the “red” flame gets that oxygen in a 
much smaller zone thanks to the presence of the simultaneous flow of air. 
 
 
Figure 2. E-FIELD Flames at Increasing Fuel Velocity (No Simultaneous Flow of Air) 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
Figure 2 shows flames at increasing fuel velocities. Although the positive electric field tends to force the 
flames downward toward the burner, the flames are lifted from the burner because they are oxygen 
starved without the simultaneous flow of air. More oxygen is required to burn higher fuel flow rates, and 
the diameter at the base of the flame correspondingly increases. The distance that the flame is lifted from 
the burner also increases with the fuel velocity, where the separation allows more oxygen to reach the 
flame. The flame length is another measure of the oxygen transport, where the flame extends until it gets 
enough oxygen to consume all of the fuel. 
 
Week 09: April 20-26 
On GMT 113, we again performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points using pure methane, but this time with a positively charged electrode mesh. Like we 
observed with 30% ethylene tests (GMT 095), these tests also showed the strong effect that an electric 
field can have on soot within the flame.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
81 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG  
In this test, just after ignition, the electric field is energized at a very low voltage. The small flame, 
with its yellow/orange top, stabilizes for several seconds. Then, the voltage is quickly increased to 
1 kilovolt. Under the influence of this electric field, you can see the flame broaden, turn all blue 
in color (i.e., become soot free), and become quite dim at the tip. When the electric field is 
deactivated just before the end of the test, the flame quickly returns to its initial condition—with 
its sooty top. 
 
Week 10: April 27 – May 3 
On GMT 117, the boot drive in the FCF Image Processor failed. As this hard drive stores all our science 
image data, we were unable to perform the planned ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames) test points. Next week, the crew will remove this hard drive, so we can boot up 
the FCF Image Processor from its other hard drive. Once this hard drive is ready to go as the new boot 
drive, we plan to get back to performing test points. 
 
ACME E-FIELD Flames Test Point Early Results 
 
Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with and without a Simultaneous Flow of Air at Increasingly Negative Electric-
field Potential (100% Methane) 
 
Figure 1 shows how the flame changes as the potential of the negatively-charged electric field is increased. 
The top row of flames benefitted from the oxygen supplied by air flowing from the burner at the same 
time as the fuel. The bottom row of flames had no extra flow of air—only the oxygen in the air-like 
environment of the Combustion Chamber. In both cases, the effect of the electric field on the flame shape 
and size is dramatic. The ion wind, an upward flow created by the negatively-charged electric field, 
enhances oxygen transport to the flame causing it to become narrower and shorter. 
 
The negatively-charged electric field also affects the ion current, or the electric current that passes 
through the flame due to the motion created by the ion wind. As the electric field continues to increase 
in strength, the ion current peaks then sharply drops to a lower ion current and the flame size increases 
correspondingly. In comparable testing in normal gravity, the ion current peaked at a lower current then 
plateaued instead of sharply dropping like the microgravity tests. Figure 2 below compares the 
microgravity tests with and without the simultaneous flow of air. The flames without the simultaneous 
flow of air peak at a lower ion current and at a lower field strength compared to flames with a 
simultaneous flow of air.

content:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
83 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG  
At the start of this test, the 100% ethylene flame is broad and bright with soot “horns.” These 
soot “horns” are caused by heavy soot production just within the flame. As the positively charged 
electric-field starts to strengthen, the flame starts to vigorously oscillate. You can see hot soot 
particles stream from the flame, where they would normally be consumed as they pass through 
the flame sheet. 
  
At about 3 kilovolts, the flame steadies and flattens because the positively charged electric-field 
tends to push the flame toward the burner. It appears that the soot is trapped within the flame 
by thermophoresis, in which the soot particles are driven from hot to cold. At about 8 kilovolts, 
the flame begins to pulse strongly in an axisymmetric fashion; whereas, the earlier oscillations 
were asymmetric. Finally, when the electric field is deactivated, the soot streams from the top of 
the flame.  
 
One of the goals of E-FIELD Flames is to gain a fundamental understanding of using electric fields 
to control soot production in flames. Results could ultimately lead to more efficient and less 
polluting combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
CLD Flame round 2 featuring ethylene 
 
E-FIELD Flames round 2 featuring the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner 
 
Week 31: September 21-27 
Sergey & Ricky: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new Manifold #4 bottle allows 
us to perform test points with ethylene fuel instead of methane fuel. 
 
On GMT 269, we successfully began the second round of testing for ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field 
Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames). The first round of testing was conducted with the coflow burner, 
which can simultaneously flow air and a gaseous fuel mixture. This round of testing uses a gas-jet burner, 
which can only flow a gaseous fuel mixture. Comparison of the results will allow an improved 
understanding of the importance of the coflow and the air entrainment on the flames.   
 
Today, we successfully ignited eleven flames using 40% methane fuel, and the electrode mesh was used 
to create a negatively charged electric field. A gradual increase in the electric-field strength caused the 
dim blue flames to intensify, lift from the burner and tilt—where lifted flames are very sensitive to flow 
conditions. At higher field strengths, the flames strongly oscillated and sometimes blew out.

10 April 2021 
84 
 
Figure 1. Two Preliminary Monochrome E-FIELD Flames Images from the Same Test (40% Methane) 
Due to a higher negatively charged electric-field strength, the right-hand flame in Figure 1 is lifted from 
the burner and tilts to the side. An electric field can strongly influence the motion of the ions produced 
by a combustion reaction. This ion motion affects the motion of neutral molecules, creating an ion wind. 
The overall result is similar to gravity’s buoyant effect on flames, where the hot gases are accelerated 
upward. 
 
Week 32/01: September 28 – October 4 
Sergey: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new Manifold #4 bottle allows us to 
perform test points with pure methane fuel instead of diluted ethylene fuel. 
 
On GMT 274, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) test 
points using 30% ethylene fuel. In contrast to the 40% methane flames from last week’s tests, these flames 
were more stable despite their greater dilution. These tests demonstrated that a moderate negatively 
charged electric field can be used with the gas-jet burner to intensify a flame without causing it to become 
unstable. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
While the light is still on at the beginning of this video, you can see the copper mesh, which is 
used to create the electric field. Before the electric field is activated, the flame is extremely dim. 
It brightens significantly and gains a sooty tip as the mesh is activated, where the electric field 
induces an ion wind enhancing the transport of oxygen to the flame. As the electric field ramps 
up in voltage, the flame shrinks dramatically in size and becomes much more intense because of 
the electric field’s strong effect on the oxygen transport. Flames grow to reach the oxygen needed 
to burn the fuel, so better oxygen transport leads to smaller and more intense flames. At a 
sufficiently high voltage, the slightly lifted flame becomes unstable and partially detaches from 
the burner. As the voltage ramps down, the flame stabilizes and grows in size. We study the 
repeated ramping of the field strength because depending on the ramp (e.g., up vs. down) subtle 
differences can be seen in the flame behavior at the same voltage. 
 
Increment 57-58 (with the rest of round 2, which features the 2.1-mm gas-jet 
burner) 
Week 02: October 5-11 
Sergey: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new Manifold #4 bottle allows us to 
perform test points with ethylene fuel instead of methane fuel. 
 
On GMT 282, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) test 
points using 100% and 70% methane fuel. With these tests, we observed that the high-concentration 
methane flames on the gas-jet burner were extremely faint and soot-free until the electric field was 
activated. As we increased the field strength of the negatively charged copper mesh, the flames narrowed, 
brightened significantly, and gained sooty tips…until they became soot-free after lifting off the burner. 
Many of the flames extinguished at higher voltages, further demonstrating the strong effect that an 
electric field can have on a flame. 
 
Methane, which is the primary component of natural gas, is an ideal gas to study for combustion research 
because its chemistry is well understood. However, our understanding of the role of ions—especially

10 April 2021 
85 
 
under the influence of an electric field—is limited. The E-FIELD Flames experiment seeks to overcome this 
shortfall and explore how electrical fields may be used to manipulate combustion for practical benefit. 
 
Figure 1 shows consecutive images of a 100% methane flame taken with increasingly longer exposure 
times. The high-voltage electric field transformed the flame into a shape similar to that of flames in normal 
gravity (i.e., narrower and with a pointed tip). Without the electric field, the flame tip is rounded, and the 
flame is much broader and soot-free. 
 
Week 03: October 12-18 
Sergey: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new Manifold #4 bottle allows us to 
perform test points with diluted methane fuel instead of pure ethylene fuel. 
 
On GMT 285 and 290, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points with ethylene concentrations of 100% and 80%. With these tests, we observed how a 
negatively-charged electrode mesh affected sooty flames at high ethylene concentrations and at different 
fuel velocities. 
 
E-FIELD Flames studies how electric fields influence flames. An electric field can strongly influence the 
motion of the ions produced by a combustion reaction. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically 
affect flame stability, structure, and soot production. The results show a strong potential for an innovative 
approach to reducing pollutant emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth. 
 
Week 04: October 19-25 
Alex: On GMT 095, great job installing the ACME Mesh Pos Power Supply and replacing the ACME igniter 
tip! You removed the negative power supply and installed the positive one to allow us to perform test 
points using a positively charged electric field to influence the flame. You replaced the igniter tip for 
preventative maintenance. We returned to performing test points later in the week. 
 
Also, thank you for checking the CIR I/O Processor Custom Cable #1 connection to the Optics Bench 
connector saver. You checked this connection because we were having communication issues with one of 
our image processors on the back of the Optics Bench. Good news! On GMT 298, we successfully 
established communication with this package! We would like a couple more successful interactions with 
this package before we’re certain the anomaly is solved, but we are hopeful!

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
86 
 
Week 05: October 26 – November 1 
Sergey: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottles this week! The new bottles allowed us to continue 
performing test points. 
 
Alex: Thank you for removing the CIR burst disks and opening all the gas chromatograph (GC) manifold 
bottles. These tasks have prepared the CIR GC system for a bakeout next week. The next ACME 
experiment—BRE (Burning Rate Emulator)—plans to use the GC to sample the chamber environment 
before and after test points. 
 
On GMT 298 and 302, we performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points with 40% methane and 30% ethylene. These tests were conducted with the positively-
charged electrode mesh, which tends to push the flame toward and around the narrow burner. This 
technology could have practical terrestrial applications in stabilizing flames burning at fuel-lean 
conditions, which generate less nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur oxides (SOx). NOx and SOx cause acid 
rain. On Earth, combustion is the principal human cause of both acid rain and greenhouse gas production. 
 
 
Figure 1. Image of an E-FIELD Flame Around the Burner Tip (40% Methane) 
 
Figure 1 shows how the flame gets pushed “down” and around the burner tip due to the electric field 
resulting from the positively-charged electrode mesh. 
 
Week 07: November 9-15 
Sergey: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold Bottle this week! The new Manifold #4 bottle allows us to 
perform test points with pure ethylene fuel instead of pure methane fuel. 
 
On GMT 312, we ignited 13 flames with 100% methane fuel for ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects 
on Laminar Diffusion Flames). To date, 500 flames have been ignited for ACME! ACME, which is planned 
to run through the end of 2019, includes E-FIELD Flames and five other experiments that use gaseous 
fuels. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
While the light is still on at the beginning of this video, you can see the positively-charged 
electrode mesh, which is used to create an electric field. The flame starts off extremely dim and 
“standing” off the end of the burner tip. The electric field pushes the flame onto the burner tip.

10 April 2021 
87 
 
You can see the burner tip glow when it gets heated by the surrounding flame. This test was 
particularly interesting because it resulted in the glowing burner as well as a small “fireworks” 
show, including both arcing and glowing particles (e.g., soot particles). The particles are charged 
and can be seen to move away from the electrode mesh and towards the methane gas flowing 
from the burner. Similar tests on this day didn’t result in such “fireworks,” so this phenomenon 
will be studied more closely. 
 
Week 08: November 16-22 
On GMT 319, we performed the final test points for the second round of testing for ACME E-FIELD Flames 
(Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames). These test points used ethylene fuel concentrations 
ranging from 25% to 100%. Today’s plan was to focus on high concentrations, namely 80% and 100%, 
where ethylene’s carbon double bond can make highly sooty flames. The soot particles are naturally 
charged and cause the flame to be strongly affected by the electric field. However, we adjusted the plan 
because the high fuel concentrations at a high electric-field strength led to electrical breakdown, sparks 
and arcing, which interfered with our measurement objectives. To reduce the extent of the electrical 
breakdown, we performed the day’s remaining test points at lower ethylene concentrations, which 
provided more useful data. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This test point video shows the strong effect of an electric field on an 80% ethylene flame. When 
the electric field is activated, the flame intensifies, and the soot, which causes the yellow flame 
color, gets brighter. As the field strength is increased, the flame becomes shorter and narrower. 
The flame then engulfs the burner outlet as the positively-charged electric field pushes the flame 
away. You can see sparks at the flame tip and later throughout the flame. The flame tip—in both 
position and soot intensity—oscillates at varying speeds, sometimes becoming steady for a 
moment. The flame continues to shrink in size until it basically encircles just the tip of the burner. 
You can see bright spots intermittently at the flame tip. At the highest voltages, soot periodically 
bursts toward the electrode mesh and arcing becomes visible at the mesh. When the electric field 
is deactivated, the flame gets bigger and dimmer until it goes out when the fuel is shut off.

Neglecting minor reformatting, e.g., re-sizing of images, the only change was an updating of a web site

The weekly recap is available from e-mail or www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/index.html. 
 
Note that hyperlinks were generally not included in the excerpts below, but they typically go to web pages 
accessible via https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/experiments/explorer/.  Those 
pages are secondary sources of information for the ACME project, for which the primary web site is 
https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/. 
 
E-FIELD Flames round 1 featuring the coflow burner 
 
Week of March 12, 2018 
Crew begins first week of new ACME operations 
The Advanced Combustion Microgravity Experiment (ACME) investigation is a set of studies of gaseous 
flames to be conducted in the Combustion Integration Rack (CIR), one of which being Electric-Field Effects 
on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames).  
 
In E-FIELD Flames, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner 
and a mesh electrode. The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are 
strongly affected by a high-voltage electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence 
the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion 
current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity enables new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
This week marks the first week of E-FIELD flames operations with a very successful first set of ten flames 
ignited for studying the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show 
that the high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy. This effect dramatically affected the 
flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production.

is in support of the Advanced Combustion Microgravity Experiment (ACME). ACME is a set of five 
independent studies researching gaseous flames in space that may enable more fuel efficient and less 
polluting technologies on Earth.

Roscosmos opened up the Combustion Integrated Rack in the afternoon and replaced manifold

the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), enable the safe research of high temperatures, flames and gases.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
97 
 
Appendix J. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The E-FIELD Flames data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for 
the other current ACME experiments.  To be clear, there is no collection of soot or other physical samples 
that are subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The E-FIELD Flames image data includes images from the ACME DataCam, the CFI intensified camera (used 
with the CH* filter), and the High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera (equipped with a red filter 
corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package).  The DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic 
Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are in a Tagged Image File (tif) 
format.  In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s 
Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
109 
 
UC Irvine (https://uci.edu). The experiment which is currently operating in the space 
station's Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) is led by Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin (right) 
and Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien (left). The fifth test day in the current round of testing 
is scheduled for tomorrow, Oct. 17. Next week, the high-voltage power supply will be 
swapped by the space station commander, Alex Gerst. The subsequent four days of 
tests will be carried out with a positively-charged electrode mesh, where the recent 
tests have been carried out with a negatively-charged mesh. The ion wind resulting 
from the electric field tends to lift the flame when the mesh is negatively charged and 
push it back toward the burner when it is positively charged.” 
 
Educational outreach related to the experiment was carried out by doctoral student Claudia Lopez-
Camara, where these presentations are just two examples: 
McBride, S., Munoz Abujder, R., Putman, E., Ramya Bhaskar, R., Lopez-Camara, C.-F., and Helmig, 
J. (2018) “A Space Science Curriculum to Initiate Student Interest in STEM,” 2018 ISS Research 
and Development Conference, San Francisco, July 23-26. 
McBride, S., Munoz Abujder, R., Putman, E., Ramya Bhaskar, R., Lopez-Camara, C.-F., and Helmig, 
J. (2018) “Space Science Outreach to Initiate Early Interest in STEM,” Annual Meeting of the 
American Society for Gravitational and Space Research Annual Meeting, Rockville, MD, Oct. 
31 - Nov. 3. 
 
Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of 
Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018 – during the first round of E-
FIELD Flames testing. 
 
Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project and specifically the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018 by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, 
“International Space Station (ISS) Combustion Experiments.” 
 
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts 
of both genders, and the general public.   His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity (for which resources are available via  http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human 
spaceflight.  But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA 
and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL.  In this 
regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online.  For example, he 
regularly presents on microgravity at  Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Educators 
Conference (SEEC).   He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, four national Boy Scout 
conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree - 
which was hosted in the U.S.  Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in 
these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually described at 
www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

content:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
13 
3.0 
EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION INTERFACES 
ACME commands originate from the ACME Ground Software (AGS) CSCI on a ground 
workstation at the Telescience Center (TSC) at Glenn Research Center (GRC).  These commands 
are then forwarded through a variety of systems until they eventually end up at the CIR on the 
ISS.   
 
Figure 1  ACME System Diagram 
 
 
3.1 
CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) Interface 
Commands sent through the CIR IOP (Input Output Processor) are in the format required by 
FCF-ICD-0076A.  See section A.1, FCF Command Protocol for a listing of the required 
command formats, including all required headers.  All commands from the ground go to the IOP 
with the FCF Command Header and User Data filled in.  Commands from ACME to the IPSUs 
and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the 
packet to the IOP for routing.

3.1.1 
ACME Commands 
Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of 
commands. 
Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a 
string is less than the available length then a terminating zero character needs to be used.  The ground command software will make 
this transparent to the normal user. 
The Common Group is so-named because it is implemented in code shared between payloads.

3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description

2

Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2)

Area for module command-dependent parameters.

FtpSendFile 
The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine. 
Command ID: 0xC015 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_FILE 
 
3.1.2.22 
FtpSendDirectory 
The FtpSendDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpLocalDirectory command 
and the FtpRemoteDirectory command to copy a directory recursively from the local machine to

FtpGetFile

ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC017 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_FILE

SetSource 
The SetSource command provides the source for filesystem commands. The path may be an 
absolute path or a relative path. If a relative path is given it is combined with the current working

CompareCrcTwoFiles 
The CompareCrcTwoFiles command performs a SHA256 (Secure Hash Algorithm) on two files 
and compares the values. Source directory is set via the SetSource command and the destination 
directory is set via the SetDestination command.  If a relative path is given for either source or 
destination it is combined with the current working directory from a single or series of 
ChangeDirectory commands to form the complete path. The file1 specified in the command is 
combined with the calculated source path and file2 is combined with the calculated destination 
path.

SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

3.1.3.3 
SystemCloseTestPoint 
The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE 
3.1.3.4 
SystemResetMotionController 
The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER 
 
3.1.3.5 
SystemCirFlowState 
The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
} 
 
 
Command ID: 0xC107 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_CIR_FLOW_STATE

IntensifiedCameraSafe 
The IntensifiedCameraSafe command  places the intensified camera in a state that is safe for 
turning on lights without harming the camera by sending commands to the IPSUG.  The filter is 
commanded to home position and a fixed delay occurs to allow this to finish (without checking 
that it is finished).  Then the filter is sent to a safe position with another fixed delay.  The gain is 
set to 2048 (reporting back 2500).  Gate type is set to pulsed and gate width is set to zero 
(reporting back 20).  The delays and safe parameters are defined in the Intensifier group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. 
 
Command ID: 0xC226

3.1.5 
ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter.

3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

IgniterMotorSetState 
The IgniterMotorSetState command disables or enables the igniter motor by setting the RST line 
on the stepper driver to 0 V or 5 V respectively.  In normal operations this command should not 
be necessary because the motor is automatically enabled as soon as the cube is active (the signal 
originates in the cube), and is disabled when the software shuts down.  For reference, the stepper 
driver module is an Intelligent Motion System (IMS) XIM481H installed on an IMS INT-481 
board with MS0, MS2, and MS3 in the on position. 
 
To reset the motion controller board instead use the SystemResetMotionController command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC307

ACME Flow Group Command Details 
For flow group commands refer to the latest revision of drawing S1101MFS004, “ACME/CIR 
Integrated Pneumatic Schematic” to see how flow devices are connected to each other.  A screen 
shot of the ACME CIA portion of this drawing (Rev A) is shown below.  Gas from the CIR 
comes in at the bottom of the diagram; fuel through QD11, nitrogen bypass through QD12, and 
static mixer through QD13.

3.1.6.1 
FlowEnableMfcs 
The FlowEnableMfcs command turns the mass flow controllers on or off.  Initially they are all 
turned on as soon as the cube boots.  After this first power-on the MFCs are queried for their 
configuration, including full scale flow which appears in telemetry.  Subsequent commanded 
power-ons do not cause a query of configuration.

3.1.6.5 
FlowMfcSerialCommand 
The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is 
specified by the registry value: Flow/MfcSerialCommandTimeoutMsec.  See Table 32.

3.1.6.11 
FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing ramping 
continues until complete.

3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

3.1.7.11 
PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)

3.1.8 
ACME E-Field Group Command Details 
3.1.8.1 
EFieldEnable 
The EFieldEnable command enables or disables the high voltage supply that powers the electric 
field mesh.  This command also effectively performs a EFieldSetVoltage command with voltage 
parameter equal to zero prior to an enable and after a disable.  Any waveforms are stopped by a 
disable. 
 
This command controls the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-6 (HV2_EN) signal.  See Table 18. 
 
The high voltage supply is an Ultravolt part number 20A12-N4-Y6-C. 
 
Command ID: 0xC601 
Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_ENABLE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description 
state 
1 
Uint8 
0 = Disable 
1 = Enable 
Disable sets HV_EN to 0V.  Enable sets 
HV_EN to 5V. 
 
3.1.8.2 
EFieldSetVoltage 
The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
stepVoltage < 0 starts at maxVoltage and steps to minVoltage (and back up if cycles 
> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

EFieldRectangularWave 
The EFieldRectangularWave command is an EFieldSteppedSignal command but there is a 
second step with its own size and duration.  The two step sizes can be the same or opposite 
polarity. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

minVoltage + stepAVoltage.

DNx-AI-207 Board 
This analog input layer in the UEI PowerDNA Cube has 16 differential input channels with an input range of +/-10 Volts and 18-bit 
resolution.  Several gains are available but ACME is using a gain of 1.

MFCA1 Flow Rate 
0 to 5 V 
Static mixer/oxygen mass flow controller flow rate. 0 to 
MFCA1_FULL_SCALE in SLPM.  Flow rate (SLPM) = Voltage / 5.0 
* MFCA1_FULL_SCALE.  Device is Teledyne Hastings HFC-D-302.  
Full scale depends on installed device. 
AIN-1 
MFCA2_FLOW 
MFCA2 Flow Rate 
0 to 5 V

* MFCA2_FULL_SCALE.   Device is Teledyne Hastings HFC-D-302.

AIN-2

0 to 5 V 
Fuel mass flow controller flow rate. 0 to MFCA2_FULL_SCALE in

installed device.

-1.5 to 1.5V 
Measurement of ion current between E-Field grid and burner. Ion 
Current (A) = 1000 * Voltage/162, where Rsense is resistance of shunt 
resistor and RDA is the data acquisition resistance.  -25 to 25 µA..

using Pressure (psia) = (Voltage – 0.5) * 14.5038 * 10 / 4. Device is
