view, blocks the flame. 
In microgravity, flames aren’t supplied oxygen through buoyant convention. As a result, low-momentum 
flames like these in a quiescent (still) atmosphere tend to be quite weak and self-extinguish. Microgravity 
is an extremely useful for environment for this experiment since a key objective is to study flame dynamics 
and extinction. 
 
Week 29: September 20 - 26 
On GMT 266, Luca Parmitano replaced the ACME Fuel Controller and the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and 
CIR Manifold #4. These changes support the next ACME s-Flame test points, which will be in a chamber 
environment of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm) and will use diluted methane fuel at faster flow 
rates. 
 
Week 5: October 25 - 31 
On GMT 297 on the back of the CIR Optics Bench, Jessica Meir removed a failed hard drive from the FCF 
Image Processor and then replaced the FCF Image Processor. On GMT 301, the CIR was powered up and 
a checkout of the new FCF Image Processor was successful. We returned to performing test points later 
in the week! 
 
Week 6: November 1 - 7 
On GMT 304 and 308, 30 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and 
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). These tests burned methane fuel diluted with nitrogen in 
atmospheres of 21% and 30% oxygen (with a balance of nitrogen). Methane is the primary component of 
natural gas. These test points focused on determining where the radiative heat loss or velocities are too 
high for the flame to be sustained, which are known as the radiative and convective extinction limits. 
Radiative heat transport is much more important under microgravity conditions because the hot gases 
don’t buoyantly rise from the flame. 
 
ACME s-Flame Images 
 
This figure shows three flames of 45% methane burning in 30% oxygen. The gaseous methane fuel flows 
from the porous sphere of the burner, which is visible in the flame’s center. The flow of fuel increases 
from left to right, which increases the size of the flame. The burner’s fuel supply tube is visible below the 
sphere. The flame loses heat to this tube causing an opening, which typically grows with time as the flame 
weakens. In the flame on the right, the opening is comparatively small, which signifies a stronger flame.

In the left and center images, the glow of a 14-micron ceramic fiber is visible above the flame. Where the 
fiber is visibly glowing, the flame’s temperature at that point can be determined via color-ratio pyrometry, 
which uses a color camera characterized for that purpose. The faint glow of a second fiber further from 
the flame can be seen at the top of the center image. When the image on the right was captured, the fiber 
array was not yet inserted into the flame. 
 
Week 8: November 15 - 21 
On GMT 323, Drew Morgan replaced the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME 
s-Flame test points using pure hydrogen fuel in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
Week 12: December 13 - 19 
On GMT 347, Drew Morgan replaced the ACME Bypass and Fuel Controllers to support the ACME s-Flame 
(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points on GMT 352, which flowed nitrogen 
and fuel at slower flow rates.  
 
Ten flames were successfully ignited on GMT 352. These tests were conducted with nitrogen-diluted 
hydrogen fuel making the flames very faint. The CIR is equipped with an intensified camera, which images 
these very faint flames by visualizing the ultraviolet emission of the OH molecule (at 310 nm) as it drops 
to a lower energy level. This process is known as chemiluminescence. Thus far, there has only been a 
preliminary review of some image data. These tests used hydrogen fuel in differing concentrations with 
both steady and ramped flow rates. The tests with ramped flow rates investigated extinction 
characteristics of the flame. 
 
Week 14: December 27 - January 2 
On GMT 358, Luca Parmitano replaced the ACME Bypass and Fuel Controllers to support ACME s-Flame 
(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points with faster nitrogen and fuel flow rates. 
 
On GMT 002, Oleg Skripochka and Luca Parmitano replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME 
s-Flame test points using a hydrogen/methane fuel mixture in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
 
2020 
Week 15: January 3 - 9 
On GMT 006, 17 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which uses spherically-symmetric diffusion flames to investigate fundamental 
processes, such as flame extinction. These tests were conducted with a mixture of hydrogen (20%), 
methane (25%), and nitrogen (55%) ejected from the porous spherical burner into a chamber atmosphere 
of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). The dim, soot-free flames exhibited local quenching due to 
radiative heat loss and reignition, which sometimes occurred repeatedly. In these cases, the dynamic parts 
of the broken flame sometimes appear to dance around the burner.  
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a non-sooty (blue) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter. The 
harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers moves in from the left to a fixed position. The glow 
from the fibers allows for a good estimation of the local temperature. The flame starts “dancing,” 
where it partially quenches due to radiative heat loss and the remaining flame stretches and 
circles around the burner through a repeated combination of quenching and reignition. The fuel

Week 16: January 10 - 16 
On GMT 013, 22 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which is a record number of sustained flames in a single day of testing for all the ACME 
experiments! Like the tests performed on GMT 006, these tests burned a mixture of hydrogen, methane, 
and nitrogen but with a greater hydrogen concentration relative to the methane concentration. Even 
though these flames were less dynamic than the “dancing” flames from GMT 006, they did break apart 
and create flamelets. The flamelets were about 1 cm across and were shaped like curved bands or circles 
rather than spheres or ellipsoids. 
 
 
This figure shows four different tests from GMT 013, where the flow rate of the hydrogen/methane fuel 
increases from left to right while the nitrogen flow rate remains constant. The burner, with its supply tube 
and porous sphere, is opposite the flame. The fuel and nitrogen both flow from the burner sphere into a 
chamber atmosphere of ~19% oxygen and nitrogen at a pressure of ~1 atm. 
 
The bright horizontal lines in each flame are the glowing 14-micron ceramic fibers, where that glow can 
be used to determine the flame’s temperature. As the fuel flow rate increases, the flames become larger 
and separate flamelets form. For these tests, the flow rate was increased to explore flame stability and 
extinction limits.

ACME s-Flame test points using pure hydrogen fuel in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm).

Diffusion Flames). These tests were conducted with nitrogen-diluted hydrogen fuel making the flames 
very faint. Even though the flames were barely visible, their presence was obvious due to the 
measurements of various instrumentation, including thermocouples, radiometers, and photomultiplier 
tubes. The glowing ceramic fibers were also a positive indication of a flame. The harp-like array of 14-
micron ceramic fibers was translated into the flame to make optical measurements of the flame 
temperature from the hot fibers’ visible glow.

be conducted with the same fuels but diluted with helium, which has much different transport properties 
than nitrogen.  
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a sooty (yellow) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter. This 
flame is burning ethylene fuel diluted by nitrogen. Ethylene’s double bond tends to make flames 
sooty. However, the soot (which is black, but thermally glows yellow) quickly disappears, leaving 
a blue soot-free spherical flame. 
 
Following ignition, the flame grows to reach enough oxygen to consume the fuel. The harp-like 
array of 14-micron ceramic fibers moves in from the left to a fixed position. The glow from the 
fibers allows for a good estimation of the local temperature. These flames are a bit like bubbles, 
where the fuel is within the flame, the oxygen is outside of it, and the light, heat, and chemical 
products are emitted at the surface where they come together and react. 
 
The base of the flame begins to retreat from the burner’s fuel supply tube due to heat loss. Both 
the flame and the glowing fibers can be seen to dim as the flame weakens. Eventually the base of 
the flame begins to oscillate. The flame locally quenches—creating a hole in the flame. This hole 
allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which in turn allows the flame to temporarily 
recover. As the oscillations grow in strength, the flame goes out. 
 
s-Flame round 2, featuring helium dilution 
 
Week 2: April 17 - 23 
On GMT 114, Chris Cassidy replaced the CIR FOMA Cal Unit on the back of the CIR Optics Bench. This 
activity allowed us to perform the calibration of the CIR’s FOMA (Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly) 
system. This calibration needs to be completed yearly to ensure that all the pressure transducers in the 
CIR are accurate. 
 
On GMT 115, in support of the CIR FOMA Calibration, Chris Cassidy closed and opened valves on the gas 
bottles installed in CIR. 
 
Week 3: April 24 - 30 
On GMT 119, Chris Cassidy replaced the ACME Fuel Controller and set the CIR Valve Timers to support the 
upcoming second round of testing for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames) starting in a couple weeks. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the 
transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth.

Week 4: May 1 - 7 
On GMT 122, Anatoly Ivanishin and Chris Cassidy replaced three CIR Manifold Bottles to support the 
upcoming second round of testing for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames) starting next week. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the

Week 5: May 8 - 14 
On GMT 132, we began the second round of testing for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of 
Spherical Diffusion Flames) with seven flames ignited using a hydrogen/methane fuel mixture diluted with 
helium. While the first round of testing used nitrogen to dilute the atmosphere and fuels, this round of 
testing uses helium. Helium is more diffusive and has a greater thermal conductivity than nitrogen. These 
factors can strongly influence combustion, which when coupled with the microgravity environment, can 
lead to new insight and understanding. 
 
On GMT 134, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottles on the CIR Manifold #4 and the CIR Check Gas 
Manifold to continue supporting s-Flame test points.

In this test point video, a porous sphere at the end of the burner’s fuel supply tube is used to 
create spherical flames. The gaseous fuel is ejected from this sphere, and the flame is ignited with 
a retracting hot-wire igniter. The flame “retreats” from the burner’s tube due to heat loss leaving 
just a flame “cap.” As the igniter retracts, a second ignition occurs while the flame “cap” is still 
burning. This second flame, which is large and spherical, is initially bright but quickly fades and 
extinguishes. We’re not sure what caused the second ignition, but regardless, the resulting data 
provides an opportunity to learn about the inner workings of flames.

of both soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames 
in microgravity are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion 
chemistry and details of the transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less 
polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

Diffusion Flames). These tests burned a hydrogen/methane fuel mixture diluted with helium but with a 
different ratio of flammable gases than investigated in the first test day. The results from both days will 
be compared with those from a third ratio, which will be tested on our next test day. On GMT 140, Anatoly 
Ivanishin replaced the bottles at CIR Manifold #1 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points 
using the third hydrogen/methane fuel mixture diluted with helium.

In this false-colored preliminary image, the flame encompasses the porous spherical burner and its fuel

flame’s heat. Where the fibers are visibly glowing, the flame’s temperature at that point can be 
determined by color-ratio pyrometry, which uses a color camera characterized for that purpose. 
Qualitatively, a yellow glow is hotter than orange, which is in turn hotter than red—just like metal in a 
forge. Given the extremely fine fibers, the measurement effectively provides the flame temperature, 
which can be compared with the results of computational modeling.

soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity

transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth.

Week 8: May 29 - June 4 
In support of ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points, Chris 
Cassidy replaced the ACME Igniter Tip and the ACME Fuel Controller on GMT 154. The next day, nine 
helium-diluted hydrogen flames were successfully ignited for s-Flame, where most of these tests were 
performed in a chamber environment of ~30% oxygen with a balance of helium. Previously, similar tests 
were performed with nitrogen dilution, but helium is dramatically different than nitrogen. Helium is more 
diffusive and has a greater thermal conductivity than nitrogen. Studying these differences can enable new

One benefit of performing combustion research in microgravity is spherical flames. This image 
(preliminary and false-colored) shows a spherical flame of diluted hydrogen ~25 mm in diameter. 
Reducing the flame geometry to a single dimension dramatically simplifies analysis and modeling. It also 
enables computation focused on chemical kinetics and transport phenomena rather than fluid dynamics

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
84 
 
The two bright lines above the flame are 14-micron ceramic fibers, which are visibly glowing because of 
the flame’s heat. The temperature distribution along the glowing fiber can be quantified through Thin 
Filament Pyrometry, where the hue is indicative of the temperature. Flame measurements are also made 
with intensified cameras, thermopile detectors, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. All this data 
is used to improve and validate flame modeling and through that enable improvements in practical 
terrestrial combustion. 
 
Week 9: June 5 - 11 
On GMT 160, 12 helium-diluted methane flames were ignited in oxygen/helium atmospheres for ACME s-
Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). Compared to other gaseous hydrocarbon 
fuels, methane (CH4) is more difficult to ignite because of its lack of carbon-carbon bonds. Methane 
ignition hadn’t been an issue in earlier testing with nitrogen dilution, but it was challenging in this week’s 
tests because of helium’s much greater thermal conductivity. Nonetheless, the recently installed coiled 
igniter tip enabled us to ignite these flames.  
 
The results from the current series of s-Flame tests will be compared with the results from the previous 
tests using nitrogen dilution. In that earlier testing, it was found that radiative extinction (i.e., extinction 
caused by radiative heat loss) is a common event, which had been predicted computationally. However, 
we did not observe this in preliminary ground-based testing. It was also seen in the on-orbit tests that 
radiative reabsorption extends the flame size at extinction. Another type of extinction was sometimes 
observed, where the gas velocities caused nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames (under certain conditions) to 
blow out. It will be interesting to see what the future comparisons will reveal about the nature of flames. 
 
On GMT 162, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points 
using 20% ethylene fuel diluted with helium. 
 
Week 10: June 12 - 18 
On GMT 164, 11 helium-diluted ethylene flames were ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames). This is a shift in testing for the s-Flame experiment from non-sooty fuels 
(i.e., hydrogen, methane, or hydrogen/methane blends) to a sooty fuel. Ethylene (C2H4) tends to be a 
sooty fuel because it has a carbon double-bond. Soot forms when hot fuel combines with itself in the 
absence of oxygen, where the union of fuel molecules is facilitated by the double bond. The flames in 
these tests were sooty at ignition, but the soot quickly disappeared resulting in blue flames, where blue 
is the natural color of flames with hydrocarbon fuels. On GMT 168, Anatoly Ivanishin replaced the bottles 
at CIR Manifold #1, CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points using 25% 
ethylene fuel diluted with helium.  
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This test point video runs at half speed to better show what is happening with the flame. A flame 
of 20% ethylene fuel ignites in a chamber atmosphere of about 30% oxygen (both diluted with 
helium). The flame is initially very bright. Although the soot particles are black, their glow depends 
on their temperature, where yellow is hotter than orange which is in turn hotter than red. While 
some soot clusters escape the flame, much of the soot becomes trapped within the flame by the 
temperature gradient.

temperature distribution where the fibers are glowing. Despite their 14-micron diameter, the

The flame becomes all blue and retreats from the fuel supply tube because of heat loss.  The 
opening in the flame allows fuel and oxygen to directly mix, where they are normally separated 
by the presence of the flame shell. This mixing enhances flammability and the reinvigorated and 
locally brighter flame flashes back to the supply tube reestablishing the nominally spherical flame. 
But it is short-lived, and the flame quickly retreats again until it is just a “cap” on the left. Mixing 
again leads to another flame flash, but it quickly extinguishes due to radiative heat loss, heat loss 
to the supply tube, and conductive heat loss enhanced by the helium’s high thermal conductivity. 
 
Week 11: June 19 - 25 
 
On GMT 170, 20 flames were ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion 
Flames). These flames burned a 25% ethylene/75% helium blend; whereas, the flames on GMT 164 burned 
a 20% ethylene/80% helium blend. Comparing these data will enable analysis of the effects of this 
fuel/inert blend on flame dynamics, such as extinction behavior and structure. On GMT 171, Anatoly 
Ivanishin replaced the bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME s-Flame test points using a 30% 
ethylene/70% helium blend. 
 
ACME s-Flame Test Point Image 
 
In this image (preliminary and false-colored), the flame on the right has a higher ethylene concentration 
than the flame on the left. As expected, the flame on the right is larger where the spherical flame expands 
until the fuel reaches enough oxygen to be consumed. 
 
These flames, which are non-premixed, are like bubbles in that the gaseous fuel is inside the bubble and 
the oxygen is outside the bubble. The flame shell, like the film of a bubble, is a thin sheet where the fuel 
and oxygen come together and react, producing light, heat, and chemical products, such as carbon dioxide 
and water vapor.  Meanwhile, the helium—which readily diffuses—is free to cross the flame shell.

However, diffusion was minimal because the helium concentrations within the fuel and the surrounding 
atmosphere were similar.  
 
Both flames were bright and sooty at ignition, but these images are from late in each test when the flames 
became dim. The bright lines at the top are the 14-micron ceramic fibers used for optical determination 
of the flame temperature using a camera characterized for that purpose. 
 
s-Flame’s goal is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both 
soot-free and sooty flames. Without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity 
are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the combustion chemistry and details of the 
transport phenomena. Results may lead to more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for 
use on Earth. 
 
Week 12: June 26 - July 2 
GMT 176 was a record-breaking day for ACME with 23 flames ignited—the most we’ve ignited in one day! 
We’ve now ignited over 250 flames for s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) 
and over 1000 flames for ACME since it started in Nov. 2017. The tests on GMT 176 were performed with 
30% ethylene in helium for comparison with the results from the two preceding test days, which burned 
20% and 25% ethylene/helium blends.  
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, helium-diluted ethylene fuel is ignited with a low fuel flow rate to limit 
the soot produced with ignition. After ignition, the flow rate is tripled in a smooth ramp, so that 
the flame response can be observed. As expected, the flame quickly grows, where it must expand 
to reach enough oxygen to consume all the fuel.   
 
Before the fuel flow rate has completely tripled, the flame retreats from the burner’s fuel supply 
tube because of heat loss—creating a hole in the flame near the tube. This hole allows for 
increased mixing of the ethylene and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame shell. 
This mixing causes the flame to momentarily reestablish around the burner tube with a bright 
flash of light. Mixing again leads to another flame flash, after which the flame fully extinguishes. 
The fuel flow rate did completely triple before the flame extinguished. 
 
Although not visible in the video, the measured OH* and CH* chemiluminescence was relatively 
constant throughout this test with the important exceptions of ignition and the bright flashes of 
light prior to extinction. In contrast, the measured chemiluminescence declined with time in 
similar tests with constant fuel flow rates. OH* and CH* are molecules at an elevated energy state 
which emit a photon of a specific wavelength as their energy level drops a level. The CH* emission 
is the source of most of the blue in a hydrocarbon flame, while the OH* emission is in the 
ultraviolet. ACME uses the latter measurement as an indicator of ignition and extinction because 
it is insensitive to the hot-wire igniter and hot burned gases. 
 
Using this unique microgravity data, the s-Flame investigation seeks to test and improve 
computational models, which may enable improvements to practical combustion on Earth.

Week of January 13, 2020 
Other investigations on which the crew performed work: 
• 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is a set of six independent studies of 
gaseous flames conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  ACME supports spacecraft 
fire prevention as well as improved fuel efficiency and reduced pollutant production in practical 
combustion on Earth. 
• 
The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), part of the ACME project, 
advances prediction of the structure and dynamics of soot-free and sooty flames.  Results could 
contribute to engines with improved efficiency and reduced emissions on Earth. 
 
Week of January 27, 2020 
Other investigations on which the crew performed work: 
• 
The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), part of the ACME project,

2019 July 30: GMT 211 
Combustion Integration Rack (CIR)/ Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
Manifold Bottle Exchange: The crew replaced the 40% O2 gas bottle with a 30% O2 bottle. They also 
replaced the ethylene fuel bottle with a hydrogen/methane mixture fuel bottle. Telemetry showed a slow 
leak in the hydrogen/methane bottle and teams are discussing a recovery plan. Flame Design part 1 
investigation is complete and preparations are in work for transition to the s-Flame investigation. The 
purpose of s-Flame is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction 
and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of 
lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. 
 
2019 July 31: GMT 212 
Combustion Integration Rack (CIR) Manifold Bottle Inspection:  Following yesterday’s discovery of a slow 
leak, the fuel bottle connection was demated, inspected, cleaned, and remated to the CIR manifold.  The 
pressure was subsequently monitored and the leak was reduced, but still present.  The crew then looked 
for the leak source (suspected to be either the quick-disconnect or pressure relief valve) with the 
ultrasonic leak detector but were unable to isolate the source of the leak. The fuel bottle valve was closed 
and teams are discussing a forward plan. This fuel bottle will be used for the upcoming s-Flame 
investigation.

experiment series includes five independent studies of gaseous flames. The primary goals of ACME are to 
improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollutant production in routine fuel combustion activities on Earth.  Its 
secondary goal is to improve spacecraft fire prevention through innovative research focused on materials 
flammability.

29 July 2021 
106 
 
Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The s-Flame data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments.  To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The s-Flame image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used with CH*, formaldehyde, and UV fused silica filters, but where only 
a single filter was used in each test 
3. Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera, equipped with an OH* filter 
4. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, 
HiBMs, and LLL-UV cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format.  In contrast, the analog video 
was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

The three images are snap 
shots 
of 
a

expanding flame in different

shows 
the 
ideal, 
reference case of a stable, 
smooth flame surface in a 
quiescent

pressure. 
The 
middle flame is taken under 
elevated pressure simulating 
that 
within 
an 
internal 
combustion engine. The flame 
surface is hydrodynamically 
unstable and develops cells, 
causing the flame to burn faster 
due to the increased flame 
surface area. The bottom flame 
is taken in a highly turbulent 
environment which simulates 
another aspect of the engine 
interior. Now the flame surface 
is distorted by the multi-scale 
turbulence, which again leads 
to an increase of the burning 
rate.

Both Princeton and Rutgers have promoted awareness of the s-Flame investigation online, for 
example, through Rutgers’ 2019 article, “From the Ground Up: Conducting International Space Station 
Experiments from a Rutgers Office.” 
 
Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of 
Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018. 
 
Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018 
by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion 
Experiments.” 
 
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts 
of both genders, and the general public.   His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity (for which resources are available via  http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human 
spaceflight.  But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA 
and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL.  In this 
regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online.  For example, he 
regularly presents on microgravity at  Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Educators 
Conference (SEEC).   He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, four national Boy Scout 
conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree 
(which was held in the U.S.).  Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in 
these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually described at 
www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

content:
BASS-2 Engineering Requirements
General Requirements
Each Burning And Suppression of Solids-2 (BASS-2) solid fuel assembly is mounted inside the Experiment Assembly via a magnetic interface such that it can be installed and removed by the crew.
Solid fuel ignition will be done with a hot-wire Kanthol material igniter.
Nitrogen gas to be used from 0 to 500 SCCM N2.  Instead of connecting the Experiment Assembly to the gas bottle it is connected via the GN2 hose to the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) gaseous nitrogen (GN2) supply interface.
3.2 mm normal length and 3.2 mm short length burner tubes will be manifested and used for BASS.
The Control Box will be modified to allow the fan flow adjustment to stop the fan when set to its minimum as a safety mechanism to extinguish flame.
Parameter Measurement
Measurement of the GN2 Flow rate, Fan Voltage, Co-Flow velocity, and flame radiation will be measured and overlaid on the video.
The data acquisition rate as measured by SPICE hardware is 4 Hz.
The measurement accuracy of ±10% was met by the SPICE hardware prior to its launch.  The measurement accuracy will meet the requirements for BASS-2.
Imaging Requirements
The Field of view of the video is fixed for BASS-2 can not be changed from SPICE.
The Still Image requirements are the same as for SPICE.  The BASS-2 still image requirements will be met with the Nikon model D300s digital still camera.

BASS-2 Engineering Requirements
Acceleration
BASS-2 testing will be scheduled around planned thruster firing or spacecraft dock or undock.
The acceleration environment will be measured by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) during BASS-2 testing which will be installed into the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) Work Volume.
Oxygen Concentration
The BASS-2 experiment will include steps in crew procedures to install a Compound Specific Analyzer (CSA-O2) into the MSG to measure the Oxygen concentration.  There is also a Major Constituent Analyzer available to measure the Columbus Module concentration. 
Crew inserts fuel sample and adjusts igniter and fuel base to desired position
Sample Frame Assembly is designed to allow for adjustment of the position of the BASS-2 solid fuel sample.
The Igniter has a wire extension that the crew will be able to position as required to ignite the solid fuel sample.

content:
Spreadsheets folder has test matrix and fan calibration information.
Test Matrix explanation
Tabs in spreadsheet for each PI.
Subrata Bhattacharjee burned various thickness of very thin pmma films.
Paul Ferkul burned Nomex III and a candle to round out the BASS-I testing.
Fletcher Miller burned various thickness and widths of thick pmma slabs (one sided and two sided burns).
Sandra Olson burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly clear), igniting the upstream end for a stagnation flame / concurrent flow geometry.
Carlos Fernandez-Pello burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly black), igniting the downstream end for an opposed flow flame spread geometry.
James T’ien burned mostly SIBAL fabric (75/25 cotton/fiberglass blend).  Also had 1 sample/2 tests with 4 cm pmma spherical section.
Columns in test matrix:
Date:  actual date of experiment.  Video display is one day later than actual date due to a leap year the on-board computer did not account for.
GMT- number is day of the year.  ISS runs on Greenwich mean time, so their clock reads as GMT – Year – Day - time
Test number:   Initial of PI name followed by test number from the initial matrix.   If multiple runs with same sample on same day, a and b are used to designate.
Sample number:   some samples were used for multiple runs.
Material:  self explanatory
Flow restrictors:  perforated plates that could be attached to the inlet screen to increase the flow restriction and thus reduce the flow range.   0 is highest flow, lowest restriction; and 2 is lowest flow, highest restriction.  
Fan display:  instantaneous fan voltagex10 on the video display.  Maximum was 122, or 12.2 volts.  Also listed sometimes are pot settings on the control box.  10 is max.
Air display:  flow speed measured in the duct in cm/s on the video display.  Response time is very slow (~ 1 min), so reading is only steady for long times at the same flow setting.
Radiometer gain:   Uncalibrated radiometer gain, radiometer is displayed on the video.   Adjusted to avoid saturation.  Useful for relative flame intensity readings and flame dynamics (like pre-extinction oscillations).  Video display data rate is 5 Hz.
Total frames:  digital Nikon still image frames shot, includes test and post-burn sample images.  
Calibrated initial and final O2:   The O2 sensor was out of calibration, so the MCA ISS reading was used to correct the initial ISS ‘air’ reading of the sensor for the day via a constant offset.     
CO2 readings:  CDM sensor readings. 
CO readings:  CSA-CP sensor readings.  OR = over range (> 1000 ppm)
Videos:   most test videos have the test number (PI initial+ # from test matrix)  In the Misc video folder, there are backup test recordings, recordings of crew operations, etc.

content:
BASS-II SCIENCE REQUIREMENTS
•
General Requirements
–
20 samples for each of the 5 PIs will be flow (including 20 clear pmma rods, 20 
black pmma rods (varied diameters for both); 19 SIBAL samples, 1 4 cm pmma 
spherical section,   20 pmma films (varied thicknesses) and 20 pmma slabs (varied 
thicknesses and 1 sided or 2 sided holders).  Also 3 Nomex-III samples.
–
27 additional igniter wires will be flown.  Solid fuel ignition uses a Kanthal hot wire.
– ISS nitrogen gas will be used (0 to 500 SCCM N2).  Instead of connecting the 
Experiment Assembly to a gas bottle it is connected via the GN2 hose to the MSG 
GN2 interface.  GN2 is used to vitiate the MSG working volume to desired O2 levels.
–
8 additional flash cards will be flow for the still camera.
•
Parameter Measurement
– Measurement of the GN2 flow rate, fan voltage, air flow velocity and direction, 
and flame radiation will be measured and overlaid on the Video.
– The acquisition rate of 4 Hz can not be changed from SPICE/BASS.
– The measurement accuracy of ±10% was met by the SPICE hardware prior to 
its launch.
•
Imaging Requirements
– The field of view of the video can not be changed from BASS.
– The D300s still image requirements are the same as for BASS.
4/14/2010

BASS-II SCIENCE REQUIREMENTS
•
Acceleration
– BASS-II testing will be scheduled around planned thruster firing or 
spacecraft dock or undock.
– The acceleration environment will be measured by a nearby SAMS 
during BASS-II testing.
•
MSG Working Volume Gas Concentrations
–
Project will include steps in crew procedures to install a Compound Specific 
Analyzer (CSA-CP) and the CO2 sensor (CDM) into the MSG to measure the 
Oxygen concentration.  These devices will provide readings before and after 
each burn of the MSG working volume well mixed gas concentrations.  
Calibration checks will utilize the Columbus and Node 3 O2 and CO2 readings.
•
Crew support
–
Crew time is needed to conduct the BASS-II experiments.  As part of the nominal 
ops, the crew establishes the desired test ambient atmosphere and flow.  The 
crew  manually inserts  the fuel sample, adjusts the fuel location and igniter 
position within the camera fields of view.   The crew manually ignites the sample 
and triggers the still camera.   The crew performs flow calibration and soot 
cleaning as needed.  
–
The crew works closely with the BASS-II PI team to determine test settings and 
provide real-time feedback during each burn.

content:
9
BASS-II Science Overview
Relevance/Impact:  Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) tests the hypothesis 
that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than 
the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, 
oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.).  
Objectives:  
•
To identify what is the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft 
environments, and how does that compare to the terrestrial upward burning used to 
screen the materials for safe use aboard spacecraft.
•
To determine how quickly a fire in space can grow and if the flames reach a finite size 
or continue to grow.  This has implications for firefighting strategies in spacecraft.
Primary variables:  The main variables to be tested are the effects of ambient oxygen 
concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness, and geometry.  
Development Approach:
BASS-II will utilize the on orbit BASS hardware launched originally for SPICE on STS-126.  
New samples, igniters, and more flash cards will provide new data.  Crew is required to 
set up and operate the experiment.  Video and data down-linked to the ground for 
evaluation.

content:
Approach: 
 
♦Microgravity combustion tests were performed 
aboard the International Space Station using the 
BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) 
hardware. 
 
♦The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, 
and a level of containment.  
 
♦Cotton-fiberglass blend fabric samples were 
mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could 
impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. 
 
♦The effects of airflow speed on flame appearance, 
flame growth, and spread rates were determined 
in both the opposed and concurrent flow 
configuration.

Science Applications:  
 
Understanding of long-duration microgravity solid material burning and extinction  
Improved strategies for NASA spacecraft materials selection; link actual burn 
behavior in microgravity to Earth-based selection methods 
Improved combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection 
and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth  
Validated detailed combustion models in the simpler flow environment of 
microgravity build more complex combustion models needed to capture the 
important details of flames burning in normal gravity; models have wide 
applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion 
problems.

content:
Summary 
 
♦For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady 
spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an 
intermediate value of flow speed.  
 
♦These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this 
geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in 
the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).  
 
♦For the concurrent flow configuration, a limiting length and steady 
spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds. For these 
conditions, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow.  
 
♦This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was 
obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity. In addition, by 
decreasing concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 
cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.  
 
♦The valuable results from these long-duration experiments validate a 
number of theoretical predictions and also provide the data for a 
transient flame growth model under development.

content:
Approach: 
 
♦Microgravity combustion tests were performed 
aboard the International Space Station using the 
BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) 
hardware. 
 
♦The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, 
and a level of containment.  
 
♦Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind 
tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 
40 cm/s. 
 
♦The effects of airflow speed on flame appearance, 
flame growth, and spread rates were determined 
in both the opposed and concurrent flow.  
 
♦More recent tests varying oxygen (below 21%) 
have been completed.

Science Applications:  
 
Understanding of long-duration microgravity solid material burning and extinction  
Improved strategies for NASA spacecraft materials selection; link actual burn 
behavior in microgravity to Earth-based selection methods 
Improved combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection 
and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth  
Validated detailed combustion models in the simpler flow environment of 
microgravity build more complex combustion models needed to capture the 
important details of flames burning in normal gravity; models have wide 
applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion 
problems.

Summary 1. Thin Fuel: Flame Spread and Extinction 
 
 
♦Opposed flow:  
•
flame quickly reached steady spread 
•
spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed 
 
♦Concurrent flow:

Flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow. 
•
Quenching extinction was observed (around 1 cm/s) 
 
♦This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in 
purely forced flows in microgravity.  
 
♦Long-duration experiments validate a number of theoretical predictions and 
also provide the data for a transient flame growth model under development.

Science Background: 
 
♦Combustion of solid fuels in micro-
gravity has been an active area of 
research 
 
♦Numerical models predict that 1-g 
buoyant flows profoundly affect fuel 
flammability 
 
♦Ground-based facilities have verified 
this behavior but only for thin fuels in 
opposed flow 
 
♦Flow speeds below the buoyant limit 
are of interest

content:
Approach: 
 
♦Microgravity combustion tests were performed 
aboard the International Space Station using the 
BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) 
hardware. 
 
♦The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, 
and a level of containment.  
 
♦Cotton-fiberglass blend fabric samples were 
mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could 
impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. 
 
♦The effects of airflow speed on flame appearance, 
flame growth, and spread rates were determined 
in both the opposed and concurrent flow 
configuration.

Science Applications:  
 
Understanding of long-duration microgravity solid material burning and extinction  
Improved strategies for NASA spacecraft materials selection; link actual burn 
behavior in microgravity to Earth-based selection methods 
Improved combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection 
and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth  
Validated detailed combustion models in the simpler flow environment of 
microgravity build more complex combustion models needed to capture the 
important details of flames burning in normal gravity; models have wide 
applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion 
problems.

Summary 
 
♦For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady 
spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an 
intermediate value of flow speed.  
 
♦These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this 
geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in 
the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).  
 
♦For the concurrent flow configuration, a limiting length and steady 
spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds. For these 
conditions, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow.  
 
♦This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was 
obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity. In addition, by 
decreasing concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 
cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.

Summary 
 
♦For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady 
spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an 
intermediate value of flow speed.  
 
♦These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this 
geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in

♦For the concurrent flow configuration, a limiting length and steady 
spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds. For these

♦This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was 
obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity. In addition, by 
decreasing concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 
cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.  
 
♦The valuable results from these long-duration experiments validate a 
number of theoretical predictions and also provide the data for a 
transient flame growth model under development.

content:
INTRODUCTION 
•
Three investigations will be performed:   SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.   
•
These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
•
SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which 
flew on STS-87 in 1997. 
•
SPICE hardware is already on-orbit.  It has successfully completed all of its 
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. 
Spare gas onboard will now be used to collect additional data.  New fuel is 
being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. 
•
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. 
•
SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to 
smoke.  
•
SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted 
from the fuel nozzle.   
•
BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

content:
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find 
the laminar smoke-point properties of 
nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the 
properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion 
flames that do not emit soot) for two fuel types 
under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity 
configurations.  
 
SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, 
measure the overall flame shape to validate the 
theoretical and numerical predictions, measure 
the flame stabilization heights, and measure the 
temperature field to verify flame structure 
predictions.

Target Setting: The target setting is just above the setting that 
produces a distinct edge (only a small portion of the tip will emit 
smoke). The smoke will probably emerge from the center of the tip 
but may emerge at the tip edges (horns) for the larger nozzle. The 
pictures show the onset of smoke points for various fuels on the 
KC-135. The size of the flame when it emits smoke is a fuel 
property. The expected size sequence will be Propylene, Ethylene, 
Propane and Methane (probably no smoke point). The diluted 
propylene smoke points will be longer than pure propylene. 
 
SPICE Smoke Point Determination Cue Card  
Background:  The smoke point is the flame length, 
above which, soot particles are no longer consumed in 
the flame and instead emerge through the flame tip 
and glow as they cool. The glowing soot causes a 
change from a sharp edge to a gradual transition 
between the bright flame and black background. 
 
Advisory note: For the test points with the 0.4 mm 
nozzle, the possibility exists that the flame could blow 
off. When this happens, the blue flame-base no longer 
touches the nozzle. When the base of the flame starts 
to separate from the nozzle, reduce the flow rate until 
it is well attached as the smoke height is not 
achievable.

SLICE Science Background 
•
The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting 
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and 
stabilizes at a downstream position.  
•
The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and 
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) 
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in 
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
6

content:
BASS Science Background 
•
The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well 
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being 
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).  
•
To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended 
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this 
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of 
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate 
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft).  Practical, 
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames 
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire 
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).  
•
There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on 
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the 
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and 
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of 
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially 
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame 
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is 
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the 
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. 
7

content:
Earth Applications 
•
SPICE 
 
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat 
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to 
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of 
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our 
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point, 
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical 
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces). 
•
SLICE 
 
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced 
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is 
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system 
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before 
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other 
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and 
improve our global environment. 
•
BASS 
 
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for 
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the 
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual 
material flammability in microgravity 
9

content:
Introduction 
•
Three investigations will be performed:   SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.   
•
These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
•
SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which 
flew on STS-87 in 1997. 
•
SPICE hardware is already on-orbit.  It has successfully completed all of its 
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. New 
fuel is being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. 
•
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. 
•
SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to 
smoke.  
•
SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted 
from the fuel nozzle.   
•
BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find 
the laminar smoke-point properties of 
nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the 
properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion

under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity 
configurations.

measure the overall flame shape to validate the 
theoretical and numerical predictions, measure 
the flame stabilization heights, and measure the 
temperature field to verify flame structure 
predictions.

Target Setting: The target setting is just above the setting that 
produces a distinct edge (only a small portion of the tip will emit 
smoke). The smoke will probably emerge from the center of the tip 
but may emerge at the tip edges (horns) for the larger nozzle. The 
pictures show the onset of smoke points for various fuels on the 
KC-135. The size of the flame when it emits smoke is a fuel 
property. The expected size sequence will be Propylene, Ethylene, 
Propane and Methane (probably no smoke point). The diluted 
propylene smoke points will be longer than pure propylene. 
 
SPICE Smoke Point Determination Cue Card  
Background:  The smoke point is the flame length, 
above which, soot particles are no longer consumed in 
the flame and instead emerge through the flame tip 
and glow as they cool. The glowing soot causes a 
change from a sharp edge to a gradual transition 
between the bright flame and black background. 
 
Advisory note: For the test points with the 0.4 mm 
nozzle, the possibility exists that the flame could blow 
off. When this happens, the blue flame-base no longer 
touches the nozzle. When the base of the flame starts 
to separate from the nozzle, reduce the flow rate until 
it is well attached as the smoke height is not 
achievable.

SLICE Science Background 
•
The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting 
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and 
stabilizes at a downstream position.  
•
The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and 
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) 
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in 
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
6

content:
BASS Science Background 
•
The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well 
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being 
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).  
•
To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended 
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this 
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of 
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate 
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft).  Practical, 
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames 
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire 
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).  
•
There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on 
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the 
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and 
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of 
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially 
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame 
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is 
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the 
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. 
7

content:
Earth Applications 
•
SPICE 
 
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat 
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to 
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of 
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our 
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point, 
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical 
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces). 
•
SLICE 
 
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced 
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is 
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system 
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before 
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other 
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and 
improve our global environment. 
•
BASS 
 
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for 
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the 
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual 
material flammability in microgravity 
9

content:
8th U. S. National Combustion Meeting
Organized by the Western States Section of the Combustion Institute
 and hosted by the University of Utah
May 19-22, 2013
Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and 
Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity
Paul V. Ferkul1     Sandra L. Olson2     Michael C. Johnston3     James S. T’ien3
1National Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH  44135
2NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH  44135
3Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH  44106
Microgravity combustion tests burning fabric samples were performed aboard the International Space Station.  The cotton-fiberglass blend samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose air flow speeds up to 40 cm/s.  The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment.  The effects of air flow speed on flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent-flow configuration.  For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed.  These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).  In the concurrent-flow configuration, flame size grew with time during the tests.  A limiting length and steady spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds (≤ 10 cm/s) for the short-length samples that fit in the small wind tunnel.  For these conditions, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow.  This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity.  In addition, by decreasing flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.  The valuable results from these long-duration experiments validate a number of theoretical predictions and also provide the data for a transient flame growth model under development.
Introduction
The combustion of thermally-thin fuels burning in low-speed flows has been studied extensively [e.g. Olson et al., 1988; Olson, 1991; Ferkul and T’ien, 1994; Grayson et al., 1994; T’ien and Bedir, 1997; Shih and T’ien, 1997].  The importance of radiative loss is evident in leading to flame extinction when the flow velocity (or ambient oxygen concentration) is reduced sufficiently.  This quenching extinction occurs when the flame power output decreases, and the radiative heat loss rate becomes a significant fraction of the total combustion heat release from the flame.
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.  This is shown for a specific thermally-thin fuel in Fig. 1 produced by a computational model.  A flame can only exist inside the U-shaped curve.  The flammability boundary consists of two branches, as shown.  Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system).  The flames in microgravity are very sensitive to flow speed, especially as the flame approaches the extinction boundary.  This has implications for Figure 1.  Flammability boundary for a thin solid fuel from model computation.  Much of the boundary is inaccessible for study in 1-g because of the ever-present buoyant convection flows of at least 20 cm/s.
Figure 1.  Flammability boundary for a thin solid fuel from model computation.  Much of the boundary is inaccessible for study in 1-g because of the ever-present buoyant convection flows of at least 20 cm/s.
both the fundamental understanding of mechanisms leading to diffusion flame extinction as well as practical significance for spacecraft fire safety.  Materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity with all other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.). 
Figure 1.  Flammability boundary for a thin solid fuel from model computation.  Much of the boundary is inaccessible for study in 1-g because of the ever-present buoyant convection flows of at least 20 cm/s.
Figure 1.  Flammability boundary for a thin solid fuel from model computation.  Much of the boundary is inaccessible for study in 1-g because of the ever-present buoyant convection flows of at least 20 cm/s.
There have been few experiments examining concurrent-flow flame spread over thin fuels in the long-duration microgravity environments available in space.  In Sacksteder et al. [1997], the number of tests was limited and only simple diagnostics were possible, but valuable insight into the burning behavior of thin paper samples was attained, including a visual record of the flames and measurements of spread rate and flame temperatures.  The fuel tended to crack when it burned, causing the flame to respond in a non-predictable way.  In Olson et al. [2001], ignition was initiated in the center of a paper fuel sheet so that only a portion of some of the flames spread in the concurrent mode.  Depending on the flow speed, the flame would either spread entirely into the flow (opposed flow) or the ignition flame would split into an opposed and concurrent-flow flame spreading simultaneously away from each other.
Understanding long-duration microgravity solid material burning and extinction is important for improving strategies for NASA spacecraft materials selection.  The goal is to link actual burn behavior in microgravity to Earth-based selection methods.  From a more fundamental point of view, improved combustion computational models using the experimental results can be developed to aid in the design of fire detection and suppression systems both in microgravity and on Earth.  Validated detailed combustion models in the simpler flow environment of microgravity can help build more complex combustion models of flames burning in normal gravity.  Better models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems.
Methods
Combustion tests burning fabric sheets are conducted aboard the ISS (International Space Station) using the Microgravity Science Glovebox Facility [Butler, 2008].  The sheets are mounted in a holder which sandwiches the fabric between two thin stainless-steel frames.  The exposed fuel measures 8.5 cm in length and 1 or 2 cm in width.  One short edge of the fuel is not framed, and ignition is achieved across the sample on this edge.  See Fig. 2.  A 29-gage Kanthal wire spans the sample and is resistively heated to provide ignition.  Typically the igniter resistance is 1 ohm and a current of around 3.7A is supplied for ignition, which occurs within about 2 s.  The samples each have their own integral igniter, the leads of which are glued flat along the frame to minimize any flow disturbances.  The igniter leads come off the back of the sample and go to a connector which is plugged in during installation.  
The custom-made fabric (sometimes referred to as SIBAL fabric) is a blend of cotton and fiberglass.  The threads consist of fibers of cotton and fiberglass which are spun together.  A simple weave patter is used with a spacing of 60 by 40 threads per inch (Fig. 3).  The overall area density is 18.0 mg/cm2, with 75% by mass cotton and remainder fiberglass.  This fabric was developed with the idea that the fiberglass matrix would be left behind after all the fuel is consumed, so that the sheet would not curl or crack.  Either of these geometrical changes could affect the flow in a non-predictable way and so are undesirable.  As will be seen later, the flame is very sensitive to small air flow changes in microgravity.

The samples are burned in the SPICE apparatus which is a small flow duct with a cross-sectional area of 76mm x 76mm [Dotson et. al. 2010].  The front window of the duct can be opened so that samples can be installed one at a time.  See Fig. 4.  There is a tab with alignment holes on the sample holder which permits quick and accurate installation onto small rare-earth magnets inside the flow duct.  Samples can be flipped 180 degrees so that the igniter is on the upstream or downstream end of the fuel.  In this way, both concurrent-flow and opposed-flow tests can be conducted.  The electrical connector is plugged into a socket inside the duct and the wires are tucked into a corner to minimize flow disturbances.  A variable-speed fan is used to generate air flow speeds from 0 to 40 cm/s.  Air speed is the principal variable for this experiment.
The flow duct is housed within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) which provides power, imaging, and a level of containment (Fig. 5) [Butler, 2008].  It is very advantageous that the astronaut can perform hands-on operation of the experiment while viewing the flame directly.  Sometimes the flame is very dim or has features which the camera misses.  The astronaut can make observations in real-time to the research team on the ground which is in direct audio and visual communication.  The researchers on the ground in turn provide guidance and clarification is being performed while at the same time benefitting enormously from the direct involvement of the ISS crew member.

After all the appropriate electrical connections are made between the duct and the MSG, the cameras are set up.  The cameras provide the bulk of the data for this experiment.  A digital still camera takes high-resolution pictures through the top window at rate of about one frame per second.  A video camera captures the edge view of the flame through the front window at 30 frames per second.  There is a character overlay on the video image to display fan setting, flow speed (from a hot-wire anemometer), radiometer output from a wide-angle sensor inside the duct, and time.

After the sample is installed, the MSG volume is sealed and the lights are turned off.  The experiment is operated using a control box which is external to the MSG and can adjust flow speed, igniter on/off, and radiometer gain.  In addition to the camera views which are available live to both the astronaut and the ground team, the astronaut can look into a port to view the flame directly.
Figure 5.  Fish-eye view of the inside of the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the flow duct installed.  The MSG provides power, imaging, and a level of containment.  The astronaut can easily access the hardware which permits valuable hands-on operation.  The digital still camera can be see viewing down at the duct, and a video camera and mirror image the sample through the front window.
Just before the test is initiated, the flow is set to the desired value and the cameras start recording.  Ignition is turned on and a flame is established within about 2 seconds.  The flame spreads across the sample, ultimately consuming all the fuel and then goes out.  In some tests, the flow speed is changed while the flame is burning to gage its effect.  After the flame goes out, the duct is allowed to cool and vent for several minutes until the old sample can be removed and a fresh one installed for the next test.

Video overlay information is shown at the top right.  Flow speed direction is as indicated yielding a concurrent-flow configuration. (Test 1)
Results and Discussion
Figure 6 shows typical flame images from both cameras for a concurrent-flow test at 10 cm/s and a 2-cm wide fabric.  On the left, the digital still high-resolution image is shown looking down through the top window.  The flame leading edge is mostly blue, but there is a significant amount of yellow which indicates the presence of soot.  Dark charring on the surface is visible indicating the area of significant fuel pyrolysis.  The base of the flame advances, leaving behind mostly fiberglass but with some remnants of cotton.  This is evident by the bright orange smoldering occurring in the fuel matrix.  Eventually, the smoldering ceases.  On the right, the view of the flame from the front window video camera is shown.  This view is important for determining flame symmetry and 2-D structure.  While this camera lacks the sensitivity and resolution of the digital still camera, it records images at a much higher rate of 30 frames per second.  For all cases, the two flame halves were symmetric and the flame spread uniformly without any disturbances caused by fuel burnout (cracking or curling).  The text overlay indicates the fan setting, flow speed, radiometer level, date, and time.  The minimum measurable air flow speed is 1 cm/s.

Most of the samples were 2 cm in width, and most of the tests were performed in the concurrent-flow configuration.  The opposed flow configuration was amenable to air flow speed changes during the burn since the flame was found to reach steady state quickly after the flow was changed.  This is not the case for concurrent flow where the flame response time (and fuel length required) is significantly larger.
Figure 7.  Effect of concurrent-flow speed on flame structure.       Left: 10 cm/s.  Right: 5 cm/s. (Tests 7 and 8)
Figure 7.  Effect of concurrent-flow speed on flame structure.       Left: 10 cm/s.  Right: 5 cm/s. (Tests 7 and 8)
Figure 7 shows the comparison of concurrent air flow speeds of 5 and 10 cm/s on flame structure for a 2-cm wide sample.  The images are taken about 20 seconds after ignition.  The flame base for the wider samples in concurrent flow is rarely horizontal; rather there is always a slight tilt.  The spread rate of the base of the flame does reach steady state during the available observation times for air flow speeds of 20 cm/s and less.  However, the flame tip spread rate is still growing for air flow speeds equal to and higher than 10 cm/s. To put it another way, the flames only reach a steady length for flow speeds less than 10 cm/s.  
In Fig. 8, a summary of the spread rates is presented.   Results are plotted for both opposed flow (velocity > 0) and concurrent flow (velocity < 0).  For opposed flow, the flame responds very rapidly to flow changes and steady state flame spread rates and lengths are obtained.  As a result, a single burn can yield multiple data points if the flow is changed in a step-wise fashion.  For concurrent flow, the flame takes a relatively long time to respond to flow changes so it is not feasible to attempt to get multiple data points per burn by changing flow speed.  For concurrent flow, the flame base spread rate is plotted and reaches a steady state for all points shown.  However the flame tip spread rate was increasing for the 2-cm wide samples above 5 cm/s air flow speed.  The concurrent-flow flames burning the 1-cm wide samples did however reach a steady length.
Concurrent-flow flame spread rate increases linearly with flow speed, and linear curve fits are shown.  Spread rate is width-dependent for the two widths studied.  For concurrent flow, extinction was observed at a low but finite flow speed of less than 1 cm/s (shown by the dashed vertical line).  Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds, in good agreement with previous research [Olson, 1991].  An opposed flow extinction test was attempted by decreasing the flow in a stepwise fashion, however extinction was not observed before the flame reached the end of fuel.  Based on the trends however, it appears that an opposed-flow quenching extinction limit can be extrapolated to exist at an air flow speed of less than 1 cm/s.  This implies that for this fuel, there is a small range of flow speeds near zero within which the flame cannot be sustained in either direction (concurrent or opposed).

Figure 9.  Flame growth to steady state spread for 1 cm sample width in concurrent air flow of 11 cm/s. (Test 10)

The flame spread measurements are made by tracking the flame base and tip position from the recorded images.  The resolution and picture quality of the digital still images are far better than the video images.  However, both can be used to determine flame spread rate.  A sample tracking plot derived from the digital still images is shown in Fig. 9.  The case shown is for a 1-cm wide sample burning in a concurrent flow of 11 cm/s.  Ignition occurs at t=0.  There is some initial development time when the flame grows, but after about 20 seconds the flame reaches steady state.  This is obvious as the slopes of the base and tip positions become parallel for about 30 seconds and the flame length becomes constant.  Furthermore, the visual images indicate the flame shape and intensity become nearly invariant during this period.  Finally, when the flame runs out of fuel, it shrinks and goes out.

The opposed-flow flames all reach a steady length and spread rate as long as the air flow speed is held constant for around 5 seconds.  The 1-cm wide concurrent-flow flames also all reach a steady state.  The concurrent-flow flames burning the 2-cm wide samples all have constant flame base spread rates over the available test duration.  However, only air flows less than 10 cm/s yield steady flame lengths.  The concurrent tests performed right at 10 cm/s give Figure 10. indications that the flames are approaching a steady length, but the fuel samples are too short to conclude this with certainty.

In Fig. 10, the still image sequence is shown for 1-cm wide fuel sample in 11 cm/s concurrent air flow.  The ignition, flame development, steady state spread, and extinction portions of the burn can be seen.  In addition, the flames tend to leave behind a small amount of fuel when they spread.  Since the fuel is very hot and now exposed to fresh oxygen, there is the development of an interesting pattern of smoldering visible as a bright orange glow in the fuel matrix beneath the flame.  This surface reaction may have some effect on the stabilization of the flame.
For concurrent-flow flames, the fuel preheating depends on the entire flame and hot plume which means that the flame response time to flow changes is a strong function of the flame size.  On the other hand, opposed-flow flames tend to respond quickly to flow changes since the fuel preheating ahead of the flame (which controls spread) only depends on the small region around the stabilization zone.  One can take advantage of this aspect by performing a series of step-wise flow changes to get the spread behavior as a function of flow speed in a single test.  In Fig. 11, the flame images from such a test are shown for a 2-cm wide sample burning in opposed flow.  The flow is decreased from 10 cm/s all the way to nearly zero, and the spread rate is measured at each set flow speed.  From this single burn, six different conditions are studied.  The flow speed changes are indicated in the figure.  The flame responds within a couple seconds, but the flame is allowed to burn at this speed for about 10 to 15 seconds so that a good spread rate determination can be made.
Figure 11.  Digital still camera images showing a flame burning a 2-cm wide cotton-fiberglass fabric in opposed flow.  Images are taken every 1.25 sec (starting at top and moving from left to right). The flow is decreased in discrete steps from 10 cm/s all the way down to less than 1 cm/s.  The flame response to flow changes is very rapid, and the flow effects on the flame and its spread rate are dramatic.  Total burn time is 90 sec.  Flow changes are indicated by numbers. (Test 9)
