While the numerical modeling eﬀorts continue to progress toward including particulate sooting
eﬀects, the work has already predicted that that carbon dioxide substitution for nitrogen in the
burning of large carbon number hydrocarbon liquid droplets leads to a signiﬁcant eﬀects partly
through increased heat capacity within the gaseous diﬀusion ﬂame, but mostly because of modifca-
tions in spectral radiative coupling in the gas phase. Eﬀects of sooting and slow gas-phase/droplet
convection remain to be considered in future numerical modeling studies. The work also shows
that the modeling methodologies can be developed to evaluate the eﬀects of chemical inhibitors in
the liquid and gas phases.
The BCDCE program has produced results that are of relevance to the proposed FLEX program.
Speciﬁcally, BCDCE expertise can contribute to FLEX by quantifying ﬁber inﬂuences analytically
and computationally) and interpreting data in terms of inﬂuences of droplet shapes, internal ﬂows,
liquid mixing rates and product dissolution. The BCDCE research has also developed a 3-d com-
putational model of a droplet on a ﬁber, including capillary ﬂows induced by the ﬁber. A cross
ﬂow can be modeled, which is relevant to a droplet anchored on a moving ﬁber. However, the
computational model presently covers only vaporizing droplets. It is planned to extend this model
to include combustion, depending on funding levels. UC Davis also has a working drop rig that
can be used for experiments up to about 10 atm.
A.2
Fiber Supported Droplet Combustion Experiment (FSDC)
FSDC was the ﬁrst droplet combustion experiment conducted in space. In this Glovebox experi-
ment, in a procedure somewhat similar to the current project, a shuttle crew member deposited a
measured amount of fuel droplet (initial diameters varied between 2 and 5 mm) on a silicon-carbide
ﬁber (80 µm diameter) and ignited them in cabin air environment using a hot-wire igniter. The re-
sults of these experiments are summarized in Dietrich et al. (1996) and Shaw et al., (2001a, 2001b).
This experiment, for the ﬁrst time, produced the radiative extinction of large methanol droplets
in a quiescent, microgravity environment. In the forced convective part of FSDC-1 experiments,
droplets were burned initially in a quiescent environment and then forced convective ﬂow (gener-
ated by a fan) was turned on so that both spherically symmetric and convective droplet burning
were observed. The dynamics of ﬂame response were also documented. The convective velocities
in these experiments were of the order of 10 cm/s and radiative extinctions were not observed for
the methanol and heptane/hexadecane fuel droplets studied.
A.3
Fiber Supported Droplet Combustion Experiment - 2 (FSDC-2)
FSDC-2 experiments were conducted during the MSL-1 mission (STS-94) of the space shuttle
Columbia in April 1997.
In these experiments radiative extinction for ethanol, methanol, n-
heptane, and n-decane fuels were observed in a quiescent environment. Flow eﬀects on sooting
and non-sooting were also investigated in the intermediate Reynolds number regime Re ∼O(100)
(Colantonio et al. 1998). The FSDC experiments clearly demonstrated the feasibility of performing
ﬁber supported droplet combustion experiments as well as the experimental technique of extracting
ﬂame position as function of time from the Si-C ﬁber radiation. These experiments strongly support
the feasibility of the proposed experiments. Results from the FSDC-2 experiments are described
by Shaw et al. (2001a).
A.4
Droplet Combustion Experiment (DCE)
The Droplet Combustion Experiment is a high ﬁdelity experiment conducted inside a pressure ves-
sel onboard the Spacelab during MSL-1 mission. Free ﬂoated, n-heptane droplets were burned in

oxygen/helium environments at three diﬀerent pressures (0.25, 0.5, and 1 atm.). At low oxygen
concentrations and at large initial droplet sizes radiative extinction was observed (Nayagam et al.,
1998). All the radiative extinctions observed during these experiments were essentially in a quies-
cent environment (droplet drift velocities ∼2 mm/s) and the ﬂames were spherical. Extinction
occurs suddenly and with no obvious preferential starting point (within the time resolution of ob-
servation 1/30 sec). At high oxygen concentrations, when the drift velocities of the order a few
mm/s were present, only ‘diﬀusive extinctions’ were observed. Diﬀusive extinction of this nature,
however, was hardly perturbed by the slow convective eﬀects. One of the lessons learned during
these experiments relevant to the proposed study is that it is very diﬃcult, if not impossible, to
control the droplet/gas relative velocities in a free ﬂoated droplet combustion experiment. This
fact has led us to use the small Si-C ﬁber to support the droplet and produce precisely controllable
velocities by translating the tethered droplet in a quiescent environment.
A.5
Ground-based studies of Soot Formation/Destruction
Controlling the degree of sooting is important for developing an accurate understanding of its inﬂu-
ence on droplet burning, ﬂame dynamics, and ﬂame extinction. All of the independent experimental
variables (initial droplet diameter, diluents and suppressants, oxygen mole fraction, pressure, fuel
type, convection) to be used in the FLEX experiments have been demonstrated in previous micro-
gravity experiments to strongly inﬂuence the degree of sooting and droplet burning behavior which
will thereby aﬀect ﬂame extinction. The background section on droplet combustion clearly showed
how initial droplet size and forced convective ﬂow velocity inﬂuence sooting behavior. The FLEX
team has conducted additional experiments to show how diﬀerent inert gases (or suppressant gases)
inﬂuence sooting behavior.

The residence times of the fuel vapor within the region bounded by the droplet surface and the
ﬂame front were calculated and the results are summarized along with the burning rate and ﬂame
temperature measurements in Table 1 for the three inert cases. Residence times of ethanol fuel vapor
in the oxygen/helium inert case is a factor of two lower than the oxygen/nitrogen and oxygen/argon
inert cases. This is mainly due to the higher Stefan ﬂux associated with increased burning rates
in the oxygen/helium inert case. Since the residence time in both argon and nitrogen inert cases
are very similar, the large diﬀerence in the soot yield is not caused by the inﬂuence of residence
time. Comparisons of the ﬂame temperatures indicate that the oxygen/argon inert case exhibits
the highest temperature, followed by the oxygen/nitrogen and oxygen/helium cases, respectively.
Therefore, the combination of higher fuel vapor residence time and higher temperature accounts for
the dramatic increase in sooting for the oxygen/argon case compared to the oxygen/helium case.
Figure 10 displays the laser-backlit view of ethanol droplets burning in 30% and 40% con-
centrations in nitrogen at 2.4 atm pressure (Yozgatligil et al., 2005). These experiments clearly
demonstrate the strong dependence of sooting behavior of ethanol droplets on ambient pressure and
oxygen concentration. As the oxygen concentration is increased, the sooting propensity (based on
visual observation of the opacity of the sootshell) appears to vary in a non-monotonic fashion, ﬁrst
increasing and then decreasing with increasing oxygen concentration. The maximum soot volume
fractions ({v, max) were also measured for these experiments. At 21% O2 in N2 , the maximum
soot volume fraction is approximately 10 ppm, while at 30% O2 in N2 , the maximum soot volume
fraction is approximately 17.5 ppm. As the oxygen concentration is increased, the maximum soot
volume fraction decreased from 11 ppm at the 35% O2 in N2 to less than 5 ppm at the 45% O2 in
N2 case.
Increases in the oxygen concentration result in smaller droplet ﬂames and higher rates of burning
which causes reductions in the fuel vapor transport time. Both of these eﬀects will tend to reduce
the time for soot formation and growth.
At the same, increases in the oxygen concentration
will produce higher ﬂame temperatures which increase the rate of pyrolysis reactions leading to
greater degree of soot precursor and soot formation. The non-monotonic behavior is believed to be
caused by the competition between soot formation and soot oxidation. Numerical calculations also
indicate that concentrations of soot precursors such as benzene display a non-monotonic behavior
with oxygen concentration (Mehl et al., 2005).

droplet combustion. Figure 11 displays the laser-backlit image at t = 0.5 sec after ignition for n-

A.6
Ground-based studies of Soret Diﬀusion
Aharon and Shaw (1998) developed analytical models to describe transport of O2 to droplet ﬂames
under quasisteady conditions, with a particular emphasis of evaluating Soret transport as well as
multicomponent diﬀusion eﬀects that occurs as a result of variations in binary diﬀusion coeﬃcients.
Their models predicted that Soret transport can oppose transport of O2 to a reaction zone if the
diluent has a small molecular weight relative to the molecular weight of O2 , which is the case for
He . Conversely, transport of O2 to a reaction zone is enhanced via Soret eﬀects if the diluent
molecular weight is large relative to the molecular weight of O2 , which is the case for SF6 (or
Xe).
For a diluent such as N2 , which has a molecular weight that is close to the molecular
weight of O2 , Soret eﬀects are small. It was also shown that multicomponent diﬀusion eﬀects
can be important if signiﬁcant diﬀerences between binary species diﬀusion coeﬃcients are present.
The relative inﬂuences of Soret transport and multicomponent diﬀusion eﬀects on an eﬀective O2
diﬀusion coeﬃcient, DO are given in the following relationship.
DO = β φ DIO
(8)
where β accounts for Soret transport, φ multicomponent diﬀusion (accounting for the presence
of combustion-generated CO2 and H2O) and DIO is the binary diﬀusion coeﬃcient of O2 in the
diluent (e.g., He ) (Aharon and Shaw, 1998). When β > 1, Soret transport enhances O2 transport
to ﬂame zones, and when β < 1 Soret transport opposes O2 transport to ﬂame zones. These same
conclusions also apply to φ, which accounts for diﬀerences between binary diﬀusion coeﬃcients in
a multicomponent gas mixture.

content:
molecular weight inert (in this case, Xe) signiﬁcantly promotes transport of oxygen to the ﬂame
zone from Soret eﬀects (β = 1.46), though multicomponent diﬀusion is not signiﬁcantly enhanced
(φ = 1.03). Based on these results, it is clear that varying the molecular weight of the inert
component in the ambient over signiﬁcant ranges strongly inﬂuences the contributions of Soret
transport and multicomponent diﬀusion on transport of O2 to ﬂames.
Further drop tower experiments along these same lines have been performed by Wei and Shaw
(2005). Reduced-gravity experiments involved burning individual propanol droplets that were ini-
tially about 1 mm in diameter. The environment was composed of an O2 -inert mixture, where
He , Ar, Xe and N2 were used separately as inerts. The O2 mole fraction in the environment was
0.21 or 0.50, and the pressure ranged from 0.03 MPa −1.0 MPa. Data from the experiments
indicate that combustion characteristics depend signiﬁcantly on the inert species. He produced
larger and apparently cooler ﬂames while Xe produced ﬂames that were signiﬁcantly smaller and
hotter (for approximately the same initial droplet diameter). N2 and Ar produced intermediate
results. Extensions of these experiments to other fuels (methanol and heptane) and other diluents
(CO2 and SF6) are presently being pursued.
The ground-based experiments described above were limited to smaller droplets (≈
1 mm
in diameter or smaller) that can be burned to completion (or near completion) in drop towers.
Larger droplets, e.g., up to 5 mm initially or larger, which have long burn times, cannot be studied
using ground-based reduced-gravity facilities because of experiment time limitations, which means
that inﬂuences of extended length and time scales relevant to spacecraft environments cannot be
investigated unless space-based experiments are performed.
A.7
Summary
The analytical and numerical modeling work accompanying the above experimental eﬀorts has
guided the development of test matrices for the speciﬁc experiments as well as interpreted the
data obtained from these eﬀorts have signiﬁcantly advanced understanding of the dynamics of
droplet combustion, inclusive of the dynamics of ﬂame position during droplet burning, including
extinction processes, the eﬀects of combustion product dissolution, multi-component vaporization,
non-luminous radiation coupling, sooting, Soret transport, multicomponent diﬀusion, and slow
convection on burning rate parameters, ﬂame structure, and extinction, The sub-models developed
for chemical kinetics in these studies have been extensively used in industry, particularly in the
aircraft gas turbine development eﬀorts at both GE aircraft and United Technologies Research
Center. A bibliography of references that detail the speciﬁcs of these theoretical works and their
comparisons with the above experiments are attached as Appendix

2.7 Passive Rack Isolation System  
The Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) hardware is installed on the CIR ISPR structure in 
order to passively isolate the rack from on-orbit vibrations.  The combination of integrated rack 
and PaRIS provides vibration isolation in both dynamic load path directions (i.e., attenuating 
vibrations imposed on the rack by the ISS vehicle as well as attenuating vibrations induced on 
the ISS vehicle by the rack, without consuming any ISS power, thermal, or data/command 
system resources.  It will attenuate vibratory accelerations above 1 Hz to the ISPR by suspending 
the ISPR from the International Space Station (ISS) module structure using passive dampers and 
springs.  The utility umbilical assembly provides a low bias force and spring rate connection 
between the module structure and the payload rack structure for utility pass through. 
 
The PaRIS is composed of the following: 
 
x Upper isolation strut adapter/interface assembly 
x Upper lock–down/snubbed assembly 
x Lower isolation adapter/interface assembly 
x Lower lock–down/snubbed assembly 
x Utility umbilical assemblies 
x Passive isolation units 
x Installation/adjustment/maintenance hardware 
 
PaRIS utilizes the spring / dampers to isolate the rack from the ISS module structure at 
frequencies above 0.5 Hz.  Unique utility cables and hoses are designated to all PaRIS 
applications.  The utility services have a service loop between the ISS vehicle interface and the 
PaRIS host rack to help in removing the force induced by them.  The utility umbilical assembly 
interfaces with the module at the Utility Interface Panel (UIP) connectors.  
2.8 Science Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) 
The Science Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) is an ISS based system that collects 
acceleration data and distributes this data to the science community.  The distributed architecture 
of SAMS allows many sensors to be deployed at once, each independently collecting 
acceleration data and sending the data to a main control unit.  The control unit can handle 
different types of sensors collecting data at different rates at the same time.  The control unit then 
stores the data on its hard drive and sends the data to Payload Information Management System 
(PIMS) on the ground.  PIMS can then distribute the desired data to the user on the ground.  CIR 
includes a SAMS Tri-axial Sensor Head Ethernet stand alone (SAMS TSH-ES) sensor that 
extends this SAMS system into the rack. 
 
Users on the ground contact the PIMS or SAMS ground operations to have them issue 
commands or provide data.  Ground controllers issue commands to the sensor include starting 
acceleration data collection, changing the acceleration data’s frequency range, and stopping 
acceleration data collection.  Nominally, the CIR TSH begins data telemetry on rack power-up. 
The SAMS is mounted on the front of CIR Optics Bench allowing it to measure accelerations on 
a structure rigidly coupled the combustion chamber.

CIR CONFIGURABLE CAPABILITIES AND RESOURCES 
The CIR provides a set of equipment that provides capabilities above those identified in the base 
configuration described in section 2.0.  This hardware is launched in a stowage configuration and 
installed by the flight crew as required to support a particular science investigation.  Consumable 
resources such as pressurized gas bottles, adsorber cartridges and I/O Processor hard disk drives 
are also included as configurable capabilities.  Much of this hardware is currently manifested on-
orbit and is available for use.  Hardware not currently on-orbit will need to be manifested 
3.1 Science Diagnostics Packages 
The CIR science diagnostics are complete avionics packages including software ready for 
installation and operation in the CIR.  These capabilities include illumination, imaging, image 
acquisition and processing.  A summary of capability and specification is provided in TABLE IV 
and 0  
The CIR specific Diagnostics Packages include: 
x Image Acquisition Modules (IAM) 
x Diagnostic Packages 
x High Bit Depth Multispectral Package (HiBMs) 
x Low Light Level Ultraviolet Package (LLL-UV) 
x Illumination Package.  
 
The Diagnostic Packages are mounted on the Optics Bench using common interfaces to permit 
movement of packages to various window locations for maximum science support flexibility.  
This approach emphasizes packaging modularity for operational flexibility and maintainability. 
Standardized optical interfaces (referred to as the flange mounts) are used between modules.  
These interfaces permit module arrangements to be reconfigured on orbit if required by science.

3.1.1 
Illumination Package 
The Illumination Package FIGURE 14 consists of a laser diode source and a collimating optical 
system, which is used to provide monochromatic illumination with a center wavelength between 
650 - 660nm. 
Two laser diodes are installed in the Illumination Package.  One is the primary laser diode and 
the second is included as a spare.  Both laser diodes are fiber coupled, each with its own FC/PC 
type fiber-optic connection at the Illumination Control Module (ICM), so the output from both 
cannot be used at the same time.  Each laser diode contains a photodiode to provide feedback of 
power output and a temperature transducer to monitor the diode temperature.  The laser diode is 
operated below the lasing threshold current and serves as a non-coherent illumination source.   
The Illumination Package can be used together with the HiBMs Package as a uniform 
illumination background source for soot absorption measurements in soot volume fraction 
applications, for shadowgraph measurements or for droplet diameter measurements.  The 
modular design supports future growth considerations.   
Illumination Package Specifications and Features:  
x 90 mm diameter CW beam 
x Collimation: 0.339° maximum divergence 
x 8-bit programmable output level (0-255) 
x Output power < 5 maw typical; used below lasing threshold current 
x 60% Illumination field uniformity 
x Peak Wavelength: between 650 and 660 nm 
x Spectral Bandwidth: < 10 nm maximum at 50% points 
 
Laser Diode Characteristics: 
x 300-350 maw max output power 
x Continuous Wave (CW) operation  
x Center Wavelength: 650-660 nm 
x Fiber Pigtailed; 0.22 Numerical Aperture

Low Light Level Packages

monochrome camera with a 1024x1024, frame transfer CCD array, providing 12 bit digital 
imaging capability.  The CCD is directly coupled to an 18 mm Gen-II-UV Micro-channel Plate 
Intensifier to provide maximum response at short wavelengths, including the OH emission line at 
310 nm.  The intensifier includes gating control that allows varied exposure times.  This function 
is used both to protect the Intensifier from overexposure and as a means to match the intensity of 
the event being viewed, such as a flame.  The package includes fast numerical aperture optics 
with high UV transmission characteristics and provision for spectral filtering of the transmitted 
illumination (Figure 14).  The LLL-UV Package is provided to produce images of events or

3.0   FCF OVERVIEW 
3.1   Fluids and Combustion Facility  
The FCF is a modular, multi-user facility developed by Glenn Research Center (GRC) 
for permanent installation in the ISS US Lab Module to support technology development 
and validation in support of Space Exploration.  This facility establishes an initial 
operational capability for microgravity fluid physics and combustion science on-board 
ISS.    FCF’s  scope  started  with  design  and  progressed  through  development,  
production, deployment and operation in ISS.  
FCF consists of two powered racks and sufficient on-orbit stowage in ISS for FCF and 
payload hardware.  The two racks are the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the 
Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR).  FCF operates together with payload experiment 
equipment and ground-based operations facilities to perform fluids and combustion 
science experiments within available FCF and ISS resources. 
3.2   Combustion Integrated Rack  
The CIR is designed to support a wide variety of combustion sciences in space.  Solid, 
liquid and gas fuels are burned in a Chamber.  Diagnostics are used to capture 
important attributes of the combustion event such that scientists may better understand 
the combustion process.   
Components located in the CIR will consist of two (2) types of hardware; permanent 
facility hardware, designed to serve multiple Principal Investigators (PI), and PI-specific 
hardware, designed to be replaced as part of each experiment to be performed.  The 
CIR design is to be installed in a standard Boeing ISPR.  A folding door is used over the 
front of the assembled rack.

4.0   CIR/MDCA INTERFACE SECTION 
CIR and MDCA hardware was launched on STS 126/ULF-2from Kennedy Space Center 
in November 2008.  After delivery, CIR was installed in the United States Laboratory 
Module, and MDCA was installed into the CIR.  It is anticipated that FLEX2 hardware 
will be manifested on ATV2 or ULF5 in 2010, and will be integrated into MDCA by the 
crew after the completion of FLEX and FLEX-Helium experiments.   
4.1   MDCA/FLEX2 Experiment Overview 
4.1.1   Payload Description 
MDCA is designed to support experiments that investigate the fundamental 
combustion/suppression/extinguishment aspects of fuel droplets under different 
pressures and ambient oxygen concentrations for a range of fuel droplet sizes.  The 
MDCA/FLEX2 experiments include hardware that is based on the design of the 
MDCA/FLEX hardware, with minimal changes made to accommodate droplet array 
experiments.  The most extensive design changes are with regard to the Retractable 
Index Fiber (RIF), and the igniter tips, as will be described in section 5.  The FLEX2 
hardware that has no changes from the FLEX design consists of gas bottles, and an 
adsorber cartridge, both of which are CIR provided.  Additional needle assemblies and 
fuel reservoirs are provided by FLEX2 and are also identical to those used in FLEX.  
The fuels loaded into the reservoirs, however, will differ from those used in FLEX, as is 
discussed in section 5.      
4.1.2   Experiment objectives 
The objective of MDCA is to provide the apparatus for dispensing, deploying, and 
igniting fuel droplets while the CIR provides the diagnostics, structure, supporting 
avionics, and infrastructure for recording, processing, and downlinking the data from the 
combustion event.  The MDCA initial experiments consist of the FLEX investigations.  
FLEX utilizes pure Methanol and pure Heptane as fuels.  FLEX2 is a follow-on 
experiment planned to begin after the completion of FLEX and FLEX-Helium (He), and 
utilizes pure Ethanol and Decane fuels as well as mixtures of fuels, and provides the 
added capability of igniting arrays of fuel droplets tethered to a beaded fiber. 
4.1.3   Experiment Hardware Description 
The MDCA hardware consists of three distinct hardware components.  The Chamber 
Insert Assembly (CIA) provides the mechanisms for initiating the combustion event.  
The Avionics Package is the center of control and power distribution for the MDCA.  PI 
Specific Diagnostic Packages consist of diagnostics provided by CIR that are necessary 
to meet science requirements and are not provided by MDCA.  An example of this is the 
additional Image Processing Unit (IPSU) and High Bit Depth/Multispectral (HiBMs) 
camera that FLEX2 requires for its operations.  CIR will also be responsible for the 
negotiation of the up-mass of replacement components for MDCA hardware and 
consumable items that are supplied by CIR as specified in CIR-MDCA Integration 
Agreement (FCF-IA-MV-MDCA).  The consumable items required by FLEX2 include an

5.0   MDCA STRUCTURAL/MECHANICAL 
5.1   Chamber Insert Assembly 
The MDCA CIA (See FIGURE 3 and FIGURE 4) is a multi-functional apparatus 
designed as the major platform used for mounting integral sub-system hardware to 
perform combustion science.  The CIA consists of the Internal Apparatus, which is the 
functional hardware of the experiment, the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS), upon 
which the Internal Apparatus is structurally based, and electrical and thermal 
interconnects.  The Internal Apparatus is capable of dispensing, deploying and igniting 
fuel droplets with small velocities relative to the field of view of the diagnostic 
equipment.  The Internal Apparatus of MDCA consists of two fuel dispensing systems, 
dual needle deployment mechanism, two hot wire igniters, an indexing fiber support 
mechanism, radiometers, pressure-sensitive igniter switch, and thermistors.   
During the mission, the crew may replace igniters, the fiber support mechanism, fuel 
reservoir, and deployment needles.

5.2   Internal Apparatus 
5.2.1   Fuel Dispensing System 
There are two fuel dispenser systems on the CIA.  Each fuel dispenser system has two 
subassemblies; the replaceable fuel reservoir assembly and the dispenser motor 
assembly.  The fuel reservoir is composed of a syringe and attached latching solenoid 
valve, an aluminum housing, and a transparent plate of Lexan F2100.  The dispenser 
motor assembly is composed of a drive screw, a stepper motor, an incremental 
encoder, and structural base.  During the software controlled dispensing sequence, fuel 
is dispensed from one syringe, through the latching solenoid valve to its own 
deployment needle.  The solenoid valve is sent a voltage pulse that switches the valve 
to its alternate state.  The syringe valve will be closed immediately following the 
dispensing of the fuel droplet.  
Two identical dispenser systems are present for improved reliability when using a single 
type of fuel.  Alternatively, each syringe may contain a mixture of fuels.  In addition, the 
entire fuel reservoir assembly may be replaced if necessary by separating the fuel line 
bayonet, the valve power connectors, and loosening the captive fasteners.  To monitor 
the temperature of the fuel, each syringe is outfitted with a thermistor. 
FLEX2 requires the use of Ethanol, Decane, and a set of fuel mixtures.  Additional 5 ml

5.2.2   Fuel Reservoir System 
While the fuels loaded into the reservoirs differ between FLEX and FLEX2, the fuel 
reservoir design is identical.  The fuel reservoir is a gas-tight glass syringe and stainless 
steel plunger.  The plunger tip is covered by Teflon, which forms a dual wiper seal 
against the inside of the syringe.  The syringe is covered by a tygon sleeve that is 
epoxied to the syringe at its top.  The tygon-enshrouded syringe body is lightly clamped 
between a transparent cover and the housing.  The syringe feeds fuel directly to an 
attached latching solenoid valve.  It is also epoxied to the solenoid valve at its bottom.  
The fuel is fed from the valve through polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tubing to the 
dispenser needles.  A quick disconnect in the tubing is necessary to allow removal of 
the fuel reservoir.   
Each syringe has two levels of containment.  In addition to the tygon sleeve, the syringe 
is enveloped in an aluminum sleeve that is covered by a transparent Lexan 9604 barrier 
to protect against impact.  See FIGURE 6. 
Each syringe can contain 5.0 ml of fuel.  Nearly all of the fuel in the syringe is capable of 
being dispensed.

5.2.3   Deployment System 
The FLEX2 deployment mechanism is identical to that of MDCA/FLEX, and consists of 
two replaceable deployment needles mounted on brushless servo motors and bi-stable 
brakes.  The deployment needles are flared tubes (See FIGURE 8) connected to the 
Dispenser System via .012 inch OD, .01 inch ID, PTFE tubing.  The deployment 
needles are inverted relative to each other and opposed 180 degrees as illustrated in 
FIGURE 9.  During deployment, the needles move in a plane common to the igniters 
and fiber.  Each needle is moved by a brushless servo motor, which rotates the needles 
to a pre-determined position verified by motor encoder feedback.  Just before 
dispensing fuel, the needles are positioned in close proximity to each other.  Fuel from 
each of the fuel dispenser systems is routed to its dedicated deployment needle tip to 
create a single droplet of a desired size.  Upon completion of fuel dispensing, the 
deployment motors actuate again, rotating to increase the gap between the needles and 
to minimize the needle surface contact with the droplet.  Finally, the needles are rapidly 
withdrawn simultaneously.  The rapid synchronized retraction of the needles causes the 
fuel droplet to detach from the deployment needles with little or no residual motion.  
Either deployment needle may be used to dispense the droplet via its fuel dispenser 
system.  The needles may be replaced by separating the bayonet assembly in the fuel 
line and unfastening the needle fixture on the motor axis.  Per the replacement 
procedure, which is performed at the ISS provided work bench, the deployment needles 
will be removed only after its cover has been installed.  This cover, shown in FIGURE 
10, prevents contact with the needle during removal/installation.  Each needle has its 
own cover that remains attached during stowage.  Needles will be individually bagged 
upon replacement to contain any residual fuels and broken material.

5.2.4   Ignition System 
While the MDCA/FLEX igniter tips uses two identical round heating elements with single 
loops, the FLEX2 ignition tips consist of two heating elements with a dual loop 
configuration.  The elements are Kanthal hot wire igniters mounted on removable 
ceramic mounts (See FIGURE 11).  The elements have  can simultaneously ignite a two 
bead droplet array on the retractable index fiber.  The ceramic mount is mounted to a 
bracket on the drive shaft.  Each drive shaft is driven by a rotary stepper motor and an 
enclosed drive screw.  Each hot wire igniter is positioned opposite the other.  The rotary 
stepper motor moves the igniter linearly into the deployment area to a predetermined 
position just before dispensing of the droplet.  Motor encoders automatically verify the 
igniter position.  The fuel is dispensed, the droplet is deployed, and a wait period passes 
to allow some fuel vaporization.  Then both igniters are pulsed with a brief current to 
heat the igniter and ignite the fuel vapor surrounding the droplet.  Finally, the igniters 
rapidly retract out of the field of view of the diagnostic equipment.  Each igniter may be 
replaced by pulling the ceramic mount from the bracket.  The electrical connection is 
made when the ceramic mount is plugged onto the bracket. 
The igniter tips will be stowed in bags.  The crew will be required to wear gloves while 
performing this procedure.  Additionally, during this operation, which is performed at the 
ISS provided work bench, the covers for the deployment needles will be installed to 
prevent inadvertent contact. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
FIGURE 11 FLEX AND FLEX2 IGNITER TIPS  
 
5.2.5   Fiber Support System 
The FLEX2 fiber support mechanism is based on that of MDCA/FLEX, with the addition 
of crossing fibers for tethering an array of droplets.  The FLEX2 experiments employ a 
set of 79 micron diameter, 229 mm long silicon carbon-carbide fibers with  an additional 
set of crossing fiber pairs of the same material to suspend fuel droplets in an array of 
predetermined dimension.    The main fibers are supported at both ends by the arms of 
a U-shaped bracket.  The lower portion of the U- bracket is mounted to an axle.  The 
axle is attached to a rotary stepper motor that rotates the bracket and fiber

approximately 120 degrees about the axle so that the fiber is in the center of the fuel 
deployment area. Retractable Indexing Fiber (RIF) Sub-Assembly design features 
replaceable Fiber Arm, both rotational and linear over travel hard stops. Stepper Motors 
are protected by use of slip clutches.  See FIGURE 12. 
The droplet may be deployed at various intersections of the crossing fiber pairs with the 
main fiber.  There are 3 pairs of crossing fibers with two pairs 12mm apart, and 1 pair at 
24mm apart.  They are attached by epoxy to a cross member that is attached to the U-
shaped fiber arm bracket.  A second rotary stepper motor actuates a rack and pinion 
mechanism.  The rack and pinion mechanism allows the fiber to be indexed along the 
axis of the fiber.  Deployment onto the fiber is limited to the central 129 mm of the fiber 
because using the extreme ends of the fiber would bring the bracket arms close enough 
to interfere with the combustion event.   
When a tethered droplet array is desired, one of the crossing fibers is moved into 
position, the droplet is dispensed onto the cross fiber, and the fiber is translated the 
distance of the cross fiber pair spacing.  There are two crossing fiber pairs spaced 
12mm apart, and one pair spaced 24mm apart.  The next droplet is then dispensed onto 
the second cross fiber pair.  The deployment needles retract, and the igniters ignite the 
droplets.  
The hardware-restricted spherical volume around the center of the droplet is called the 
zone of exclusion.  When the fiber is not being used, the fiber will be in the retracted 
mode, clear of the deployment area and diagnostic fields of view.  Rotational retraction 
speeds of the RIF are nominally from 2°-6°/sec. 
The fiber support mechanism may be replaced in case of damage with stowed spares 
by unfastening the captive fasteners shown in FIGURE 13.  The Fiber Arm is replaced 
at the ISS provided work bench after the CIA is removed from the chamber.  It requires 
no complicated alignment techniques and no electrical power.  Included in the Fiber 
Arm replacement procedure is the installation of the protective cover for the fiber which 
prevents inadvertent contact.  The Fiber Arm is stowed with this cover installed.  To 
prevent handling damage, each Fiber Arm Assembly is shipped with a protective cover 
(FIGURE 14).

5.2.6   Water Cooling System 
The details of the water cooling system are unchanged by the FLEX2 operations, and 
are included in the MDCA safety data package MDC-DOC-1679.  The CIA will take in 
water from the CIR Water Thermal Control System through the IRR.  CIA intake and 
exhaust lines will connect to the IRR.  The CIA water lines provide the interface 
between the CIR IRR and the MDCA CIA structure. The coolant system will connect to 
the CIR IRR with quick disconnects. 
 
5.2.7   Pressure Sensitive Igniter Switch 
The details of operation of the pressure sensitive igniter switch are unchanged by the 
FLEX2 operations, and are included in the MDCA safety data package MDC-DOC-
1679.  While the physical and electrical operation of the switch is unchanged, its role no 
longer functions as a hazard control in FLEX2.  The updated detonation analysis shows 
that the fuel to O2 mixture ratio drops below the flammability limit as pressure 
increases.  Therefore no hazard is associated with high pressure operations.      
 
6.0   MDCA ELECTRICAL/AVIONICS  
6.1   MDCA Avionics Package Hardware 
The MDCA Avionics Package is made of aluminum alloy, 6061-T6.  Some structural 
components may be composed of corrosion resistant stainless steel, A286. 
The Avionics Package is an aluminum box that provides a physical housing, an EMI 
shield, and connection to the CIR Optics Bench electrical interconnects.  The housing 
will be mounted on the Optics Bench at the Principal Investigator Location (PIL).  This 
housing has inlet and exhaust vents to interface with the CIR Air Thermal Control 
System.  The housing is illustrated in FIGURE 15 and FIGURE 16.

FLX-REQ-0001 
February 04, 2010 
PREFACE 
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a modular, multi-
user experimentation mini-facility for conducting droplet combustion science experiments in the 
microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS).  This facility, called the 
Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), resides in Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR), a component of the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF) on-board the ISS.  The Flame 
Extinguishment Experiment 2 (FLEX-2) uses the MDCA platform to conduct droplet 
combustion tests. 
This document will define the engineering and science requirements necessary to successfully 
complete the FLEX-2 experiments.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1  
Purpose 
This document will define the engineering requirements necessary to successfully complete the 
science and safety requirements.  This document will be used by the FLEX-2 design engineers to 
develop the systems necessary for FLEX-2.  Interface and carrier requirements levied on FLEX-
2 are documented in the CIR-MDCA Interface Control Document (FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA).  
FLEX-2 will use the existing Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) hardware and 
software platform already developed as a baseline for meeting many of the requirements found in 
this document.  Safety requirements are documented in the CIR/MDCA Integrated Hazard 
Reports and the MDCA Hazard Reports (Re-Flight). 
1.2  
Scope 
This FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements Document (ERD) serves to document two sets of 
requirements:  Science Requirements and Derived Engineering Requirements.  The FLEX-2 
Science Requirements Document (SRD) is created by the experiment’s Principle Investigators 
(PI’s) and defines the requirements that are necessary to accomplish the FLEX-2 science 
objectives.  The purpose of this document is to provide traceability to the SRD and to formalize 
these requirements.  Also, it defines the engineering requirements derived to establish the 
capabilities for a system that achieves the science requirements in conjunction with existing CIR 
and MDCA capabilities.

content:
FLX-REQ-0001 
February 04, 2010 
3.0 
MDCA OVERVIEW 
3.1  
Payload Description 
The Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus is a mini-facility designed to support Principal 
Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of droplet combustion in a microgravity 
environment.  MDCA will be integrated into the Fluids and Combustion Facility’s (FCF) 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space Station (ISS).  Currently, the 
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) and the Flame Extinguishment Experiment 2 (FLEX-
2) have been selected for use in the MDCA. 
3.2  
MDCA Mission 
The MDCA mission is to perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame 
extinguishment investigations using the CIR.  The MDCA will allow investigation using pure 
liquid fuels and mixtures of liquid fuels at various chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, 
and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity environment allows for measurement and 
observation of flame extinguishment processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The 
modular design of the MDCA allows for flexibility in configuring for specific experiments and 
easy maintainability of the hardware.  This hardware will provide the apparatus for dispensing, 
deploying and igniting fuel droplets.  When new droplet experiments are proposed, the additional 
experiment specific hardware will be provided.  This requirements document reflects such a 
case, including only the requirements of the FLEX-2 investigation. 
3.3  
FLEX-2 Requirements Flow 
Figure 1 represents the requirements flow for all of the FLEX-2 requirements.  The requirements 
in the Science Requirements Document (SRD) are agreed upon by the FLEX-2 Principle 
Investigators (PI’s), and this document serves as the top level source of those requirements 
necessary to achieve the FLEX-2 science objectives.  Derived requirements come from 
engineering requirements and are set by the FLEX-2 Project Team.  These two sets of 
requirements are incorporated into this the FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements Document (FLX-
REQ-0001).  
Safety requirements are contained in the updated FLEX-2 safety review hazard reports from the 
Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP).  The carrier requirements are found in the CIR/FLEX-2 
Interface Control Document (FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA).

FLX-REQ-0001 
February 04, 2010 
3.4  
MDCA Hardware Description 
The FLEX-2 investigation will be using the existing MDCA hardware and software.  MDCA 
should be considered the platform on which the FLEX-2 experiments are carried out.  The 
MDCA hardware consists of three hardware domains:  the Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA), the 
Avionics Package, and MDCA Diagnostics.  The CIA provides the mechanism for the 
combustion event.  The Avionics Package is the center of the control and power distribution for 
the FLEX-2.  The FLEX-2 hardware is discussed in detail below.  If more detail is desired, 
please refer to MDC-DOC-1364, MDCA Baseline Systems Description. 
3.4.1  
MDCA Chamber Insert Assembly 
The MDCA Chamber Insert Assembly provides all the necessary hardware and interfaces to 
perform science on one platform.  Most experimental functions occur within the CIA structure 
and many associated systems are found on the CIA.  The CIA consists of the Internal Apparatus 
(IA), which is the functional hardware and the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) upon 
which the IA is structurally based.  Other subsystems found on the CIA include the Droplet 
Dispensing System, the Droplet Deployment System, the Fiber Support System, and the Ignition 
System. 
3.4.1.1  
Experiment Mounting Structure 
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA and acts as the primary mechanical interface 
with the CIR combustion chamber.  It consists of two endplates, the support structure, and the 
removable shrouds to protect the IA during crew activity. 
3.4.1.2  
Internal Apparatus 
The IA provides the primary mounting platform for all experiment specific hardware and 
functions such as droplet dispensing, deployment and ignition.  The IA encompasses all motors 
used in MDCA, as well as a cooling plate, radiometers, and some avionics hardware.  The IA is 
also available for future add-on hardware for different PIs. 
3.4.1.2.1  
Fuel Dispenser System 
There are two separate fuel dispenser systems on the CIA.  Each fuel dispenser system consists 
of a motor housing and a replaceable reservoir.  The motor housing is permanently fixed to the 
IA and contains the motor, encoder, and lead screw assembly.  The encoder verifies position of 
the motor and allows ground operators to keep account of fuel usage.  The replaceable reservoir 
is composed of the syringe, the latching solenoid valve, the reservoir housing, and a transparent 
Lexan cover.  The replaceable reservoir assembly is located on top of the motor housing.  The 
syringe is covered in a Tygon sleeve and contained in aluminum housing.  The syringe is 
connected directly to a fuel isolation, latching, solenoid valve.  The polytetraflouroethylene 
(PTFE) fuel line tubing is attached to the valve with a removable fitting to disconnect the

stepper motor, which in turn pushes the plunger on the syringe. 
3.4.1.2.2  
Deployment System 
The deployment system consists of two deployment needles made from .010-inch O.D. stainless 
steel tubing supported by a ceramic sleeve.  Each needle tip is flared to aid in the droplet 
deployment.  The needles are mounted to individual rotary servomotors with a specially designed 
coupling that allows replacement of the needles and maintains the precise alignment of the 
system.  The motors rotate the needles to a pre-determined location where they are nearly tip-to-
tip.  Metered fuel from the dispenser is routed via the PTFE tubing to one needle forming a 
droplet of very precise volume.  The deployment motors then actuate again, creating a slight gap 
between the needles.  This causes the droplet to center itself between the needle tips and 
minimizes the contact area with the needles.  Finally, the needles are rapidly accelerated apart, 
deploying the droplet off the needle tips.  The rapid acceleration leaves the droplet in place with 
little or no residual motion. 
3.4.1.2.3  
Fiber Support System 
The fiber mechanism consists of a 235 mm long, 79μm diameter silicon carbide fiber fastened 
between two arms with epoxy to a tension of 15000 psi.  There is a succession of small stainless 
steel beads secured to the fiber at 12mm intervals.  The use of the fiber mechanism allows fuel 
droplets to be deployed onto, and thus tethered to, the beaded fiber at specific locations during 
experimental burn and observation.  The beads act to constrain the position of the droplets on the 
fiber, which is especially necessary for the FLEX-2 droplet linear array experiments, where two 
droplets are burned simultaneously.  When used, the fiber is rotated 68o into the deployment area 
using a rotary stepping gear motor.  To deploy a linear array of droplets and to provide a clean 
portion of the fiber for successive burns, linear translation of the fiber through the deployment 
zone is achievable using a similar gear motor driving a pinion gear attached to a rack on the fiber 
mechanism assembly.  This translation can also be used to provide a low velocity flow over a 
single burning droplet. 
3.4.1.2.4  
Ignition System 
The ignition system uses the original MDCA configuration for single droplet ignition and for the 
array experiments, modified dual droplet igniter tips are employed.  The original MDCA ignition 
system consists of two hot wire igniters opposed 180o, controlled by individual actuators.  These 
ignition wires are 4mm diameter loops of Kanthal A-1 wire, 30 AWG.  These loops are mounted 
into ceramic tubes and comprise the igniter tip assembly.  This assembly has two pins that mate 
with sockets on the igniter-mounting interface.  This interface is fixed to the igniter motors, 
which move the igniters into the deployment area linearly in precise steps and quickly retract the 
igniters after ignition.  The MDCA igniter tips are designed to be crew replaceable and for the 
array experiments these will be replaced with the dual droplet igniter tips, which are based on the 
original MDCA design and comply with all MDCA requirements.

3.4.1.2.5  
Cooling Plate System 
A cooling plate is provided to conductively cool the IA.  The tubing is a stainless steel 3/8-inch 
O.D. with .028-inch wall thickness.  CIR compatible quick disconnect coupling fittings will 
connect the cold plate to the EMS endplate.  A flexible conductive lined Teflon hose with 
stainless steel braiding will provide the coupling from the MDCA CIA to the CIR Interface 
Resource Ring (IRR).  Mating Preece connectors will be used for this interface with CIR’s IRR.  
CIR’s color coding scheme will be maintained by MDCA for the inlet and outlet connectors.   
The cooling system will circulate ISS cooling water flow controlled by CIR to satisfy FLEX-2 
requirements.  Prior to launch, the cooling system will be pre-filled to capacity with cooling 
water.  A gaseous nitrogen charged accumulator bottle installed inline will provide automatic 
CIA protection from fluid over expansion in the system specifically during storage periods where 
ambient temperatures may significantly change. 
3.4.1.2.6  
Radiometers 
The Radiometers will provide relative measure of flame radiation and emissions through the 
combustion event.  The Radiometer Package consists of two Radiometers contained in a single 
housing, mounted on the CIA, providing a direct view of the combustion event.  The Broad-Band 
Radiometer will measure total flame energy from combustion over a wavelength range covering 
0.6 μm – 5.0 μm, while the Narrow-Band Radiometer will provide spectrally filtered 
measurements for specific H20 emissions at 1.87 μm, using a narrow bandpass filter.  Power to 
the Radiometer Package is provided by MDCA Avionics. 
3.4.2  
MDCA Avionics 
The Avionics Package provides power conditioning and power distribution, system control, data 
acquisition, and operator interface for the MDCA.  The Avionics Package will house the main 
electronics for the MDCA hardware and will be mounted on the CIR Optics Bench. 
3.4.2.1  
Data and Control 
A processor is responsible for automating the sequencing of operational events along with 
acquiring, downlinking, and storing experiment data.  Experiment control and sequencing will be 
automated by the MDCA software, which is resident on the main processor.  The main processor 
communicates with the CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP).  The interface to the CIR IOP is 
necessary for transferring commands, downlinked data, and images and to receive the ISS video 
and health and science (H&S) data.

3.4.2.2  
Power Control and Distribution 
MDCA receives its direct current, 28-Volt power from the CIR’s Electrical Power Control Unit 
(EPCU) through the Avionics Package.  In the Avionics Package, the power is conditioned by 
filters and dc-dc converters for use by the processor, eight Axis Motor Controller, A/D and 
Signal Conditioning Boards, and CIA interface board. 
3.4.3  
MDCA Diagnostics 
MDCA Diagnostics provide acquisition and storage of all optical information concerning droplet 
deployment and combustion. 
3.4.3.1  
Color Camera Package 
The MDCA Color Camera Package will provide an overhead view of the combustion event.  The 
Color Camera Package consists of a Sony FCB-EX470L CCD camera, which includes a built-in 
Zoom Lens with RS-232 controllable zoom and focus functions.  The camera is completely 
enclosed in a housing container and mounted to the CIA upper structure, internal to the chamber.  
An aluminum broadband coated turning mirror is used to fold the view from the experiment to 
the color camera.  The Color Camera Package analog video output is converted to twisted pair, 
via the Color Camera Interface Package, which then routes the output to the CIR Image 
Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU-A) for viewing and storage.  Power to the Color Camera 
Package is supplied by MDCA Avionics. 
3.4.3.2  
White Light Illumination 
The White Light Illumination Package supports the Color Camera Package prior to and 
following the experiment event, to provide direct overhead lighting of the droplet deployment 
area during dispensing, deployment and ignition for troubleshooting purposes.  The White Light 
Illumination is powered off upon droplet ignition, as the experiment provides its own light.  The 
package consists of two clusters of nine White Light LEDs mounted on the CIA upper structure.  
Power to the White Light Illumination is supplied by MDCA Avionics.

3.5  
Interfaces 
3.5.1  
External Interfaces 
3.5.1.1  
Launch Configuration Interfaces 
FLEX-2 provided hardware is non-operational for launch.  FLEX-2 hardware will be stowed in 
standard containers provided by FLEX-2 and will only have physical and structural interfaces 
with the containers.  
3.5.1.2  
On-Orbit External Interfaces 
FLEX-2 has no direct external interfaces on-orbit.  All interfaces with the FCF, US LAB, ISS 
and the ground are indirectly through CIR. 
3.5.2  
Internal Interfaces 
The internal interfaces between MDCA and CIR are listed below and the requirements for these 
interfaces will be defined in FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA, Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus 
Interface Control Document. 
• Structural/Mechanical and Stowage 
• Electrical Power 
• Command and Data Handling 
• Payload and Diagnostics 
• Thermal Control 
• Exhaust Vent 
• FOMA Gas Delivery 
• Environmental

4.0 
REQUIREMENTS 
This section details all science and derived engineering requirements that have been levied upon 
FLEX-2.  Verifications for these requirements are documented in the FLEX-2 SEVP (FLX-PLN-
0002). 
4.1  
Science Requirements 
 This section is a flowdown of the science requirements from the FLEX-2 SRD dated December 
6, 2009.  Upon being signed, this FLEX-2 ERD becomes the formal FLEX-2 project requirement 
document. 
4.1.1  
Experimental Fuels - Alcohol  
FLEX-2 shall require the use of ethanol. 
4.1.2  
Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon 
FLEX-2 shall require the use of decane. 
4.1.3  
Experimental Fuels – Alcohol Mixture 
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a propanol/glycerol mixture. 
4.1.4  
Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon Mixture 1 
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a heptane/hexadecane mixture. 
4.1.5  
Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon Mixture 2 
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a heptane/octane mixture. 
4.1.6  
Experimental Fuels – Other Mixture 
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a decane/propylbenzene mixture. 
4.1.7  
Fuel Purity 
FLEX-2 shall use fuels of research grade with purity greater than 99.5% by volume. 
4.1.8  
Fuel Quality 
FLEX-2 fuels shall be anhydrous prior to loading into fuel reservoirs.

4.1.9  
Fuel Degassing 
FLEX-2 pure fuels shall be degassed prior to loading into fuel reservoirs.   
4.1.10  
Fuel Quality Assurance 
Certification of test samples shall be provided prior to flight. 
4.1.11  
Fuel Temperature 
The fuel temperature at the start of each test shall be in the range of 18 ºC – 27 ºC.  
4.1.12  
Droplet Size Tolerance 
FLEX-2 shall dispense droplets with diameters of 1.5 – 5 mm with a tolerance ± 0.25 mm. 
4.1.13  
Droplet Size Reproducibility 
FLEX-2 shall dispense droplets with diameters of 1.5 – 5 mm with a reproducibility of ± 5%. 
4.1.14  
Fiber Size 
FLEX-2 shall provide a support fiber with a diameter < 100 µm.   
4.1.15  
Fiber Material Thermal Diffusivity 
FLEX-2 shall provide a fiber material with a thermal diffusivity no greater than 2.3 cm2/s.   
4.1.16  
Fiber Material Emissivity 
FLEX-2 shall provide a fiber material with an emissivity comparable to that of 80 micron. 
diameter Silicon Carbide.   
4.1.17  
Droplet Anchoring Capability 
FLEX-2 shall provide a support fiber capable of anchoring a fuel droplet at a fixed location by 
use of bead structures. 
 
4.1.18  
Droplet Arrays 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to create droplet arrays in a binary linear configuration with 
bead spacing of 12mm and 24mm.

4.1.19  
Bead Material  
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads are made of an impervious material. 
4.1.20  
Bead Shape 
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads are of a shape that is as close to spherical as possible. 
4.1.21  
Bead Size 
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads have a diameter that is as small as possible, but of sufficient 
size as to allow consistent droplet deployment and positioning for the full range of initial droplet 
diameters. 
4.1.22  
Bead Surface 
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the surface of the beads and the fiber interface contain no pores or 
areas where gas can be trapped. 
4.1.23  
Bead Spacing 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to create droplet arrays in a binary linear configuration with 
a bead spacing of 12mm. 
4.1.24  
Ignite in Flow 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to ignite a droplet in a quiescent atmosphere and with gas 
flowing past. 
4.1.25  
Igniter Material 
FLEX-2 shall provide hot wire igniters as the droplet ignition source. 
4.1.26  
Igniter on Time 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to power on the igniters for between 1 to 5 second durations. 
4.1.27  
Ignition Timing 
FLEX-2 shall wait 10 seconds after deployment of a droplet before initiating the ignition 
sequence to allow for droplet deployment induced oscillations to damp adequately. 
4.1.28  
Ignition Disturbance 
FLEX-2 shall provide the command controllable ability to apply the minimum necessary energy 
input to the droplet during ignition.

4.1.29  
Igniter Position Control 
FLEX-2 shall provide capability to reposition the igniter tip between tests to 1 – 5 initial droplet 
diameters from the droplet surface, ± 0.5 mm. 
4.1.30  
Igniter Retraction 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to retract the igniter tips from the field of view of the droplet 
view diagnostic after ignition of the droplet. 
4.1.31  
Igniter Control 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to change the igniter position, power, and duration of 
operation by command.  
4.1.32  
Hardware Exclusion  
FLEX-2 shall provide for removal of all objects (except the fiber) inside the spherical boundary 
of a radius of 10 initial droplet diameters from the deployment site after ignition during all tests. 
4.1.33  
Non-Quiescent Test Point Timing 
When running a non-quiescent test point, the translation of the support fiber shall begin at the 
same time as igniter retraction. 
4.1.34  
Chamber Atmosphere Pressure 
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient pressure ranges from 0.5 – 3 atm, with a tolerance of ± 0.05 atm.   
4.1.35  
Chamber Atmosphere Pressure Rise 
FLEX-2 shall maintain the chamber pressure throughout any given test point to within ± 10% of 
the initial chamber pressure.  
4.1.36  
Oxygen Mole Fractions 
FLEX-2 shall provide oxygen mole fractions ranging from 0.1 to 0.4 with a tolerance on the 
initial charge of ± 0.005 for O2. 
4.1.37  
Chamber Atmosphere Temperature 
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient temperature within the range of 18 – 27 °C.

4.1.38  
Atmospheric Mixing 
FLEX-2 shall provide well-mixed chamber gasses before ignition. 
4.1.39  
Atmospheric Quiescence 
FLEX-2 shall provide quiescent gasses prior to ignition. 
4.1.40  
Atmospheric Humidity 
Atmosphere shall have a Relative Humidity of < 10% for all tests. 
4.1.41  
Chamber Atmosphere Test Set 1 
FLEX-2 shall provide gas mixtures of O2/N2. 
4.1.42  
Chamber Atmosphere Test Set 2 
FLEX-2 shall provide gas mixtures of O2/He. 
4.1.43  
Flow Field Production 
FLEX-2 shall provide relative motion between the drop and the ambient gas by translating the 
fiber. 
4.1.44  
Flow Field Velocity Ranges 
FLEX-2 shall provide flow velocity ranges from 0.1 to 5cm/s with an accuracy of ±1%.   
4.1.45  
Flow Field Control 
FLEX-2 shall provide for control of the acceleration and deceleration of the flow field. 
4.1.46  
Test Point Initiation 
FLEX-2 shall wait at least two (2) minutes after a chamber atmospheric fill before beginning a 
test point to ensure the gas, temperature and pressure to stabilize. 
4.1.47  
Display of Diagnostic Views 
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to downlink the color camera view in near real time. 
4.1.48  
Downlink of Chamber Temperature Data 
FLEX-2 shall provide near real time downlink of the chamber temperature data.

4.1.49  
Downlink of Chamber Pressure Data 
FLEX-2 shall provide near real time downlink of the chamber pressure data. 
4.1.50  
Atmospheric Fuel Vapor 
The test atmosphere prior to each test point shall have fuel vapor mole fraction of < 0.005. 
4.1.51  
Atmospheric Purity 
The test atmosphere prior to each test shall consist of < 0.02 mole fraction (for each product 
species) CO, CO2, and any other by-products of combustion. 
4.1.52  
G-Level 
FLEX-2 shall ensure acceleration levels are < 1 x 10-4 m/s2 on three (3) axes. 
4.1.53  
Microgravity Measurement 
FLEX-2 shall provide capability to measure acceleration near the CIR with an accuracy of 1 x 
10-6 m/s2.  Frequency range shall be 0.01 – 125 Hz.  Sampling rate shall be 1 – 5 times the 
frequency. 
4.1.54  
Diagnostics Imaging  
All MDCA diagnostics shall acquire images pre-ignition, during ignition, at droplet extinction 
and post-extinction.  
4.1.55  
Droplet Imaging Orientation 
FLEX-2 shall provide a droplet view with the focal plane parallel to the support fiber and 
coplanar with the droplet. 
4.1.56  
Droplet Imaging FOV 
FLEX-2 shall provide FOV of 3.0 cm diameter centered about the deployment site for the droplet 
view.     
4.1.57  
Droplet Imaging Spatial Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide spatial resolution of 30 µm over the entire FOV for the droplet view. 
4.1.58  
Droplet Imaging Temporal Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide a nominal minimum framing rate of 30 fps for the droplet view.

Droplet Imaging Temporal Resolution Additional Capability 
The FLEX-2 droplet view camera shall have the ability to use a framing rate of between 60 to 
100 fps at a resolution of 60 µm. 
4.1.60  
Droplet Imaging DOF 
FLEX-2 shall provide a DOF ≥ 3.0 cm for the droplet view.   
4.1.61  
Droplet Imaging Illumination 
FLEX-2 shall provide capability to back light the droplet with a uniform, collimated light source 
of sufficient intensity to allow the droplet’s edges to be clearly detected.

OH Flame Imaging Orientation 
FLEX-2 shall provide a flame view with a focal plane parallel to the support fiber.

OH Flame Imaging Emission 
FLEX-2 shall provide color imaging detection with emission centered for wavelengths of 310 
nm (± 5 nm). 
4.1.65  
OH Flame Imaging Spatial Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide a spatial resolution of 150μm over the entire FOV for the OH flame view. 
4.1.66  
OH Flame Imaging Temporal Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide framing rate of 30 fps for the OH flame view.   
4.1.67  
OH Flame Imaging DOF 
FLEX-2 shall provide a DOF no less than 5mm for the OH flame view.   
4.1.68  
OH Flame Imaging Gain 
The gain on the OH flame imager shall be adjustable prior to each test point.

4.1.69  
Color Imaging Orientation 
FLEX-2 shall ensure the MDCA color camera provides a full view of the droplet and flame with 
the focal plane parallel to the fiber providing viewing of the droplet dispensing and deployment 
sequence.  
4.1.70  
Color Imaging FOV 
FLEX-2 shall provide a FOV  ≥ 5.0 cm diameter, positioned so the entire flame is imaged for the 
MDCA color camera.  
4.1.71  
Color Imaging Spatial Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide a spatial resolution of 100μm for the MDCA color camera.  
4.1.72  
Color Imaging Temporal Resolution 
FLEX-2 shall provide framing rate of 30 fps for the MDCA color camera. 
4.1.73  
Color Imaging DOF 
FLEX-2 shall provide a DOF of no less than 5.0 mm for the MDCA color camera. 
4.1.74  
Color Imaging Zoom 
FLEX-2 shall provide a zoom capability with the MDCA color camera, upon request of the PI, in 
order to adjust the FOV. 
4.1.75  
Narrow Band Radiative Emission 
FLEX-2 shall provide a narrow band radiometer to measure radiant emissions in the luminous 
and non-luminous flames at a wavelength in the H2O band centered at 1.87 µm. 
4.1.76  
Narrow and Broad Band Radiative Emission Sampling Rate  
FLEX-2 shall provide a narrowband and broadband radiometer sampling rate of 30 Hz.   
4.1.77  
Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission Placement 
FLEX-2 shall place the narrowband and broadband radiometer at least 15 cm from the droplet. 
4.1.78  
Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiometer Isolation 
FLEX-2 shall shield the narrowband and broadband radiometers from igniter wire radiation, both 
reflected and direct.

Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission Accuracy 
The FLEX-2 narrow band and broad band radiative emission accuracy shall be 5% of full scale

FLEX-2 shall provide a full view of the droplet and flame with a preferred orientation such that

Soot/Fiber Temperature Field of View 
FLEX-2 shall provide a soot /fiber temperature diagnostic with a full view of the droplet and

4.1.97  
Temperature Measurement Accuracy 
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient temperature measurement accuracy to within ±0.5 C in the range 
of 18-27º C. 
4.1.98  
Synchronization of Measurements 
FLEX-2 shall reference time measurements to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) and have all data 
time stamped and synchronized to within ± 0.03 sec. 
4.2   
Derived Requirements 
This section specifies the additional derived requirements needed to support the training, testing, 
operations, design, and development of the FLEX-2 project within the MDCA and CIR carriers.  
4.2.1  
Fuel Dispenser System 
The following requirements refer specifically to the MDCA/FLEX-2 fuel dispenser system. 
4.2.1.1  
Fuel Mixture Ratio Accuracy 
FLEX-2 shall develop a procedure to ensure that accurate fuel mixtures are loaded into the fuel 
reservoirs.  Mixture ratios shall be accurate to within ±0.5%.   
4.2.1.2  
Fuel Material Compatibility 
The materials exposed to the fuels within the dispensing system shall be compatible with FLEX-
2 identified fuels as follows: 
1. Ethanol 
2. Decane 
3. Heptane 
4. Hexadecane 
5. Octane 
6. Propylbenzene 
7. Glycerol 
8. Propanol 
4.2.1.3  
Purity Degradation 
Purity degradation is in direct correlation to the fuels’ exposure to outside environments.  Fuel 
purity degradation shall be ensured by sealing the fuel reservoir assembly to a maximum leak 
rate of 1 x 10-6 scc/sec of gaseous helium.  
4.2.2  
Atmospheric Conditions 
The following requirements refer specifically to FLEX-2 chamber atmospheric conditions.

CO2 Removal

FLEX-2 shall provide the means to remove fuel vapor from the chamber atmosphere to the 
acceptable levels detailed in the Science Requirements section, requirement 4.1.50.

Internal Apparatus 
The following requirements refer specifically to the hardware components found on the MDCA 
Internal Apparatus. 
4.2.3.1  
Oxygen Compatibility 
All components developed for FLEX-2 located in the CIR chamber shall be compatible with 
40% oxygen at 3 atm. 
4.2.3.2  
Igniter Compatibility 
FLEX-2 shall provide igniter tips that comply with the existing MDCA igniter drive circuitry.  
The igniter shall be constructed of 26 AWG Kanthal type A1 wire 75.8 mm long with a total DC 
resistance of 1 Ω ± 0.250Ω at 20°C.  
4.2.3.3  
Igniter Hoop Diameter 
The igniter hoop diameter shall be able to radiatively heat droplets spaced up to 24mm apart. 
4.2.3.4  
Fiber Alignment with Needles 
The fiber shall be oriented orthogonal to the needle line of action within ± 5 degrees.  This value 
shall be maintained for all replaceable units (when a component is replaced, it shall have the 
same alignment).

Fiber beads must not generate localized boiling in the droplet prior to flame contraction.  Porous

APPENDIX B 
DEFINITIONS 
B.1 
Scope 
This appendix defines special terminology used in this document. 
B.2 
List of Definitions 
Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) – Configured equipment placed inside the combustion 
chamber to perform an experiment.  Usually consists of an experiment mounting structure and an 
internal apparatus. 
Critical Items List (CIL) – For critical failure modes, the CIL contains specific rationale, which 
justifies the retention of the critical item in the system.   
Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) – Hardware that provides the structural interface from 
the combustion chamber to the internal apparatus. 
Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) – Procedure by which each credible failure mode 
is analyzed (failure mode occurrence, methods of detection the failure, corrective action) to 
determine the effects on the system and to classify each potential failure mode in accordance 
with the severity of its effect. 
Internal Apparatus (IA) – The IA provides the primary mounting platform for all experiment 
specific hardware and functions such as droplet dispensing, deployment and ignition.  The IA 
encompasses all motors used in MDCA, as well as a cooling plate, radiometers and some 
avionics hardware.  The IA is also available for future add-on hardware for different PIs. 
Telescience Support Center (TSC) – The NASA ground facility that provides the capability to 
execute ground support operations of on-orbit ISS and Space Shuttle Payloads from the Glenn 
Reseach Center (GRC).

content:
ISS FLEX Experiments - Background
•
Microgravity droplet combustion experiments aimed at
understanding the flammability boundaries of liquid
fuels in a variety of ambient conditions – spacecraft fire
safety
•
Sooting and non-sooting fuels are burned in nitrogen,
helium, carbon dioxide, and xenon environment at
various oxygen concentrations at different pressures
(effectiveness of fire suppressants in spacecraft
environments – CO2 is used in ISS)
•
Conventional understanding has been that the droplet
flame can extinguish via two modes:
•
Diffusive extinction (high Oxygen, small droplet) or
•
Radiative extinction (low oxygen, large droplet)
•
Pure evaporation following extinction
•
Existing theories and numerical simulations supported
this view

content:
ISS FLEX “Cool Flame” Combustion
•
Over 50 years of microgravity droplet combustion experiments (drop-
towers, parabolic-flights, and space shuttle) and the 2nd stage low-
temperature combustion has never been observed
•
Initial attempts at explaining this behavior using pure vaporization could
not agree with quasi-steady d-square law behavior. Diffusion controlled
surface catalytic reaction models required unacceptably high diffusion
coefficients for oxygen
•
low heat release rate
•
quasi-steady burning
•
2nd extinction
•
lower activation energy
Passes “the duck test” – it must be cool-flame supported combustion!

content:
Potential applications
•
Fire safety
•
On Earth spontaneous combustion and explosion of liquid fuel
vapors in chemical industry is a major concern
•
In space “cool flame” can persist after hot flame extinction and
generate combustible vapor that can reignite (similar to smoldering
combustion in solid fuels)
•
Recent results show re-ignition with decane

content:
Concluding Remarks
•
A new phenomenon where a hot flame extinction leads
to a low-temperature, “cool-flame” burning in
microgravity has been observed for the first time
•
These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and
potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety
concerns in spacecraft environments
•
Existing, widely-used detailed chemical kinetic models
do not accurately predict the 2nd stage cool flame
extinction and need further improvement
•
Improved low temperature chemistry will have wide
ranging applications including advanced internal
combustion engine design and development
•
The new phenomena may lead to new innovative
burner designs and fuel reforming technologies

Methanol as an experimental proxy fuel 
Aside from obtaining a better understanding of combustion of MeOH as a fuel in 
practical applications,  MeOH serves as an excellent experimental proxy for 
refining our understanding of basic combustion phenomena … 
•
Chemical kinetics are relatively simple … oxidation reaction is adequately captured in a 
reduced 2 step mechanism (Zhang, '96)  
•
Only trace amounts of CH3 resulting in very little soot production 
•
Stoichiometry results in relatively small flame stand-off distances … minimizing radiative 
effects 
•
 Water vapor produced from combustion diffuses back to the droplet surface, condenses 
(Tb= 64.7°C) … can serve as a useful model for studying condensed phase mixing and 
bi-component fuels.

content:
28th Annual Meeting  of the American Society of Space and Gravitational Research  
Dynamics of Water Absorption and Evaporation During Methanol Droplet 
Combustion in Microgravity 
4 of 15 
MeOH Droplet Extinction Theory  
•
Initially, water produced in the  flame diffuses back to the 
droplet surface and condenses  
•
During the second half of the burning period the water is 
absorbed and gradually builds up in the droplet  
•
Two “idealized” limiting cases for describing the possible 
mixing mechanisms of the binary liquid mixture  
-
diffusion limited … no internal convection in the droplet 
resulting in a thin boundary layer of water that quickly begins to 
evaporate with the fuel   
 -
convection limited … binary mixture is homogenous throughout the droplet resulting in a 
greater amount of water in the droplet and an increase in the concentration of water that 
vaporizes with the fuel   
•
At a certain mixture threshold water begins to evaporate with the fuel and is 
convected back to the flame zone 
•
As water reaches the flame zone the flame temperature decreases,  the reaction time  
increases, and eventually the reaction time reaches the limit beyond which the 
residence time is insufficient to sustain the oxidation reaction … at which point  the 
flame extinguishes

28th Annual Meeting  of the American Society of Space and Gravitational Research  
Dynamics of Water Absorption and Evaporation During Methanol Droplet 
Combustion in Microgravity 
5 of 15 
Previous Work 
•
Implications of water condensation on the surface of evaporating  MeOH droplets first 
investigated in the context of a theoretical study of spray evaporation (Law & Binark, '79) 
-
condensation heat release could augment evaporation rates 
-
water produced from combustion could "back diffuse" to fuel surface,  having a similar effect to 
environmental humidity  
•
Experiment performed on evaporation rates of suspended MeOH droplets in cold humid 
environments (Law et al., '87) 
-
latent heat of condensation at droplet surface initially increase evaporation rates which gradually 
decrease as the droplet becomes concentrated with water 
•
The effect of water condensation and absorption at the droplet surface during rapid 
evaporation (e.g., combustion) first reported by Choi et al. ('88, '89) and extended in later 
studies (Cho et al. '90; Lee & Law, '92;  Yang et al.'90; Dietrich et al., '96) 
•
 A considerable amount of theoretical and numerical work has been performed through 
the years increasing our basic understanding of the complicated processes occurring 
during MeOH combustion – condensed phase transport, burning rate dependencies, 
extinction mechanisms, radiative transport, etc. (Chao et al., '90;  Marchese et al., '96; 
Zhang et al., '96, '97, '98; Okai, et al., 2000;  Dwyer et al., '96, 98, Kazakov et al., '03, 
Farouk et al., '12)

Isolated Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity: “Cool 
Flames” 
 
Tanvir Farouk1 and Frederick L. Dryer2 
 
1Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina,  
Columbia, SC 29208 
2Department of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, 
 Princeton, NJ 08544 
 
  
Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) Experiment Program has been conducting isolated droplet 
combustion experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) with an overall goal to 
determine and analyze burning behavior, limiting oxygen index, and extinction mechanisms as a 
function of fuel, drop diameter, pressure, oxygen index, and dilution (using various diluents, 
including helium, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide). In recent experiments anomalous combustion of n-
heptane droplets are observed; high temperature combustion followed by radiative visible extinction 
and a transition to a second stage (‘cool flame’) burn characterized by loss of visible flame emission. 
In the cool flame regime the droplet regression continues eventually resulting in extinction diameters 
characteristic of diffusive extinction.  Experimental examples of the two stage burning and 
extinction characteristics of isolated n-heptane droplets under microgravity conditions are presented 
and analyzed numerically using a novel spherosymmetric droplet combustion code that includes full 
two-stage detailed chemical kinetics, multi-component transport, and spectral radiative interactions. 
Simulations are presented for a wide range of droplet sizes as well as different diluents.  Radiant heat 
loss from the larger diameter cases results in the transition to the “cool-flame” configuration. 
Simulations further show that ambient diluent conditions and initial droplet sizes that favor enhanced 
radiative heat loss transition from a high temperature combustion stage to a “low temperature” 
diffusive combustion stage and continues to diffusive extinction. Numerical results are analyzed in 
detail to identify key controlling experimental parameters and detailed kinetic properties that result 
in the noted observations. Special attention is given towards identifying the dominant kinetic 
pathways responsible for the cool diffusion flame behavior as well as extinction. Predictions are 
found to be in good qualitative agreement with the experimental measurements. The generic 
character of these results as they pertain to other alkanes-fuels will also be discussed. 
 
1. Introduction 
 
Since 2009, the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) Experiment has been conducting isolated droplet 
combustion experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The overall goal of these 
experiments is to determine and analyze burning behavior, limiting oxygen index, and extinction 
mechanisms as a function of fuel, drop diameter, pressure, oxygen index, and dilution (using various 
diluents, including helium, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide) [1]. Unique to microgravity experiments is the 
ability to study a wide range of initial drop diameters so as to characterize both radiative and diffusive 
extinction phenomena.  In the first phase of the program, methanol was utilized to obtain data on a non 
sooting fuel which absorbs combustion products over its burning history, notably water [1, 2]. More 
recently, the study of hydrocarbons was initiated using n-heptane as the fuel.  In the case of methanol,
