Figure 2 – Software Development Environment 
2.2.5.1 Hardware 
Project software will be developed on an x86 computer running Windows XP or better using the tools 
listed below.  Compiled embedded control software and the operating system image for the DACU will 
be transferred to the DACU CPU’s data storage over a private ethernet network.  The DACU CPU is an 
x86 single board computer located on a PC/104 electronics board.  The DACU can be run by resetting or 
re-powering or, in debug mode, by initiating payload software from the development computer.  An 
RS422 interface between the development computer and DACU CPU simulates and tests the 
communication link between the payload and MSG. 
2.2.5.2 Operating Systems 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be developed to run under the QNX Real-Time Operating 
System (RTOS) by QNX Software Systems Ltd.  (The QNX RTOS is also known as Neutrino.)  It is a 
scalable, POSIX compliant, deterministic, and multi-threaded operating system.   
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer will be developed to run under Windows NT 4.0, 
or as directed by MSG (an upgrade is possible in the near future). 
Custom project software for ground control at the TSC will be developed to run under Windows XP and 
will use the Telescience Research Kit (TreK) from MSFC to communicate with ISS command and data 
interfaces.

2.2.5.3 Languages 
Wherever possible the project will use C++ as the programming language. 
2.2.5.4 Coding Standard 
The project will use 60081-STD-0066, BXF Software Coding Standard, to provide coding guidelines to 
promote style consistency, ease of reading, and maintainability by different programmers. 
2.2.5.5 Compilers 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be compiled using QNX Momentics Integrated 
Development Environment (IDE) version 6.x.x by QNX Software Systems Ltd. 
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer and custom software for ground control will be 
developed using Microsoft Visual Studio .NET. 
2.2.5.6 Version Control / Software Repository 
All project software, including low control level software, will be placed under version control.  Version 
control allows the project to maintain a database of the source code, library modules, and COTS 
packages.  This database will provide change tracking information and simultaneous user access.  The 
version control database will be automatically archived using the existing ZIN network backup system. 
Version control will be achieved using Subversion by tigris.org. 
2.3 
Verification and Validation Plan 
Verification addresses whatever steps a project is going to use to assure that the requirements are 
completely and correctly incorporated in the software product.  Validation states how the project intends 
to get confirmation that what is being designed, built, and delivered meets those requirements. 
The project will perform verification by inspection.  SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, will 
provide traceability to each specific requirement in SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document.  
Verification will be completed prior to source code implementation and will involve a design review as 
specified in SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance Plan. 
The project will perform validation by testing.  SAME-TST-001, Software Acceptance Test, will be 
developed and executed to ensure that the software performs as expected.  In addition to nominal 
operations, this test will validate appropriate reaction, as defined by the software requirements, to off-
nominal and boundary conditions.  A mission sequence test will be developed and executed at the project 
level to ensure validation of the entire system, hardware and software.  The crew display will be 
additionally validated by a usability test at Johnson Space Center (JSC).  Integrated testing of the 
experiment with MSG will be performed as well, as required by MSFC-RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation 
Interface Requirements Document.  Prior to, and in-between releases of software, informal module testing 
will be performed to ensure functionality of each module. 
2.4 
Organizational and Technical Interface Descriptions 
This section describes all interfaces between the development organization and the users, customers, 
product assurance, and suppliers.  Interface descriptions define the boundaries of responsibility for each 
part of the software product and the way that technical information will be transmitted between all parties.

2.4.1 Project Manager (GRC) 
The GRC Project Manager is responsible for the overall management of the project including milestone 
reviews, cost review, schedule, technical status, issues, and technical interchange to assure understanding 
of all requirements 
2.4.2 Principal Investigator and Science Team (GRC, NCMR, NIST)  
The Principal Investigator’s (PI) team is responsible for specifying the science requirements for the 
experiment.  These requirements will be captured in SAME-DOC-002, Engineering Requirements 
Document.  The science team will review and accept the verification and validation of the SAME 
software. 
2.4.3 Project Lead/Lead Engineer (ZIN) 
The Project Lead will provide a management function for the monitoring, control, and reporting of the 
project effort.  The Project Lead shall provide to NASA reporting and insight into the project status, and 
technical performance.  Acting also as the Project Lead Engineer, the Project Lead is responsible for 
coordinating issues between the various project disciplines. 
2.4.4 Lead Software Engineer (ZIN) 
The Lead Software Engineer is responsible for software requirements gathering, overall design, 
implementation and testing of the various software systems.  The Lead Software Engineer ensures that 
software is provided for system verifications, such as environmental testing. The Lead Software Engineer 
coordinates with the Ground Operations Engineers to achieve needed ground software support. The 
Software Lead is also responsible for maintaining the software schedules. 
2.4.5 Ground Operations Engineers (ZIN and TSC) 
The Ground Operations Engineers assist the Lead Software Engineer in obtaining the necessary command 
and data interfaces at the TSC.  The Ground Operations Engineers also provide ground software and 
procedures used for viewing data of the MSG host system onboard ISS. 
2.4.6 GRC Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate (SMAD) 
SMAD is responsible for NASA programmatic oversight related to Safety, Reliability, Quality Assurance 
and Security.  It provides advice and guidance in the planning and implementation of Security and 
supports flight projects to assure all safety requirements are met and mission success is consistent with 
the Center's goals. 
2.4.7 ZIN Quality Assurance 
ZIN Quality Assurance is responsible for implementation of the ZIN quality system during the life of the 
project.  It is responsible for ensuring that the quality assurance requirements identified in SAME-PLN-
006, Software Assurance Plan, and in SAME-PLN-003, Product Assurance Plan, are met.

The ZIN Configuration Management Officer is responsible for implementation and maintenance of

2.7 
Software Assurance Plan 
In order to ensure conformance of software to established requirements, development methodologies and 
standards a software assurance plan shall be developed.  Refer to SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance 
Plan. 
2.8 
Risk Management Plan 
Risk management is addressed at the project level through SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan.  However, 
procedure P04003, Design Control Procedure for Software, of QM001, ZIN Technologies Quality 
Manual requires that the software risk level be assessed, and that will be done here. 
Following the guidelines of P04003 it is determined that the software risk for the project is Medium.  A 
medium level of risk is characterized as “In-use software failure risks significant property damage or 
significant negative impact upon the customer”.  The influencing point in this decision is the fact that 
samples are destroyed in testing and therefore science data losses during the test cannot be recovered by 
re-running the sample test.  There is not a risk of significant property damage, only of negative impact 
upon the customer. 
2.9 
Configuration Management Plan 
For released software the configuration management plan is contained within SAME-PLN-002, 
Configuration Management Plan, which also contains requirements for releasing software.  Prior to 
release, software will be stored and tracked using the version control method specified in Section 2.2.5.6.

Not required for medium control level software.

3.0 
PRODUCT SPECIFICATION 
There are number of software-related product specification documents recommended by GRC-P2.6.4.  
The manner in which these are implemented by the project are listed below. 
3.1 
Concept Documentation 
Not required for medium control level software.  Refer to SAME-DOC-001, Concept Description 
Document, for the project-level concept. 
3.2 
Requirements Documentation 
The project will develop SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document, which will contain all 
software requirements pertaining to systems, facility, safety, operations, telemetry, software interfaces, 
functionality and performance.  This document will also contain any limitations or constraints on the 
system and will specify the required responses to off-nominal and boundary conditions. 
3.3 
Design Documentation 
The project will develop SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, which will contain both the 
architectural software design and the detailed software design.  It is expected that these sections will be 
added at separate times. 
The architectural design will lay out the basic structure for the software defining the high level interfaces 
between software and hardware and any other systems as well as define the domains, objects, modules, 
functions and operations needed to meet the requirements.  Operational scenarios and use cases will be 
documented as part of the design to assure the design covers all the aspects of operation. Timing diagrams 
and flow charts will be used to convey the architecture and the real-time command and data flow.  
Network diagrams may be used to describe the physical and data interactions on the network in the final 
installation. 
The detailed software design will specify details that are worked within and between the modules, classes, 
and/or objects. For Object Oriented Design (OOD), the public versus private sectors will be determined. 
Parameter and variable types and values will be established. Global versus private flags, variables, and 
parameters will be determined. Methods, attributes, calculations, and algorithms will be captured. 
3.4 
Version Description 
The project will create Version Description Documents (VDD) to capture the as-built state of released 
software. A VDD will be necessary for each ground support software and flight software release and will 
be captured in SAME-DOC-010, Ground Software Version Description Document, and SAME-DOC-
011, Flight Software Version Description Document, respectively.  VDDs are not required for test support 
software.  The VDD will indicate compatability with other package versions.  For example, “This version 
of ground software will work with versions 1.0–2.5 of flight software.” Additional requirements for the 
VDD are listed in SAME-PLN-002, Configuration Management Plan.  It is suggested that the VDD 
contain the sections shown below.

PROCEDURES 
See the Validation and Software Assurance Plan in previous sections for the use of procedures by the 
project.  This section describes the content of the procedures. 
4.1 
Testing Procedures 
The project will develop SAME-TST-001, Software Acceptance Test,  which will perform all internal 
validation tasks on released software.  This procedure will contain a requirements matrix which will 
indicate the source of each requirement and the step(s) in the procedure in which it is tested.  The 
procedure will clearly delineate pass/fail criteria for each test within the procedure.  The results of the 
procedure will be documented in a report numbered according to SAME-PLN-002, Configuration 
Management Plan. 
The mission sequence test procedure for full instrument validation for the PI is specified at the project 
level. 
Any integrated testing with MSG will follow procedures developed by MSG with input from the project.  
Procedures for usability testing of the crew display software will be developed by JSC personnel with 
input from the project.

5.0 
RECORDS 
This section describes how the recommended software records listed in  Table 2 are implemented and 
handled in this project.  Most of these records are a result of following subsections of the software 
management plan, Section 2.0. 
5.1 
Project Approval/Work Authorization 
A record of approval/work authorization for the software effort of the project is part of the record for the 
entire project.  Refer to the project level document, SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan. 
5.2 
Design Review Records 
During software design reviews, with occurrence as dictated by SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance 
Plan, minutes will be taken and a summary report will be generated that is signed off by all design review 
members.  At this point SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, will be modified to either 
reference a document containing the summary report or the report content itself will be appended to 
SAME-DOC-006.  In addition, for each review a memo describing the results of the review will be sent to 
the GRC Project Manager. 
Minutes from other software meetings will be stored and backed-up electronically. 
5.3 
Review or Board Records 
Record of project level reviews and board response, for example the Verification Readiness Review and 
the Pre-Ship Review, are kept at the project level according to SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan. 
5.4 
Problem Reports / Corrective Action Reports 
As specified in SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance Plan, the project will record and track to closure 
any problems found in software using procedures P13001, Procedure for The Control of Nonconforming 
Product, and P14001, Corrective and Preventive Action Procedure, of QM001, ZIN Technologies Quality 
Manual.  The project shall use the non-conformance tracking and corrective action reporting as described 
in the Quality Manual once the software has passed software acceptance testing. 
5.5 
Verification and Validation Results 
Verification results consist of the record from the software design review.  See Section 5.2 for more 
information. 
Internal validation results for the project software releases will be in the form of a signed Software 
Acceptance Test Report.  Results of the validation accomplished by the mission sequence test will be 
generated at the project level according to SAME-PLN-003, Product Assurance Plan. 
External validation results, such as from the crew display usability test and any integrated MSG testing 
may exist as a memo or e-mail, in which case the text of the results will be stored electronically in a 
backed-up folder.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 
Purpose 
This document defines the specific requirements to be satisfied throughout the implementation of the software for 
the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument.  The information contained within this document 
provides the technical requirements to be implemented and enables the development team to assess whether or not 
the completed software complies with the requirements of the system.  The data included in this document provides 
the criteria for acceptance of the integrated software configuration. 
1.2 
Scope 
The requirements specified herein apply only to SAME instrument software and custom MSG Laptop Computer 
(MLC) software.  All ground based telemetry data processing and command uplink software requirements will be 
identified in future documents as required.

content:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 2 
2.0 
INSTRUMENT OVERVIEW 
The SAME instrument is designed to quantify the size and distribution of smoke particulate in low gravity so that 
this information is available for the future design of effective low gravity smoke detectors.  The instrument will also 
be used to evaluate the performance of two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detectors and one commercial smoke 
detector.  Measurements will be made for the smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the 
effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time and aging. The primary targets are materials that 
produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. 
 
 
Figure 1 
SAME Instrument Assembly Inside MSG WV 
The instrument is installed and operated in the MSG Work Volume (WV) which provides a minimal level of 
containment (see Figure 1).  A general description of the major subsystems follows below.  See SAME-DOC-001, 
Concept Description Document, for more detail. 
• 
Sample Carousel Turning Module, Sample Carousel and Heater Wire Coil 
These components are used to select and heat a sample in order to generate smoke. 
• 
Camera 
A camera and light(s) are mounted to see the sample and production of smoke. 
• 
Aging Chamber 
The aging chamber has a piston and two gate valves for holding the smoke for a time before releasing it 
downstream.  The piston is moved by pressure and vacuum provided by MSG and controlled by SAME. 
• 
Thermal Precipitator Module 
This assembly collects samples of smoke on TEM grids for post-flight inspection.  It has access to smoke 
before and after the aging chamber.

content:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 3 
• 
Smoke Diagnostics  
After the aging chamber, the smoke is passed to several diagnostics:  the TSI P-Trak™ particle 
concentration counter, the TSI DustTrak™, a residential-grade ionization detector, the ISS photoelectric 
smoke detector and the STS ionization smoke detector. 
• 
Fluids Control Unit 
Pressure and vacuum supplied by MSG is controlled for smoke aging chamber piston movement and for all 
other fluid flow to and from the diagnostic equipment. 
• 
System Diagnostics  
Besides the diagnostic instruments measuring smoke characteristics, there are pressure transducers, 
temperature gauges, and voltage and current sensors to monitor system performance. 
• 
External Interfaces  
External interfaces provided by MSG include power, video recording, temperature control, post-
pyrolization venting, nitrogen and air supply/vacuum, an RS-422 interface for commanding and telemetry, 
ethernet for file transfer, and a laptop for crew access to the SAME experiment.  A SAMS unit measures 
local µg and vibrations and forwards that data to the ground requiring no SAME or MSG processing. 
• 
Avionics 
Contained in the Data Acquisition Control Unit (DACU) box, the SAME avionics conduct automated 
experiments, controlling the other sub-systems to produce and analyze the smoke.  Commands from the 
ground are processed.  Experiment data is saved to files on a local storage medium and forwarded to MSG 
for subsequent downlink.  Housekeeping data is downlinked every second and supplied to MSG.  Off-
nominal conditions are reported to MSG and the ground.  In addition, a means for the crew to access 
SAME data and control is provided.

content:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 4 
3.0 
AVIONICS OVERVIEW 
SAME avionics are located in the DACU within the MSG Work Volume (WV).  Cables will stretch to the SAME 
diagnostic hardware for control and feedback, to J311 of the WV for command and data transfer, and to J404 of the 
WV for ethernet connection to the MSG laptop computer (MLC) for file transfer and crew display operation.  There 
is also a cable for the camera. 
3.1 
Data Interfaces 
To interface to the MSG, and subsequently to ground systems, the DACU CPU will communicate primarily to the 
MSG Rack Controller, also known as the SPLC (Standard Payload Computer) using an RS-422 interface (see Figure 
2).  SAME will use this interface to receive uplink commands and send health and status (H&S) data and low rate 
telemetry (LRT) data. 
 
 
Figure 2 
SAME to MSG Data Interfaces 
Payload commands are transmitted from the ground through the ISS Payload MDM and eventually to the SPLC via 
MIL-STD-1553.  The SPLC abstracts this interface from the payload developer, relieving the burden of knowing the 
details about the 1553 bus and command validation. 
A packet containing SAME health and status is automatically transmitted in the reverse direction on the 1553 bus 
and is received on the ground.  Also included in the payload health and status packet is the Experiment Control 
Word or ECW, a single dedicated memory word that represents the status of the payload.  The ECW is monitored by 
various ISS subsystems and provides a quick alert if an off-nominal condition is indicated in it.

content:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 5 
File-based SAME science data such as experiment measurement data and instrument ancillary data will be 
transferred to the MLC using FTP utilizing a 10BaseT ethernet connection.  Once these files are stored on the MLC, 
the MSG Operations Team at the Payload Operations Integration Center (POIC) will periodically initiate their 
downlink and forward them to the SAME Operations Team.  Since SAME is not permitted to transmit data on the 
ISS LAN, the DACU will automatically switch the active network connection from the MLC to SAME and ISS 
using a custom designed ethernet switch when the FTP transfer is required.  In its normal state, the MLC will be 
connected to ISS LAN. 
The camera looking at the SAME sample is hooked up via an NTSC cable to a feedthrough inside the WV which is 
then patched on the outside to a video recorder channel in the video drawer. 
3.2 
DACU Overview 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control.  It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and 
interfacing with the environment external to SAME.  It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate 
experiments.  A brief list of its major responsibilities is as follows:  
1. Receive, validate and process commands from the MSG. 
2. Periodically transmit SAME system status and select parameters to the MSG. 
3. Transmit completed and requested data files to the MLC via FTP. 
4. Manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium. 
5. Autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed tests. 
6. Provide diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
7. Control the MSG video recorder(s) capturing SAME images. 
8. React to sensor(s) out of tolerance by notifying MSG and ground systems, and performing software inhibits 
or other actions as appropriate. 
3.3 
Crew Display Overview 
During long periods of LOS or failure of telemetry, it is beneficial to provide limited visibility into SAME 
operation.  Payloads may utilize the MLC to present payload status to the crew and provide a mechanism to control 
the payload directly from it.  Two options for providing the SAME Crew Display are possible.  Option 1 is the 
preferred solution at this time because of a likely delay in an upgrade to provide a dedicated ethernet link between 
the MLC and an experiment. 
3.3.1 Option 1 - Custom Win32 or Java Based Application 
All data transmitted to the SPLC via H&S and LRT is also transmitted to the MLC via the MSG 1553 bus, and is 
therefore available on the MLC.  SAME may develop a custom Win32-based or Java-based application that displays 
a limited set of the SAME downlink data for the crew to see and provides commanding to the SAME instrument. 
3.3.2 Option 2 - Embedded Web Pages 
A dedicated ethernet interface between the MLC and SAME may be leveraged to provide a web-based interface into 
the DACU using the MLC native web browser.  The operating system running on the DACU is capable of running 
an embedded web-server such as Apache or NASA’s Tempest servers.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 6 
4.0 
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
4.1 
System Status 
4.1.1 Update Rate 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-1-1-1] 
The DACU software shall update its internal status once per second. 
4.1.2 LED Status Indicators 
The DACU will control two LEDs mounted on the outside of the DACU enclosure using discrete outputs.  These 
LEDs are described in Table 1. 
 
Table 1 
Status LEDs 
LED Name 
Description 
OK STATUS 
Indicates nominal operation of the entire 
SAME apparatus. 
TEST RUNNING 
Indicates that a test is currently running. 
 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall illuminate the OK STATUS LED while the CPU is 
properly running.  If the software detects an internal fault or error condition, 
the LED shall be extinguished. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall illuminate the TEST RUNNING LED while a test is 
running.  Upon completion, the LED shall be extinguished. 
4.2 
Data Communication 
There are three two-way paths of data communications connected to the DACU.  An RS422 interface is used for 
communications with the SPLC.  An ethernet interface is used for communications with MLC.  An RS232 interface 
is available while not on orbit for development, maintenance, and debugging activities. 
4.2.1 SPLC Communications 
4.2.1.1 
Serial Port Configuration 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-1-1] 
A single bi-directional RS422 channel between the DACU and the SPLC 
shall be used to communicate with the MSG systems.  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-1-2] 
RS422 serial port settings shall be 19200 baud, no parity, 8 data bits, and 1 
stop bit.

4.2.1.2 
Data Format 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-1] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the ESTEC Data Link Format as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-
0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 3.5.1.1. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-2] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the byte and bit order as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, 
MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 1.4.3. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-3] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the word alignment as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, 
MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 2.3. 
4.2.1.3 
Health and Status Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-1] 
Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a health and status 
packet containing information such as voltages, currents, and pressures 
necessary to verify safe and proper operation.  Included in this information 
are the C&W flags which indicate nominal or off-nominal operation to the 
rack systems.   
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-2] 
The content of the health and status packet shall conform to the format 
specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control 
Document. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-3] 
The Cycle Counter field in the health and status packet shall be incremented 
once per second up to the value 0xffff, then roll over to 0. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-4] 
The C&W flags fields in the health and status packet shall be asserted only 
upon the conditions listed in Section 6.2. 
4.2.1.4 
Low Rate Telemetry Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-1] 
Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a low rate telemetry 
packet representing the current state of the instrument.   
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-2] 
The content of the low rate telemetry packet shall conform to the format 
specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control 
Document. 
4.2.1.5 
Video Command Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-1] 
The DACU shall have the ability to control MSG video drawer functions by 
sending video command packets to the SPLC.  The controllable video 
drawer functions are determined by the requirements of the video drawer 
command group, Section 4.4.5. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-2] 
The content of video drawer packets issued by the DACU shall conform to 
the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface 
Control Document. 
4.2.1.6 
Time of Day Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-6-1] 
The DACU shall accept time of day packets from the SPLC when they 
adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW 
Interface Control Document.

 8 
4.2.1.7 
Experiment Command Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-7-1] 
The DACU shall accept experiment command packets from the SPLC when 
they adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC 
ASW Interface Control Document. 
4.2.2 MLC Communications 
Upon completion of a science run, all data files will be stored on DACU internal storage.  A copy of these data files 
will automatically be forwarded to the MLC via FTP on a point-to-point cross-wired ethernet cable.  The SAME 
Operations Team will submit a request to the MSG Team at MSFC to downlink the files on the MLC at the earliest 
possible time.  The downlinked files will then be electronically forwarded to GRC.  Because the connection is made 
directly to the MLC, no bandwidth restrictions are necessary to ensure ISS LAN resource availability. 
4.2.2.1 
FTP Usage 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-1-1] 
All data files stored on the DACU local storage shall be automatically 
forwarded to the MLC via FTP for backup and downlink. 
4.2.2.2 
Network Details  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-1] 
A dedicated standard 802.3 (10BaseT) ethernet connection from the MLC 
to the DACU shall be used to perform the FTP transfer. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-2] 
Communications with the FTP server shall be done utilizing a server IP 
address of 192.168.1.1, port 21. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-3] 
The DACU will automatically switch the ethernet source from MLC→ISS 
to MLC→SAME when communication to the MLC is required.  When the 
transaction is completed, the original MLC→ISS connection will be 
restored. 
4.2.2.3 
SAME File Maintenance  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-3-1] 
The DACU shall provide the ability to remove SAME files from the FTP 
server as needed to ensure proper storage space utilization. 
4.2.3 Remote Console Communications 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-1] 
The DACU shall provide a telnet console login session on an RS232 port.  
All administrative features and capabilities available via telnet shall be 
supported. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-2] 
The telnet console RS232 serial port settings shall be, 19200 baud, no 
parity, 8 data bits, and 1 stop bit.

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 9 
4.3 
Data Storage Requirements 
The data storage requirements reflect two main needs.  First, that a record of all status, measurements and events is 
preserved beyond the flight of the instrument.  And second, that individual values of status, measurements or events 
can be easily located in stored data. 
4.3.1 Storage Media 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall store all files on a media that can preserve all generated 
files for extraction after payload down-mass.  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-2] 
The storage media shall have a capacity of at least 520 megabytes. 
4.3.2 File Conventions 
4.3.2.1 
Directory Structure 
Because the execution of ISS instrument experiments are highly scheduled, the date and time that procedures and 
ground commanding is performed is usually reliably recorded by NASA cadre and experiment ground operation 
teams.  As such, finding the data files for a previously run experiment or for a particular logged event is facilitated 
by a data storage structure based on the date.  Therefore, 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-1-1] 
All files created shall be organized into a hierarchical directory structure 
based on the date that files were created. 
4.3.2.2 
File Names 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-2-1] 
All files created shall have unique file names. 
4.3.3 Stored Data 
4.3.3.1 
Housekeeping Data 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-1] 
Once per second data relating to the status of the instrument shall be stored 
to a file. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-2] 
Each second of housekeeping data stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
4.3.3.2 
Messages 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-1] 
Messages generated by the instrument shall be stored to a file. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-2] 
Each message stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
4.3.3.3 
Experiment Results 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-1] 
Experiment results shall be stored to a file 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-2] 
Experiment results stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-3] 
DELETED.

Command Requirements 
Commands are the primary means of initiating SAME instrument operations.  Commands to an instrument are 
typically formatted into an array of data and inserted into command packets and then transmitted from the ground 
operation station or from the crew display on the MSG MLC on-board the ISS.  When command packets reach the 
DACU the command data within is extracted and interpreted and the appropriate software functions are executed. 
The command requirements below deal mainly with the functions required by the instrument and not with how those 
functions are implemented or with how the command data is formatted.  See SAME-DOC-005,  Software Interface 
Control Document, for the latter information.

SUBSYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
5.1 
Sample Carousel 
5.1.1 Sample Selection 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control a motor to rotate the sample carousel to a specified 
sample number. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall use four proximity sensors to confirm correct positioning 
of the correct sample carousel. 
5.1.2 Sample Positioning 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall mate the selected sample tube with the smoke generation 
duct and the sample contacts with heater wire coil contacts by controlling a 
linear actuator. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall confirm correct mating of a sample tube and sample 
contacts by monitoring the resistance between the two heater wire coil 
contacts. 
5.2 
Sample Heater (Heater Wire Coil) 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-1] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
sample surface temperature and duration of the heating. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-2] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall achieve 
steady state temperature of the heater within 5 seconds. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-3] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall set the 
temperature of the heater wire coil to any temperature between 50 and 500 
degrees Celcius. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-4] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall provide 
active temperature control of the heater. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-5] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
heater temperature and duration so as not to ignite the sample. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-6] 
The DACU shall measure and store the sample temperature at least once per 
second. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-7] 
The DACU shall measure and store the gas plume temperature at least once 
per second.

Aging Chamber 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward velocity to 
achieve 1 to 10 cm/s average flow velocity in the smoke generation duct. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the vacuum line, by sensing and controlling a 
mass flow controller on the vacuum line, and by sensing a pressure 
transducer monitoring the drive side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward velocity in 
order to provide smoke at the rate required for the particular diagnostics in 
use. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-4] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the GN2 line, by sensing and controlling a mass 
flow controller on the GN2 line, and by sensing a pressure transducer 
monitoring the sample side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-5] 
The DACU shall control a mixing fan in the aging chamber to be on during 
a specified portion of the residence time.

[SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-1-1-1]

precipitator module so that at most only one valve is open at a time. 
5.5.2 Heater Control 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-2-1-1]

precipitator module heater at a time.

The DACU shall control the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port.

keypad using custom electronics.

The DACU shall receive data from the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall sample DustTrak data at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz.

6.0 
OFF-NOMINAL AND CONTINGENCY REQUIREMENTS 
6.1 
Maintenance Mode Operation 
The software will contain provisions to allow experiment operations to continue in the event of the following: 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-1] 
In the event of a loss of the ability to write to the data hard drive, the system 
shall continue to accept uplink commands and transmit status data to ensure 
safe operation. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-2] 
In the event of a loss of ethernet communication between the DACU and 
the MLC, operations shall continue.  Data recorded on the flight avionics 
may be manually commanded for retransmission once communication is 
regained. 
6.2 
Caution and Warning 
Three discrete bits in the health and status packet are used to indicate to MSG the presence of a payload condition 
warranting a warning, caution, or advisory classification and reaction.  See MSFC-RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation 
Interface Requirements Document, Section 3.11 for details of each level.  The specific payload conditions that result 
in warning and caution levels are determined by the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) during Phased Safety 
Reviews.  Automatic safing will be performed if the warning or caution bit is set. The advisory bit can be used to 
reflect errors and off-nominal conditions seen only in the low rate telemetry data to the health and status data.  If, 
due to limited communication coverage or communication error, the health and status data is received while the low 
rate telemetry is not, then these off-nominal conditions will still be noted and time-tagged. 
6.2.1 Warning 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 2 -Warning” condition and a subsequent set of the Warning bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.2 Caution 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 3 - Caution” condition and a subsequent set of the Caution bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.3 Advisory 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 4 - Advisory” condition and a subsequent set of the Advisory bit in 
the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.3 
Automatic Safing 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-1] 
In the event of a GN2 regulated pressure reading of over 21 psig, the DACU 
shall automatically shut off the main GN2 valve. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-2] 
In the event of a vacuum pressure reading of over 19 psia, the DACU shall 
automatically shut off the main vacuum valve.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 
Scope 
This plan applies to all Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) hardware, software, and 
operating procedures developed under the Microgravity Research, Development, and Operations Contract 
(MRDOC).  This plan establishes the methods and responsibilities for verifying the SAME requirements. 
 The requirements for the SAME project, including investigation, engineering, product assurance, safety, 
and carrier requirements, are in Appendix A of this document.  The verification methods and sources of 
these requirements are also included in Appendix A.  This plan defines the verification process, leading to 
certification of the SAME flight hardware. 
1.2 
Purpose 
This document defines the verification activities required to show that SAME complies with its 
requirements.  These activities include the verification of investigation requirements from the Exploration 
Investigation Requirements Document (EIRD) for SAME, software engineering requirements from the 
Software Requirements Documents, product assurance requirements from the Project Product Assurance 
Plan (PAP), safety requirements from the Hazard Reports, and carrier requirements from the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox (MSG) Interface Control Document (ICD). 
This document includes all of the requirements to be verified by SAME and serves as the Engineering 
Requirements Document to organize and list all necessary requirements. 
1.3 
TBDs 
TBDs are used as a place-holder for requirements, verifications, or document numbers that are not known 
at the time of the latest release of this document.

content:
SAME-PLN-005 Rev F 
 3
4.0 
VERIFICATIONS 
4.1 
General 
The SAME Project Office will verify all the requirements imposed on the SAME System.  The primary 
sites for verification activities will be the Glenn Research Center (GRC) and the item developer’s site 
unless otherwise directed by the MSG or International Space Station (ISS) programs.  All requirements 
will be recorded in this document and disseminated to the design team.  This document will provide 
traceability from the parent requirement through the subsequent derived requirements.  It will also 
identify the verification source document and verification method.  
SAME will be building and verifying more than one set of flight hardware. Consequently, a certain 
number of verifications must be repeated for each serialized assembly. A subset of the requirements is 
designated as series requirements.  
4.1.1 Verification Methods 
The methods used to complete the verifications are analysis, test, inspection and demonstration.  The 
method(s) required for the SAME verifications are listed in the requirements matrix in Appendix A.  The 
methods of verification are defined in MSFC-RQMT-2888 as stated in Sections 4.1.1.1, 4.1.1.2, 4.1.1.3, 
and 4.1.1.4. 
4.1.1.1 Analysis 
Analysis is a technical evaluation that relates equipment design and use parameters for prediction of 
actual design and operation.  Analysis may be used to verify requirements, provided established 
techniques used are adequate to yield confidence, or where testing is impractical.  Included in this 
category is analysis of similarity to items previously verified to the same criteria or more stringent 
criteria.  Verification accomplished by analysis shall be evidenced by an analysis report. 
4.1.1.2 Test 
Test is actual operation of equipment under simulated conditions or the subjection of equipment to 
specified environments to measure responses.  Verification accomplished by test shall be evidenced by a 
test report. 
4.1.1.3 Inspection 
Inspection is a physical evaluation of equipment and associated documentation.  Inspection may be used 
to verify construction features, drawing compliance, workmanship, and physical condition.  It includes 
determination of physical dimensions.  Verification accomplished by inspection shall be evidenced by an 
inspection report. 
4.1.1.4 Demonstration 
Demonstration is the qualitative determination of compliance with requirements by observation during 
actual operation or simulation under preplanned conditions and guidelines.  Some human factor 
requirements where the method of closure is a demonstration require the investigation to be set up in its 
on-orbit configuration in the MSG Engineering Unit (EU) to verify that the requirement is satisfied.

content:
SAME-PLN-005 Rev F 
 4
4.1.2 Tools (Requirements Matrix and Verification Tracking Log) 
A matrix has been compiled in an Excel spreadsheet to include all requirements to be satisfied by SAME. 
 It identifies the source of each requirement, the discipline under which it falls, the verification method to 
be used for closure, and resources necessary to perform the verification. It also identifies series 
requirements. The matrix, in Appendix A, will be provided to the engineering team for use in verification 
activities, and will be included in the released (.pdf) version of this document. 
The verification tracking log (VTL) will be used to track the status of the verifications and the 
documentation provided as evidence for the completion of the verifications. It is an Excel workbook that 
includes five worksheets: the VTL itself, a statistics page, the current version of the requirements matrix, 
a summary of applicable ECOs, and a notes/explanation page. The VTL will not be configuration-
controlled as it is a summary of the state of controlled documentation and it will not be included in the 
released version of this document. It will be available in the project team’s shared directory. 
4.2 
Planning 
4.2.1 Verification Definition Sheets 
A Verification Definition Sheet (VDS) will be used to complete the carrier requirements from MSFC-
ICD-3462.  The corresponding VDS for each carrier requirement is listed in the requirements matrix and 
can be found in Appendix E of MSFC-RQMT-2888.  The VDS provides instructions, definitions, 
references, and guidelines for verification activities associated with each requirement. 
4.2.2 Test Plans and Procedures 
The controlled requirements matrix will be distributed to the engineering team so that the requirements 
can be grouped into meaningful test plans or procedures that will allow for efficient testing and closure of 
the requirements.  Test plans and procedures will be written to include the verification statements to 
ensure that the requirements are clearly stated, understood, and closed out by the test.  Test plans and 
procedures containing carrier requirements will also contain the corresponding VDS. 
Test plans and procedures will be a project team effort lead by the Systems Engineering team.  Plans and 
procedures will use exact language from the requirement sources to convey the objective of the test as 
completion of these verifications.   
The template of how the requirements will be incorporated into the documents is shown in Figure 1.  This 
table, along with the introductory text, will be included in test plans and procedures intended for 
verification activities. 
4.2.3 Implementation and Reporting 
4.2.3.1 Implementation 
Test verifications in the matrix will be logically grouped into similar items that can be completed in a 
single test.  The test plans and procedures will be written accordingly.  Some of the verifications will be 
closed on the functional model or other similar flight-like hardware when the testing of flight hardware is 
not necessary or cannot be accomplished due to the nature of the test.  Otherwise, testing will be done on 
the flight hardware.  The tests performed on non-flight hardware are indicated in the requirements matrix.

SAME-PLN-005 Rev F 
 5
Inspections will be done at the time of hardware assembly and will be done on flight hardware or flight 
drawings.   
Analyses will be done using the flight configuration of hardware for the calculations.   
Demonstrations will be done on the flight hardware.   
All Human Factors (HFIT) verifications will be done once the hardware is delivered to MSG and the 
HFIT evaluation is performed.  Additional verifications require integrated setup or testing in the MSG EU 
and will be completed after the hardware is delivered to MSG.  These verifications are identified in the 
requirements matrix. 
 
Figure 1: Example of Verification List in Documents 
4.2.3.2 Reporting 
Test, analysis and inspection reports will be written as evidence that the tests, analyses and inspections 
were performed to satisfy the requirements.  Reports will include the requirement statements, as shown in 
Figure 1, to indicate what verifications were performed and are closed by the report.  Reports and other 
necessary documentation will be kept by the Systems Engineering team and Configuration Management 
as evidence that the verifications were performed.  
The final report generated against a carrier requirement will be a comprehensive report intended to close 
out the requirement, upon which a Certificate of Compliance is issued. 
Certificates of Compliance will be generated to close verifications by demonstration.

SAME-PLN-005 Rev F 
 6
4.3 
Certificate of Compliance  
As the carrier verification activities are completed, the SAME team will generate and sign Certificates of 
Compliance.  With the completion of all verifications identified in this document and their associated 
Certificates of Compliance, all of the requirements and verifications of MSG compatibility, functionality, 
and safety will have been met. 
4.4 
Maintenance of the Certificate of Compliance 
Any changes to SAME occurring after the verification activities are completed will be reviewed to assess 
their impacts on the individual requirements and their associated verification certificates.   If such a 
review determines that re-verification is warranted, the changes to SAME and the proposed additional 
verification activities will be presented to the MSG payload program office for concurrence before 
verification activities are completed.  
4.5 
Requirement Sources  
4.5.1 Investigation Requirements 
The investigation requirements for SAME are found in the EIRD for SAME.  These, along with derived 
engineering responses to these requirements from the various engineering disciplines, can be found in the 
requirements matrix in this document.  These engineering responses will be verified to show that the 
investigation requirements are met.  The Project Scientist for SAME will approve all reports containing 
investigation verification close-outs.    
4.5.2 Software Engineering Requirements 
Software engineering requirements can be found in SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document, 
and are included in the requirements matrix in this document.  These requirements include detailed 
responses to the investigation, safety, and MSG carrier requirements, and requirements to establish good 
engineering practices. 
4.5.3 Product Assurance Requirements 
Product assurance requirements can be found in SAME-PLN-003, Product Assurance Plan.  The 
requirements found in the Product Assurance Plan are derived from the Space Assurance Requirements 
and Guidelines (SARG) as they are applicable to the SAME project.  Statements containing “shall” 
require a formal documented closure of the requirement, as defined in the Product Assurance Plan, and 
are included in the requirements matrix.  Statements containing “will or must” are requirements to be 
fulfilled but do not require a formal documented closure, as defined in the Product Assurance Plan.  The 
“will or must” requirements which have a direct impact on the SAME project budget, schedule, and 
design are included in the requirements matrix. 
4.5.4 Safety Requirements 
SAME safety requirements are identified according to the payload safety process described in NSTS 
1700.7B, Safety Policy and Requirements for Payloads Using the Space Transportation System, and 
NSTS 1700.7B ISS Addendum, Safety Policy and Requirements for Payloads Using the International 
Space Station, using NSTS/ISS 13830, Payload Safety Review and Data Submittal.

content:
SAME-PLN-005 Rev F 
 7
The SAME safety requirements are found in the SAME hazard reports and are included in the 
requirements matrix in this document.  The requirements are included in the matrix to provide visibility 
and to allow them to be grouped with other requirements in verification activities (i.e. test plans and 
procedures) for efficient completion. Although closure information will be included in the VTL, the 
safety requirements will be officially tracked in a Safety Verification Tracking Log (SVTL) and 
maintained by the SAME Safety Engineer.  The SVTL and documentation used to close the safety 
verifications will be provided to the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) for approval at the Phase III 
Safety Review. 
4.5.5 MSG Carrier Requirements 
Requirements for interfacing with the MSG are found in MSFC-ICD-3462, Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) Interface Control Document for SAME, and are included in the requirements matrix in 
this document.  MSFC-ICD-3462 contains a Verification Applicability Matrix to indicate what 
requirements from MSFC-RQMT-2888 are applicable to SAME.  The Verification Applicability Matrix 
also identifies the appropriate verification method, the applicable VDS, and other comments associated 
with the completion of the verification.  All information given in the Verification Applicability Matrix is 
duplicated in the requirements matrix in this document.  The complete text of the requirements as well as 
the VDS is found in MSFC-RQMT-2888. 
4.5.6 Space Shuttle and ISS Requirements 
MSG interfaces with Johnson Space Center (JSC) concerning payload interface requirements.  Therefore, 
all Space Shuttle and ISS requirements should be documented in MSFC-ICD-3462, as identified in 
Section 4.5.4. 
4.5.7 KSC Facility Requirements 
SAME is not planning to operate at Kennedy Space Center (KSC). 
4.6 
Staffing 
Implementation of the SAME verification process requires all members of the SAME team to support the 
verification activities. 
4.6.1 Roles and Responsibilities 
The Systems Engineering team will prepare documentation necessary for the performance of verifications 
and the reporting of the results of verification activities.  All plans and procedures for verification 
activities will be checked by a member of the Systems Engineering team to insure that the applicable 
requirements are included.   One member of the Systems Engineering team will be responsible for 
updating the VTL to track the status of the verification activities and to include the document number for 
the reports generated to close the verifications.   
Hardware and Software Engineers will provide assistance writing test plans and procedures and 
performing verification activities. 
The Safety Engineer will track and maintain all safety verifications from the hazard reports in the SVTL. 
The Project Scientist will approve all documentation that completes an investigation requirement. 
Quality Assurance (QA) personnel will be involved if the requirement in question is a QA requirement.

Verification procedures will be prepared for each functional and 
environmental test activity as appropriate at the component, 
subsystem, and experiment levels. These procedures will 
describe the configuration of the article, specific environmental 
parameters, and how each activity contained in the verification 
plan will be implemented.  These procedures will be prepared 
and released in accordance with the SAME defined configuration 
management approach.

3.4.1

Engineering
Safety Critical and Fracture Critical Structures
All structural elements including associated interfaces, fasteners, 
and welds in the primary load path are considered Safety Critical 
Structures (SCS) and shall be analyzed per the guidelines of 
NASA-STD-5003 and SSP 52005.  
Fracture Critical components are a subset of 
SCS and are defined as ones whose failure 
would present catastrophic hazards, i.e. they 
are not fail-safe. Through analysis SAME has 
determined that there are no Fracture Critical 
Components as part of the payload. 
A

Engineering

SAME will demonstrate compliance with structural loads 
requirements by conducting the appropriate inspections, 
analyses, and/or tests. Flight hardware will be designed to 
maintain structural integrity and functionality during all phases of 
the expected life cycle.  Verification of the structures and 
systems will consider static and dynamic loads encountered 
during assembly, testing, transportation, launch, ascent, space 
operations, descent and landing. NASA-STD-5002 will be utilized 
for defining methodologies, practices and requirements for 
conducting load analyses in the verification plan.

and test factors, as well as service life factors, to be used for 
flight hardware development and verification.

assurance shall be shown by analysis to have positive margins of 
safety.  The minimum margins of safety for all credible failure 
modes shall be determined.

The SAME Project will verify structural integrity by analysis alone 
without strength testing using the criteria and design factors 
specified in SSP 52005. Criteria and rationale will be reviewed 
and approved by the Payload Carrier/Integrator. For payloads 
launched on the Space Shuttle such as SAME, the Space Shuttle 
Payload Safety Review Panel will approve these criteria.

3.4.8

Engineering

All SAME flight hardware will be flown in a stowed configuration, 
packed in foam.  SAME will use a combination of random and 
sinusoidal vibration testing (Protoflight vibration) to demonstrate 
the ability of the system to withstand launch requirements.
See table in SAME-PLN-003, Section 3.4.8 for 
major system components and their vibration 
testing levels.

3.4.8

For a Class D experiment such as SAME, the workmanship 
vibration testing is a guideline.  Vibration sensitive components, 
such as optical components or particle sensors, and 
irreplaceable mission critical parts will see qualification program 
levels of vibration testing while in the “soft” stowage configuration 
that they will see for launch.  
See table in SAME-PLN-003, Section 3.4.8 for 
major system components and their vibration 
testing levels.

electronics boards will only be tested as a part of the final

performed to reveal inadequacies in workmanship.  
See table in SAME-PLN-003, Section 3.4.8 for 
major system components and their vibration 
testing levels.

Systems under test that contain electronic (EEE) parts shall be

hundred hours of failure-free operation is required for SAME 
components, subsystems or systems prior to hardware turnover. 
The one hundred hours includes operational time accumulated

subsystems and functionality are sufficiently robust to meet the 
design goals.

mission operations system, including the ground processing 
equipment and software in order to fully demonstrate operational 
compatibility and the ability of the entire system to perform as

The SAME Project Office (PO) shall conduct appropriate safety 
analyses both at the system and subsystem levels.  Each system 
and subsystem shall be evaluated to determine the applicability 
of each technical safety requirement. 
SAME will implement a system safety program 
that will assure the identification and control of 
hazards during design, fabrication, test, 
transportation, ground operations, launch, and 
retrieval. The SAME system safety program will 
be tailored to meet carrier-specific 
requirements, as outlined in the SARG. SAME 
will also meet the interface and safety

170.01.a
SAME-PLN-003 
7.1
Systems 
Engineering
Reliability, Availability & Maintainability - General Requirements
SAME will plan and implement a reliability program that interacts 
effectively with other program disciplines, including systems 
engineering, hardware design, and product assurance.  The 
preferred development approach is to develop prototype 
hardware/software to provide the final flight design for experiment
hardware/software. The reliability effort will be conducted 
throughout the design process, to the final design of the flight 
hardware.  Much of the reliability will be demonstrated through 
component and assembly testing.  Reliability and availability 
analyses will be performed concurrently with design to indicate 
areas of risk, promote design improvements, and increase 
system reliability and supportability. 
NVR
170.01.b
SAME-PLN-003 
7.1

Engineering
Reliability, Availability & Maintainability - General Requirements
All non-conformances that occur during build-up or testing of 
flight hardware shall be reported and tracked to completion per 
the ZIN-Tech Quality Management System (QMS).

SAME-PLN-003 
7.2.1
Systems 
Engineering
Reliability Allocation and Prediction Analysis
The SAME project shall perform a low-fidelity reliability prediction 
and failure mode analysis. The system level reliability for the 
mission duration and duty cycle will be improved to the greatest 
extent possible with a combination of highly reliable components 
and flight spares complemented with alternate (off-nominal) 
procedures.
A
X
170.02.1.b
SAME-PLN-003 
7.2.1
Systems 
Engineering
Reliability Allocation and Prediction Analysis
When using a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) component, 
SAME will procure the optimal reliability component. The 
selection will be based on the following:
1) Acceptable vendor screening program to the project 
requirements (burn-in, thermal cycle and vibration levels)
2) Acceptable vendor quality control program
3) A Mean-Time Between Failure (MTBF) which yields a reliability
of 90% or greater for the expected life cycle of the component, 
whenever this data and these parts are available from the vendor
4) Radiation hardness and minimized EMI susceptibility, as 
needed
NVR
170.02.2
SAME-PLN-003 
7.2.2
Systems 
Engineering
Burn-In Periods
The SAME project shall provide a statement of the burn-in 
periods (both total burn-in and failure free) that will be required 
for all equipment prior to delivery, and how the periods relate to 
the overall equipment life.
Experiment run times will be provided (log 
books.)
A
X
X
170.02.3
SAME-PLN-003 
7.2.3
Systems 
Engineering
Failure Modes and Effects Analysis and Critical Items List
The SAME project will perform a Failure Analysis, performed on 
the major assembly/component level in order to determine the 
criticality of its internal hardware devices, relative to mission 
success and safety. Critical items are those components or 
subassemblies whose failure modes are safety critical or mission-
success critical. In those instances where critical failure modes 
cannot be designed out of the intended system, the hardware will 
be designed for minimum risk or a spare component will be flown.
NVR

There are no single point failures for loss of life or vehicle in the 
SAME Experiment.  Any single point failures that could result in 
injury, loss of life, vehicle, or science mission, will be determined 
from the Hazards Analysis and the FMEA.  Single point failures 
that would compromise mission success will be determined and 
documented as a result of the FMEA and will become part of the 
SAME risk list to be accepted with rationale, watched, or 
mitigated as they are evaluated.

Worst-case analysis will be performed by the project on all

design parameters, including those that are subject to variations 
that could degrade performance, will be included in the analysis.

The SAME project will build and maintain spare subsystem 
components as required by the customer.  The spare unit will be 
composed of flight parts and will be identical to the flight unit.  
The Fit/Functional Model hardware is intended to be composed 
of some flight-like parts and procedures. This unit may be 
available for sparing of some parts or subsystems.  Information 
and support will be provided to the Project Manager for sparing 
and logistics planning.

The project shall perform a maintainability allocation and

allocations allow, where failures are likely and unavoidable.  
Procedures shall be developed to troubleshoot, fix, or work 
around malfunctions.

7.4.2

Limited Life Items
Limited storage life items have a specified storage time limit 
(shelf-life), which is less its planned storage time. Examples of 
limited storage-life items are solid chemicals, chemical mixtures 
and/or solutions, solvents, lubricants, epoxies, or even hardware 
devices.  The project controls limited storage-life items by the 
expiration date indicated on any limited storage-life item. Whether
dated by the manufacturer or by the project at receiving/creation, 
any expiration date is checked before use and recorded in the 
process plan or log book. For safety critical operations, this is 
validated by a QA sign-off.

The Project shall perform qualitative maintainability analysis to 
assure that the system is maintainable and that there is an 
effective maintenance capability to restore functions to their full 
capacity throughout the intended operational life of the system.

SAME-PLN-003 for list of design features.

SAME will operate a closed-loop nonconformance control system 
for failures and discrepancies and provide documentation of each 
nonconformance per the ZIN P13001 Procedure for the Control 
of Nonconforming Product.  In this process ZIN F13001 
Nonconformance Report is initiated.  ZIN Quality monitors the 
disposition of the Nonconformance.  The non-conformance is

developed which assures that limited-life items have not been 
degraded or damaged during storage. The plan will address 
proper handling, including environmental conditions, to mitigate 
damage or prolong life, and testing to assure the stored items 
meet required specifications. Limited-life items not meeting the 
requirements set forth in the plan will be considered 
nonconforming, and handled in accordance with paragraph 8.9. 
Limited life items will be identified on a list and a log of their 
remaining life maintained. (The definition and requirements for

Load Requirements
Investigations will be designed to withstand the launch and 
landing conditions when stowed in the MPLM, Middeck or other 
transportation vehicles. For design consideration the 
Investigation will use the acceleration loads defined in Table I 
when stowed in the MPLM or Middeck. These loads are based 
on a worst case condition of the Middeck and MPLM. The IIT will 
provide the investigator with the acceleration and random 
vibration data of the carrier the investigation is manifested on. 
Additional requirements or data may be required depending on 
the configuration of the investigation and the requirements of the 
carrier.
It is assumed that the loads imposed by the random vibration 
environment on stowed items in foam can be neglected in design 
consideration. The Investigation will conduct a workmanship test, 
for instance on electrical components or mechanisms, based on 
the random vibration environment defined in Table I. The 
Investigation must ensure that the hardware will survive the 
workmanship random vibration level.

Reverse Current
Investigation hardware connected to the 120 Vdc primary power 
source available in the WV must comply with the requirements 
defined in paragraph 3.2.2.4.1 or 3.2.2.4.2 for the reverse current 
into the upstream power source. Note: Investigations having 
input connected capacitances, the aggregate total of which is 
less than 25 micro-farads, are considered meeting the limits of 
paragraph 3.2.2.4.1 for US Type I RPCMs. Input connected 
capacitors are those which, by virtue of circuit arrangement, are 
able to discharge through the power source when the power 
source is short circuited. Series connected rectifier diodes and 
resistors greater than 10 Ohms are sufficient to block such 
discharges.

Reverse Current Limits
Investigations using the 120V DC primary power source shall 
limit reverse current transients that can occur when a hard fault 
occurs across the power source within the applicable transient 
envelope shown in Figures 15, 16 and 17. For purposes of this 
interface definition, the fault is 10 milli Ohms or less applied 
within 2 micro-seconds or less. For the investigation hardware 
exhibiting reverse current transient peaks within ±100 Amperes, 
the fault resistance is 40 milli Ohms or less.

Transients Partially Contained Within the Envelope
If the reverse current on the 120V DC primary power source 
exceeds the envelope limits defined in paragraph 3.2.2.4.1 for 
one or more short time intervals, the transient peak current and 
the ratio of the times of intersection with the envelope shall 
satisfy the following inequality: (ipk/ie)2 x ln(t2/t1) ≤ 1 where ln 
represents the natural logarithm, t1 and t2 correspond to the 
beginning and end times, respectively, of each interval when the 
transient is outside the envelope, ipk is the peak of the transient 
occurring between t2 and t1, and ie is the point on the envelope at 
the time of the peak ipk. For multiple intervals in which the 
envelope is exceeded, the left-hand side of this expression will 
be evaluated for each interval and the sum of all such results will 
total less than unity.  See MSFC-RQMT-2888 for more 
information.

Returns, Signals Below Four Megahertz (an exception to

Balanced signal circuits external to equipment with frequency 
content below four megahertz shall be isolated from chassis, 
structure, and any other power return by a minimum of 6,000 
ohms, individually (i.e., measured per connection, pin, wire, etc.). 
A balanced circuit means that the impedances from high and low 
sides to case or structure are equal. Typical circuits have 
balanced receiving ends and unbalanced sending ends. If the 
impedance through the sending end is very low (1%) compared 
with the isolation impedance at the receiving end, it is considered 
a balanced circuit.

Signal circuits with frequency components equal to or above four 
megahertz shall use controlled impedance transmission and 
reception media such as shielded twisted 72-ohm cable, "twin-
ax" cable, "tri-ax" cable, or "co-ax" cable. Circuits using "twin-ax" 
cable shall be balanced and referenced to primary structure at a 
single point. "Tri-ax" cable shall use the center and inner shield 
conductors for unbalanced transmission, referenced to primary 
structure at a single point with the outer shield multipoint 
grounded as an "overshield". dc isolated, single-ended circuits 
coupled by coaxial cable with the shield terminated 360 degrees 
at each end and at available intermediate points, shall be 
permitted for signals with the lowest frequency component equal 
to or above 4 MHz.

3.2.4.2
Electrical 
Engineering
Electrical Bonding 
Investigation hardware connected to the RPDA power sources 
available in the WV shall be bonded in accordance with the 
following requirements. Electrical bonding is the process of 
providing good electrical connection across mechanical 
interfaces to minimize electrical potential differences between 
equipment and individual parts of structure. Good electrical 
bonding provides: Fault current paths for protection against fire 
and personnel shock, Provides a current path for radio 
frequencies for proper operation of filters and shields, and a 
means to prevent or safely discharge static charges.
Electrical bonds are classified according to the purpose for the 
bond. There may be more than one purpose for bonding a 
specific interface, and the bond shall meet the requirements of 
each applicable class. Notes shall be provided on assembly 
drawings indicating the applicable class or classes. The material 
used in the MSG work volume is 7075 aluminum nickel struck. A 
bonding test shall be performed during integrated testing with the 
Engineering Unit.
Must test with EU, test results to be provided to 
IPIM.

requirement of bonding. Investigation hardware providers shall

Class H Bonding (Shock and Fault Protection) 
Fault current, due to short circuits to equipment case or 
structure, may cause shock or fire hazards. All electrically 
conductive equipment cases that may develop potentials due to 
short circuits shall be electrically bonded to structure. The bond 
shall minimize shock hazard voltages and allow proper operation 
of circuit protection devices such as circuit breakers or fuses. 
Bonding of structural joints in the fault current return path shall 
provide for the maximum current that may be delivered by the 
power supply until the fuse or circuit breaker disconnects. For 
personnel and fire safety the fault current return path shall be 
capable of conducting a minimum of 500% overload current for a 
time period of 0.5 second. Typical personnel protection breakers 
will trip within 0.2 second after a hard short to case. Resultant 
voltage on the enclosure of the affected component must not 
exceed 4.5 volts, and no fire or damage to the bond is allowed. 
See MSFC-RQMT-2888 for more information.

IPIM.

All electrical components which use or produce electromagnetic

contact over a large area (greater than 1 square inch) of the 
mating surfaces meet the RF impedance requirement. The bond 
from the equipment enclosure to the mounting plate furnished 
with the equipment shall also comply with these requirements, 
except that a suitable flat ground strap may be used across any 
necessary vibration isolators or other environment isolators.  See

Methods of Bonding 
Equipment and structure with metal-to-metal joints that are joined 
by processes that transform the mated surfaces into one piece of 
metal, such as by welding or brazing, are considered permanent 
and inherently bonded.  Semi-permanent joints are held together 
by screws, rivets, clamps, etc.  Semi-permanent mating surfaces 
shall be cleaned of all insulating material before connection to 
provide a good electrical bond.  Clamping pressure across the 
joint shall be adequate to assure a secure mechanical 
connection. Fasteners or their threads shall not be used as 
primary bonding paths.

anodized, or zinc-plated washers; or any cadmium-plated

Frequency or Rise/Fall Time 
For Table IX, EMC Classification, Wire Type, and Shield 
Grounding classification purposes, the fundamental component 
of steady state operation will determine the frequency of the 
circuit unless the rise/fall time (pulsed wave forms) is less than 
10 microseconds. If the rise/fall time is less than 10 
microseconds and the voltage is less than 6 volts, the circuit 
shall be classified as Radio Frequency (RF) regardless of the 
fundamental frequency. Power circuits which are switched on 
and off will be classified as HO or EO even if their rise/fall times 
are less than 10 microseconds.

Electrical

Impedance 
The actual impedance of the interconnecting circuit, i.e., the 
complex "Z" that includes resistance, inductance and 
capacitance, will be used to classify the source and load 
impedances using Table IX. These source and load impedances 
determine the magnetic and electric field coupling mode 
category. The equivalent circuit pickup resistance, i.e., the sum 
of the load and equivalent reactive/resistive components, will be 
used to identify potential areas for magnetic or electric field 
coupling.

coupling that can cause induced noise with amplitudes less than 
the source voltage that will affect measurement and/or 
conversion accuracy, circuit classification will be based upon 
circuit sensitivity considerations rather than upon frequency, 
rise/fall time, impedance, or voltage. Circuits assigned a 
classification based on sensitivity rather than on source voltage 
will be identified on all wiring diagrams containing such circuits.

treatment will be based on Table IX and the wire/cable and

Investigation I/O Interface
The MSG provides 8 analog inputs, 8 discrete inputs, and 8 
digital outputs, split equally between two connectors in the Work 
Volume. When properly configured and enabled, the Experiment 
Control Board (ECB) reads the input lines and transmits the data 
to the RC. The RC in turn transmits the data to the ISS via the 
Low Rate Data Link (LRDL) in a Low Rate Telemetry (LRT) 
packet. The digital output lines are controlled via commands to 
the RC.

WV Air Circulation System (ACS)
The WV air circulation is established by the MSG Air Handling 
Unit (AHU). The AHU heat exchanger provides 200 W of 
investigation cooling, at an airflow rate of 1200 l/min and a 
maximum velocity of 0.044 m/s at the centerline of the WV. The 
airflow can be varied between 15% and 100% depending on fan 
speed settings. The rate and velocity is calculated without an 
Investigation inside the WV. Investigation power draw data shall 
be used to determine if the AHU heat exchanger is capable of 
removing the dissipated heat load. The filtration system provides 
for particulate removal, filtration of single spillage (see section 
3.7.3), and oxidation of CO to CO2 by means of a built-in 
catalyst. Due to the hydroscopic nature of the filters, the humidity 
inside the WV will be maintained at or below cabin level. Figure

Investigations shall be designed to maintain fault tolerance or

temperature, without ground or flight crew intervention, in the

coolant loop, avionics air cooling or the vacuum and nitrogen

Chemical Releases
Investigations that use chemicals that would create a toxicity 
problem or cause a hazard to ISS or MSG hardware if released 
shall provide adequate containment.  Containment shall be 
provided by the use of a pressure vessel or the use of two or 
three redundantly sealed containers, depending on the 
toxicological hazard for a chemical with a vapor pressure below 
15 psia. The Investigation must assure that each level of 
containment will not leak under the maximum use conditions (i.e. 
vibration, temperature, pressure, etc.). The release of methanol, 
ethanol, isopropyl alcohol, n-propyl alcohol, n-butyl alcohol, 
acetone, ethylene glycol, and propylene glycol into the ISS 
habitable environment shall be prohibited. The release of these 
compounds due to normal materials offgassing is exempt from 
this requirement.

cooperative efforts of ISS Payload Label Approval Team (IPLAT)

The design of electrical connectors shall make it impossible to 
inadvertently reverse a connection or mate the wrong connectors 
if a hazardous condition can be created. Payload and on-orbit 
support equipment, wire harnesses, and connectors shall be 
designed such that no blind connections or disconnections must 
be made during payload installation, operation, removal, or 
maintenance on orbit or during ground operations at KSC unless 
the design includes scoop proof connectors or other protective 
features. For payload equipment, for which mismating or cross-
connection may damage ISS or MSG provided equipment, plugs, 
and receptacles (connectors), shall be selected and applied such 
that they cannot be mismatched or cross-connected in the 
intended system as well as adjacent systems. Although 
identification markings or labels are required, the use of 
identification alone is not sufficient to preclude mismating. See
