4.2.7 Materials Offgassing 
 
Representative SPICE hardware, flight-like cables and other miscellaneous items have been 
toxic off-gas tested in accordance with NASA-STD-6001, Test 7. See letter ED36B(03-060)  
attached to 1230 form. Offgas test results will be analyzed by NASA/GRC/SMAD  and certified 
for flight via the GRC/JSC Materials and Processes Inter-center Agreement. 
 
Materials Off-gassing is addressed in Section 7 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.8 Non-Ionizing Radiation (EMI) 
 
4.2.8.1 
Non-Transmitters 
 
SPICE is designed for compliance with the radiated and conducted emissions requirements 
specified in MSFC-RQMT-2888 as defined in SSP 30237, Space Station Electromagnetic 
Emission and Susceptibility Requirements.  All electronic assemblies have been tested for 
conformance to this specification including the determination of the maximum ripple voltage 
emissions appearing on the SPICE input power leads.  The power conversion box contains a 
filter to meet the requirements of MSFC RQMT-2888. This filter reduces the step from milliamp 
draw to 3 amp draw by the still camera when taking a picture. See figure 14. SPICE will only be 
operated inside of the MSG working volume.  The test results have been submitted to 
NASA/MSFC MSG personnel for their review and approval. An ISS Electromagnetic Emissions 
Panel approved Technical Interface Agreement has been sought for RE02 exceedance.  
 
EMI Radiation is addressed in Section 8.1 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.8.2 
Lasers 
 
There are no lasers in the SPICE experiment. 
 
4.2.9 Battery Failure 
 
The Batteries used in the SPICE experiment meet the criteria of small commercial batteries 
stated in Section 9.2 of the JSC Standardized Hazard Report JSC 1230. The following 
SPICE hardware contains small commercial batteries that are verified as permanently soldered 
into their respective electrical circuits and have completed successful verification of in circuit 
voltage measurements and verification of circuit isolation from external power sources. 
 
The NIKON D100 Digital Camera contains Button Cell 20mmX3.2mm, type Li-Mn-O2, 3 Volts 
DC 65mAh, Maxell Model No.: ML2032T6. The battery is fully contained within the Digital 
Camera and cannot be accessed unless complete Camera disassembly is performed. The 
purpose of the camera battery is to maintain date, time and camera operational settings. The 
cell is soldered to board.   
 
The Horita Video Titler Card Cell consists of two cells in series. The cells are 15.5 X6.3 mm 
Rechargeable Nickel Metal Hydride cells  1.2 VDC each, 60mAh, Model Number GP60BVH, 
Manufacturer GP Batteries International LTD.  The cells will not be charged and are prevented

the Video Control Box and cannot be accessed unless the Video Control Box is disassembled. 
The purpose of the Video Titler Card Cell is to maintain Video Titler operational settings.   
 
The Dallas Tattle-Tale Card I-Button Data Device, Model Number DS1994, contains a 
12.5mmX2.5mm Li-CFx Battery, 3VDC, 50mAh, Model No. BR1225, Manufacturer RAYOVAC. 
The Lithium Battery is soldered to the boards and fully contained within the I Button Data Device 
and the I Button Data Device is contained inside the Experiment Assembly. The purpose of the I 
Button Data Device Lithium (Li-CFx) Battery is to maintain experiment data memory when 
external power is removed from the Experiment Assembly. The documents for the I-Button Data 
Device state that it does not use any power to charge the lithium battery.  It has a limited life of 
greater than10 years based on the low power required to sit idle. Specifically there is a 
statement on page 46 that the ROM logic can be operated by the parasite power even after the 
lithium cell is exhausted in 10 years or more.  This implies that the other sections of memory 
may not be operational if the lithium battery dies.  When data is being exchanged with the I-
Button Data Device, the data line is used to charge a capacitor internal to the I-Button Data 
Device and that capacitor is used to power the read write operations.  Parasite power is an 
internal I-Button Data Device capacitor that is charged by the data line (converted RS-232).   
 
 
Battery Failure is addressed in Section 9.2 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.10 
 Touch Temperatures 
 
SPICE hardware and electronics have been designed and tested to meet touch temperature 
limits of 49°C specified in the Interpretation Letter MA2-95-048. Also during on-orbit operation, 
the SPICE hardware is enclosed inside the MSG working volume with no direct crew contact 
with the SPICE Experiment Assembly during ignition or combustion processes (experiment 
runs).  Also during post experiment runs the airflow provided by the MSG Air Handling Unit 
(AHU) during by-product clean up will also aid in the dissipation of any residual heated air within 
the MSG working volume. SPICE by design does not require external cooling during experiment 
operations.  
 
A thermal test has been conducted to verify that the touch temperature limits of MA2-95-048 are 
met. The fuel nozzles were tested and found that the worst case nozzle reached 89 degrees C 
but cooled to 33 degrees C in less than 60 seconds after flame off. This was without EA air flow 
which will be present at the end of a burn decreasing cooling time. A wait time will be imposed 
before EA chamber access after flame off.   
 
Touch Temperature is addressed in hazard report U6.     
 
4.2.11 Electrical Power Distribution 
 
The electrical power distribution system meets station interface circuit protection requirements 
of SSP 57000 (through the MSG Working Volume secondary power sources) and payload wire 
sizing and circuit protection requirements of Interpretation Letter TA-92-038.  The SPICE 
hardware will receive circuit protection from the MSG conditioned power sources (28VDC @ 7 
Amps), (+/-12VDC @ 2 Amps) and (5VDC @ 4 Amps).  SPICE will provide additional circuit 
protection in the Power Conditioning Box (5-Amp fast-acting cartridge fuses) on the +28 VDC 
and +5 VDC power lines.  The SPICE +/- 12VDC power line does not require additional circuit

conditioned power source. 
 
Besides the circuit protection provided by the MSG circuit breakers and SPICE Fuses, the 
DC/DC converters also provide additional protection by current limiting their output in the event 
of an over-current condition.  See schematic of the SPICE Power Distribution System attached 
to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11. See SPICE Wire De-rating Analysis 60054-ANA-
017. 
 
SPICE does not meet the Power Distribution Single Point Grounding requirements of MSFC-
RQMT-2888.  The Hitachi Video Camera HV-C20U-S4 video camera, (PN )7009.80.AA 
(specially modified for the MSG Program), the Nikon D100 Digital SLR Camera and other 
similar commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) cameras (modified or unmodified) violate SSP30240, 
3.2.1.2, Secondary and Tertiary Electrical Power (single point grounding) by connecting the 
incoming 12 Vdc power return to camera structure (the second time the 12 Vdc is grounded to 
structure). SPICE has submitted a Tailoring Interpretation Agreement for these occurrences. 
See schematics attached to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11.  
 
SPICE meets the bonding and grounding requirements of SSP 30245 and SSP 30240.  Bonding 
and grounding of the SPICE hardware is accomplished via several different methods; via the 
chassis conductor pin provided via Pin L at the P303 Power Connector (i.e., conductor bond 
path), via the overall shield on the P303 Power Cable (i.e., using a grounded backshell), and via 
the metal-to-metal bond of SPICE structure to the MSG mounting plate. See schematic attached 
to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11. 
 
The SPICE experiment will fail-safe in the event of total or partial power loss, i.e., the hardware 
will not be damaged or pose any hazard in the event of a power disruption.  In the event of a 
total power loss, the SPICE Experiment cannot be operated. The MFC is normally closed, so 
power loss will stop fuel flow. See Hazard Report SPICE-U5 for loss of power case effect on 
fuel flammability control. 
 
Power into SPICE is filtered to prevent surges on the MSG power supply. See Figure 14 for the 
28 volt power filter schematic.  
 
A temporary or intermittent loss of power will cause the SPICE control software to "reboot" (the 
unit will act as if it was being turn "ON" for the first time). 
 
Electrical Power Distribution is addressed in Section 11 of STD-SPICE-01.

4.2.12 Ignition of Flammable Atmospheres in the Payload Bay 
Not applicable, as the SPICE hardware is not mounted/transported in the the Shuttle Payload

4.2.13 Rotating Equipment 
 
The SPICE Experiment Assembly has one internal Fan to (1) study convective flow during 
combustion and (2) to remove combustion byproducts from the Experiment Assembly in 
between tests.  The fan is DC-powered and is made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic (See 
Sections 6 and 7 of STD-SPICE-01 for materials requirements).  The fan diameter is 3 inches, 
with a speed of 2950 RPM.  It is a brushless DC motor provided with 12 V. Although the Fan 
shroud is plastic it is also fully enclosed in aluminum housing with stainless steel mesh (Type 
304ss, 71% of open area) covering the fan inlet and outlet openings.  Analysis shows that this 
fan has a low kinetic energy level (<<<19, 310 J) and is fully contained with the Experiment 
Assembly according to NASA-STD-5003 requirements. 
 
Rotating Equipment is addressed in Section 13 of STD-SPICE-01.

during SPICE ignition is 2.8 Amps on the +5 VDC power line.  Crew procedures require that the 
MSG circuit breakers that provide power to the MSG J303 connector be turned off prior to any 
crew interface with the SPICE Experiment.

and/or keying.  In addition, they will all be labeled to help identify the connector interface in

Normal operating power draw of the Experiment is 27 Watts with a maximum power draw, which 
only occurs during ignition, of approximately 42 Watts for < 10 sec.   
 
All power connectors utilized by SPICE conform to the MIL-C-38999 Series I standard which 
feature a scoop-proof design that completely encloses the pin/socket contacts during mating 
and de-mating operations.  Additionally, the powered side of the cable connectors on SPICE are 
terminated in sockets to provide protection against inadvertent shorting that could be caused by 
external debris.   
 
Mating/Demating of Power Connectors is addressed in Section 14 of STD-SPICE-01. 
    
4.2.15 Contingency Return and Rapid Safing 
 
The SPICE experiment is not in operation mode while stowed in Shuttle for launch and landing.  
While on orbit the SPICE hardware will be either stowed in the ISS stowage, or in operation in 
the MSG.  In either case, the SPICE hardware will not interfere with the IVA envelope or impede 
emergency IVA egress to the remaining contiguous pressurized volumes. 
 
Design analysis will be performed for the SPICE hardware and planned flight operations for 
compliance to MA2-96-190.    
 
Contingency Return and Rapid Safing is addressed in Section 15 of STD-SPICE-01.      
 
4.2.16 Release of Mercury from Bulbs into Crew Habitable 
Environment 
 
There is no mercury in any of the SPICE components.  
 
4.3 OTHER SAFETY HAZARDS 
 
The previous sections close discussion on the SPICE Flight Payload Standardized Hazard 
Control Report (STD-SPICE-01).   Additional potential hazards and SPICE unique hazards are 
discussed below. 
 
4.3.1 Pressurized Systems 
 
SPICE pressurized components are the Gas Bottle Assemblies and the Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System. These components do not interface with the nitrogen or vacuum sources 
of the MSG.  
 
Even though all of the components are rated for pressures well above 230 psi, the system MDP 
is determined by the point at which the fuel can turn to liquid. This pressure also considered the 
maximum temperature that the bottle could experience. SPICE pressurized lines and fittings will 
be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 230psid. SPICE Pressurized system 
components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP

of 230 psid. The gas bottles are DOT bottles with a rated pressure of 500 psi which will be 
pressurized to a maximum of 230 psi. To prevent overpressurization this will be verified after 
filling that the bottles are the correct mixture and at the correct pressure.  The bottles have been 
proof tested to 1000 psi. The Experiment Assembly is not sealed and will not pressurize in the 
event of full open flow from the mass flow controller. The maximum flow rate of the fuel system 
is 20 liters per minute. The fan that is used to cause flow is capable of 1120 liters per minute 
with a pressure drop of parts of a psi. Therefore the flow rate through the chamber is orders of 
magnitude greater than the maximum fuel flow into the chamber. Therefore the chamber will 
have no significant increase in pressure. See hazard Report SPICE U5 for analysis of pressure 
due to burning of worst case fuel load in the EA.  In the event of power loss the Mass Flow 
Controller is normally closed, therefore fuel flow will stop.  
Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in 
accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and Processes. 
Hardware will be built in conformance with approved design drawings and specifications. The 
gas bottles will be filled to approved procedures to insure that the proper mixture of gas is 
placed in the correct bottle and each bottle is filled to the correct pressure. 
The Gas Bottle Assemblies and the pressurized portions of the Experiment Assembly Fuel 
Delivery System will be proof pressure tested to 1.5 X MDP and Helium Leak tested for an 
acceptable leak rate of 1x10E-4 scc/sec Helium in order to validate structural integrity and 
containment by design. 
 
During on orbit operations, procedures will be provided to instruct the crew on proper Gas Bottle 
Exchange, Experiment Set-up and Operation to prevent Gas Bottle and Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System leakage. 
  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U2. Flammability issues of the fuels are covered 
in SPICE-U4 and SPICE U5. Projectile issues are covered in SPICE-U3. 
 
4.3.2 Collision 
 
Calculations show that for the bottle under full pressure, the propulsive force of the worst case, 
a break off of a tube, only create 0.6 lbs of force for 0.23 seconds. The force required to break 
off the tube is 10 lbs at the worst case moment arm with all factors of safety. If the bottle is 
being held such that 10 lbs of force is on the bottle, the 0.6 lb propulsive force can easily be 
withstood. Each Gas Bottle Assembly by design incorporates a single fault tolerant design. The 
Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect are in series on the Gas Bottle Assembly. Should the 
Diaphragm Valve fail the Quick Disconnect will contain the gas. The failure of the Quick 
Disconnect is backed up by the containment of the Diaphragm Valve. Both the Diaphragm Valve 
and Quick Disconnect would need to fail simultaneously in order for the Gas Bottle Assembly to 
become a projectile. In addition there is a cap on the QC which although is not a radial vent cap 
it will restrict the flow and disperse it at an angle reducing the force. Even if both failures 
occurred the Gas Bottle Tubing at the QD end incorporates a 90 degree bend that would 
prevent the Gas Bottle assembly from gaining any significant speed (<1.5m/s), and force 
(<0.6lbf) or direction that would present a collision hazard.  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U3. 
 
 
4.3.3 On-Orbit Maintenance

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
41 
The SPICE experiment hardware does not contain limited life items. No on-orbit maintenance is 
planned. 
 
4.3.4 Fire Detection and Suppression 
 
SPICE does not have any computer control of any FD& S functions and cannot interface directly 
with the ISS caution and warning system.  SPICE flammability hazards are controlled by 
material selection, containment, and wire de-rating and circuit protection, (See Section 4.2.6 
and 4.2.11). SPICE unburned Fuel contamination hazard is controlled under unique Hazard 
Report SPICE-U1. Structural Integrity of the SPICE Experiment Fuel Delivery System is 
controlled under unique Hazard Report SPICE-U2.  
SPICE will receive Fire Detection capability from MSG through its Working Volume Rear Wall 
Temperature Sensor. The crew is required to be present during any burn per MSFC-RQMT-
2888.  Fire Suppression capability is provided by MSG through the use of a station Portable Fire 
Extinguisher (PFE) expelling CO2 into the MSG Working Volume. See Attachment D for the 
completed Fire Detection and Suppression Reporting Form 1428 for the SPICE Experiment. 
4.3.5 Crew Interaction 
 
SPICE is designed such that any required access to SPICE hardware during flight or ground 
operations can be accomplished with minimum risk of injury to personnel.  SPICE hardware 
components are designed to provide enough clearance for crew interface and usage and do not 
create a pinch or accessibility hazard.  
 
The SPICE experiment complies with the requirements for Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) 
compatibility as specified in MSFC-RQMT-2888 document.  An analysis will be prepared to 
demonstrate that that electrical equipment and any parts susceptible to damage by ESD will fail-
safe when exposed to an Electrostatic Discharge (ED) equal or less than 4,000 Volts to the 
case or any pin on the external contacts.  These (ED) voltages might be the result of charges 
accumulated and then discharged from ground personnel or crewmembers during equipment 
installation or removal.   Reference unique hazard SPICE-U8.  
 
Table 5 provides a listing of the SPICE Standard and Unique Hazards that are controlled by 
operating procedures.

content:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
45 
 
 
 
 
4.3.6 Release of Experiment Materials 
4.3.6.1 Unburned Fuel Release  
JSC toxicologist assessment of the fuels used in SPICE have a toxicity rating of 0 and a 
flammability rating of 4, See Attachment A, SPICE Hazardous Material Summary Table (HMST). 
Also see table 6 for levels of fuel in the lab module.  
 
A concern was raised at the Phase 0/I review concerning effects on the ECLSS due to leaks of 
these fuels. The action item to determine any issues with these gases in the quantities from 
SPICE was given. The results of the analysis are that leakage of the total amounts of these 
fuels is not an issue for ECLSS.  Reference the March 25, 2004 email from Tim Smith which is 
attached to hazard report SPICE-U1. Leakage of fuel from SPICE is being controlled by design 
and verified by Helium leak testing of the Fuel Delivery System and the bottle assemblies. The 
gases that have been analyzed for ECLSS will be used to fill the bottle assemblies by using 
approved procedures, by labeling each bottle assembly for contents, and then by sampling each 
bottle to test for the correct contents. 
 
Reference Attachment E Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U1. 
 
Flammability in the US Lab. Lean Flammability Limit (LFL) Calculations conducted on the 
HMST listed SPICE Fuel Concentrations that could be released inside the United States Lab 
(USL) Volume show that all 12 SPICE Gas Bottles could leak their entire contents into the USL 
Volume and still be below the LFL for the applicable Fuel. The MSG will be in the Columbus 
module at the time SPICE is run. This module has a smaller volume than the US Lab. A new 
HMST has been requested and new calculations were performed based on the volume of 64 m3 
that is being used by toxicology. See table 6 for the calculations.  
 
Flammability in Stowage. The bottles are launched packed in foam in stowage cases which 
are in turn packed in foam. The bottles have all been vibration tested in the stowage 
configuration and leak tested. The fittings are all commercial fittings rated for over 3000 psi. 
Also each Gas Bottle Assembly incorporates a single fault tolerant design, which would require 
the Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect to fail simultaneously in order for the Gas Bottle 
Assembly to leak unburned fuel through the normal flow path. This fault tolerance is 
accomplished by having the Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect in series on the Gas Bottle 
Assembly. Should the Diaphragm Valve fail the Quick Disconnect will contain the gas. The 
failure of the Quick Disconnect is backed up by the containment of the Diaphragm Valve. There 
will be no ignition sources in the Gas Bottle Assembly stowage cases (no electronics or 
batteries). The bottles will be electrically connected to the aluminum case by two redundant 
strips of aluminum tape attached to the foam which will contact each bottle. A calculation will be 
performed providing the necessary volume in stowage which must be clear of ignition sources 
assuming two worst case bottles leak. This is based on being below the LFL. See table 6. The 
current calculation with a 75 % packing factor (there is only 25 % void space) is 156 liters or a 
54 cm cube. This size is easily accommodated considering the amount of foam used. Once the 
fuel leaks into the MPLM or ISS stowage volume it was agreed that it will dissipate rapidly.  
 
Stowage for landing utilizes the same controls, including valve handle restraints. The restraint (a 
tie-wrap) is capable of withstanding 50 lbs of force, which is sufficient to prevent turning of the 
valve during launch and to prevent inadvertent turning during handling.  See figure 10b for a

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
46 
picture of the valve with the restraint. This picture is for demonstration of the concept, the flight 
version will be installed with considerations for the crew (e.g. sharp edges) They will be cut by 
the crew once the bottle is inside the MSG. The bottles are expected to be used to the point 
where no gas is available to leak out, therefore for landing there should be less fuel, but the tie 
wrap will be installed by the crew when the bottle is removed from the MSG. In addition to the 
tie wrap the foam cut outs for the bottles includes cut outs for the handles which will prevent 
them from turning.  
 
Reference Attachment E Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U4  
 
 
Flammability in the MSG.  This concern is divided into three concerns, fuel build up in the EA 
igniting, fuel leak into the MSG igniting and gas leak impinging on a crew member’s hand.  
 
For the concern of the EA filling with fuel and igniting during times with out crew access to the 
inside of the EA, the MFC has been leak tested at MDP to demonstrate that it will not leak into 
chamber when off, preventing fuel in the chamber from building up or flowing in quantities that 
could ignite. Air flow from the EA fans keep the EA internal fuel percentage below the LFL. The 
EA fan is on automatically upon power up of SPICE. Also the air flow rate is verified by the crew 
from the laptop which has a measured value of air flow rate displayed. The only ignition source 
in the EA chamber is the ignitor and the ignitor is not turned on until after the EA fan is verified 
on. The crew will turn on the ignitor before fuel flow which will eliminate fuel build up. In the 
event that the fan fails, the crew fails to verify the fan speed and there was an ignition source 
the total energy content of the EA chamber is well below the 14,240 ft-lb limit for a pressure 
vessel at worst case fuel mixture. See table 6.  
 
A flame out condition has been proposed to cause fuel build up if the fuel is not turned off or fuel 
is not ignited. For this condition to occur the EA fan would also have to be off.  Large amounts 
of air in the line could cause flame out.  An air bubble caused by changing bottles has been 
hypothesized as causing a flame out. The QC from manufacturer is “drip-less” meaning it has 
minimal air entrainment (0.3 cc). This air bubble would be pushed out in the first 2 seconds of 
operation before ignition was confirmed (before steady state operation), therefore the situation 
of a flame out or failure to ignite in 2-3 seconds would not be a surprise situation for the crew, it 
would be part of the ignition sequence. Only approved crew procedures will be used to monitor 
burn to adjust flame. In addition it has been shown that the air bubble would mix in the fuel line 
filter to a percentage of fuel/air that would not be an issue. See attachments to hazard report 
SPICE-U5 for analysis.  
 
For the MSG concern, in general Lean Flammability Limit (LFL) Calculations conducted on the 
HMST listed SPICE Fuel Concentrations that could be released inside the MSG Working 
Volume show that 2 SPICE Gas Bottles could leak their entire contents into the MSG Working 
Volume and still be below the LFL for the applicable Fuel, see table 6. Note only one bottle at a 
time will be permitted in the MSG. This assumes total mixing which is realistic considering that 
there is a minimum of 180 liters/sec of air flowing in the MSG caused by the MSG fans. The 
MSG fans are capable of the fuel concentrations below the LFL, and in addition the EA fan will 
mix the air in the MSG WV. See attachments to hazard report SPICE-U5 for analysis. There are 
no ignition sources inside MSG to ignite any leak from the gas bottles. The switches used for 
the SPICE inhibits and ignition will not produce any sparks or electrical ignition sources. SPICE 
is designed to minimize the potential for leaks, and with the use of approved crew procedures to 
ensure the MSG fans are running and only one bottle is permitted in MSG at a time there should 
not be fuel ignition in MSG. See unique hazard SPICE-U8.

content:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
47 
In the case of MSG being powered down or power failing there is a concern that a pool of fuel 
which leaks out of the Bottle Assembly or EA will ignite when the MSG is powered on. This is 
addressed in the attachment to hazard report SPICE-U5 which shows that in the worst case the 
fuel will dissipate due to molecular action in less than 28 minutes, but other factors reduce that 
time. A slow leak would mean less fuel to dissipate or allow a longer dilution time. A fast leak 
would increase mixing due to gas velocity. Since the crew is necessary for the total operation of 
SPICE, when the crew leaves the MSG it will be required that the crew turn off the hand valve 
reducing the leak potential. In the event of a power loss, when power is restored to the lab, 
racks must be individually turned back on, this includes the MSG. If a wait time of ½ hour were 
implemented it would insure adequate dilution of the fuel.  
 
In the case of impingement the leak controls mentioned before for the bottles are still valid. In 
addition, the pressurized area of the EA will be leak tested to insure that it does not leak. The 
Quick Connects (QC) softgood seal resides on the bottle side of the connection which will be 
used only once. The EA side which will mate 12 times (once for each bottle) is the metal side, 
thus reducing the risk of leakage due to seal wear. Electronics are contained inside the EA. The 
only exposed item is a switch which is a 5 volt switch. 5 volt systems are frequently used in 
flammable atmospheres (mines) due to their inability to ignite them. In addition this switch is 
sealed. The ignitor throw is a lever that the crew moves to insert the ignitor into the fuel path 
and turn on the ignitor. It is a lever on a rod which goes inside the EA to move the ignitor. There 
is a hall effect sensor (digital) which senses the proximity of the ignitor to the nozzle area  and 
electronically turns on the ignitor. Therefore there are no sparks associated with turning on the 
ignitor. There are also no sparks in the proximity of the crew’s hand to light a fuel impingement.  
See figure 16. 
 
Each Gas Bottle Assembly will be filled per approved procedure which will ensure all bottles are 
filled with the proper fuel mixtures to appropriate pressures and labeled to identify filled bottle 
contents. Structural Integrity of the Gas Bottle Assemblies including the Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System is verified by conducting proof pressure to 1.5 X system MDP of 230 psid. 
The Gas Bottle Assemblies will meet a leak rate of less than 1X10E-4 scc/sec Helium. The 
Experiment Assembly Fuel Delivery System will be verified by a decay pressure test 
 
Reference  Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U5.   
 
In the case of the crew having access to the inside of the EA and fuel leaking into it and igniting, 
the fuel is controlled by the MFC which is inhibited by the window switch (open circuit when the 
EA window is open), fuel enable on control box is off, and  the fuel switch is off.  All of these 
inhibit the MFC. In addition the Gas Bottle Assembly valve will be turned off. There are no 
ignition sources other than the ignitor itself. The inhibit switches are all 5 volt and the hall effect 
switch for the ignitor is solid state digital. The ignitor is inhibited by a window switch, the control 
box ignitor inhibit and the fact that the ignitor throw is not thrown.  Also when ever there is power 
to the experiment the EA fan will be on, which keeps the chamber below the LFL. See figure 17.  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U8.

4.3.6.2 Combustion By-Product Release 
 
JSC toxicologist assessments of the combustion by-products of Carbon Monoxide and Carbon Dioxide 
produced by the SPICE experiment have been given a toxicity rating of 0. See Attachment A, SPICE 
Hazardous Material Summary Table HMST.  To ensure that the combustion by-products are compatible 
with ECLSS, SPICE will ensure that the correct gases, mixtures, and pressure are used to fill the test 
bottles. 
  
The SPICE Experiment is operated inside the Working Volume of the Micro-gravity Science Glove Box 
(MSG) Facility. The MSG Facility provides a level of containment for SPICE Combustion By-Products.  
The amount of soot which may be created by SPICE is 2-10 mg total. This is based on ELF and ground 
testing. MSG filtering will contain any soot by-products that are produced. 
 
Reference Attachment E Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U1.

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE 
 
 
 
 
 SPICE-SDP-003 
May 2008 
50 
 
 
 
4.3.7 Acoustic Noise 
Acoustic noise generated by the small fan in the Experiment Assembly will not be a hazard. The SPICE 
Experiment will be in compliance to the Acoustic requirements of the MSFC-RQMT-2888.  
4.3.8 Stowage 
The Gas Bottle assemblies shown in Figure 10 will be pre-packed using two Gas Bottle Storage Cases, 
shown in figure 9. Each Gas Bottle Storage Case will contain 6 Gas Bottle Assemblies and a third 
storage Case will be used for SPICE Component storage. See sections 2.6 and 2.7. 
The SPICE Experiment Assembly along with the Gas Bottle and Component Cases will be soft stowed 
in the MPLM for launch and landing.  Stowage for launch is planned at L-48 hours.  The hardware 
configuration for stowage during launch and landing is still under development and is in work in 
conjunction with MSG.  
 
 
4.4 SPICE TEST FAILURES, ANOMALIES AND ACCIDENTS 
SPICE has had no safety related test failures, anomalies and accidents involving Qualification or Flight 
Hardware. The only test failure is related to EMI susceptibility of the camera. 
 
4.5  AGREEMENTS FROM PHASE 0/1 REVIEW AND 
SUBSEQUENT REVIEWS 
 
The following agreements/action items were taken at phase 0/1. After each action item is an answer or 
reference to the SDP text or hazard report which addresses the comment.

 SPICE-SDP-003 
May 2008 
51 
Phase 0/1 Agreements  
3.1 The PO agreed to perform a maintenance safety assessment to encompass fuse replacement in the 
Power Conditioning Box, and other nominal equipment changeouts. A maintenance safety assessment 
has been completed and is included as an attachment to unique Hazard Report U-7. 
3.2 The PO agreed to note that the hardware transfer case latches are not safety-critical, since the case 
will be soft stowed and packed in foam.  This information is now included in section 4.2.1. 
3.3 The PO agreed to provide more information and pictures, along with a safety assessment, for the 
valve handle tie-wrap. Figure 10 b shows the valve handle tie-wrap constraint as well as figures 
attached to the Hazard Report SPICE U-3. An assessment of the restraint is covered in paragraph 
4.3.6.1.  
3.4 The PO agreed to confirm that there would still be airflow if the Control Box Assembly fan setting 
were set to zero. The airflow is wired to be on whenever the experiment is powered. Also the 
procedures require the crew to confirm the air flow by reading the measured air flow value off the 
laptop. See hazard report U-5. 
3.5 The PO agreed to attach a shatterable materials matrix to the 1230 hazard reporting form.   This has 
been attached to the 1230 form. 
 
3.6 The PSEs agreed to provide a shatterable materials matrix example to the PO. This was provided 
by Daniel Porter and was used to generate the matrix for SPICE. 
 
3.7 The PO agreed to determine if they could use a flow straightener made of non-frangible materials.  
This was investigated. Substitute materials did not have the same properties and replacement of 
this item would be difficult. It would also cause the acceptance vibration test to be voided. See 
controls provided in the 1230 form section 5.  
 
3.8 The PO agreed to send correspondence from Nikon to the PSEs and coordinate with the PSEs to set 
up a working group meeting to discuss COTS battery systems and schematics with EP5. This has been 
initiated (there have been a few interactions with Nikon)  Removal of the battery from the camera 
before flight will be done.  The SPICE Project has determined that the removal of the battery 
reduces the reliability of the Camera and is seeking to keep the battery in place for flight.  
 
3.9 The PO agreed to provide the EMI waiver and all bonding, grounding, power, and wire sizing 
schematics as attachments to the 1230 hazard reporting form at Phase II. These items have been added 
to the end of the 1230 form. 
 
3.10 MSFC/FD31/T. Smith agreed to provide to the PO input from ECLSS concerning the effects of 
unburned fuels and combustion byproducts on the air scrubbers of Shuttle and ISS. Tim Smith 
provided this information and its conclusion has been included in 4.3.6.1 of the SDP.  
 
3.11 The PSEs agreed to compare SPICE to its predecessor, ELF, and other similar payloads to see how 
similar hazards were handled previously and how it may apply to SPICE. This was provided by John 
Fonner.

May 2008 
52 
3.12 The PO agreed to provide better rationale on the projectile assessment for the pressurized bottle 
assemblies. This analysis has been updated and attached to the hazard report U-3.  
 
3.13 The PO agreed to develop a unique hazard report to address fuel leakage in the bottle stowage 
cases and the MPLM:  SPICE-U4, Fire and Detonation in MPLM and ISS Stowage. The hazard report 
has been updated to include controls reflecting the concerns raised from the 0/1 review on fuel 
leakage in the bottle stowage cases stowed both in MPLM and ISS.  
 
3.14 The PO agreed to develop a unique hazard report to address premature/inadvertent fuel ignition, as 
well as failure to ignite fuel:  SPICE-U5, Fire and Detonation in MSG. The hazard report has been 
updated to include controls reflecting the concerns raised from the 0/1 review.  
 
3.15 The PO agreed to develop a unique hazard report for Touch Temperature, providing a wait time for 
cool-down of the burner tube prior to changeout:  SPICE-U6, Touch Temperature.  This hazard report 
has been created and added to the unique hazard reports. A wait time has been added.  
 
Post Phase 0/1Comments  
 
Create operational hazard controls matrix for Phase II per the 13830 requirements.  Many operational 
controls were identified in the hazard reports, but they will need to be listed individually in a hazard 
control matrix as well. Table 5 has been updated to include this information.  
 
Sequentially number the pages of your HR attachments for Phase II, especially the 1230 attachments.  
Hand-written numbers are fine. Page numbering has been done using Adobe on the finished 
converted file.  
 
At Phase II please provide the following:  
1. Updated information on the progress/success of removing the battery from the Nikon D100 camera. 
The battery was removed from an engineering camera and as a result the camera does not 
function properly.  The battery is now planned to remain in the camera. 
2. Value of Vcc depicted in the schematic for the Horita Titler. Power to Vcc is supplied by a 
regulator U6 (lower middle of schematic) which is an LM7805. This is a 5Volt regulator.  
3. If the I-Button reader is not to be used on-orbit, there are no other power sources that can charge the 
battery.  If the reader is to be used, information on the "Parasite Power" voltage and current protection 
for the cell will be required. Information was added to the STD SPICE 01 hazard report 
information with the rest of the battery information.  
 
As noted at the Phase 0/1 review, please do not state “adequate instructions.”  At Phase II add the 
appropriate details that are required to be in the procedures to Hazard Control 6.1.  This will make it 
clear to the PSRP what you will verify and easier on you to complete your verifications. Have added 
details to SPICE-U2 hazard control 6.1 and hazard control.

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE 
 
 
 
 
 SPICE-SDP-003 
May 2008 
53 
Phase II Agreements 
 
MINUTES FOR SMOKE POINT IN CO-FLOW EXPERIMENT PHASE II FLIGHT SAFETY REVIEW ON 
JANUARY 27,  
 
NASA JSC 
Payload Safety Review Panel 
Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment 
Phase II Flight Safety Review 
 
Minutes of Meeting 
January 27, 2005 
  
1.0 INTRODUCTION 
1.1 General:  The Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP), chaired by JSC/NA3/S. Wolf, met on January, 
2005, with representatives of GRC, the Payload Organization (PO), and MSFC at the Regents Park III 
Conference Facility for a Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Phase II Flight Safety Review 
(FSR). JSC/NC44/J. Fonner and M. Highsmith, the supporting Payload Safety Engineers (PSEs), 
introduced the meeting and attendees (see Attachment 1).   
1.2 Background: The Phase 0/I FSR was held March 3, 2004.  
1.3 Scope: This meeting focused on the Phase II FSR. The PSRP assigned no previous Action Items 
(AIs) to this payload. The PO also summarized the Phase 0/I agreement disposition.   
1.4 Conclusion: One agreement and one action item resulted from this meeting (see Attachment 2). All 
nine Hazard Reports (HRs) were signed and approved for Phase II. This meeting completed the Phase II 
FSR.  
 
2.0 SIGNIFICANT SAFETY DISCUSSION  
2.1 SPICE Science and Hardware Overview: SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena to 
understand the mechanisms controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. SPICE will 
stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and 
numerical predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to 
verify flame structure predictions. The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar 
smokepoint properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet 
diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame 
shapes under co-flow conditions. The soot point is a simple measurement that has been found useful to 
study the influence of flow and fuel properties on the sooting propensity of flames. This information 
would help support current understanding of soot processes in laminar flames and by analogy in 
turbulent flames of practical interest. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of 
buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity (ng) are well known, corresponding information for 
nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus, the measurements of the laminar smoke-point 
properties proposed here would also reduce the risk of future experiments involving hydrocarbon-fueled 
laminar jet diffusion flames in spacecraft.  
2.2 SPICE Hardware Overview: Hardware soft stowed in during launch and landing includes:

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE 
 
 
 
 
 SPICE-SDP-003 
May 2008 
54 
• Experiment Assembly: Chamber for combustion, Hot-Wire Igniter Arm, Window, Flow 
Straightener, Heat Sink/Filter, Fuel Delivery System, Nozzle, Fan, Data Logger, Radiometer. 
• Fuel Bottle Assembly: Commercial DOT bottle with Diaphragm Valve, SS tubing, QC fitting. 
• Controller Box: External to MSG, controls: radiometer, Data Recording, Fuel Enable, Ignitor 
Enable, Fuel Flow set point, Fan Flow set point and camera shutter. 
• Image Acquisition Nikon Digital still camera and a Panasonic WV-CP 654 Video Camera 
System 
• Power-Video Unit: Video Titler and Power Conditioning Assemblies. 
• Cables: Power Cable Assembly, Video Cable Assembly, Still Camera Cable Assembly, and Feed 
Through Cable Assembly. 
• Video Tapes: 30 Digital Video tapes. 
• Data Storage: 6 IBM micro drives 1 GB. 
The PO indicated that the radiometer measures the temperatures of the flames. 
2.3 Integration and Operations: The PO indicated that the fan will operate for chamber cooling on-
orbit. The crew can verify that the igniter is on prior to turning on the gas. The PO anticipates 10-14 
hours total operational time for the experiment with a set-up time of 45-60 minutes. Each experiment 
run lasts just a few minutes. The PO is hoping for use of the hardware and the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) for several hours at a time. The PO clarified that the fuel nozzle changeout is manual. 
The crew procedure hazards are listed in a table.  
2.4 Safety Assessment:  
2.4.1 Form 1428, Fire Detection and Suppression Reporting Form: Approved as discussed in the 
meeting.  
2.4.2 Form 622 - Reflown and Series Payload Hardware Reflight Assessment Reporting Sheet: Not 
applicable to this payload.  
2.5 Hazard Report Discussion: The PO provides crew procedure inputs to the Payload Operations Data 
File (PODF) at MSFC.  
2.5.1 Form 1230, Flight Payload Standardized Hazard Control Report: Approved as modified in this 
meeting. The MSG integrated/series assessment will appear at Phase III. The PO indicated that the 
controller box is velcroed in place inside the MSG and that there are no crew entanglement concerns 
with the cables associated with the hardware package. Associated with Shatterable Material Release, the 
PO indicated that the flow straightener is made of Cordierite (a ceramic) and is contained inside the fan 
housing on the Experiment Assembly (EA) with a 100 mesh screen over it. The EA will be packaged in 
a clear plastic bag and will be inspected for particles before use. Any particles that escape the EA mesh 
should be captured by the MSG filter and the MSG HEPA filter. The PO clarified that the minor 
electromagnetic exceedences affect the cameras, but this is a performance issue, not a safety issue. The 
PSRP recommended that the PO match the voltage rating of the fan with the power supply to the fan 
(12V supply).  
2.5.2 SPICE-U1, Contamination of Orbiter/ISS Habitable Areas by SPICE Unburned Fuels or 
Combustion By-Products Results in Injury/Illness: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO stated 
that the by-products consist of carbon dioxide and water, both scrubbed by the MSG filters. The 
Hazardous Materials Summary Table (HMST) is attached and under review. The PO analyzed the 
amounts, kinds, and release rates of the fuel bottle contents and determined that the contamination

May 2008 
55 
hazards are reasonably benign in this payload. The PO also stated that each bottle is individually proof 
tested.  
2.5.3 SPICE-U2, Pressure System Rupture: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO indicated that 
each gas bottle has been leak tested and filled to an appropriate pressure corresponding to the fuel 
mixtures. The PO keeps a pressure vessel log on each bottle. The QC caps will be installed during 
stowage and transit to MSG.  
2.5.4 SPICE-U3, Projectile Hazard Gas Bottle: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO deleted 
hazard cause 2 and controls 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4 as a result of the discussion.  
2.5.5 SPICE-U4, Fire and Detonation in MPLM and ISS Stowage: Approved as modified in this meeting. 
Crew procedures have the crew marking spent bottles to prevent the crew from grabbing an empty gas 
bottle for installation. The PO described the aluminum strip inside the bottle case that is the bonding 
strap to preclude electrostatic discharge inside the bottle case: the aluminum strip is stuck to the interior 
of the top of the case in such a way that it touches the metal of the bottles when the case is closed. The 
PO indicated that any labels on the bottles will be positioned to assure the metal-to-metal contact 
between the bottles and the grounding strip. Discussion of the temporary aisle stowage of the bottle case 
led the PSRP to assign AI 1 to the PO to determine if the Station-supplied fuel stowage location 
complies with the SPICE flammability assessment restrictions. The PO will provide more details at 
Phase III.  
2.5.6 SPICE-U5, Fire in MSG: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PSRP recommended that the 
PO delete the 14,242 foot pounds reference in favor of the estimates in the table as the limits of released 
energy from the gas bottles. The pressure release exceeds the MSG interface control document limit, 
which makes this a catastrophic hazard rather than the usual critical designation.  
2.5.7 SPICE-U6, Touch Temperature Injury: Approved as modified in this meeting.  
2.5.8 SPICE-U7, Maintenance Assessment Hazard Controls: Approved as modified in this meeting.  
2.5.9 SPICE-U8, Flame Impingement During Crew Access: Approved as modified in this meeting. The 
PO clarified that the igniter cools down within less than 30 seconds. The PO has not seen the nozzles 
work loose due to gas flow –a matter of running torque versus seating torque—and indicated that gas 
flow pressure is not high enough to cause a problem. The PO has four inhibits on fuel flow and three 
inhibits on ignition. The PO agreed to provide a logic diagram depicting all of the inhibits that prevent 
fuel ignition at Phase III (Agreement 3.1).  
 
3.0  AGREEMENTS 
3.1 The PO agreed to provide a logic diagram depicting all of the inhibits that prevent fuel ignition at 
Phase III.

5.     Shatterable Material Release 
 
a) 
All materials are contained.  
 
b) 
Optical glass (i.e. lenses, filters, etc.)  components 
of crew cabin experiment hardware that are non-
stressed (no delta pressure) and have passed both 
a vibration test at flight levels and a post-test visual 
inspection. 
 
c) 
Payload bay hardware shatterable material 
components that weigh less than 0.25 lb and are 
non-stressed (no delta pressure) or non-structural. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5a.1  Analysis.    ZIN Tech Engineering will ensure that SPICE design provides for 
containment of all shatterable materials (see list below) and prepare a report confirming 
design requirements have been met.   
Status – Closed 08/07/03. 60054-ANA-026, Containment of Shatterable Materials 
Analysis. 
 
5a.2  Inspection.   ZIN Tech Quality will verify that the as-built flight hardware conforms to 
the approved drawings and record results in an inspection report.   
Status – Closed 03/01/07. SPICE-INS-020-R1, As-Built Inspection Report 
 
5a.3  Inspection.    ZIN Tech Engineering will review crew procedure inputs to ensure that 
checks of containment and assessment of status prior to utilizing frangible hardware are 
included, and prepare a report confirming inclusion in the crew procedure inputs.   
Status - Closed to VTL. 
 
5b.1  Test.    ZIN Tech Engineering will arrange for SPICE flight hardware to undergo 
acceptance vibration testing and prepare a test report confirming test was successfully 
completed and passed inspection for no breakage.  Note even though this control is for 
Optics, the flow straightener has been tested, see list of all items in table B-2.  
Status - Closed to 02/07/07. SPICE-TST-007-R1.  Stowed Vibration Test Report 
 
See shatterable materials table, table B-2. 
 
6.      Flammable Materials 
a) 
A-rated materials selected from MAPTIS, or 
 
b) 
Flammability assessment per NSTS 22648 
 
 
 
 
6ab.1  Analysis.   ZIN Tech Quality will compile a MIUL that records materials specified in 
approved design documents, evaluate the materials identified per NSTS 1700.7B / ISS 
Addendum requirements and current MAPTIS material ratings, and generate MUAs to 
substantiate usage of all non-A-rated materials.  Any required flammability assessment 
per NSTS 22648 will be included in usage rationale of the MUAs.   
Status – Closed to VTL. 
 
6ab.2  Analysis.   NASA/GRC SMAD reviews the MIUL and MUAs and when approved 
provides a material certification memorandum in accordance with intercenter agreements.   
Status - Closed to VTL. 
 
 
7.      Materials Offgassing 
Offgassing tests of assembled article per  NASA-
STD-6001 (previously published as NHB 8060.1C). 
 
7a.1  Test .    ZIN Tech Engineering will arrange offgas testing in accordance with NASA-
STD-6001, Test 7 and prepares a report.   
Status – Closed 2/09/07. SPICE-RPT-001.  Toxic Off-gas Test Report 
 
7a.2  Analysis.  NASA/GRC SMAD reviews offgas test report and when approved provides 
material certification memorandum in accordance with intercenter agreements.   
Status – Closed to VTL.

a)

protection requirements of Letter TA-92-038. 
 
b) 
Station-powered payloads – Meets station interface 
circuit protection requirements of SSP 57000 and 
payload circuit protection requirements of Letter 
TA-92-038. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
11b.1  Analysis .    ZIN Tech Engineering will perform an analysis of the SPICE design to 
verify proper wire sizing for circuit protection provided by MSG and prepare a report 
confirming design requirements have been met.  
 Status – Closed 6/3/03. Report 60054-ANA-017, SPICE Wire Derating Analysis

bonding and grounding methodology for compliance with SSP 30245 and SSP 30240.

content:
SPICE-MEM-010 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 1 of 2 
 
Memorandum SPICE-MEM-010 
 
 
 
 
 
TO: 
 
Tibor Lorik, SPICE Project Lead, ZIN Technologies, Inc. 
 
FROM: 
Kevin Magee, Project Engineer, ZIN Technologies, Inc. 
 
SUBJECT: 
SPICE Flow Duct Velocity Measurements 
 
DATE:  
July 6, 2009 
______________________________________________________________ 
 
This Memo addresses the SPICE flow duct velocity measurements, which were performed by Kevin 
Magee on the flight hardware from June 16-24, 2008.  A hot wire anemometer probe was used to 
measure the air velocity at various points within the flow duct.  This probe was passed into the duct 
through a special multi-piece top window with probe ports at the desired locations.  Unused ports were 
taped shut on the inside and outside to prevent leakage and minimize flow disturbances.  The window 
itself was assembled and sealed with Kapton tape around its perimeter. 
 
The probe used was a TSI, Inc., Model 1261A miniature boundary layer probe (S/N# 012077) with a 
T1.5 (coated tungsten platinum) wire and a 56 ohm control resistor to give a 260oC operating 
temperature.  Its calibration was performed in a free jet facility on April 28, 2006. 
 
Measurements were taken at two axial stations of 13 and 56 mm as measured by the permanent scale 
bonded to the floor of the duct.  These locations are where the tip of the probe was located, not where 
the ports were located since the probe curves forward into the air flow.  At each axial station, 
measurements were taken at three width locations: the duct centerline, 20 mm off the centerline 
towards the back wall (called the “inside” position), and 20 mm off the centerline towards the front 
window (called the “outside” position).  At each width position, measurements were taken at three 
heights: 19, 36, and 57 mm off the floor of the duct.  It should be noted that the 36 mm height 
corresponds to the height of the nozzle, which was installed for the tests.  However, no flow out of the 
nozzle was done during the tests.  All locations are shown in Figure 1. 
 
At each measured position, the anemometer probe’s velocity readings were recorded for FAN dial 
settings of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10.  The FAN and AIR readings were also noted.  Plots were then created 
to compare the probe velocity, AIR reading, and FAN reading for the different FAN dial settings.  
Velocity profile plots were also generated at the various axial stations in both width and height.  These 
plots and the raw data can be found in the spreadsheets at the following location. 
 
(Z:) Zindata1\zinapp\Shares\MRDOC\60107_086_SPP\SPICE\Duct Flow Data

1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The purpose of this document is to identify the science requirements for the SPICE Experiment 
manifested to fly on the ISS.  The science requirements are traced to the Science Requirements 
Document. 
 
2.0 
VERIFICATION CLOSURE RECORD 
 
Appendix A contains each Science Verification Sheet, which identifies the science requirement, 
verification method, and verification closure summary.  The verification summary identifies the 
SPICE project document that addresses the verification closure.  All SPICE project documents 
are under configuration control and available upon request.  This document will be updated 
periodically to reflect the closure status of the verifications. 
 
3.0 
CURRENT VERIFICATION STATUS 
 
There are 18 verification requirements.  All requirements have been closed.  One verification, 
Radiometer accuracy is not compliant.

The Co-Flow Velocity shall be measured with an accuracy of 10% of the 
reading, at a sampling rate of 4 Hz, and over a range of 5 – 50 cm/s. 
 
IMPLEMENTATION 
The Oxidizer Velocity and Co-Flow Velocity are the same measurement and 
they will be measured by an Air Velocity Transducer made by TSI with Model 
number 8475.  The output is routed to an amplifier for scaling with the output 
monitored by the A/D Converter on the Tattletale board.   
 
VERIFICATION 
VERIFICATION METHOD:  INS 
Verify that the Velocity Probe is capable of supporting the required range and 
accuracy. 
 
If time permits the probe will be calibrated. 
 
VERIFICATION STATUS: CLOSED - COMPLIANT 
The specification sheet for the Velocity Probe states that the velocity range is 
from 0.05 to 2.54 m/s (5 -254 cm/s) which is within the range of 5 – 50 cm/s 
required. 
The fact that the fan is always on limits the lower range that the Velocity Probe 
reaches.  The measurement displayed on the video monitor and in the data 
ranges from 15 to 53 CFM for minimum fan velocity to maximum fan velocity. 
The accuracy is stated to be ±3% of the reading ±1% of the selected range.  This 
is within the required accuracy. 
Inspection of the data acquired and stored in the Experiment Assembly shows 
that 4 samples per second are acquired.

content:
1
Executive Summary
This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke
aerosol relative to smoke on Earth.
We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with
the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle
interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is
expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain,
convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con-
ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity,
buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling re-
moves large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼40 µm and the mode
particle size to ∼5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmet-
ric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity
when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large
particles (> 20 µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and
smaller particles (< 10 µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large
particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature re-
circulation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle
diameter in microgravity is ∼10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that
future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot,
recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The
ﬁnal document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.
UTILIZATION OF THE SAME DATA FOR ADVANCED MODELING AND SIMULATION OF SMOKE GENERATION IN
MICROGRAVITY
3
SEAN C. GARRICK

2
Introduction
Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convec-
tion modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles,
condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the
aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles
with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high
temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems
(Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity
smoke particles to be 2 −8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the Interna-
tional Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may
not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al.,
2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke
growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated
sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The
intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and
to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two cross-
ﬂow velocities of sufﬁciently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.
Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis,
particle settling, and ﬂow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and
modeling methodology, followed by a description of the ﬂow geometry and the parameter space under
consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower
of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar ﬁelds as a means to describe
particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the
hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle ﬁelds interact with the ﬂuid
dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, ﬂow
geometry, and the higher ﬂow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize ﬁndings
relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.
UTILIZATION OF THE SAME DATA FOR ADVANCED MODELING AND SIMULATION OF SMOKE GENERATION IN
MICROGRAVITY

4
Results
4.1
FLOW CONFIGURATION
We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels
DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experi-
ments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is
shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sam-
ple. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected
downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation
to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling
is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments).
4.2
PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
Constant ﬂuid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are
provided in Table 2.
The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is
deﬁned for DBP as cnuc = 3.2 × 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000).
The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale, Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated
in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K. We consider two
inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster
ﬂow of Uo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces
(Twall = To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a ﬁxed temperature of Ts = 473.2 K, and releases
DBP vapor at a constant mass ﬂux of q′′ = 8.4 × 10−5 kg/m2 · s. The mass ﬂux has been selected to be
representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions
are imposed for all species and particle ﬁelds at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is
considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.
The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying
Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two ﬂow speeds and
gravitational levels is given in Table 3. The ﬂags “EG” and “MG” identify the “Earth gravity” and “micro-
gravity” conditions, while 1 and 2 identify the Uo = 0.08 m/s and Uo = 0.1 m/s conditions, respectively.
Case 1MG is therefore deﬁned to have an inlet velocity of Uo = 0.08 m/s and go = 0 m/s2, corre-
sponding to a Reynolds number Re = 22.3 and a Froude number Fr = ∞. In addition to the four base
cases listed in Table 3, we examine the aerosol development sensitivity to: (1) particle settling, (2) ther-
mophoresis, and (3) the ﬂow geometry. For this purpose, a series of additional cases, deﬁned in Table
3, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. Case 1EG-NS (where NS
stands for “no settling”) is identical to Case 1EG, but the settling mechanism has been neglected. Case
1MG-NT (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”) is identical to Case 1MG, but the thermophoresis
transport mechanism has been neglected. Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R (where R stands for “rotated”) are
identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. In all cases,
data is collected and presented at a time of t = 7 seconds.
4.3
NUMERICAL SPECIFICATIONS
The domain is non-uniformly discretized by 960 grid points in the x direction and 240 grid point in
the y direction. The governing equations are solved on this computational mesh with a second-order
MacCormack scheme. The particle size space is discretized by 45 particle nodes, with the volume of
each successive node increased by a factor of 2.25, i.e. vk = 2.25 × vk−1. The volume of the ﬁrst node
is selected to be the volume of a DBP molecule, v1 = vm = 4.44 × 10−28 m3. Boundary conditions are

implemented by considering the characteristic relations for the Euler equations accounting for gravity
(Poinsot and Lele, 1992). The computational tool used for this work has been well-validated and used
for prior studies of aerosols (Garrick, 2011, 2015, Garrick and Khakpour, 2004, Garrick et al., 2001,
Khakpour and Garrick, 2003, Modem and Garrick, 2003).
4.4
PHYSICAL ASSUMPTIONS
All assumptions utilized in this work are listed below.
• From the perspective of thermal conductivity and viscosity, the condensing vapor phase is con-
sidered sufﬁciently dilute such that µ and k are computed for air as a function of temperature and
density (Kadoya et al., 1985). Both the air and the condensing vapor are considered calorically
perfect gases with constant properties deﬁned in Table 1.
• The Mach number M is only important for ﬂows with M ≳0.3. Although the physics are insen-
sitive to variation in Mach number when the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to
convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often
remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large
density variations. Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the
number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales. We instead use a scaled dynamic
pressure as the reference pressure Po = ρo (c1Uo)2, such that P ⋆= ραRαT
Po
, where c1 is speciﬁed
to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s. The ﬂow ﬁeld was found to be independent of c1
for the values used.
• All particles are assumed to be spherical.
• Condensed phase DBP properties are deﬁned by their continuum values.
• There is no momentum exchange between the particles and the ﬂuid (the air/DBP vapor mixture);
the particle velocity equals the ﬂuid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the
stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the
domain (including the large particles).
• The ﬂuid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature.
• Particle diffusion coefﬁcients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge
due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors. For this reason, the mini-
mum diffusion coefﬁcient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds
to the ﬁfth particle size node – any node greater than the ﬁfth node is assigned the particle diffu-
sion coefﬁcient of the ﬁfth node.
• The mass ﬂux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially
uniform temperature.
• Particles that impact a solid surface “stick” with 100% efﬁciency, and are removed from the ﬂow.
• The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly)
in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation
is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous intro-
duction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal ﬁelds, conversely, become steady
after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features
develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic ﬁelds. We therefore present all
results at time t = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state. At his time, all
ﬁelds are either steady, or changing at a rate that does not affect the conclusions drawn from the
simulations.

4.5
FLUID FLOW, TEMPERATURE, AND MASS FRACTION
The velocity ﬁeld controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles.
Vorticity ω, deﬁned as the curl of the velocity vector
ω = ∇× u,
(31)
is positive in regions of the ﬂow where ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise, and is negative in regions where
the ﬂuid rotates clockwise. The sign and magnitude of vorticity therefore identiﬁes the location, orienta-
tion, and intensity of vortices and boundary layers.
Figure 2 shows the steady dimensionless vorticity. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows
Case 1EG. The grey rectangles represent the heated vapor source. Red ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise
(positive vorticity) and blue ﬂuid rotates clockwise (negative vorticity). Immediately upon entering the
channel, the ﬂuid at the walls is brought to rest by the no slip condition, signiﬁed by the large vorticity
gradients in the upper and lower left corners of panels (a) and (b). As the ﬂuid travels downstream
from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous
diffusion. Further downstream, the heated rectangle reduces the cross-sectional ﬂow area, and the
pressure ﬁeld accelerates the ﬂuid through ﬂow paths above and below the heated vapor source. The
microgravity case in panel (a) remains symmetric near the heated vapor source, whereas the Earth
gravity case in panel (b) develops an asymmetry with the majority of ﬂuid passing below the heated
vapor source (indicated by larger vorticity magnitudes below than above). Comparatively low vorticity
values on the downstream side of the rectangles indicate the presence of low speed, recirculating
wakes. The microgravity wake in panel (a) is symmetric, whereas the Earth gravity wake in panel (b) is
asymmetric. As the ﬂuid continues to ﬂow downstream, the boundary layers thicken in both cases and
the ﬂuid exits the domain to the right. Variations in density due to heat transfer from the rectangle have
inﬂuenced the vorticity ﬁelds via baroclinic torque and buoyancy. Because there is no gravity in Case
1MG in panel (a), density variations due to heating do not disturb the symmetry of the ﬂow ﬁeld. The
asymmetry apparent in panel (b) is due to buoyancy effects.
Temperature ﬁelds with overlaid velocity vectors are shown in Fig. 3 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a)
shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG. The downstream portion of the domain has been
expanded for clarity. Velocity vectors in panel (a) show a symmetric wake proﬁle with two counter-
rotating vortices surrounded by dividing streamlines. Panel (b) shows an asymmetric buoyant wake,
also with two counter rotating vortices: one near the lower right corner of the heated vapor source, and
another near the upper right corner of the heated vapor source. Both panels show hot ﬂuid in white,
warm ﬂuid in red, and room temperature ﬂuid in black. Thermal energy diffuses from the heated vapor
source to the adjacent ﬂuid. Hot ﬂuid convects energy downstream and cools while diffusing energy
to cooler ﬂuid and the isothermal upper and lower walls. The highest temperatures appear near the
heated surface and in the wake. In both cases, the gas in the center of the channel exits the domain
at greater than 350 Kelvin. The microgravity case maintains a symmetric temperature ﬁeld because
there is no gravity, and therefore no asymmetric coupling between the vorticity and temperature via
buoyancy. In panel (b), buoyant convection resulting from gravitational forces caries the low density, hot
ﬂuid towards the upper surface. As the hot ﬂuid encounters the isothermal upper surface, a thin thermal
boundary layer develops. Hot ﬂuid cools rapidly when in close proximity to the upper surface due to the
thin thermal boundary layer.
DBP vapor mass fraction is shown in Fig. 4 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and
panel (b) shows Case 1EG. Consistent with the vorticity and temperature, the DBP vapor mass fraction
is symmetric in Case 1MG and asymmetric in Case 1EG. The highest mass fractions of DBP (approx-
imately 0.05) appear in white on the immediate downstream side of the heated vapor source in both
panels (a) and (b). The recirculating wakes in both cases contain a small concentration of DBP vapor,
but are encompassed by streaks of DBP vapor issuing from the upper and lower surfaces of the heated
vapor source. In Case 1MG, the DBP vapor streaks interact via diffusion at the downstream side of the
wake and eventually merge. In Case 1EG, merging velocity characteristics, indicated by the merging
velocity vectors at the downstream side of the wake, rapidly combine the upper and lower vapor streaks.
In both Case 1MG and Case 1EG, the majority of the vapor is consumed before the domain outlet.

PARTICLE NUCLEATION, NUMBER DENSITY, AND SIZE
The particle nucleation rate is a function of vapor mass fraction and temperature (and pressure). Figure
5 shows the DBP nucleation rate at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1EG in

Figure 8 shows the particle number densities for Cases 1MG and 1EG at downstream measurement
plane x′ = 26 at time t = 7 seconds. Case 1MG is shown in red and Case 1EG is shown in black.
The Case 1MG distribution contains particle diameters ranging from hundreds of nanometers to tens
of micrometers, with a small percentage of particles approaching one hundred micrometers. The most
frequent size is approximately 5 µm. The Case 1MG distribution contains two local maximums: one at
5 µm and another at 30 µm. The Case 1EG distribution contains only one local maximum at 5 µm. Case
1EG contains a larger number density than Case 1MG for all particle sizes < 20 µm, and Case 1EG
contains no particles > 40 µm – these large particle settle out of the system. Case 1EG contains orders
of magnitude more particles < 5 µm than Case 1MG.
4.7
EFFECT OF PARTICLE SETTLING
In order to isolate the effects of particle settling, we modify Case 1EG by neglecting the settling mecha-
nism (by setting uss⋆
j,k = 0). This case is referred to as Case 1EG–NS, where NS stands for “no settling”.
Figure 9 compares size distributions for Case 1MG, Case 1EG, and Case 1EG–NS at measurement
plane x′ = 26 at time t = 7 seconds. The Case 1EG–NS distribution is considerably wider than the other
cases. It contains particles ranging in size from nanometers to 100 µm. Case 1EG–NS also contains
two local maxima in the particle size distribution, much like Case 1MG and unlike Case 1EG. Eliminating
the settling mechanism has expanded the size distribution to include both smaller and larger particles,
and has also introduced a new local maximum in the size distribution near 35 µm.
4.8
EFFECT OF THERMOPHORESIS
Figure 10 shows particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case
1MG-NT in panel (b) (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”). When thermophoresis is active, as in
panel (a), particles do not appear adjacent to the surface of the heated vapor source; the temperature
gradient is large normal to the surface, and thermophoresis forces the particles out of this region.
When thermophoresis is inactive, particles are able to remain near the hot surface. In this region, the
temperature is sufﬁciently high to cause evaporation. Small particles are able to diffuse out of the wake,
resulting in lower particle number densities inside the Case 1MG-NT wake than the Case 1MG wake.
Downstream of the wake, larger particle number densities are present in Case 1MG-NT relative to Case
1MG, following from the decreased number of particles trapped in the Case 1MG-NT wake vorticies.
Figure 11 shows particle size distributions for Cases 1MG and 1MG-NT at time t = 7 seconds. Consis-
tent with Fig. 10, the peak number density in Case 1MG-NT is greater than Case 1MG by approximately
a factor of ﬁve – the most frequent particle size is ∼5 µm for both cases. A local maximum appears in
both distributions around dp = 30 µm. This local maximum contains fewer particles in Case 1MG-NT
than in Case 1MG, potentially because this local maximum is comprised of particles that have inter-
acted with the wake region. In Case 1MG-NT, some of these particles have undergone evaporation and
shifted to smaller particle sizes.
4.9
EFFECT OF HEATED VAPOR SOURCE ORIENTATION
Figure 12 shows the particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG-R in panel (a)
and Case 1EG-R in panel (b) (where R stands for “Rotated”). Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are identical
to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. The wake regions
of Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R are considerably smaller than Cases 1MG and 1EG, and neither Case
1MG-R nor Case 1EG-R contain particles in their wakes. The results from Case 1MG-R differ from
Case 1MG in that they do not prominently display two high particle number density streaks around the
symmetry line, but instead contain large particle number densities everywhere near the symmetry plane.
Case 1EG-R presents large particle number densities near the cool upper surface, similar to Case 1EG.
Unlike Case 1EG, Case 1EG-R does not contain particles inside its comparatively small downstream
wake region, but instead contains particles in a large recirculation region that appears above the heated
vapor source. The number density of particles in the recirculation region directly above the heated
vapor source is lower than the particle number density downstream of the recirculation region. Settling
