Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure.  Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion 
systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a 
much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of 
characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  
The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many 
microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames 
advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  
For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low 
concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for 
evaluating the minor species chemistry.  With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to 
new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational 
environment of the combustion application. 
 
 
VI.  Methods/Research Operations 
B. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, 
by the ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set 
of tests.  The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  No CFI-G tests were 
conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception 
of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature 
has reached a critical value. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
38 
 
 
VII.  Results 
G. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 280 hot flames were ignited (or in some cases naturally reignited) for the CFI-G 
experiment during Increments 64-66, where 33, 225, and 22 flames were ignited in the 
three increments, respectively.  Testing began near the end of Increment 64 and the final 
test day was conducted at the start of Increment 66.  Cool flame evidence was seen in 
some tests and 15 cool flames, listed and discussed later, have been identified thus far. 
 
The CFI-G experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment.  The 
tests were instead conducted burning various gaseous fuels, including ethane (C2H6), 
propane (C3H8), and n-butane (n-C4H10).  These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which 
the hot flame chemistry is reasonably well understood, but where there is much 
remaining to be learned about the cool flame chemistry. 
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for CFI-G; all of the investigation’s data was 
electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all current 
ACME experiments. 
 
Summary logs of the flames ignited for CFI-G for the two rounds of testing are found in 
Tables 1 and 2.   The first round of testing featured normal flames in which the fuel flowed 
from the burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere.   In contrast, the second round was 
largely conducted with inverse-flame tests in which an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed 
from the burner into a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel.  The round two exception 
was the final test day (at the start of Increment 66) which was again conducted in the 
normal-flames mode.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
41 
 
 
H. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
3. Mission anomalies  
On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record 
the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU-G, also 
known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working.  Only the first two 
tests on that day were successful, where two tests aborted due to an IPSU error, and 
three tests failed to ignite.  In closing checkout, it was determined that the hot-wire 
igniter tip had also failed.  With the IPSU-G failure, the test day was nearly a total loss.  
Except for a small number of sample images downloaded during the midst of testing, 
the primary image data from even the successful tests was lost.   Furthermore, there 
was no more propane available for use in inverse-flame testing, so the test day could 
not be repeated.  However, astronaut Mark Vande Hei replaced the failed igniter tip 
on Sept. 8 and the failed hard drive in the IPSU-G on Sept. 10, and CFI-G testing 
successfully resumed on Sept.  13, just 2 weeks after the double failure.  
 
Looking back to Increment 64, the Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU1) used 
with the High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and the opposed CIR 
illumination package ceased functioning on March 29 (GMT 088).  Tests 21088M1-M3 
aborted due to an error with IPSU1 communication, where test M4 was successful 
when the test was run without use of the HiBMs camera.   The troublesome IPSU1 
was replaced by astronaut Megan McArthur on May 18 (GMT 138), but it was not 
available during the intervening test days.  However, this wasn’t particularly a loss to 
CFI-G because that camera, with its red filter, is only sensitive to the red backlight 
from the CIR illumination package and visible thermal radiation, e.g., from glowing 
soot particles.   Furthermore, the illumination could make it more difficult to discern 
cool flames, so the HiBMs camera, illumination package, and IPSU1 were rarely used 
for CFI-G.  The principal exception was during the second round of testing.  With the 
inverse-flame tests, the soot is generated outside of the flames, so this photography 
was used to track potential soot deposition on the chamber windows, etc.   However, 
the end-of-day imaging did not appear to change over time, suggesting that the soot 
was not an issue for the chamber windows.  However, the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) 
modules and radiometers were closer to the flame than the windows and might had 
been adversely affected by soot. 
 
4. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their 
presence.  Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-
premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can 
occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames.  Tests intended to directly 
ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames.  Meanwhile, 
evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the 
testing.  During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after

21 November 2022 
42 
 
 
hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly 
shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion. 
 
In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated 
hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low-
temperature combustion.    It is likely that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 
cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition.  The exposed type-B 
thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons.  The 
catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the low-
temperature combustion in these tests. 
 
A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI 
intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, 
while the intensifier gain is set high. 
 
When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow 
Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., 
where actual flow rate differed from that desired. 
 
Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce 
spherically symmetric flames.  While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the 
flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center.  More specifically, 
the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of 
the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical 
burner.  In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric.  At 
sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can 
appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape.  In the latter case, the flame locally 
quenches near the supply tube. 
 
During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that 
the lowest of the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry 
(TFP) fiber array had broken.  Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 
2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array.  Unfortunately, the 
next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 
5 mm apart.  Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also had months of 
remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers 
(instead of 5) for the final BRE testing and the subsequent CLD Flame and CFI-G tests.  
This was a minor loss, where the fiber array was only occasionally used in CFI-G 
testing.

content:
ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
43 
 
 
I. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The experiment’s proposal to CASIS and NSF stated: 
“It is assumed here that approximately 50 ISS flames can be conducted.  
These will include approximately 12 chamber fills following evacuation.” 
Far more testing was carried out for this experiment, where that included the ignition of  
280 hot flames in 23 days of ISS testing, some of which included multiple chamber fills.  
Although some of the flames were short lived, the testing far exceeded the quantity that 
had been proposed. 
 
The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) 
over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a 
degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). 
 
Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is done because of 
operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day.  
Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to 
allow additional tests to be conducted.  This is intentionally done to maximize the 
scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. 
 
J. Status of Data Analysis  
[provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] 
Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate (for normal 
flames), the oxidizer mass flow rate (for inverse flames), O2 concentration, fuel dilution, 
and pressure were obtained for all the normal and inverse flame test days.  The raw test 
measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes 
(PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test.  
The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec.  
 
The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements.  The 
transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis.  In addition, test images 
recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME 
DataCam have been analyzed to investigate the presence of cool flames and to find flame 
diameters.  Of these the intensified camera is of most value, and all of its images to date 
have been converted to video files and reviewed.  Since the intensified camera images 
were taken under the maximum possible gain applied, the images were averaged and 
filtered to decrease the overall noise level, and the intensity of the images was increased 
by a factor of 50 to facilitate the search of intensity peaks.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
44 
 
 
Particular attention has been given to the PMT-2 measurements due to its sensitivity to 
wavelengths of 230 – 700 nm for CH2O* to investigate the presence of cool flames.  PMT-
2 measurements have been analyzed to determine flame durations as well.  Because cool 
diffusion flames were identified through the readings of radiometers after the radiative 
extinction of hot flames, the radiometer data was carefully analyzed. Burner 
temperatures were analyzed to find their correlation to the ignition and diameter of cool 
flames.  
 
K. Preliminary Research Findings  
[provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] 
A total of 280 hot diffusion flames were observed. Among them, 189 flames experienced 
radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, 
either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated.  Of those that 
extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames.  These cool 
flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% n-
butane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates 
between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s.  
 
Cool diffusion flames were initially identified by the readings of radiometers after the 
radiative extinction of hot flames.  Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows 
that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. 
Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped 
flowing.  Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot-cool flame transitions.  The first cool flame, the 
first drop of the radiant heat flux, followed the radiative extinction of the first hot flame.  
In a few seconds, the heat flux abruptly increased due to reignition of a hot flame.  This 
cycle of radiative extinction, transition to a cool flame, and reignition of a hot flame 
continued until the flow was terminated.  The observed cool flames are summarized in 
Table 3.  
 
Cool flames were also identified by processed images taken from the intensified camera. 
When cool flames appeared after the radiative extinction of the hot flames, no flame 
luminosity was evident for about 1 s, after which cool flames appeared.  For test points 
21174C3, C4, C6, and F1, the cool flames lasted for approximately 14 s and disappeared 
as soon as the fuel flow stopped.  For the tests of multiple hot-cool flame transitions, 
21291A1 and 21291C1, the first cool flame lasted longer than the following cool flames.  
The intensified camera images of hot and cool flames were used to find flame radii as 
well.  The radii of hot flames were measured at the time just before the flame oscillation.  
 
Representative images of a hot flame and a cool flame are presented in Fig. 2.  It is shown 
that the hot flame is brighter and larger than the cool flame.  While a flame sheet is clearly 
indicated in the hot flame image, the intensity of a cool flame gradually decreases from 
the peak along radial direction, which implies that the reaction zone of the cool flame is

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
51 
 
 
Appendix F. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 
 
2021 (for all of CFI-G) 
First round (normal flames) 
Increment 64 
Week 21: March 5-11  
On GMT 062, the final test points were performed for ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion). The 
Principal Investigator, Marshall Long from Yale University, considers the experiment to have been very 
successful. On this day, 11 flames were ignited, which contributed to the over 300 that were ignited for 
all of CLD Flame. Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to 
normal gravity. Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the 
lack of buoyancy. We have gathered a superior set of experimental data to be used for improving our 
ability to computationally model highly diluted flames. This capability could be implemented in design 
tools resulting in more efficient and less polluting combustion here on Earth. 
 
On GMT 068 & 069, Kate Rubins configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME 
experiment, CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually 
low temperatures known as cool flames. These flames were discovered in 2012 with the first subrack 
payload to use CIR, but this investigation only used liquid fuels. ACME’s hardware will allow CFI-G to study 
gaseous fuels to gain valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines. 
 
The time-lapse CLD Flame image associated with this submission is not included in this report. 
 
Week 22: March 12-18  
On GMT 075, Mike Hopkins lubricated the CIR GC Argon QDs and replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold 
#2 and CIR Manifold #4. These tasks prepared the CIR for supporting the next ACME experiment, CFI-G 
Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually low temperatures 
known as cool flames. These flames were discovered in 2012 with the first subrack payload to use CIR, but 
this investigation only used liquid fuels. ACME’s hardware will allow CFI-G to study gaseous fuels to gain 
valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines. 
 
Week 24: March 26 – April 1 
On GMT 088, the first test points were performed for ACME CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with 
Gases) with 14 ethane flames, sometimes diluted with nitrogen, ignited in various oxygen/nitrogen 
atmospheres. CFI-G studies flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames, which were 
discovered in 2012 with droplet combustion research being conducted in CIR at the time. That experiment 
burned liquid fuel droplets, which shrink as they burn. Instead, CFI-G will burn gaseous fuel ejected from 
a porous spherical burner to investigate cool flames under quasi-steady conditions. Cool flame chemical 
kinetics are important to ignition and the results could lead to cleaner burning and more efficient internal 
combustion engines.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
52 
 
 
 
Figure 1. Preliminary False-Colored Image of Hot Ethane Flame for CFI-G 
 
This false-colored image shows a spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity without the 
buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by 
reducing the flame structure to a single dimension, which allows computational models to focus on 
chemical kinetics and transport phenomena.  
 
The hot flame in Figure 1 has a hole at the bottom because of heat loss to the fuel tube, which supplies 
the ethane to the porous sphere. The three bright lines passing through the flame are 14-micron ceramic 
fibers, which were translated into the flame to determine temperature measurements from the color of 
the glowing fibers. Residual soot clusters, like the fibers, are glowing because of their high temperature. 
These soot clusters were “pushed” to the bottom half of the flame by the insertion of the fibers. 
 
Week 26: April 9-15 
On GMT 102, nine nitrogen-diluted butane flames were ignited for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation 
with Gases). Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were 
discovered in 2012 with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. CFI-G’s goal is to study non-
premixed cool flames using gaseous fuels, which have not been observed before and so far have not been 
observed in CFI-G testing. It is still possible that they may be detected in a more thorough review of the 
data. Whether cool flames are present or not, we are still acquiring useful results, such as data about soot 
processes. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a bright, sooty spherical flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter. 
Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters. Many clusters 
escape the flame while trapped soot eventually fades as it cools.  
 
On its right side, the flame starts to open due to heat loss to the burner’s fuel supply tube. With 
increasing heat loss, the flame nearly extinguishes, which creates a larger hole. This large hole in 
the flame shell allows for the direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which causes the flame to

Increment 65 
Week 2: April 16-22 
On GMT 106, additional tests were performed with nitrogen-diluted butane for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases). While last week’s tests with this fuel were performed at a chamber pressure of 
1 atm, this week’s tests were performed at half that pressure. Ten hot flames were ignited, and the data 
is being analyzed to determine if a cool flame occurred after the hot flame extinguished. In 13 other tests, 
data is being analyzed to determine if a cool flame was ignited directly with a low-energy ignition. 
Meanwhile, the data collected from the hot flames contribute to an earlier ACME experiment, Flame 
Design, which only tested with ethylene fuel. On GMT 109, Mike Hopkins replaced the gas bottles at CIR 
Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CFI-G test points. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This clip from a test point video shows a 50% butane flame ignited in a chamber atmosphere with 
elevated oxygen at 0.5 atm. The flame is bright and sooty, where the soot is formed when the fuel 
molecules within the flame combine in the absence of oxygen, which is outside the flame. The 
flame is like a bubble that separates the two reactants. The flame shell, like the film of the bubble, 
is a thin sheet where the fuel and oxygen come together and react, producing heat, light, carbon 
dioxide, and water vapor. 
 
Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters. Some of these soot 
clusters escape the flame—being pushed by the outward flow of the fuel from the burner. Others 
are trapped in the flame as a temperature gradient drives them away from the flame shell and 
toward the cooler burner. These opposing forces cause some soot clusters to just “dance” in 
place. 
 
After the video clip ends, the soot continues to fade as the flame temperature drops, where hardly 
any soot remained when the flame extinguished. 
 
Week 3: April 23-29 
On GMT 112, ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test points were performed using 
propane fuel. Flames with unusually low temperatures, known as cool flames, were discovered in 2012 
with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. CFI-G’s goal is to study cool flames using gaseous 
fuels to gain valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines. On GMT 118 and 119, Shane 
Kimbrough replaced an ACME controller and the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of 
CFI-G test points. 
 
Week 4: April 30 – May 6 
On GMT 125, ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test points were performed using 
nitrogen-diluted butane fuel at both elevated and normal oxygen concentrations. The data is being 
analyzed to determine if the elusive and hard-to-detect cool flames were burning after the hot flames 
extinguished or if they ignited directly. Regardless, the testing is providing valuable results that will add 
to our understanding of flammability limits and soot production, clustering, and oxidation.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
54 
 
 
CFI-G studies flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames, which were discovered in 
2012 with droplet combustion research being conducted in CIR at the time. That experiment burned liquid 
fuel droplets, which shrink as they burn. Instead, CFI-G will burn gaseous fuel ejected from a porous 
spherical burner to investigate cool flames under quasi-steady conditions. Cool flame chemistry is 
important to ignition, and the results could lead to cleaner burning and more efficient internal combustion 
engines. 
 
 
Figure 1. CFI-G Hot Flame of Nitrogen-Diluted Butane 
 
Figure 1 shows a hot flame of nitrogen-diluted butane in an atmosphere of elevated oxygen. The porous 
spherical burner of sintered stainless-steel sits on top of the tube that supplies the gaseous fuel. The blue 
flame shell is spherical, which is only possible in microgravity without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s 
gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by reducing the flame structure to a single 
dimension, which allows computational models to focus on the chemistry and transport phenomena 
rather than the prediction of the flame shape.    
 
The yellow particles are clusters of soot. Their color is the result of thermal radiation and is indicative of 
their temperature. Soot is formed when the fuel molecules within the flame combine in the absence of 
oxygen, which is outside the flame. The flame is like a bubble that separates the two reactants. The flame 
shell, like the film of the bubble, is a thin sheet where the fuel and oxygen come together and react, 
producing heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor. 
 
Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters. Some of these soot clusters 
escape the flame because they are pushed by the outward flow of the fuel from the burner. Others are 
trapped in the flame as a temperature gradient drives them away from the flame shell and toward the 
cooler burner.

On GMT 130, ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test points were performed using 
nitrogen-diluted propane fuel at chamber pressures of both 2 and 3 atm. Fifteen hot flames were ignited.

content:
ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022 
57 
 
 
Week 10: June 11-17 
On GMT 162, 12 nitrogen-diluted ethane flames were ignited for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation 
with Gases) at ambient pressures. Some tests were performed in atmospheres with 21% oxygen, while 
some tests were performed in higher oxygen concentrations of 35-40%. During two tests, the 14-micron 
ceramic fibers were translated into the flame to optically measure the flame temperature through a 
technique known as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). On GMT 165, Mark Vande Hei replaced the gas bottles 
at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CFI-G test points. 
 
 
Figure 1. Flame Temperature Measurement of CFI-G Hot Flame 
 
Figure 1 shows two images of the same nitrogen-diluted ethane flame. The right-hand image has been 
enhanced to show the faint spherical flame. The color of the fibers’ glow in the left-hand image is 
indicative of the temperature, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red. Using 
a camera characterized for quantitative measurements, we can determine a radial temperature 
distribution across the flame by analyzing the color variation along the length of a fiber. 
 
The top fiber is outside of the flame. Its glow can be used to determine the temperature near the flame, 
where it is obviously cooler despite its proximity. The fibers that pass through the flame are much brighter 
except for their centers, which are dimmer and cooler. The flame shell separates the fuel and the oxygen, 
where the heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor are created at its surface, so the flame is hottest 
at its shell. 
 
Week 11: June 18-24 
On GMT 174, we ignited 16 nitrogen-diluted butane flames in the final tests for the first round of ACME 
CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Cool flames remained elusive, where there has been no clear 
evidence of these low-temperature phenomena during this round of testing. In the coming weeks and 
months, we will review the data more closely to assess their potential presence. Regardless, we gathered 
a wealth of valuable data that will improve our fundamental understanding of soot process and flame 
dynamics. Since CFI-G tested with different fuels, these data expand upon the results gained from the 
other ACME experiments.  
 
Next week, the ACME Chamber Insert will be configured to support the second and final round of CFI-G 
testing. This testing will explore the potential existence of cool flames in an inverse configuration. The 
flow direction will be reversed, where a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen will flow from the burner into the 
Combustion Chamber, which will be filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel. As a result, the 
flames will be inside out, where, as an example, the soot will be formed outside of the flame.

In this test point video, soot that forms at ignition escapes from the flame, especially opposite of 
the burner’s supply tube (toward the left). The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss 
experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole 
allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, 
thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again 
due to heat loss. This repeated opening and closing of the flame creates a visually dramatic flame 
that swirls around the porous spherical burner. 
 
Second round (inverse flames except for the final test day)  
Week 12: June 25 – July 1 
Recent data analysis shows evidence of cool flames!  
 
Data from several of the ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) tests on GMT 174 indicate 
the presence of cool flames. These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-
diluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during 
testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements 
after the hot flames quenched. 
 
Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were discovered in 2012 
with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. Now, we’ve achieved non-premixed cool flames 
using gaseous fuels! Cool flame chemistry is important to ignition and the results could lead to vehicles 
that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution.

The images in Figure 1 are from an intensified camera filtered to look for the very faint emissions of a cool 
flame (associated with the excited formaldehyde molecule, CH2O*). The sequence shows the quenching 
of the hot flame due to radiative heat loss, followed by a comparatively dark period lasting roughly a 
second, after which the cool flame becomes evident. As expected, the cool flame is much smaller than 
the hot flame. The dark center in each cool flame image is the porous spherical burner and its fuel supply 
tube can be seen extending to the right. 
 
Week 13: July 2-8 
On GMT 183, Mark Vande Hei configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases). CFI-G studies flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames. 
Part 2 testing will explore the potential existence of cool flames in an inverse configuration. The flow 
direction will be reversed, where a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen will flow from the burner into the 
Combustion Chamber, which will be filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel. As a result, the 
flames will be inside out, where, as an example, the soot will be formed outside of the flame. Cool flame 
chemistry is important to ignition and the results could lead to vehicles that experience less wear on 
engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution. 
 
Week 14: July 9-15 
On GMT 193, Megan McArthur replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support 
the start of CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test points. 
 
Week 15: July 16-22 
On GMT 196, the first test points were performed for ACME CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames Investigation with 
Gases), where inverse flames were ignited in space for the first time. We ignited seven sustained inverse 
flames with diluted ethane fuel at both elevated and reduced pressures. With inverse flames, the diluted 
oxygen flows from the burner into a chamber filled with diluted gaseous fuel. As a result, inverse flames 
are inside out, where, as an example, the soot is formed outside rather than inside the flame. On GMT 
200, Megan McArthur replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CFI-G Part 2 
(Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test points.

Figure 1 shows a bright blue, spherical inverse flame. The porous spherical burner of sintered stainless-
steel sits on top of the tube that typically supplies gaseous fuel for normal flames. Instead, for inverse 
flames it supplies oxygen, which may be diluted with nitrogen. 
 
Week 16: July 23-29 
On GMT 202, we ignited 11 inverse flames for CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). For 
these tests, an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner into the Combustion Chamber filled with 
an ethane/nitrogen mixture. We observed that flames in 12% ethane burned longer than those in 6% 
ethane. Tests were performed at a chamber pressure of both 1 and 2 atm, and some tests used the array 
of 14-micron ceramic fibers to make flame temperature measurements. On GMT 207, Megan McArthur 
replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CFI-G Part 2 test points. 
 
 
Figure 1. Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Oxidizer Flow Rates 
 
Figure 1 compares the flames from three tests with different flow rates of oxidizer from the burner. The 
flame size is dependent on the limiting reactant, which for inverse flames is the oxygen. 
 
The porous spherical burner and its supply tube are visible within each spherical flame. Heat loss to the 
supply tube causes the flame to locally quench and creates an opening. This opening leads to direct mixing 
of the reactants, which would otherwise be separated by the flame shell. Mixing enhances the combustion 
and brightens the flame at the opening. 
 
Week 17: July 30 – Aug. 5 
On GMT 209 and 216, we ignited 23 inverse flames in a Combustion Chamber filled with ethane and 
nitrogen for CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). These two test days ignited flames in 
different fuel concentrations and pressures while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the porous 
spherical burner. We gained valuable information about the conditions that influence soot formation. On 
GMT 214, Mark Vande Hei replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4. On GMT 215, 
Shane Kimbrough opened the valves on these two bottles. These tasks were performed to support 
continuation of CFI-G Part 2 test points. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This test point video of a CFI-G inverse flame is at 3x normal speed. The flame is initially blue but 
overtime an orange band appears just outside the flame. This orange band is made up of soot 
particles, which are black but glow because of their high temperature—just like metal in a forge.

The soot is formed when the fuel, at a high temperature, reacts with itself in the absence of 
oxygen. The temperature is highest at the flame’s surface, and for inverse flames, the fuel is 
outside the flame. Therefore, in this test, the soot forms just outside the flame. 
 
The glowing soot doesn’t fully encompass the flame because of heat loss to the burner’s supply 
tube and because the flow from the burner is not quite uniform. However, in this instance, these 
shortcomings reveal the sensitivity of soot formation to temperature, residence time, and 
reactant mixture.

of concentrations from the spherical burner into the fuel-filled chamber. The testing today was limited to

pressure.

but a greater nitrogen flow on the right.

on the right had a greater nitrogen flow rate, making the oxygen more dilute and the total flow rate

Figure 1. Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Flow Rates 
 
This composite image compares inverse flames with multiples of oxygen/nitrogen flow rates from the 
porous spherical burner faintly seen within the flames. The oxygen flows outward until it reaches sufficient 
fuel to be consumed. As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. 
Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames. The 
oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent in this 
trio of tests.  
 
These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame. 
The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully 
extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens 
of seconds. Meanwhile, some flames are quasi-steady despite the opening. This is one example of how 
these spherical flames are not as simple as had earlier been imagined. 
 
Week 20: Aug. 20-26 
Shane Kimbrough replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #2 on GMT 232 and the gas bottle at CIR 
Manifold #4 on GMT 235 to support CFI-G Part 2 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). We then ignited 
eight sustained inverse flames in a Combustion Chamber filled with a 20% propane mixture at two 
different pressures. These tests also varied the flow rate and concentration ratio of the oxygen/nitrogen 
mixture flowing from the burner.

heated to a high temperature by the flame, combines in the absence of oxygen, which is inside 
the flame. 
 
The flame cools due to both radiative heat loss and conductive heat loss to the burner, especially 
to the tube supplying the oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The soot lasts the longest away from the 
supply tube where the flame is hottest. To visibly glow due to their temperature, materials must

oxygen/nitrogen mixture issuing from the burner. This marks the completion of CFI-G Part 2! 
 
 
Figure 1. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame 
 
This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than 
inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the 
absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the 
inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., 
carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the high-
temperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature. 
 
At ignition, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some 
asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical 
burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot 
free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this 
have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation. 
 
Week 27: Oct. 8-14 
On GMT 285, Megan McArthur configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support an extra day of testing 
for CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Part 1 studies normal flames as opposed to inverse 
flames like Part 2. For normal flames, the gaseous fuel flows from the burner into a Combustion Chamber 
filled with diluted oxygen. The reverse is true for inverse flames, making them inside out. The purpose of 
this extra day is to recreate the test conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing. The 
goal of CFI-G is to study these low temperature flames to gain valuable insight into the combustion 
processes in engines. Also, to support this extra day of testing, Shane Kimbrough set the CIR Valve Timers 
and replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 on GMT 286 and Megan McArthur 
replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 on GMT 287.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 
 
21 November 2022

Increment 66 
Week 1: Oct. 15-21 
On GMT 291, we performed the last 12 tests for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) during 
an extra day of testing with normal flames. The purpose of this extra day was to recreate the test 
conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing, and we successfully achieved cool flames! 
In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they 
reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane 
reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames. Cool flame chemistry is important for 
ignition in internal combustion engines and an improved understanding would aid the development of 
vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This video clip is from the end of a test in which the hot butane flame repeatedly extinguishes and 
reignites. While the low-temperature cool flames between the hot flames aren’t visible in this 
video, they cause the closest thermocouple to warm enough to visibly glow prior to reignition. 
 
Reignition causes the temperature to abruptly increase, but then it drops while the hot flame 
burns and weakens. When the hot flame extinguishes and transitions to a cool flame, the 
temperature starts increasing again until another temperature spike caused by the next 
reignition. 
 
In another test, we saw evidence of a cool flame where the temperature temporarily rose after 
the hot flame extinguished but not enough to reignite a hot flame.

Appendix G. Crew Activity per Space Station Science Highlights  
The subsequent text and images are from the weekly highlights prepared by the Lead Increment Scientist 
and made available via e-mail and online via www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/.   
 
With the major exception of the Space Station Science Highlights, links were generally not included in the 
excerpts herein because they typically go to secondary sources of information for the ACME project, for 
which the primary web site is https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/.  
Clarifications have been added in red. 
 
2021 (for all of CFI-G) 
First round (normal flames) 
 
Week of March 8, 2021 
Other investigations on which the crew performed work: 
• 
ACME is a set of six independent studies of gaseous flames. ACME’s goals are to advance fuel 
efficiency and reduce pollutant production in practical combustion on Earth, and to improve 
spacecraft fire prevention. 
 
Week of April 26, 2021 
Observing flames 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) include six independent studies of 
flames that seek to improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollution from combustion on Earth and help 
prevent fires in spacecraft. ACME investigations are conducted in the space station’s Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR), which includes a combustion chamber, gas bottles, and five cameras for observing 
flames. The research aimed at spacecraft fire prevention examines different materials, including how to 
put them out when burning, conditions needed for a material to continue burning, and the effectiveness 
of existing methods to screen and select materials for spacecraft. The crew replaced controllers for ACME 
during the week. 
 
Week of June 7, 2021 
Other investigations on which the crew performed work: 
• 
ACME includes six independent studies to improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollution from 
combustion on Earth and help prevent fires in spacecraft. The spacecraft fire prevention studies 
examine different materials, conditions needed for them to burn, how to extinguish them, and 
the effectiveness of methods to screen and select materials for spacecraft. 
Note that only one of the six ACME experiments was focused on spacecraft fire safety and that was 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), not CFI-G.

Week of October 11, 2021 
Coolest flames in space 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is a set of six independent studies 
of gaseous flames conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The researchers’ goals are to gain 
information that can lead to improved fuel efficiency, reduced pollutant production in practical 
combustion on Earth, and improved spacecraft fire prevention. One of the ACME studies currently being 
conducted is known as the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. A cool flame is one that burns at about 
600 degrees Celsius. A candle is about two times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius. The 
results of this investigation could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This past 
week, a crew member was tasked with replacing a butane bottle in preparation for the experiment.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments.  To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and 
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format.  In contrast, the analog video was 
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

N.3 Awards 
In 2021, CFI-G Principal Investigator Peter Sunderland was inducted as a Fellow of the Combustion 
Institute for his “significant contributions to understanding laminar flame dynamics and soot 
formation and oxidation.” 
 
While the awards proceed the CFI-G experiment, CFI-G Co-Investigator Forman Williams was 
recognized by the Combustion Institute with the Silver Combustion Medal (1978) and the Bernard 
Lewis Gold Medal (in 1990).  He furthermore was induced in the inaugural 2018 class of Fellows of the 
Combustion Institute for his “pioneering investigations in energy and combustion including nitric 
oxide emissions, spray and turbulent combustion, chemical kinetics and fire research.” 
 
N.4 Outreach

where some entries are specific to CFI-G.  He continues to administer these sites, where most content 
thus far has been about the ACME project of which CFI-G is a part.  As an example of educational 
outreach, a simple board game related to the ACME’s spherical flames experiments can be 
downloaded 
from 
https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/downloads/.

be downloaded from that page.  Printed copies of fact sheets have been distributed at meetings of

CASIS and NSF, which selected the experiment for spaceflight, promoted awareness of the research 
as can be seen through these links:

Gravity’s grip on heat and fire to be studied in space 
• 
Science in Space: NSF & ISS Briefing 
• 
The National Science Foundation and the ISS National Lab Announce Three Selected Projects

Space Station 
• 
Unusual "cool flames" discovered aboard International Space Station 
 
Tweets and Facebook posts from the investigators’ organizations and NSF are found on subsequent 
pages, where there could easily be more. 
 
Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of 
Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018. 
 
Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018 
by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion 
Experiments.” 
 
A photo collage and 1-paragraph article on ACME by Michael Greshko titled “Cosmic Combustion” 
was published on page 22 of the Oct. 2022 issue of the National Geographic Magazine, for which there 
is an online version.  While general to ACME, the article addresses CFI-G with a statement about the 
flames: “In microgravity they can swell into ethereal … orbs that can burn at a surprisingly cool 900 
degrees Fahrenheit (a gas stove burner’s high setting is about 3100oF).”  Despite its brevity, 
Sunderland and Stocker were both interviewed for the article. 
 
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts 
of both genders, and the general public.  His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of 
microgravity and human spaceflight, for example through microgravity design challenges which he 
helps create and administer. But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes 
speaks on ‘NASA and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in 
Metropolis, IL.  In this regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and 
online.  For example, he regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space 
Exploration Educators Conference (SEEC).   He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, 
five national Boy Scout conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 
World Scout Jamboree (which was held in the U.S.).  Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in 
NASA’s participation in these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually 
described at www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

Computational Fluid Dynamics Analysis of Flame 
Dynamics in Partial Gravity Environments in a 
Rotating Centrifuge 
 
Ankit Sharmaa,1, Arland Zatania Lojoa,1, Ya-Ting T. Liaoa,*, Paul V. Ferkulb,c, 
Michael C. Johnstonc 
 
aCase Western Reserve University, Cleveland, Ohio 44106, USA 
bUniversities Space Research Association, Brook Park, OH 44142, USA 
cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 44135, USA 
 
 
______________________________________________________________ 
 
Abstract 
The safety of spacecraft and crew members is a critical concern for space research and exploration missions. It is 
already known that fire hazards in a microgravity environment present unique challenges, primarily due to the 
absence of buoyancy, which significantly alters fire behavior. The NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to send 
humans to the Moon, introduces a new set of challenges due to the Moon partial gravity compared to the Earth. 
This necessitates a better understanding of fire behavior in partial gravity conditions. However, conducting 
experiments in true partial gravity environments is challenging, and the use of centrifuges to create artificial 
partial gravity introduces complications, including the Coriolis force and limitations in chamber siz e. 
Consequently, there have been limited studies on flame dynamics in partial gravity. To address these challenges, 
this research employs Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) techniques to investigate flame behavior in a partial 
gravity environment created by a rotating centrifuge. The numerical model is validated against NASA's previous 
experiments and provides information on the effects of the Coriolis force and flow recirculation in the chamber. 
The analysis reveals that the interaction between buoyancy, Coriolis force, and flow recirculation plays a 
significant role in flame behavior. The flame tilt angle observed in both the experiments and the numerical results 
is caused by the combined effects of these forces and their variations along the flame length. In conclusion, this 
research contributes to our understanding of how flames behave in partial gravity environments created by 
rotating centrifuges. It emphasizes the complexity of flame dynamics in such conditions and provides valuable 
insights for future centrifuge experiments, with the goal of improving space exploration safety and understanding 
flame behavior in unique partial gravity environment. 
 
Keywords: Partial gravity; Flames; Coriolis force; Centrifuge.

the numerical examination of flame dynamics in 8 
artificial partial gravity created by rotating 9 
centrifuges, revealing how the Coriolis effects and 10 
flow recirculation inside the chamber may complicate 11 
the results. The findings provide insights on how to 12 
interpret existing data and guide the design of future 13 
centrifuge experiments. Through these, this study 14 
addresses the knowledge gaps in fire dynamics in 15 
partial gravity environment, and contributes to safety 16 
and success of future space exploration. 17

normal gravity. It has also been observed that steady 5 
flame spread can be achieved in microgravity in 6 
concurrent flows [2, 4], whereas on Earth, flame 7 
spread is usually regarded as an accelerating process 8 
for typical fuel bed sizes [5–7]. These fundamental 9 
differences in flame behavior have prompted many 10 
experimental studies to develop a better 11 
understanding of fire dynamics in reduced and 12 
microgravity conditions using drop towers [3, 8], 13 
parabolic flights [9–12], space shuttles [13] , and 14 
facilities aboard the International Space Station [14–15 
16]. 16 
For future missions such as NASA’s Artemis 17 
program, there are plans to send humans to the Moon 18 
for exploration and research. This program will 19 
include the establishment of a new space station in 20 
Lunar orbit (Gateway) and eventually the creation of 21 
a habitable Lunar base. These new missions bring a 22 
unique set of challenges due to the gravity level on the 23 
Moon, which is 1/6th of the Earth’s gravity (g e). It is 24 
well known that buoyancy plays a significant role in 25 
fire growth processes in normal gravity [5–7, 17, 18]. 26 
However, reduced buoyancy conditions in partial 27 
gravity can create more severe fire hazards compared 28 
to normal gravity [19–22]. The expected weaker 29 
buoyant flow in partial gravity can lead to smaller 30 
convective heat loss and a longer residence time of 31 
reactants in the flame stabilization zone. As a result, a 32 
material may be combustible over a wider range of 33 
oxygen concentrations and pressures in partial gravity 34 
than in normal gravity. Therefore, studying how a fire 35 
would behave in these partial gravity conditions 36 
becomes very important for the safe continuation of 37 
space exploration in such environments. 38 
There have been only limited studies [1, 9–11, 21, 39 
22] on partial gravity flame behavior due to difficulty 40 
in performing experiments in partial gravity 41 
conditions (e.g., parabolic flights). Feier et al. [9] 42 
performed upward, and downward flame spread and 43 
extinction experiments over a thin solid in a partial 44 
gravity environment created in an airplane flying 45 
parabolic trajectories. A linearly increasing 46 
relationship with gravity was observed for flame 47 
spread rates and pyrolysis lengths with proportionality 48 
constants dependent on the pressure and sample 49 
width. They also developed a three -dimensional 50 
numerical model and obtained good agreement with 51 
the experiment. Similarly, Kleinhenz et al. 52 
[10]conducted parabolic flight experiments on 53 
upward flame spread over thin solid samples in 54 
different pressure and gravity conditions. Through 55 
pressure modeling, they successfully corelated the 56 
flame spread rates to pressures and gravity levels 57 
(with an empirical exponent for the pressure term, V f 58 
~ p1.8g). In a recent study, Konno et al. [11] conducted 59 
parabolic flight experiments on downward flame 60 
spread over electric wire samples (i.e., metallic core 61 
wrapped by low -density polyethylene insulation). In 62 
their results, the limiting oxygen concentrations and 63 
flame spread rates were deduced and found to have 64 
different dependencies on gravity levels for different 65 
oxygen concentrations, forced flow speeds, and wire 66 
characteristics (e.g., insulation thickness, core 67 
material). 68 
 Another way to generate artificial gravity is by 69 
using a centrifuge. This technique has been used in 70 
various previous studies [23–29] to generate hyper 71 
gravity by rotating the centrifuge in Earth’s normal 72 
gravity and allowing the sample fixture to swing in 73 
order to align it with the net acceleration vector. In 74 
order to generate artificial partial gravity levels, the 75 
centrifuge needs to be rotated in a microgravity 76 
facility (e.g., drop tower, sounding rocket). 77 
One of the complications of using a centrifuge 78 
facility is the introduction of the Coriolis force [20, 79 
25, 29–31]. When hot combusting gas “rises” toward 80 
the axis of rotation, it experiences a Coriolis force 81 
orthogonal to the velocity vector, tilting the flow 82 
stream and hence the flame away from the radial line. 83 
In previous hyper gravity centrifuge studies, Coriolis 84 
force was assumed to cause negligible effects on the 85 
flame. For example, in the study of Durox et al. [25], 86 
for a 15 cm -long methane diffusion flame in a 5m -87 
arm-length centrifuge, the lateral deflection caused by 88 
the Coriolis effect was deduced to be less than 6 % of 89 
the flame length. In another study by Altenkirch et al. 90 
[24], errors caused by the Coriolis effects in flame 91 
length measurement were considered less than 6 % 92 
and was neglected . However, these effects have not 93 
been thoroughly evaluated for microgravity 94 
centrifuge. Furthermore, burning experiments using a 95 
centrifuge will need to be contained in a closed 96 
combustion chamber. If the chamber is not large 97 
enough, additional challenges, including induced flow 98 
due to recirculation in the limited space of the 99 
chamber, and oxygen depletion (especially for thick 100 
samples), are present. For a microgravity centrifuge, 101 
the experiment time duration is also limited by the 102 
hosting microgravity platform (e.g., ~5 s for drop 103 
tower, 20-30s for parabolic aircraft flights, and 1-5 104 
minutes for sounding rockets) and operations can be 105 
costly. Due to these difficulties in setting up an 106 
artificial partial gravity environment, there have been 107 
only a handful of experimental studies on flame 108 
dynamics in partial gravity. 109 
 These challenges can be addressed using 110 
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) techniques to 111 
understand experiment results and to guide future 112 
partial gravity tests. Some previous studies have 113 
developed numerical models for studying partial 114 
gravity flame spread in parabolic flights [32, 33]. 115 
However, there is lack of numerical studies that 116 
specifically investigated the effect of flame behavior 117 
in the partial gravity environment created using a 118 
rotating centrifuge, the objective of the present study. 119 
In this work, a numerical model is developed and 120 
validated against previous NASA microgravity 121 
centrifuge experiments [20]], and the effects of 122

The developed model, with potential to be extended 2 
to different chamber geometry and fuel type, can 3 
serve as a tool to provide suggestions for the design of 4 
future centrifuge tests. It will also provide information 5 
on interpreting results from existing and future 6

2. Numerical Model 9 
A numerical model is developed using CFD 10 
software ANSYS FLUENT 20.1. Details of the 11 
numerical model can be found in [30, 31]. Below is a 12 
brief description of the model setup. 13 
The geometry is based on previous experiments 14 
performed at the NASA Glenn Research Center using 15 
a microgravity centrifuge operated in a 5.2 s drop 16 
tower [20]. The experiments consisted of a simulated 17 
candle (i.e., a wick made of a porous, sintered bronze 18 
cylinder inserted into a small liquid fuel reservoir) 19 
mounted horizontally on a turntable (XZ plane) inside 20 
a dome-shaped chamber as shown in Fig. 1a. Heptane 21 
liquid fuel was replenished in the wick through 22 
capillarity as combustion took place. As the chamber 23 
fell in the drop tower, different artificial gravity levels 24 
were created by rotating the turntable at different 25 
angular velocities. Two cameras were fixed inside the 26 
chamber to record the flame growth process. 27

In this numerical study, a CAD model is 33 
constructed based on the experimental setup, as 34 
shown in Fig. 1b. Dimensions of the model and wick 35 
are shown in Fig. 2. The wick is fixed on the rotating 36 
table such that its tip is at 32 cm from the axis of 37 
rotation (at x = -32 cm). Heptane fuel is assumed 38 
coming out of the wick at a constant mass flow rate of 39 
2.083×10-6 kg/s (corresponding to a 100 W candle 40 
flame [34]). All chamber walls are defined with no-41 
slip (with respect to the rotating frame) and adiabatic 42 
conditions. 43

To generate the artificial gravity, the 1 
computational domain is rotated around the vertical 2 
(i.e., negative y -) axis. The rotational speeds are 3 
selected to match the tested conditions in the 4 
experiments: 0.003 ge, 0.012 g e, 0.075 g e, 0.2 g e, 0.3 5 
ge, 0.59 g e, and 1 g e (ge: earth gravity = 9.81 m/s 2). 6 
While the wick is located at 32 cm from the axis of 7 
rotation, the rotational speeds are selected so that the 8 
desired artificial gravities are achieved at 30 cm since 9 
this location is approximately the center of the flame. 10 
Conservation of mass, momentum, species and 11 
energy are solved using Finite Volume Method 12 
(FVM). Turbulence is modeled using the Reynolds -13 
averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations with a k-14 
omega SST model. For the gas -phase combustion, 15 
single step overall stoichiometric combustion is 16 
adopted: C7H16 + 11O2 → 8H2O + 7CO2. The reaction 17 
rate is assumed to be controlled by turbulent mixing 18 
(fast kinetic) and is calculated using the eddy 19 
dissipation model. 20 
The initial conditions are set to 300K and zero 21 
relative velocity (with respect to the rotational 22 
chamber). This is to mimic the experimental setup. In 23 
the experiments, the chamber was spun up for a period 24 
of time before it was dropped (i.e., chamber gas was 25 
considered to rotate as a solid body). The initial gas 26 
composition is air. Small traces of combustion 27 
products (H2O and CO2) are included, as required by 28 
the eddy-dissipation reaction rate model in Fluent 29 
(initial mass fraction of the gas: 23.13% O2, 76.77% 30 
N2, 0.05% H2O, and 0.05% CO2). 31 
Non-uniform meshing is used to optimize 32 
computational time and resources with finer meshes 33 
allocated near the wick where the flame is expected to 34 
grow. Finer meshes are also allocated near the walls 35 
to resolve the thermal and viscous boundary layers. A 36 
grid independence study is performed to ensure that 37 
the mesh resolution is appropriate [30]. Based on the 38 
results, final mesh selected consists of 8.14 million 39 
cells with the largest cell of volume 8.89 ×10-7 m3 and 40 
the smallest 8.21 × 10-12 m3. A constant time step of 41 
0.01 s for a total of 500 timesteps is employed to 42 
capture 5 seconds of data aligning with the drop tower 43 
experimental duration. The simulations are performed 44 
on the Case High Performance Computing Cluster 45 
using 16 cores and 32 GB memory. The simulation 46 
time is ~ 16-24 hours for each case. 47 
 48 
3. Comparisons between Numerical and 49 
Experimental Results 50 
3.1 Transient flame growth process 51 
Figure 3 shows a side -by-side comparison of the 52 
flame growth process in the experiment [20] (left 53 
panes) and in the numerical simulation (right panes) 54 
for artificial gravity at 0.3 g e. A video version of this 55 
comparison can be found in the supplemental 56 
material. Numerical results on the right panes display 57 
the temperature contour with a 5% oxygen isoline 58 
(black line). The numerical simulation predicts a close 59 
resemblance of the flame shape observed in the 60 
experiment throughout the flame development 61 
process. After ignition, the flame grew “upwards” 62 
towards the center of rotation and tilted to the left due 63 
to the effect of Coriolis force in both the experiment 64 
and numerical simulation. 65 
When the artificial gravity exceeds 0.075 g e, both 66 
experimental and numerical results exhibit the 67 
phenomenon of flame pulsation. This phenomenon 68 
has been observed for a wide range of fuel types, 69 
burner diameters, heat release rates, and Reynolds 70 
numbers [35-39]. Previous study suggested that it is 71 
caused by Kelvin-Helmholtz instability of the buoyant 72 
flow [39]. In this study, it is more obvious at a higher 73 
simulated ge (i.e., larger buoyant flow velocity) . To 74 
illustrate this, Fig. 4 shows one cycle of the pulsation 75 
in the experiment (top row) and in the numerical 76 
simulation (bottom row) at 1g e. The corresponding 77 
video can be found in the supplemental material. 78

In Fig. 4, experimental images are 17 ms apart 5 
(total duration is ~ 0.11s) and the numerical images 6 
are ~65 ms apart (total duration ~ 0.41 s). The 7 
numerical simulation significantly underpredicts the 8 
pulsation frequency (7-9 Hz in the experiments versus 9 
~2.5 Hz in the numerical results). Multiple possible 10 
reasons contribute to this discrepancy. Previous 11 
research for pool fires and candle flames showed that 12 
the pulsation frequency is negatively corelated to the 13 
fire power. For pool fires, the pulsation frequency is 14 
corelated to square root of gravity over the square root 15 
of pool diameter ( 𝑓𝑓~�𝑔𝑔/𝐷𝐷) [35]. For a bundle of 16 
candles, the pulsation frequency decreases linearly 17 
with the number of candles [36, 37]. It is possible that 18 
the constant uniform mass flux assumed on the 19 
wicked surface in the simulations overestimates the 20 
fire power (and hence the model underpredicts the 21 
pulsation frequency). While this research focuses on 22 
the Coriolis effect and the overall behavior of the 23 
flames in the centrifuge, the model can be fine -tuned 24 
in the future work to capture the pulsation frequency. 25 
Figure 4 shows that in the first half of the pulsation 26 
cycle (Fig. 4 a-c in the experimental result and Fig. 4 27 
h-j in the numerical results), the flame is short and 28 
exhibits a similar shape as in lower artificial gravity 29 
(e.g., 0.3 ge). At the second half of the cycle (Fig. 4 d-30 
f and Fig. 4 k-m), the flame bends in the middle with 31 
the top portion tilting to the left at a larger angle. As 32 
the flame grows, the bending location moves upward. 33 
This flame pulsation and bending phenomenon 34 
observed in the experiment was captured reasonably 35 
well by the numerical model (except for the pulsation 36 
frequency). 37

In this study, the blowing velocity on the wick 20 
surface (in the order of mm/s) is negligible compared 21 
to the buoyant flow. The Froude number ranges from 22 
~0.6 to ~ 0.002 and t he flame is considered as 23 
buoyancy controlled in all simulated cases [40, 41]. In 24 
Reynolds–Froude scaling analysis , flame length is 25 
negatively correlated to the gravity level (e.g., ~𝑔𝑔−1/5 26 
by Delichatsios [40], ~𝑔𝑔−1/3 by Altenkirch et al. [42] 27

air jet diffusion flame length was observed to decrease 30 
with 𝑔𝑔−1/3 for gravity level greater than 2 g e, 31 
consistent with the Reynolds–Froude scaling analysis. 32 
However, between 1 g e to 2 ge, the flame length was 33 
observed to remain constant or even slightly increase 34 
with the gravity. They attributed this to interactions 35 
between vortices above the flame and the tip of the 36 
reaction zone. In the study of Sunderland et al. [28], 37 
flame lengths of laminar hydrogen, methane, ethane, 38 
and propane flames from various experiments were 39 
comprehensively examined. The collected data 40 
covered a wide range of gravity level (1–15 ge). Their 41 
results showed that t he Reynolds scaling ( i.e., non-42 
dimensional flame length scales with Re) accurately 43 
correlated the flame length measurements at both 44 
Earth and elevated gravity , within experimental 45 
uncertainties. They concluded that the stoichiometric 46 
flame lengths at normal and elevated gravity are 47 
independent of the gravity level. T his is also 48 
consistent with the observations for simulated partial 49 
gravity above 0.012 ge in this study. 50

The results for the 1 g e case are shown in Fig. 12. 13 
Similar to the 0.3 g e case, the gas temperature and 14 
hence the buoyancy force increase, reach maximum 15 
values, and then decrease along the flame length. 16 
However, the Coriolis force exhibits a different 17 
variation compared to the 0.3 g e case. At the flame 18 
bottom (between x 1 and x 2), at this larger artificial 19 
gravity level, the increase of the buoyant flow velocity 20 
is more significant compared to the decrease of the 21 
local density. As a result, the flow momentum and 22 
hence the Coriolis force increase with the flow 23 
velocity. In the middle portion of the flame (between 24 
x2 and x 3), the flow velocity and the Coriolis force 25 
decrease slightly before increasing again. This is due 26 
to the dynamic effects of the flame pulsation (a bubble 27 
of higher speed flow rises up to the flame tip in each 28 
pulsation cycle). After that (between x3 and x4), as the 29 
flame temperature drops, buoyant flow velocity 30 
decreases gradually along the flame length while the 31 
gas density increases at a faster rate. As a result, the 32 
flow momentum and the Coriolis force increases 33 
throughout the remaining flame region. 34

When inspecting the net force and its angle (shown 5 
in Fig. 10c and Fig. 12b), the flame tilt angle is 6 
predicted to remain roughly constant at 20° at the 7 
bottom portion of the flame (between x 1 and x2). In 8 
the top portion of the flame (between x 3 and x4), the 9 
buoyancy force responsible for keeping the flame 10 
vertical starts diminishing along the flame length (due 11 
to decrease in gas temperature) while the Coriolis 12 
force intensifies (due to increase in density and 13 
comparatively lesser decrease in relative velocity). 14 
This results in a more pronounced tilt of the flame 15 
towards the direction of Coriolis force and explains 16 
the second bending angle observed in cases with 17 
larger artificial gravities in Fig. 5. Near the flame tip 18 
(x = x4), the angle of the net force reaches ~40°. These 19 
predicted flame tilt angles are once again consistent 20 
with the observation in Fig. 5. 21 
Notably, the magnitudes of buoyancy and Coriolis 22 
forces are very different in 1 g e and 0.3 ge, as shown 23 
in Fig. 13. This is because both Buoyancy and 24 
Coriolis forces are positively corelated to the artificial 25 
gravity level (Eqs. 3 and 4). Also note that in all 26 
simulated cases, flows exhibit tangential component 27 
in the flame region (see Fig. 7). This tangential 28 
component of the flow leads to Coriolis acceleration 29 
in the radial direction because the Coriolis force 30 
always acts orthogonally to the flow direction. If the 31 
radial component of the Coriolis force is comparable 32 
to the centrifugal acceleration, it will contaminate the 33 
artificial gravity and should not be overlooked. 34

4.3 Flow recirculation 39 
Since the chamber is closed, buoyant flows can 40 
eventually recirculate back to the flame region and 41 
affect the flame behaviors. To explore this, 42 
simulations are extended to 7s (~ 2s longer than the 43 
original drop tower experiment duration). Figure 14 44 
compares the flame growth and dynamics of the flow 45 
for the 1 g e case at 1s and 7s. In this study, the 46 
centrifuge is rotating clockwise (viewed from the top), 47 
the Coriolis force is always to the left with respect to 48 
the flow direction. This results in a counterclockwise 49 
circulation of the flow (see the white streamlines in 50 
Fig. 14). 51

From Fig. 14, it appears that this establishment of 4 
recirculation flow within the chamber eventually 5 
pushes the flame towards right (+Z) i.e., in the 6 
direction opposite to the Coriolis force. This 7 
recirculating flow can also contribute to the 8 
underestimation of the flame angles (Angles B and C) 9 
in Fig. 5. 10 
Notably, this process of flame tilting in the 11 
opposite direction was not observed in the 12 
experiments. It is because the recirculation effect only 13 
becomes prominent in the simulation after ~ 5s (7 s 14 
for 1ge and longer for lower artificial gravity cases) 15 
while the experiments durations were limited to 5.2 s. 16 
Another factor that has likely reduced or 17 
eliminated the recirculating flow in the experiments is 18 
the presence of equipment such as cameras, sensors, 19 
cables, and other materials within the chamber. These 20 
components act as obstructions disturbing the 21 
recirculation flow and preventing the recirculating 22 
flow from pushing the flame to the opposite direction. 23 
It is important to note that the simulation results 24 
presented in this study assume that the chamber is 25 
empty and does not consist of any obstructions, except 26 
the liquid wick. In additional simulations with random 27 
obstructions inside the chamber [30], flow 28 
recirculation is not observed even at longer durations. 29 
 30 
5. Conclusions and Future Works 31 
A numerical model is developed to investigate the 32 
dynamics of flames in simulated partial gravity 33 
environments in a microgravity centrifuge. The 34 
objective is to develop fundamental understanding of 35 
how the Coriolis force affects the flame 36 
characteristics. Various artificial partial gravity levels 37 
ranging from 0.003 g e to 1 g e are achieved by 38 
adjusting the centrifuge's rotational speed. 39 
Simulations are compared with previous NASA’s 40 
experiments and the effects of Coriolis force and flow 41 
recirculation are presented. Key findings are as 42 
follows. 43 
The model is shown to be able to capture the 44 
overall fire behavior observed in the experiments. 45 
This includes the flame shapes and flame tilt angles at 46 
different artificial gravity levels. Flame pulsation and 47 
bending behaviors at larger artificial gravities are also 48 
captured. However, the pulsation frequency is 49 
underestimated. Further tuning of the model is 50 
warranted to further investigation on the pulsation 51 
phenomenon. 52 
In both experimental and numerical results, as the 53 
artificial gravity increases from 0.003 g e to 0.012 ge, 54 
flame transits from spherical to elongated shapes. At 55 
0.075 ge, the flame starts exhibiting lateral tilting due 56 
to Coriolis effect, and at and above 0.59 ge, the flame 57 
exhibits two -angle bending phenomenon. Detailed 58 
examinations of local Coriolis and buoyancy forces 59 
provided insights into the transition of flame shapes. 60 
The Coriolis force tilts the flame in the tangential 61 
direction while the buoyancy force is responsible for 62 
keeping the flame vertical. The Coriolis acceleration 63 
and the buoyancy forces are both positively corelated 64 
to the artificial gravity level. As a result, the flame tilt 65 
angle remains similar in all simulated artificial 66 
gravities. 67 
The variations in temperature, density, velocity, 68 
and various forces along the flame length are 69 
examined in details. For all simulated artificial 70 
gravities, the buoyancy force, directly linked to the 71 
gas temperature, initially rises, reaches a maximum in 72 
the flame region, and subsequently diminishes. 73 
Conversely, the Coriolis force, influenced by flow 74 
momentum exhibits different trends in lower and 75 
higher artificial gravities. At low ge, the Coriolis force 76 
remains roughly constant along the flame length. For 77 
artificial gravity at 0.59 g e and higher, the Coriolis 78 
force remains similar in the bottom portion of the 79 
flame but increases in the top portion of the flame due 80 
to the increase in the local density and comparatively 81
