content:
NASA Engineering and Safety Center Technical Bulletin No. 26-03
National Aeronautics and Space Administration
Flammability Testing Configuration and Approach of Barrier Material 
Assemblies Designed for Space Flight Applications
The NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) partnered with Materials and Processes and Flammability subject matter experts from the Johnson 
Space Center, White Sands Test Facility, and the Marshall Space Flight Center to design and develop a test for evaluating the effectiveness of material 
assemblies to serve as a barrier between a potential cabin ignition source based on typical flammable materials in the habitable volume of spacecraft.
www.nasa.gov For more information, contact Dr. Morgan Abney, morgan.b.abney@nasa.gov. nasa.gov/nesc 11/04/26 DOC ID: 20260001542
Background on Barrier Material Flammability Testing
The standard “three-legged” approach to material flammability mitigation, 
including material controls, ignition source controls, and robust fire response, 
outlines a fire safety management plan in which misses or weaknesses in 
one leg are compensated for by others. The material control leg is based 
on selecting non-propagating materials for use in spacecraft. Verification of 
non-propagating materials is based on NASA-STD-6001B, Flammability, 
Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures (in this 
case, Test 1 for upward flammability). However, when not all materials 
pass the upward flammability test, additional mitigation strategies are 
required. Some of these include designing layups to serve as heat sinks, 
inhibiting propagation paths through controlled spacing and surface area, 
and shielding or enclosing flammable materials using barrier layups. Barrier 
materials are those designed to provide shielding between ignition sources 
and flammable materials. Their use for storage and broad acreage cabin 
surfaces has historically provided a hazard control justification for the 
use of highly flammable items such as crew clothing, hygiene items, etc. 
Accordingly, they must be “non-breaching” in addition to “non-propagating.” 
The standard “Test 1” materials test for flammability does not evaluate 
breaching, resulting in a gap in test capability to assess these flammability 
mitigation designs.
In 2023, testing of fully assembled barrier hardware and material lay-ups 
was performed at White Sands Test Facility to evaluate their effectiveness in 
providing flammability protection. The testing identified gaps with the current 
test approach outlined in the NASA standard, particularly for combinatorial 
configurations (e.g., seams, zippers, etc.). In 2024, NASA Johnson Space 
Center materials and processes engineering community released a memo 
(JSC-ES4-24-030) explaining that the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 upward 
flammability test is not sufficient to evaluate the materials and layups used in 
barrier hardware. In response, the NESC undertook development of a test to 
evaluate barrier materials and layups. Subject matter experts from multiple 
centers collaborated with the NESC in designing, developing, testing, and 
evaluating the new methodology.
Barrier Flammability Testing Development
Development of the barrier test methodology involved determining the 
parameters associated with barrier hardware testing. Assessed parameters 
were ignition energy including determining temperature and burn duration 
encompassing possible ignition sources, barrier material test configuration 
(“L” shape of pliable materials with challenge material “inside”), challenge 
material makeup, number of replicates, and pass/fail criteria. The team 
tested barrier assemblies and challenge material configurations to envelope 
the maximum burn time and temperature of flight-like potential ignition 
sources and materials. The team tested multiple ignitor configurations, 
different chemical types, and a range of ignitor quantities to envelope the 
potential burn durations and peak temperatures of common cabin materials 
including batteries. Ignitor configurations were tested with control materials 
to ensure the ignitor was not overly conservative but informing margin 
and that the test encompassed the range of currently proposed barrier 
material configurations. A statistical analysis of the Materials and Processes 
Technical Information System (MAPTIS) database for Test 1 data helped 
determine the appropriate number of replicates needed to provide further 
confidence and reliability in the test process and results. The new barrier 
test calls for 5 replicates as a baseline. However, if charring is observed on 
the interior of the barrier greater than 3” away from the ignitor impingement 
point material or if challenge material heat affected lengths are observed 
to be greater than 3”, then the number of replicates is increased from 5 to 
10 to reduce uncertainty. Pass/fail criteria was determined with the goals 
of ensuring that a cabin fire of known cabin flammables could not lead to 
a larger fire due to ignition and propagation of the barrier assembly itself 
or of shielded flammable materials due to a barrier breach. Details of the 
test protocol and assessment criteria will be presented at the International 
Conference on Environmental Systems. 
Barrier Flammability Testing Configuration/Parameters
Test Fixture: 
• Large fixture to eliminate edge effects (12” width x 24” length, 1” bend radius).
• “L” shaped fixture eliminates concerns for oxygen depletion and tests 
 potential upward propagation component in the event of barrier breach/ 
 flame propagation.
Challenge Materials: 
• Based on worst case autoignition temperature (AIT) materials that may 
 be present in the cabin. 
• Materials: Polyethylene (AIT 306°C), Cellulosic dry wipes (AIT 386°C), 
 (AITs at 100% oxygen, 1500 PSI).
• Suspended vertically above ignitor fire impingement point as in Test 1. 
 Lower edge of challenge materials configured with ½” wide, 1.5” long slits 
 with lower edges in contact with inner layer of barrier material under test.
Ignition Source (Size/ Energy):
• “Simulated Single Cell Battery Failure” Ignitor: Standardized ignitor bounds worst 
 case realistic temps/ durations by simulating a single cell battery failure. 
Pass/ Fail Criteria: 
• Full upward propagation of assembly materials - FAIL
• Sustained combustion of challenge material - FAIL 
• Burn through hole observable with the naked eye post-test - FAIL
• If charring observed on the interior of the barrier greater than 3 inches 
away from ignitor impingement point material OR if challenge material 
heat affected lengths are observed to be greater than 3”, then the num-
ber of replicates is increased from 5 to 10 to reduce uncertainty (samples 
in the 5 additional replicates demonstrating heat affected zones greater 
than 3 inches away from intimate contact area will not constitute failure 
but reduce uncertainty that ignition of the challenge material is unlikely).
References
1. NASA-STD-6001B, Flammability, Offgassing, and Compatibility 
 Requirements and Test Procedures, June 9, 2025
2. ES4-24-030 NASA STD-6001 Clarification, 2024

51st International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2022-219 
10-14 July 2022, St. Paul, Minnesota 
Opposed-flow spreading flames: Effect of sub-atmospheric 
pressure on spread and burning rates 
Luca Carmignani1, Priya Garg2, Michael J. Gollner3, Carlos Fernandez-Pello4 
University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, 94720, USA 
Maria Thomsen5 
Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Santiago, Chile 
and 
David L. Urban6, Gary A. Ruff7 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, 44135, USA 
Flame spread over solid fuels is a canonical problem in fire science, due to its direct 
implications on material flammability and importance in fire development. Flames in a 
microgravity environment can behave very differently than on Earth, posing additional risks 
for spaceflight life safety. Sub-atmospheric pressures in ground-based experiments have been 
proposed to approximately replicate the burning behavior of solid fuels in reduced gravity 
conditions because of similar effects on heat and mass transfer mechanisms from the flame to 
the solid. In opposed-flow flame spread, the solid fuel is heated by the flame ahead of its 
leading edge, and this process is strongly affected by the ambient conditions. In this work, we 
consider flames spreading over flat thin acrylic samples exposed to a forced flow of 20 cm/s, 
and pressures between 30 and 100 kPa. When radiation losses and chemical kinetic effects are 
neglected, experimental and theoretical results suggest an independence of the spread rate on 
pressure. However, the spread rate shows a decreasing trend with lower pressure in the range 
30-60 kPa. The mass burning rate, calculated from the samples weight measured before and 
after the experiments, shows a similar trend. The flame length, on the other hand, shows a 
non-monotonic behavior, reaching a maximum at 60 kPa. Additionally, gas emissions 
measured during the experiments are used to estimate the heat release rate of the spreading 
flames. The comparison of the heat release rate obtained from the measured emissions and 
the estimated mass burning rates, suggests that chemical kinetics is not driving the decrease 
in flame spread observed at low pressures, whereas radiation losses could be responsible in 
analogy to what has been observed in micro and partial gravity studies. These results could 
provide more information to guide future Earth-based material flammability testing for 
spacecraft applications.

I. Introduction 
HE flammability of solid combustible materials determines the fire hazard characteristics of the material and thus 
is important in fire safety1. Measured parameters include the material ease of ignition, the rate of flame spread, 
the heat release rate, and the toxicity of the combustion products. Ambient conditions such as pressure, oxygen 
concentration, gas flow, and gravity level, together with the material thermo-physical properties and scale affect these 
flammability properties, and thus it is of interest to determine these effects. 
Material flammability in sub-atmospheric pressures has application in determining the fire hazard in urban areas 
at high altitudes2-4, aircraft5, and spacecraft6,7. Furthermore, since ambient pressure affects the buoyant characteristics 
of a fire, it has the added application of using pressure modeling to simulate fires at different scales8-10. 
Following a similar approach, low pressure environments have been proposed to study the fire behavior in reduced 
gravity conditions11-15. By decreasing the ambient pressure, flames over solid fuels tend to move away from the 
burning surface, and diffusive processes become more important, in analogy with the effect of reduced buoyancy at 
low gravity levels. In microgravity the buoyant flow field is extremely weak and comparable to diffusive flows, and 
flames may not spread without externally generated flows, such as the low velocity flows generated in spacecraft by 
Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS). Spreading flames are generally divided into two main 
categories: concurrent flame spread, where the direction of propagation is the same as that of an oncoming flow field, 
including upward-spreading flames on Earth, and counter-current or opposed-flow flame spread, where the flame 
moves against an incoming flow. Concurrent-flow flame spread is known to be more hazardous than opposed-flow 
flame spread in a terrestrial environment. However, it has been shown that in a low-gravity environment opposed-
flow flames can grow more easily than concurrent spreading flames because of a fresh supply of oxidizer16, and 
sometimes burn under conditions where extinguishment would occur on Earth17-19. Previous experiments suggest that 
reduced pressures ranging between 20-40 kPa may be able to simulate flames in microgravity in terms of flame spread 
rate and flame length13,15, at least for thin combustible materials. However, there are some limitations to the 
comparison between low gravity and low pressure. Numerical studies and scaling analyses have highlighted the 
importance of diffusion processes and radiation losses in reduced pressure environments11,14,20. 
As the flame spreads over the surface of the solid, it leaves behind a burning solid that releases heat depending on 
the physico-chemical characteristics of the process. The resulting heat-release rate (HRR) is an important parameter 
used to characterize the flammability of a material, since together with the flame spread rate they determine the growth 
of a fire. The HRR can be derived from the rate of fuel consumption, which is usually calculated using the mass loss

The primary objective of this work is to provide information about the flammability of materials in spacecraft 
environments, although the results have applications to other reduced pressure conditions. Specifically, we study the 
effect of ambient sub-atmospheric pressure on the flammability of thin solid materials, through their rate of flame 
spread, emissions, and the heat release. We consider the opposed/downward spread of flames over thin acrylic samples 
(polymethyl methacrylate, or PMMA), at ambient pressures between 30 and 100 kPa. The flames are exposed to a 
forced velocity of 20 cm/s in addition to the self-generated buoyant flow. The analysis of the flow velocity controlling 
the flame spread developed by Thomsen et al.15 is expanded to correlate the experimentally measured variation of 
flame characteristics such as spread rate and flame length scales with pressure. Additionally, the gas concentrations 
of the combustion products are used to estimate the HRR of the spreading flames, which is shown to decrease with 
pressure. When compared to the HRR estimated from the average mass loss rate of the fuel, the results suggest that 
chemical kinetics is not a driving factor for these conditions. 
II. Experimental setup 
The experiments were conducted in an apparatus 
previously developed to study the flammability of solid 
combustible materials under varied ambient conditions23. 
The apparatus consists of a laboratory scale combustion 
tunnel that is inserted in a pressure chamber as shown in the 
schematic of Figure 1. The tunnel has a 125 mm square cross 
section and a 600 mm total length. The first 350 mm section 
of the duct serves as a flow straightener, the other 250 mm 
segment of the duct is used as the test section. 
The chamber is provided with a flow system that 
provides constant supply and exhaust of gases to avoid 
vitiation problems. Compressed dry air was supplied through 
critical nozzles (O’Keefe Controls) to the bottom of the duct 
while constantly evacuating to maintain constant pressure 
inside the chamber. The chamber pressure was controlled by 
a high-capacity vacuum pump (Welch DuoSeal 1376), and 
measured with an electronic pressure transducer (Omega 
Engineering, Inc. PX309-015A5V). The tests were 
conducted in air at pressures between 30 and 100 ± 2 kPa. 
The forced flow was adjusted to provide 20 cm/s at the 
respective chamber pressure for all tests. This velocity was selected to be consistent with the flow of air induced by 
the ECLSS inside of a spacecraft. In addition to the forced flow, the flame is exposed to a self-induced buoyant flow 
that varies with pressure. Thus, during the experiments the flame is exposed to a mixed (free and forced) flow 
condition. 
Gas measurements were recorded using a gas analyzer Enerac 700. This device provides real-time concentrations 
of oxygen (O2), nitrogen oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), oxides of nitrogen (NOx), and sulphur dioxide (SO2) 
using an electrochemical sensor. Carbon dioxide (CO2), carbon monoxide (CO), and unburnt hydrocarbons (HC) were 
calibrated against propane using a NDIR sensor. The flow rate of the sampling pump was set at 1.5 SLPM, and the 
sampling probe was connected to the exhaust system downstream of the vacuum pump (see schematics in Figure 1). 
The fuel samples were thin sheets of cast PMMA, with a thickness of 0.7 mm. The rectangular samples were held 
between two identical stainless-steel frames 0.6 mm thick, with a rectangular opening of 150 mm long by 50 mm wide 
that served as the test area. Each sample was placed vertically at the mid-plane of the test section, and they were 
ignited at the top with a 26-gauge Kanthal wire. The igniter was energized using a controlled current power supply 
(BK Precision 1785) set to deliver 50 W for about 10 s, or until the flame appears on both sides of the sample. The 
flames were extinguished by flushing the system with nitrogen after they had spread over the entire sample region. 
The experiments were repeated three to six times for each test condition to address experimental uncertainty. 
The ignition and subsequent flame spread were video recorded with a resolution of 1920 by 1080 at 30 frames per 
second using a Sony RX10-III camera for the front view, and a second Nikon D3200 camera for the flame side view. 
The camera settings were kept constant during the experiments, although they slightly differ between front view and

Figure 2 shows the front and side views of downward

The front view of the experiments was used also to measure the variation of the preheating and pyrolsysis lengths with 
pressure. Both length scales are inversely proportional to pressure as shown in Figure 5, but with different 
dependencies as discussed in the next section. 
Figure 6 shows the variation of the flame length 𝑥# (see Figure 3), and the total thickness of the flame 2𝑦# 
(measured from the side view of the experiments). The flame length shows a non-monotonic behavior, reaching a 
maximum at 60 kPa and decreasing at higher and lower pressures, as qualitatively observed in Figure 2. This variation, 
however, is limited to less than 20%, with an average value of about 25 mm. The flame length was multiplied by the 
total thickness of the flame and the width of the sample (52 mm) to estimate the flame volume, which values are 
shown in Figure 6. The flame length and standoff distance have the same initial trend and the flame volume increases 
by reducing pressure, although it approaches a constant value below 60 kPa. 
The flame ignition and extinction times in the experiments were matched between the cameras and the gas analyzer 
recordings, thus it was possible to calculate changes in O2 consumption, and CO, CO2 productions. The gas analyzer 
measured the molar fractions of the gas in the combustion products, which were converted to mass fractions to estimate 
the consumption and production rates of each component. The emission recordings showed a strong initial variation 
of gas concentrations (especially CO) due to the ignition phase, before reaching steady state values. Only the values 
obtained during the steady state flame spread are considered here, and the average rates are reported in Figure 7. The 
oxygen consumption rates follow a trend similar to the one observed for the spread rate in Figure 4; it is stable in the 
range 50-100 kPa, whereas it decreases at lower pressures. The CO and CO2 production rates, follow opposite trends 
as expected, respectively increasing and decreasing 
at higher pressures. This is an indication that the 
combustion efficiency of the pyrolyzed fuel 
decreases with reduced pressure, although the 
decrease is small because of the relatively small

on pressure for opposed flame spread has not yet been 
determined, but the measured values in Figure 5 suggest a

dark red line). The Reynolds number scales with 𝑝, and 
the Grashof number with 𝑝9 (Ref. 30), therefore the term

rate in Eq. (4). This is in agreement with the thermal 
regime assumptions, and confirmed by the almost 
constant value of the spread rate in the range 60-100 kPa 
in Figure 4. However, Eq. (4) does not capture the 
decrease observed at pressures below 60 kPa. To derive 
Eq. (4), we neglected the importance of the radiative 
exchange between flame and fuel surface, and the effect 
of chemical kinetics. For opposed flame spread, numerical 
studies showed that radiation losses could play a major 
role in slowing down the flames, but chemical kinetics can become important as well at low pressures14,20. 
The concentration of the post-combustion products of a flame is an important indicator of the completeness of the 
reactions involved in the flame spread. The average O2, CO and CO2 concentrations measured during the flame spread 
experiments were used to estimate the HRR32, and the results are shown in Figure 8. The HRR can also be estimated 
from the mass burning rate of the solid fuel. Since the mass of the samples was measured before and after the 
experiments, we calculated an average mass loss rate; by assuming complete combustion of the solid fuel, we can 
obtain the HRR from the mass measurements simply multiplying the mass loss rate by the heat of combustion of 
PMMA (25.9 kJ/g). The estimated values, reported in Figure 8 as well, follow the same pressure trend of the HRR 
calculated from the emission measurements, as well as the flame spread rate, indicating that they are related to the 
amount of fuel burned as the flame spreads along the solid surface. The calculated values of the HRR from the gas 
composition and mass loss are similar, suggesting that the assumption of complete combustion gives reasonable values 
for the pressure range 30-100 kPa. Furthermore, this implies that the decrease in spread rate is not driven by the onset 
of finite rate kinetics effects; more likely, the flames are weaken by radiative losses, in analogy to what happens in a 
reduced gravity environment. 
V. Conclusion 
Experiments of opposed/downward spreading flames over thin acrylic sheets were conducted at sub-atmospheric 
pressures with the objective of studying the flammability of solid combustible materials in low pressure environments 
such as high-altitude locations, aircraft, and spacecraft. Several flame characteristics are measured from the video 
analysis of the experiments. It is found that the flame spread rate is weakly dependent on pressure in the range 60-100 
kPa, and then it decreases as the ambient pressure is reduced. The pyrolysis and preheating length on the solid surface 
are inversely proportional to pressure, whereas the flame length follows a non-monotonic behavior with a peak at 60 
kPa. The gas concentrations in the post-combustion products were used to calculate the HRR of the spreading flame, 
and the results show a similar trend with the spread rate: it is almost constant in the range 50-100 kPa and then 
decreases at lower pressures. The comparison between the HRR calculated from the gas emissions, and the HRR 
estimated from the mass loss rate suggests that chemical kinetics is not a limiting factor for the spreading flames 
considered in this work, although it seems to affect the efficiency of the gas phase fuel combustion process. It is 
possible that the flow velocity of 20 cm/s used in this work was large enough to guarantee an adequate mixing of the 
reactancts, decreasing the effect of pressure on the chemical reaction rate. The spread of the flames could also be 
weakened by radiative losses, which were neglected in the flame spread rate model. The increase in concavity of the 
burning front of the solid fuel observed at low pressures, in fact, could be caused by heat losses occurring by the 
sample sides. In summary, the reduced ambient pressure on opposed-flow flame spread over thin PMMA samples had 
similar implications to a reduced gravity level, where chemical kinetics is not important and the process is limited by 
flame radiative losses. In order to better compare opposed flame spread in reduced pressure and gravity environments, 
it will be necessary to further investigate and characterize the importance of radiation losses.

spacecraft environments that represent practical spacecraft fires. These tests spanned 1.5 to 
3.2 kW with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic met ers. The final flight in the series of six 
experiments examined concurrent spread over large samples (all 41 cm wide) including a thin 
sheet of flammable fuel (cotton/fiberglass 50 cm long); 2-sided spread over 1 cm thick 
polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) (18 cm lo ng); 1-sided spread over 0.5 cm thick (18 cm 
long); and Nomex fabric (7 cm long). Results are presented for the PMMA samples, the SIBAL 
sample, and the thin cotton samples from Sa ffire IV and V. The flame heat release is 
determined and compared to the overall temperature rise in the spacecraft and the change in 
the concentration of carbon di oxide and carbon monoxide in the spacecraft. Overall, the 
temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the 
increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. 
Nomenclature 
FFD = Far Field Diagnostics 
PMMA = polymethyl methacrylate 
Saffire = Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project 
SFU = Saffire Flow Unit 
SIBAL = Solid Inflammati on Boundary at Low Speed 
SMAC = Spacecraft Maximum Allowed Concentration 
I. Introduction 
lthough spacecraft fires have long been recognized as a potentially catastrophic hazard, the impact of a spacecraft 
fire on the vehicle habitability was not examined experimentally before the initiation of the Saffire experiment 
series. In terrestrial fires, the smoke and its constituents are generally a greater hazard than the heat from the fires. In 
the confined space of an orbiting spacecraft, any of these hazards can become a critical hazard for the mission and the 
crew. Specifically, excessive temperature rise will potentially cause thermal injury, while increase in the levels of 
carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide may pose a more significant and acute hazard to the crew. Given the difficulty 
in predicting the impact of the heat and pressure rise from a spacecraft fire compared to the hazardous products, one 
of the major goals of the Saffire VI flight was to provid e such a comparison. This in creased understanding of the 
relative impact of various fire impacts can be used to guide spacecraft designs. Other than the thin cellulose samples 
on prior flights, the heat release on Saffire IV and V for the thick PMMA samples was not determined. The first three 
flights have been discussed previously.1,2 and flights IV and V were presented in Urban et al. 2021 3. As described in 
Refs. 1,2, and 3 the prior flights had a significant impact on our understanding of flame spread and growth in long 
duration and large-scale experiments . The prior flights revealed that, under typical spacecraft conditions, fires can 
develop to significant size. Overall, the average temperature and pressure ri se were not particularly of concern 
however the increase in hazardous products (carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide) were enough to be of health 
concern. However, the utility of these results as referen ce data sets for model validation was limited owing to the 
absence of heat release data for the PMMA (high heat rele ase) cases. Improvements were made for the final Saffire 
VI flight to ensure accurate heat re lease measurements. Further analysis of the burning of the structured PMMA 
sample on Saffire V are presented in Ref. 4, and details of the smoke and product transport are presented in Ref. 5. 
II. Experimental Hardware 
The Saffire Flow Unit (SFU) for flights IV - VI was very similar to that used for Saffire I-III 1,2 with the addition of 
side view cameras, and gas sensors in the inlet and outlet to measure the oxygen consumption and production of carbon 
oxides. On Saffire IV and V, the outlet gas sensor location was found to have been moved from the location where 
mixing had been verified and therefore not see a fully mixed outlet flow, so the gas measurements were not useful. 
For Saffire VI it was moved to the verified location at the end of the duct to provide oxygen consumption calorimetry 
needed to enable measurement of the heat release from th e flame. To accommodate the second set of cameras, the 
duct half-height was reduced from 25 cm (for Saffire I-III) to 15 cm for Saffire IV-VI (perpendicular to the sample 
surface) preserving the 45 cm width. The locations of the Saffire units are show n in Figure 1 with the Saffire Flow 
Unit near the end cone of the Cygnus vehicle and the Fa r Field Diagnostics (FFD) containing the smoke cleanup 
system and smoke sensors was installed in a mid-deck lo cker accommodation location adjacent to the hatch. Six

and V, the tests were conducted in a rectangular flow tunnel that was 30 cm high by 45 cm wide by 109 cm long. The 
ends of the ducts were equipped with flow straightener s that connected to plenums. The inlet and outlet ducts 
connected to these plenums and were parallel to the flow duct producing a folded geometry. These ducts enabled flow 
mixing and measurement of the temperature and concentrations of oxygen, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide on 
the inlet and outlet. The flow was induced by a fan in the inlet duct and measured by a vane anemometer at the entrance 
of the inlet duct. The samples were affixed to a metal frame (Figure 2) in the middle of the duct. Similar to Saffire IV 
& V, the sample materials were: “SIBAL” fabric (75% cotton and 25% fiberglass)1 with a total area density of 18.05 
mg/cm2; or flat, cast, polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) (either one-sided 5 mm thick or two-sided (10 mm thick). 
The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper. The 
exhaust gases exited the SFU and entered the forward port standoff of the spacecraft. 
The overall flow in the spacecraft carried the gases to the FFD in the hatch area. The 
FFD contained aerosol and sp ecies diagnostics and a sm oke cleanup system. More 
details of the smoke transport and preliminary FFD results are in Fortenberry et al.5. 
III. Results and Their Fire Safety Implications 
Representative front-view images of the flames are shown in Figure 3. Overall, the 
flame growth and spread were consistent with prior Saffire flights discussed 
previously3. The SIBAL sample (left image) achieved a steady size and spread rate 
quite rapidly where the two PMMA samples grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced. This continued 
growth is evident in Figure 4 where the outlet duct temperature rises continuously. Likewise, the oxygen consumption 
(Fig. 5) and the CO and CO2 (Fig. 6) concentrations at the SFU outlet increase continuously until the flow is reduced 
at 1120 seconds. At the same time the temperatures and gas temperature at the outlet of the SFU outlet is significant 
(70 °C) the temperature near the FFD (z enith) only changes slightly from the prior baseline. The CO and CO 2 levels 
are also very high exiting the SFU, but they are also attenuated at the location of the FFD (Fig. 6). The increase at the 
FFD is reported in Table 2. Since carbon dioxide scrubbing only occurred twice on the Saffire flights and there was 
limited carbon monoxide removal, the values reported here are the increases in the average concentration in the space 
craft due to each test. 
Figure 5 presents the heat releas e calculated from the oxygen consum ption using the method of Huggett 6 where 
the heat release is estimated for a wide range of combustible s to be 13.1 kJ per gram of oxygen consumed. The heat 
release can be seen to be consistent with the radiometer. These results are tabulated in Table 2 with the thin fuel results 
from Saffire IV and V and all the successful ignitions from Saffire VI. The fires were ge nerally of 1.5 to 3 kW in 
intensity which is a small fire by terrestrial standards. The table also includes the heat release calculated using the fuel 
consumption rate for the thin materials. For the thick materials, much of the material burning is from the surface which 
cannot be detected by the cameras, so it is not possible to estimate the heat release from the flame imaging. For the 
VI-2 sample (SIBAL) both methods were used and agree within 15% which is reasonable for this type of analysis.

Figure 7 presents the smoke concentrations at the FFD 
and the response of a terrestrial ionization detector. The 
smoke levels can be seen to rise rapidly and subsequently 
decrease, presumably due to particle loss from impaction 
on multiple surfaces. Selecting 1 mg/m3 as a relatively 
tight alarm threshold, the FFD detector reached that 
threshold at 981 seconds. By this point, much of the 
hazardous gas release had occurred. This is comparable to 
predictions based on smoke versus hazardous product 
emission by overheated materials9. Although the CO and 
CO2 diluted rapidly in these tests, the increases observed 
from these tests are quite significant from a toxicology standpoint. For carbon monoxide, NASA establishes a 
Spacecraft Maximum Allowed Concentration (SMAC) value based on the exposure duration. For carbon monoxide, 
the 1-hour SMAC is 425 ppm, and the 24-hour SMAC is 100 ppm7. For carbon dioxide, which is prevalent in manned 
spacecraft, the limits are established differently in NASA-STD-30018 which limits the 1-hour average CO2 partial 
pressure to no more than 3 mm Hg. As can be seen in Table 2, the allowable CO2 level was exceeded by both of the 
PMMA tests on Saffire VI. For carbon monoxide the levels were well above the 24-hour SMAC and quite close to the 
1-hour level.

6 
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
 
IV. Conclusion 
Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 
19 cubic meters. Despite these fires, the temperature only increased significantly very near to the fire itself. However, 
the ambient concentrations of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide rose significantly with the PMMA tests exceeding 
the 1-hour carbon dioxide limit and the 24-hour carbon monoxide limit. The smoke from the fire event was readily 
detected by an ionization detector and a light scattering system but a typical alarm threshold was only achieved at 981 
seconds. By this time most of the hazardous gas release had occurred. Collectively these results demonstrate that the 
human hazard from a fire in a spacecraft is very similar to terrestrial fires wh ere the heat from the fire is not the 
principal hazard and rather the smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern. These results are helpful for 
defining fire response approaches for spacecraft. Further wo rk will be needed to extend these results to the partial 
gravity environment expected on future mission to the moon and Mars. Additional analysis and modeling of these fire 
scenarios will be the topic of future articles.

The authors acknowledge the support of the NASA Mars Campaign Office, for the sponsorship of the Spacecraft 
Fire Safety Demonstration Project and the Saffire experime nts. In addition, the authors acknowledge the support of

Conclusions
21
• Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft
with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters.
• The temperature only increased significantly very near to the fire itself.
• Ambient concentrations of carbon monoxide exceeded the the 24 ‐hour carbon
monoxide limit. (for PMMA tests)
• Ambient concentrations of carbon dioxide exceeded the 1 ‐hour carbon dioxide limit
(for PMMA tests)
• The smoke was readily detected at 981 seconds (after most of the hazardous gas
release had occurred)
• The human hazard from a fire in a spacecraft is very similar to terrestrial fires where
the heat from the fire is not the principal hazard and rathe the smoke and gaseous
products are a much greater concern.

54th International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2025-156 
13 - 17 July 2025, Prague, Czech Republic 
 
 
Vehicle Modeling During the Burn Events in the Saffire VI 
Experiments 
Justin Niehaus1, John Brooker2, David Urban3, Gary Ruff4 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 44135, USA 
 
In order to design a fire -safe environment inside a spacecraft, knowledge of the transport of heat and 
combustion products in a reduced gravity environment is needed. After a resupply mission to the ISS, the 
Saffire project provided large -scale fire data in a microgravity environment inside of Northrup Grumman’s 
Cygnus vehicle. Solid materials were burned, including a thin cotto n-based sample and thick thermoplastic 
samples, to study a large -scale fire’s effect on a spacecraft. Sensors were placed in Cygnus that measured 
temperature and species concentration at four different standoffs, as well as nadir and zenith locations. 
Pyrosim was used to develop a model to predict the three burn events from Saffire VI using inlet and outlet 
data from the Saffire payload . The convective heat transfer coefficient between the cargo and the cabin air 
that was previously calibrated in the Saffire V model was used to predict the temperature response in the 
Saffire VI burn events. Good predictions of the CO 2 and temperature responses for the remote sensors 
throughout Cygnus were realized.

content:
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
2 
I. Introduction 
ire events present some of the most catastrophic risks to a spacecraft. Previous programs such as Apollo and 
Skylab have undergone full -scale fire testing to help quantify this risk 1-3. It is also standard practice in ground 
systems and submarines4,5. As planned oxygen levels in spacecraft begin to rise, it is important to have full -scale fire 
tests to help determine the spread of heat and combustion products. The Saffire project has provided such data in a 
microgravity environment. The sixth campaign , which took place on Northrop Grumman ’s (NG) Cygnus vehicle 
after undocking from a resupply mission to the ISS, burned a cotton -based fabric, two Polymethyl (Methacrylate) 
(PMMA) samples and attempted to burn a Nomex fabric. The data collected from these tests, such as flame 
temperature and spread velocity will be useful to combustion scientists and fire-safety engineers in designing a safer 
spacecraft. 
The first three Saffire campaigns focused primarily on the large -scale flame spread inside the Saffire payload 6-9, 
while the next three Saffire campaigns expanded the experiments to investigate the effect of a fire on the spacecraft. 
Sensors were placed throughout the vehicle t o measured temperature and species concentration, such as CO 2. These 
far-field gas and particle sensors will provide data that will increase understanding of smoke plume and combustion 
product transport within an orbiting vehicle 10-13. In addition to the burn events, the test campaign includes flow 
visualization events, CO 2 scrubs, and gas releases. Six remote sensors (RS) were utilized in Saffire IV -VI to 
measure temperature and product concentration at various locations in the cabin. A far-field device (FFD) was also 
placed in the zenith section , representing the cabin’s average temperature and species concentration s. All Saffire IV 
through VI campaigns used a cotton-based fuel and PMMA for the burn events. 
This paper presents the development of a model of the Cygnus vehicle during the Saffire VI experimental 
campaign and the simulation of the three burn events. The vehicle’s geometry and the trash and cargo placement 
after the resupply mission were determined from a map provided by NG, as well as photographs taken by the ISS 
crew. Inlet and outlet sensor data from the Saffire payload was used to calculate the heat input and species 
generation rate from Saffire to the Cygnus vehicle. The effective convective heat transfer between the cargo and the 
cabin air that was calibrated in the work describing model development of Saffire V is also used in this work 14. The 
primary verification mechanism of the model was temperature and CO 2 data provided at the RS locations. 
Developing verified models using full-scale fire tests is an excellent way to gain knowledge of the unknown and 
move towards a safer environment in space. 
II. Saffire Experiment 
The Saffire campaign of experiments ha s taken place on the NG Cygnus vehicle during a resupply mission to the 
ISS. Figure 1 shows a schematic of the Saffire experiment within the Cygnus vehicle without the trash and cargo 
that form standoffs for heat and combustion product transfer. Vital instrumentation and the vehicle Environmental 
Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) are illustrated. The size of the pressure vessel is nearly 3 meters in 
diameter by 4 meters in length. 
 
Figure 1. Schematic of Cygnus vehicle without forward side pallet foam. 
F

In between the arrival and departure of the Cygnus vehicle from the ISS, trash and cargo were placed to make a 
free air volume that would allow for control of the oxygen concentration when O2 bottles are released in between 
specified events in the campaign. The placement of the cargo, shown in Figure 2, creates channels or standoffs that 
transport heat and smoke from the Saffire payload at the nadir end of the vehicle to the zenith end of the vehicle. In 
the model, a mass generation rate (MGR) and a heat addition rate (HAR) are applied to the Saffire outlet, which has 
a surface area of 50 cm2, to apply heat and combustion products into the domain. 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 2. Saffire Experiment Model. A) This view shows the Cygnus vehicle on the forward side, highlighting 
the forward port standoff without the pallet foam. Heat and combustion products flow through the standoff over 
RS3 and into the zenith section where RS6 and the FFD are located, and the air gets recycled through the Cygnus 
ECLSS system. B) This view shows the Cygnus vehicle on the aft side, highlighting the aft port standoff without 
the pallet foam. Air flows out of the ECLSS outlet where RS1 is located and into the aft port standoff where the 
Saffire inlet and RS4 are located. 
 
 Nine events occurred during the Saffire VI experimental campaign, including the three burn events that are 
simulated in this work. These events are described in Table 1 . Similar to previous Saffire campaigns, Saffire VI 
started with pulling cabin air through the FFD to scrub the vehicle of CO2. A scrub was also performed during event 
7, between the two PMMA burn events. During event 2, CO 2 was released into the vehicle to calculate the free 
volume in the cabin and aid in analyzing the O 2 that would need to be released during the burn events. HCl was also 
released during event 2 to study acid gas adsorption to surfaces. After all the planned burns were completed, a flow 
visualization test was performed during 9 to determine any major differences in the Saffire Flow Unit (SFU) from 
event 3. An attempt to burn Nomex occurred during event 4, but no ignition was successful. Event 5 burned SIBAL 
fabric at 31.0% O 2 and is the first event simulated in this work. This work also simulates the two -sided PMMA burn 
and one-sided PMMA burn in events 6 and 8 , respectively. The initial atmospheric conditions for the experimental 
campaign at the start of the burn events were 54.1 kPA and 31.0% oxygen, with a temperature of approximately 
24.3°C. 
III. Modeling 
A model was developed to predict the effect of the three burn events of the Cygnus vehicle by utilizing the Fire 
Dynamics Simulator (FDS), a code developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST ). This 
code is optimized for large -eddy turbulent simulations and for low -speed flows usually found in compartment 
fires17. The graphical interface that was used to develop the vehicle model is Pyrosim TM 18. Figure 2 provides a 
picture of this model , highlighting the important flow boundary conditions and sensors . This geometry was

sensitivity analysis was completed to determine the effect of mesh size on accuracy of results. 
The model was primarily compared to the experiments using the CO 2 and temperature readings at the locations 
of the six remote sensors. All six of these sensors can be seen in Figure 1, while the cargo hides RS2 and RS5 in 
Figure 2 , which has also been described in detail in previous papers about Saffire IV and V 14-16. The initial 
temperature of the cabin used for each simulation was the initial temperature of RS3 since that was closest to the 
Saffire outlet , which created the greatest response for comparison. Since the initial temperature of all the remote 
sensors was different in the experiment, the other remote sensor simulation curves were adjusted after the simulation 
to match the initial temperature of the experimental curves. 
 The flow rates used for the boundary conditions in the simulations are provided in Table 2, which are provided 
experimentally. The SFU used a flow rate of 0.028 m 3/s to give a flow of approximately 20 cm/s over the samples 
during times of burning but was ramped down at certain times to promote flame extinguishment. The heat from the 
burn event is captured at the outlet of the Cygnus vehicle by the HAR, which is calculated using the inlet and outlet 
temperature of the SFU. The HAR is calculated using Eq. 1 and demonstrated in Figure 3 using data from event 5. 
Since no flame or combustion properties are inputted into the model, the SFU simply acts as an object that intakes 
cool cabin air and outputs combustion products and hot air. Radiation from the SFU has been assumed to be 
negligible. The initial atmospheric conditions of the Cygnus vehicle are shown in Table 3. The density and specific 
heat of the air used to calculate the HAR are taken at the initial temperature since the outlet of the SFU does not 
exceed 75°C during any burn . Density and specific heat would also be negligibly affected by the increase in main 
combustion products CO2 and H2O in the atmosphere, which reaches no more than 2% during any burn event .

IV. Results and Discussion 
 The initial experimental RS CO2 values for the SIBAL burn event ranged from 5,078 to 5,704 ppm, giving an 
average of 5,381 ppm as given by Table 3. This average value was used for the initial cabin CO2 concentration for 
the event 5 simulation, and then the prediction curves were increased or decreased after the simulation to match the 
initial experimental values. This method was used consistently for event 6 and 8 as well. Figure 6 shows the 
experimental CO 2 results at the six RS locations against the simulated results. An excellent agreement is realized 
once the curves reach ed steady state. This is expected since the CO 2 added to the cabin from the MGR (46.5 g) was 
close to the average CO 2 rise predicted from the six remote sensors (46.8 g). However, the rise in the curve is 
underpredicted by the model at all locations. The largest overshoot of the steady state was RS3 and RS6, which were 
in the direct path of the Saffire outlet flow. RS2 also had a considerable overshoot in the experimental curve , which 
was the RS below RS3, indicating that the flow was able to be diverted down into the starboard standoff . It is clear 
the total amount of CO 2 being delivered into the cabin from Saffire is accurate, but how much reaches various parts 
of the cabin early on during the burn event is inaccurate. If this was a con sistent problem among all three burn 
events, a reasonable conclusion would be that the cargo in the model, especially at the FP standoff needs to be 
adjusted for more flow to go over RS3. However, as will be discussed later, the CO 2 predictions are better during 
event 6 and 8.

experimental model. Besides RS3 and RS6, which are the two in the most direct path of the Saffire outlet flow, there 
was negligible increase in temperature observed during the burn event compared to the sensitivity of the 
thermocouples (+/ - 0.25 °C). Th e model predicted this behavior . The total amount of heat input into the Cygnus 
cabin from Saffire was 124 kJ, which can be calculated by integrating the HAR provided by Eq.1 and Figure 4. This 
agrees well with the cotton sample in Saffire V that provided 110 kJ of heat into the Cygnus vehicle from the 
payload.

Figure 7. Saffire VI Temperature RS response curves during the SIBAL burn test (event 5). 
 
 Figure 8 shows the CO2 RS predictions for the two-sided PMMA burn during event 6 . Excellent agreement 
between prediction and experimental data during the ramp -up phase and steady-state part of the curve is realized for 
all RS locations. Unlike the SIBAL burn, the experimental curves did not overshoot the steady state quite as much, 
which was predicted well in the model. The average increase in the RS data was 8164 ppm, representing a 128.1 g 
increase in CO2. This matches well with the total input from the MGR of 127.8 g. 
 The predictions for RS temperature response during the two -sided PMMA burn are provided in Figure 9. As 
discussed above, only RS3 and RS6, which are in the direct path of the Saffire outlet flow, are shown here since they 
are the only locations that register a temperature response. A good agreement can be seen during the ramp -up phase 
from RS3 and RS6. However, the model does overpredict the max imum temperature. A slight overprediction in 
temperature rise is realized during the SIBAL burn, but it is less noticeable due to the lower heat input. Other 
surfaces besides the trash and cargo are set to be adiabatic in the model , but could be contributing extra heat loss 
(rails, straps, etc.) . Integrating the heat addition rate for this event gave a total energy addition of 497 kJ. This is 
significantly higher than the 233 kJ calculated by a similarly sized PMMA burned during Saffire V. This is likely 
attributed to the higher O2 level in Saffire VI (30.3%) as compared to Saffire V (26.5%).

Figure 10 shows the CO2 RS predictions for the one -sided PMMA burn during event 8. This simulation provides 
the best prediction out of the three burn events, which gives added evidence that the bulk cargo placement and air 
flow within the model are well represented. The average increase in the RS data was 8229 ppm, representing a 1 30.3 
g increase in CO2. This matches well with the total input from the MGR of 130.8 g. 
 
Figure 10. Saffire VI CO2 RS response curves during one-sided PMMA burn test (event 8). 
 
During the two PMMA burn events, a dip in CO2 concentration is observed at the RS2 location after the ramp up 
before quickly recovering. This is not captured by the model. One explanation for this dip is that RS2 is close to the 
ECLSS outlet, which cycles on and off in an attempt to keep the conditions of Cygnus within certain parameters. 
RS3 is also close to the ECLSS outlet, but also close to the hot gas coming from the Saffire outlet, which likely 
dictates its behavior. RS2 can be reasonably assumed to be more influenced by slight changes in vehicle flow 
patterns. 
The temperature RS predictions for the one -sided PMMA burn during event 8 are presented in Figure 11. An 
excellent agreement is realized for RS3, while an over -prediction is realized for RS6. The experimental data for RS6 
appears nonresponsive, similar to the other four locations. While it can be explained why the heat from the fire does 
not reach those locations, RS6 has been responsive in the previous two burn events, as well as burn events in the 
previous two Saffire campaigns 14,15,16. This indicates that RS6 might not be responding properly during the burn 
event.

International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
12 
 
Figure 11. Saffire VI Temperature RS response curves during one-sided PMMA burn test (event 8). 
 
These large -scale experiments and numerical models highlighted the effect a spacecraft fire has on a vehicle, 
such as heat transfer and product mixing. The results from this work demonstrate the feasibility of predicting a fire’s 
impact on a spacecraft’s habitability . These verified model s from Saffire IV to Saffire VI can be used to predict 
“worst-case” fire scenarios. For example, heat release rates from experimental calorimetry experiments, such as Li-
ion batteries, could be provided as input to the model, or the gravity level could be adjusted to study the buoyant 
effects of heat transfer inside a vehicle under lunar or Martian gravity. 
 
V. Conclusions 
 The effects of the Saffire burn events on the Cygnus vehicle were revealed using a model developed using FDS. 
Inlet and outlet sensors to the Saffire payload se rved as the main inputs into the model, while six remote sensors 
placed throughout the cabin served as the verification of the model. In previous work, an effective convective heat 
transfer coefficient of 150 W/m 2-K for the cargo in the standoffs that was calibrated at RS3 for the Saffire V cotton 
burn was used for the three simulations in this work and provided adequate temperature predictions in the cabin. 
Besides a couple of locations during specific burn events, the model predicted CO 2 and temperature throughout the 
cabin well. These results, and the simulations of the other Saffire campaigns demonstrate the feasibility of predicting 
a fire’s impact on the habitability of an orbiting spacecraft. With validated models in place, other fire sources, such 
as Li -ion batteries, can be used to determine the effect of that type of fire in a spacecraft. Similar methods of 
modeling could also be incorporated with other spacecrafts and gravity levels .

content:
53rd International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2024-310 
21 - 25 July 2024, Louisville, Kentucky 
 
Vehicle Modeling during the Burning of Thermally Thick 
Samples in the Saffire V Experiments 
Justin Niehaus1, John Brooker2, David Urban3, Gary Ruff4 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 44135, USA 
 
In order to design a safer spacecraft in terms of fire prevention, detection and cleanup, the transport of 
combustion products and heat must be predicted. Large -scale fire data was provided by the Saffire payload 
within Northrup Grumman’s Cygnus vehicle after a resupply mission to t he ISS. Solid materials, including 
thick thermoplastic samples were ignited to study flame spread and the effect a fire has on a vehicle. Sensors 
that measured species and temperature were placed within Cygnus. A model using Pyrosim was developed to 
predict the thick fuel burn events from Saffire V by using sensor data from Cygnus. The heat transfer 
coefficient between the cabin air and cargo was previously calibrated using the cotton fuel burn event, and 
provided a good prediction of the temperature respon se within the vehicle during the two thick fuel 
experiments. The difference between the Saffire inlet CO2 sensor, and the forward port standoff CO 2 sensor, 
which is the closest to the Saffire outlet, was used as an input into the model. This method provided an excellent 
prediction of the CO2 response in the other parts of the Cygnus.

content:
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
2 
I. Introduction 
spacecraft fire poses one of the greatest risks to the crew and mission success. There is a need to predict the 
consequences of a fire event to reduce the risk for long -duration missions. Most flame spread testing has been 
executed in 1-g or has not been large-scale1,2,3. The Saffire project has provided valuable data on large flame spread 
in a microgravity environment while acting as a test bed for novel gas species sensor technology 3,4. These series of 
experiments have taken place during the end of a resupply mission to the to the International Space Station (ISS) on 
Northrop Grumman’s (NG) Cygnus vehicle. After Cygnus undocks from the ISS, the experiments take place and the 
data is downlinked before destructive re-entry into the earth’s atmosphere. The data collected will help designers and 
modelers predict the effects of a large-scale fire in a microgravity environment in order to design a safer spacecraft. 
 The focus of the first three Saffire missions was on flame spread 5,6,7,8, while the Saffire IV and V expanded the 
experiment to include gas release events and sensors throughout the vehicle. These sensors include diagnostic tools to 
determine the temperature increase due to the fire and transport of combustion products such as CO 2. The data 
collected from these far-field gas and particle sensors will provide insight into smoke plume and combustion product 
transport within the vehicle9,10,11. The test events include flow visualization at the beginning and end of the campaign, 
CO2 scrubs, gas releases, and burn events. Both Saffire IV and V experiments utilized six remote sensors (RS) spread 
throughout Cygnus that measure temperature and product concentration, such as CO 2, as well as a Far Field Device 
(FFD) that is representative of average t emperature and species concentration in the cabin. Both Saffire experiments 
had cotton based and Polymethyl (Methacrylate) (PMMA) samples as fuel for the burn events. 
The focus of this paper is on the two PMMA burn events in Saffire V. Similar to previous work12,13, the effect of 
burning the PMMA samples on the vehicle temperature and combustion product spread are predicted. The geometry 
and cargo configuration for Saffire V is the same that was used in previous work that explored the cotton sample in 
Saffire V13. The effective convective heat transfer between the cargo and the cabin air that was calibrated in that same 
work is also used in this work, which was calibrated to fit the closest RS to the Saffire outlet. The development of this 
model will aid in the prediction of heat and mass transfer throughout a spacecraft after a fire. 
 
II. Saffire Experiment 
Saffire I – V have all take n place on the NG Cygnus vehicle . The experimental data collection and downlink ing 
happened after the cargo from the resupply mission was unloaded onto the ISS and the trash was packed into Cygnus. 
A schematic of a nearly empty Cygnus vehicle is provided in Figure 1 before the cargo is loaded , highlighting the 
Saffire payload and instruments used to collect data. The pressure vessel is approximately 4 meters in length and 3 
meters in diameter. The Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) recirculated flow throughout the 
vehicle by taking air from the zenith side, near the (FFD), and expelling it on the nadir side where Saffire is located. 
 
Figure 1. Schematic of Cygnus vehicle with FFD and Saffire payload.

content:
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
3 
Trash and cargo were placed by the crew in a manner which constructed interconnected channels of approximately 
triangular shape form, as shown in Figure 2. These channels, referred to as standoffs, transported species, smoke, and 
heat from the outlet of the Saffire payload during a gas release or burn event. The heat addition rate (HAR) and the 
mass generation rate (MGR), which supply the heat and combustion products from the Saffire payload to the Cygnus 
cabin, are applied to the Saffire outlet, which has a surface area of 50 cm2. The flow of gas generally went towards 
the zenith section of Cygnus from the Saffire outlet through the forward port (FP) standoff. From there, heat and 
species would either diffuse towards the other three standoffs, or flow back to the nadir section through the ECLSS 
system. 
 
 
Figure 2. Saffire Experiment Model. A) This view shows the forward side of the Cygnus vehicle where the outlet 
of the Saffire payload can be viewed. This highlights the most direct path of the flow through the FP standoff, where 
RS is positioned, to the zenith section where RS6 and the FFD are lo cated. B) This view shows the aft side of the 
Cygnus vehicle where the inlet of Saffire takes in air from the aft port standoff, where RS4 is located, and the ECLSS 
outlet, where RS1 is located. 
 
 
Table 1 presents the experimental events completed in the Saffire V campaign. Similar to Saffire IV, Saffire V 
started with a CO 2 scrub by pulling cabin air through the FFD. Event 2 released CO 2 in the cabin to help determine 
the free volume used to calculate the amount of oxygen that needed to be added between b urns. In addition to CO 2, 
HF was released to study its decay in the atmosphere since it tends to adsorb to surfaces more than other combustion 
products such as CO2. A flow visualization test was performed to determine any major differences in the Saffire Flow 
Unit (SFU) after all the planned burns were completed in event 3 and 9 . Event 6 burned a one-sided PMMA, while 
event 8 burned a thicker structured PMMA with grooves and ridges of increasing dimension or separation 9. The 
atmosphere for the experimental campaign was approximately 0.71 atm and 29% oxygen, with an initial temperature 
of approximately 24.1°C. 
 
III. Modeling 
By using Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), a code developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology 
(NIST), a model was constructed that predicted the effect of the PMMA burn events from Saffire V on the Cygnus 
Vehicle. The focus of this large-eddy turbulent simulation code is the low-speed flow created by a compartment fire 
as well as smoke and heat transfer14. PyrosimTM 15 is the graphical interface that was used to run the FDS simulations 
and develop the vehicle model. A picture of this model highlighting the FFD, SFU, ECLSS system and RS locations 
is provided by Figure 2. A cargo placement map and photographs provided by NG were used to construct the geometry 
in Pyrosim, as was discussed in a previous paper discussing the cotton burning sample (event 5)13.

content:

The six remote sensors served as the main comparisons between the model and experiments. While all remote 
sensors are visible in Figure 1 without the cargo, some of the remote sensors are not visible due to the stowed material 
in Figure 2. Starting with the nadir section of Cygnus where Saffire is lo cated, RS1 is positioned in the bulkhead. RS 
2 -5 are in the standoffs at the midplane (zenith to nadir). Starting at the forward starboard (FS) where RS2 is located, 
the others are numbered by moving counterclockwise about the other standoffs: RS3 - forward port (FP), RS4 - aft 
port (AP), and RS5 - aft starboard (AS). RS6 is in the zenith near the hatch. In both burn events, the initial RS reading 
for the CO 2 was within 5% of the average, and hence thi s average was used for the initial CO 2 in the simulation of 
each event. The initial temperature reading of the RS varied more than this in each event, hence the initial reading of 
RS3 was used as the initial temperature of the cabin since that is the RS th at created the greatest response. The 
simulation curves of the other remote sensors were then adjusted so the initial values matched. 
 Table 2 gives the flowrates used within Cygnus and Saffire. The flow rate of 0.028 m3/s utilized by the SFU gave 
a flow of 20 cm/s over the samples, which is ramped down at certain times to extinguish the flame. In order to capture 
the effect of the burn event on the temperature of Cygnus, the HAR was calculated using the inlet and outlet 
temperature of the SFU, as given by Eq. 1, and demonstrated in Figure 3 using data from event 8. This method was 
utilized in previous work12,13, and is described as the sensible enthalpy rise method highlighted by the Society of Fire 
Protection Engineering Handbook 16. No combustion or flame properties are modeled, hence the Saffire payload is 
modeled simply as an object that takes in cool cabin air and outputs hot air and combustion products. Any radiation 
from the Saffire unit or the hot exhaust gases has been assumed to be negligib le. Other properties of the initial 
atmospheric conditions of the Cygnus vehicle are provided by Table 3. The properties of air at initial conditions (24°C) 
are used to calculate the HAR since the temperature at the outlet does not exceed 45°C, and the difference in the main 
combustion products (CO2 and H2O) are only in the 1000s of parts per million (ppm), making a negligible difference 
in cp and density between SFU inlet and outlet conditions.

IV. Results and Discussion 
 
 The initial experimental CO2 values for burn event 6 ranged from 7,375 to 7,973 ppm, giving an average of 7,597 
ppm as given by Table 3. This average value was used for the initial value for the event 6 simulation, and then the 
prediction curves were incr eased or decreased to match the initial experimental values. Figure 7 shows the model 
prediction with the experimental results for the CO2 response of the six remote sensors. An excellent agreement is 
realized in each case. There is slight over prediction during the increasing part of the curve in RS 3 and a moderate 
overprediction of this part of the curve in RS6, which are in the direct path of the flow from Saffire from the FP 
standoff. While the model has solid trash and cargo lining the edges of the FP standoff, these solids are porous in 
reality, allowing for more mixing of air and combustion products on the way to RS3 and RS6, which would bring the 
peak of the combustion product response down. 
 
 
Figure 7. Saffire V RS CO2 responses during one-sided PMMA burn test (event 6). 
 
Figure 8 provides the temperature prediction during the one-sided PMMA burn . A convective heat transfer 
coefficient of 150 W/m2-K was used for the surfaces, calibrated at RS3 from the cotton burn in the previous work13. 
The model initial condition used the RS3 initial condition (24.1 °C) since that was the RS that had the largest response.

However, the remote sensors ranged from 19.2 to 24.3 °C initially. Since the initial temperatures of the remote sensors 
were all different, the prediction curves were adjusted so that the initial value matched that of each location, in order 
to compare the increase in temperature. There was very little response besides RS3, which increased approximately 1 
degree at the peak and reached steady state at about a half degree increase. There was negligible temperature difference 
in the starboard standoffs (RS2 and RS5) compa red to the sensitivity of the thermocouples (+/ - 0.25°C). This was 
predicted well by the model. 
 Figure 9 presents the RS predictions for the structured PMMA. Excellent agreement is realized again for all RS 
values, especially at steady state where both p rediction and experiment show about a 2,500 ppm increase or a 36% 
increase in CO2 throughout the cabin. The model did predict a larger maximum value of CO 2 for both RS3 and RS6 
which are in the direct flow path of the Saffire combustion products. It is possible that the bags of trash, which are not 
perfectly rigid, partially blocked those sensors, making the CO 2 have to diffuse around the bag to get to the sensor, 
allowing for a smoother response. Fluctuations in both the CO2 and temperature response of the model can be observed 
by the remote sensors within the flow path and are placed in a more open part of the cabin outside of the standoffs, 
such as in RS6. This is likely due to the turbulent nature of the model. The reason these fluctuations are not as 
pronounced in the data is the remote sensors use a pump to suck combustion products the location to the actual sensor. 
Even if it is a small area, it is averaging the concentration around the probe area, likely smoothing out the effect of 
turbulence.

Figure 9. Saffire V RS CO2 responses during structured PMMA burn test (event 8). 
 
 The predictions for RS temperature response during the structured PMMA burn are provided in Figure 10. The 
Saffire V temperatures during the structured PMMA burn, similar t o the one -sided PMMA burn case, provide very 
little response outside of RS3 and RS6, which is predicted by the model. Integrating the heat addition rate from Figures 
4 and 5 provide a total energy addition of 233 and 275 kJ for event 6 and event 8 respectively. Despite this moderate 
difference in total heat added, the temperature response remains nearly the same for both burn events. The results from 
the experiments and model , with regards to the specific spacecraft and test conditions, indicate that the fire does not 
have a large effect on the vehicle temperature, except close to the fire. 
 An interesting phenomenon is observed by looking at the temperature profile in RS4 for both burn cases. The 
experimental profile decreases at some point below the initial temperature. One theory is the ECLSS system on Cygnus 
is known to cycle on an off to keep the conditions of the spacecraft within certain parameters. RS4 is in the direct path 
of the ECLSS system, and on the opposite side of the hot Saffire outlet, which is why it makes sense its profile is 
dictated more by the ECLSS system as opposed to the fire. RS1, which is even closer to the ECLSS outlet, shows a 
less pronounced decrease in temperature, but since it is close to the Saffire outlet, its behavior is more dictated by the 
burn event.

Figure 10. Saffire V RS Temperature responses during structured PMMA burn test (event 8). 
V. Conclusions 
 A FDS code was developed to determine the effects of the Saffire V PMMA burn events on the Cygnus vehicle. 
Measurements of CO 2 and temperature were taken throughout the vehicle, specifically at six RS locations. The 
combustion product generation rates were calculated based on the scaled difference of RS3 and the SFU inlet CO 2 
readings and the stoichiometry of PMMA combustion, while the heat addition rate was calculated based on the inlet 
and outlet Saffire temperatures. Parts of the model cargo were hollowed out in order for the model volume to match 
the volume calculated from the CO2 release events. The convective heat transfer coefficient that was calibrated at RS3 
for the Saffire V cotton burn in previous work was determined to be 150 W/m2-K and gave and excellent prediction 
for both Saffire V PMMA burn events. The model did an excellent job of predicting the CO2 and a reasonable job of 
predicting temperature data. The effect a spacecraft fire has on a vehicle was highlighted by the Saffire data and model, 
such as product mixing and heat transfer. These results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the imp act of a fire 
on the habitability of an orbiting spacecraft.

content:
51st International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2022-278 
10-14 July 2022, St. Paul, Minnesota 
Model Development of Large-Scale Spacecraft Fires during 
the Saffire-IV Experiments 
 
John Brooker1 and Justin Niehaus2 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 44135, USA 
 
An accidental fire can pose dire consequences to crew safety and mission success. The Saffire Project aims 
to investigate large-scale fire behavior in microgravity in order to aid in the prediction of spacecraft fires. These 
series of experiments ignite solid materials within the Northrop Grumman Cygnus vehicle after it departs from 
a resupply mission to the International Space Station. A model of the Cygnus vehicle during the Saffire -IV 
experiment was developed using the commercial software PyroSim. The cargo arranged during the descent 
phase was used for the geometry of the model. In the model, cabin air flows into the Saffire payload while heat 
and combustion species flow out of the Saffire downstream through a standoff to a bed of sensors called the 
Far Field Diagnostic. The temperature sensors near the Saf fire payload were used to determine the heat 
addition rate at the outlet of Saffire, while the details of the combustion and stoichiometry are used to determine 
the species flow at the outlet. Gas measurements previously reported for the Saffire -IV experim ents are 
compared against the simulation results and sources of error are discussed. 
Nomenclature 
A = Sample Area 
AP = Aft Port 
AS = Aft Starboard 
ECLSS = Environmental Control and Life Support System 
FDS = Fire Dynamics Simulator 
FP = Forward Port 
FS = Forward Starboard 
HAR = Heat Addition Rate 
ISS = International Space Station 
MLR = Mass Loss Rate 
NG = Northrop Grumman 
NIST = National Institute of Standards and Technology 
PMMA = Polymethyl Methacrylate 
SCM = Secondary Constant Mass 
SCV = Secondary Constant Volume 
RS = Remote Sensor 
SFU = Saffire Flow Unit 
SR = Spread Rate 
SIBAL = Solid Inflammatory Boundary at Low-Speed fabric 
 
I. Introduction 
fire inside of a spacecraft poses a catastrophic threat to crew health and mission success. Most of the fire testing 
that has been performed to design vehicles and determine material flammability limits ha s been performed on 
earth in 1-g or has been small in scale1,2,3,. The Saffire project aims to fill knowledge gaps of large-scale flame spread 
in microgravity. Saffire experiments have also provided opportunities to test novel gas species sensor technology in a 
realistic flight configuration, as well as a way to obtain data on the length of time to detection and detector signal level 
for a species release event in a spacecraft cabin . Five Saffire experiments have been conducted so far with one more, 
Saffire-VI, scheduled to fly in 2023. All will take place on Northrop Grumman’s (NG) Cygnus vehicle following the

content:
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
2 
completion of its resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS). The experiments and data downlink take 
place during the three weeks between undocking from the ISS and burning up during destructive reentry. 
The first three Saffire experiments focused on flame spread to compare large-scale microgravity tests to previous 
small-scale and 1-g tests4-8. Saffire IV and V incorporated gas species release events and other diagnostics tools (e.g., 
far-field trace gas and particle sensors) with the aim of gaining a deeper understanding of smoke plume transport and 
combustion products on the vehicle.9,10,11. Saffire IV has various events that include a CO 2 scrub, flow visualization, 
gas release and burn events. The burn events include a cotton/fiber-glass blend known as SIBAL and transparent rigid 
plastic polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), which is often substituted for glass, such as in shatter proof windows. Far 
field diagnostics were added for measuring smoke particles and combustion products in order to assess the impact of 
fire on the vehicle, such as product mixing. Six remote sensors (RS) that measure CO2 concentration and temperature 
are also located throughout Cygnus. 
It is important to understand the impact a fire has on the vehicle and the crew . The data collected by Saffire will 
help modelers develop tools to better predict the effect of a fire on a spacecraft . This work aims to develop a model 
that can predict the burn events in Saffire IV. The model is a closed pressure chamber of the Cygnus vehicle filled 
with trash and cargo after the resupply mission of NG -13 is completed. In the model, the Saffire unit inputs ambient 
temperature cabin air and outputs hot air and species to imitate the effect of the combustion events. The heat addition 
rate (HAR) outputted by Saffire is derived using the difference between the experimentally captured inlet and outlet 
temperature of Saffire. Downstream of Saffire, near the hatch of Cygnus (zenith) is the Far Field Diagnostic (FFD), 
where particle and combustion gas sensors are located. The model compares the experimental temperature and CO 2 
at the six RS locations throughout Cygnus and the FFD at the opposite end of Cygnus from Saffire. 
II. Saffire Experiment 
All Saffire experiments have taken place on the NG Cygnus vehicle after a resupply mission to the ISS. The first 
three Saffire missions focused on the large-scale flame spread in order to determine if tests conducted in 1 -g and at 
smaller scales are relevant to large-scale microgravity flame tests. The next three S affire tests share that focus, while 
extending to the smoke plume transport and the fire’s effect on the vehicle. 
Figure 1 shows a schematic of a Cygnus vehicle with Saffire and the FFD but with the cargo hidden. Cygnus is a 
pressure vessel that is approximately 4 meters in length by 3 meters in diameter. The Environmental Control and Life 
Support System (ECLSS) that circulates air throughout the cabin takes air in by the side with the FFD (zenith), and 
expels it on the side near Saffire, (nadir). 
The crew maintained a generally prescribed free-air volume in the vehicle, consisting of interconnected channels of 
approximate triangular geometry, made out of trash and cargo, which transported heat, species and smoke during the 
campaign events. This produced four triangular stand offs for the transfer of gas from nadir to zenith end cones, and 
back through the recirculation of air through the ECLSS system. 
 
Figure 1. Schematic of Saffire experiment. The Saffire payload (left) is integrated into the Cygnus vehicle (center). 
During the experiment, the effect of the fire on the vehicle is determined in part by the Far Field Diagnostic (right) .

specifically on the burn events, test 4 SIBAL burn and the test 5 PMMA burn. Both burns were performed at one 
atmosphere pressure, 21% O2 and with concurrent flow relative to the sample through the SFU. 
III. Modeling
