been neglected. Thus, the integrated flame emission
can be written as Si = ¯Hi∆l where the overbar de-
notes the mean along the line-of-sight. As the optical
length is equal for the different broadbands, consid-
ering a mean Hi (or for constant properties along the
optical path), a ratio of deconvoluted signalsHi (ΘH)
is equivalent to a ratio of integrated signals Si (ΘS,
see Fig. 1 for reference of where the ratios are com-
puted). This hypothesis is usually not fulfilled, but
alleviates the need for knowledge of flame geometry.
Therefore, its impact on the retrieved temperature is
assessed on a well-known flame geometry. Although
the nature and geometry of the flames compared here
is different to those encountered during the µg exper-
iments, the purpose of this section is to address the
validity of the established assumptions in the pres-
ence of high temperature and high soot volume frac-
tion gradients along the medium.
A laminar coflow ethylene-air diffusion flame was
used for validating the methodology. Details of the
experiments, calibration and simulations used in this
section can be found elsewhere [21]. The deconvo-
luted values of Hi are obtained either from exper-
imental measurements or synthetic signals of Si at
three broad spectral bands. A synthetic validation is
first performed. For this purpose, simulations of the
signals captured by the RGB camera channels were
conducted, using simulated values of temperature and
soot volume fraction from a CoFlame simulation [22]
as described in detail in [21]. The line-of-sight inte-
grated signals can then be treated to retrieve a tem-
perature that can be compared against the reference
temperature provided by the simulation, as done in
Fig. 3. The retrieved temperatures using deconvolu-
tion are very similar to the reference. The differences
are attributed to the neglect of self-absorption for this
procedure, a hypothesis that is required for the model.
This effect is not important for low optical thickness,
but may cause differences around 100 K for high soot
volume fraction zones [23]. The temperatures re-
trieved without deconvoluting the signals are shown
on the second row of Fig. 3(a). These temperatures
are always higher than those using deconvolution, es-
pecially in zones near the flame centerline, where the
flame optical thickness is highest and the hypothesis
of constant properties along the camera line-of-sight
is less correct. More detailed results supporting the
discussion are shown on Fig. 3(b) through four radial
profiles at different heights above the burner (HABs).
Although the temperature retrieved without perform-
ing the deconvolution procedure is incorrectly deter-
mined as compared to the reference, its prediction is
within 100 K and results on a higher temperature,

3.3. Calibration procedure
All the cameras used in the Saffire Experiments

bration standards using equipments certified in accor-

fied blackbody source(Mikron M360) with tempera-
tures that ranged between 973 and 1373 K. As part
of this calibration procedure, images are taken in raw
and bmp format under conditions of operation simi-
lar to those considered for the experiments. Simulta-
neously, multiple image settings are also considered.
More specifically, the exposure time was varied be-
tween 60 and 29997, and the gain value was changed
between 0 and 39 dB.
During the experiments, images of the flame as
it spreads over the solid are recorded in RAW and
JPEG formats. RAW images can then be postpro-
cessed and converted to TIFF to proceed with the
application of the broadband two color pyrometry
(B2CP) technique presented above to probe temper-
ature fields from the frames captured within visible
spectrum. To ensure that no additional processing and
alterations to the image are done during the conver-
sion process, the (B2CP) technique is applied to the
calibration images to verify the procedure. For this,
the RHS of Eq. 4 was solved using the emissivity and
temperature of the blackbody calibration source in-
stead of the Em/λ and Ts terms, respectively. Figure
5(a) shows a comparison between theoretical intensi-
ties ratios (Si/Sj) presented as solid line functions
and measured intensity ratios from calibration im-
ages ((Si/Sj)exp)) shown as circular symbols. From
the figure it can be noted that the measured inten-
sity ratio and the expected value at the temperature of
the furnace are clearly different, suggesting that the
camera adds additional processing to the files when
recording them. Furthermore, the intensity of the ob-
ject recorded by the sensor depends directly on the
camera settings used, which during the experiments
were set automatically. Thus, a correction factor is
needed in order to extract appropriate values.
Given the dependence of the intensity data
recorded by the sensor on the camera settings, a cor-
rection factor was determined as a function of the ra-
tio of intensities for each color ratio considered as
β = (Si/Sj)(Si/Sj)exp . (5)
The correction factor functions obtained from the cal-
ibration images at know temperatures are shown in
Fig. 6. It should be mentioned that, due to limita-
tions of the equipment higher temperatures could not
be tested during the calibration and thus an extrap-
olation of the data had to be made. The correction
factor functions, β, are then used to correct the ratio
of SIBAL camera images ((Si/Sj)exp)] which will
then be replaced on the LHS of Eq. 4. Figure 5(a) also
shows the corrected intensity ratios using the correc-

the flame spreads over the composite fabric, it con-
sumes most of the cotton, leaving behind the fiber-
glass mesh and some smoldering cotton residue. Dur-
ing this process, periodic images are taken of the
spread process. These images are later corrected for
perspective issues and processed to extract soot tem-
perature. Considering that the initial purpose of the
images recorded during the experiments was to use
the data to visualize the flame and track its evolu-
tion over time, i.e., pyrolysis length, flame size, etc.,
the cameras used in the experiments were set to auto-
matically modify their settings to better visualize the
flames. Due to this, some of the images would present
high levels of saturation, particularly near the center
of the flame, making it impossible to extract any rele-
vant information in the area. Thus, when performing
the color pyrometry ratios, channels green and blue
were preferred for determining the temperature.
Fig. 7: Comparison between the original data [5] (top),
B2CP temperature fields (center) and the temperature mea-
surement from the thermocouple (bottom).
Figure 7 shows the temperature field of the flame as
determined by the B2CP technique. This image was
selected to match the instant of time that the thermo-
couple measuring above the surface, in the fire plume,
reaches the peak recorded value ( T Cpeak), as shown
in the bottom portion of Fig. 7. The thermocouple
measurements have been corrected for radiation and
convection effects [25]. From the figure it is seen
that at the exact point of the thermocouple position,
B2CP gives a temperature close to 1369 K which is
relatively close to the 1426 K recorded by the device
at the same instant in time. This comparison vali-
dates both the technique and the correction functions
previously determined. The relative uncertainty asso-
ciated with the thermocouple reading has been esti-
mated following the work of Ren et al. [26]. A rela-
tive uncertainty for a type-R thermocouple of 0.25%
is considered, thus resulting in an overall correction
for radiation and convection effects of ± 6 K in the
measured value. The error for B2CP technique was
computed from a Monte Carlo propagation analysis,
considering a conservative error of 5% on the signal
ratio ΘG/R, resulting in 117 K of uncertainty for tem-
perature determination. With this, both measurements
are comparable within the error margin.
Figure 8 shows flame images at different selected
times after the test is initiated and ignition achieved,
together with the corresponding temperature fields.
At first, the flame shape for the large-scale sample
looks a bit distorted because the camera’s field of
view does not reach the entire sample holder. For
the initial 120 s, the flame kept its symmetrical shape
between the top and bottom part. After that, the top
flame seems to be pushed closer to the surface, getting
longer than the bottom flame. Towards the end of the
spread, only small smoldering spots were left burn-
ing some of the unconsumed fuel. The temperature
fields of Fig. 8 show that during the spread process
the flame temperature does not change very signifi-
cantly, staying constant at an average of 1305 K soon
after ignition and throughout the entire test. Lastly,
when looking at the results presented in Figs. 7 and
8, the reader should keep in mind that no tempera-

flame (the most luminous part) because the saturation

locations. Given that issue, temperature values were
artificially set to 0 to be able to plot the entire flame

5. Concluding remarks
The present paper presents a methodology and
analysis of broadband two color pyrometry technique
applied to a spreading diffusion flame in micrograv-
ity conditions. The proposed model is validated us-
ing numerical simulations and experimental measure-
ments of well-known coflow flames. The validation
process supports the major assumptions of the analy-
sis and shows that the technique provides an accept-
able average temperature, although it is biased to-
ward higher values. The processed RAW data from
the recorded images results in temperature in accor-
dance with thermocouple measurements of the plume
obtained during the experiment. The information ex-
tracted from the recorded images provides additional
insights of the flame characteristics observed during
the Saffire IV experiments, showing that the flame
temperature remains relatively constant during the en-
tire spread process. The application of this technique
in this configuration can be coupled with soot volume
fraction measurements in order to estimate the radia-
tive heat flux emitted by the flame, in order to design

55th International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2026-092 
12 - 16 July 2026, Rio Grande, Puerto Rico 
 
 
Spacecraft Fire Safety Predictions using Validated Saffire 
Model 
Justin Niehaus1, David Urban2, Gary Ruff3, Gordon Berger4 and John Easton5 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 44135, USA 
 
A model developed using Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) that aimed to determine the effect of a fire in a 
spacecraft was v alidated by data collected during the Saffire campaign. The model used inlet and outlet 
temperatures and CO 2 concentrations of the Saffire payload where fire spread was taking place to determine 
the amount of heat and combustion products that made it into Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus vehicle. The 
model was then validated using six remote sensors in various places in the vehicle, as well as a far field device 
(FFD) in the open zenith section that was representative of average vehicle values. Th e current work focuses 
on using the model to predict fire safety scenarios. One simulation aimed to determine the fate of HCl, which 
sticks to surfaces. The model prediction showed that the HCl was removed from the atmosphere rapidly. This 
compared well against the FFD data in the Saffire VI campaign event where a bottle of 5% HCl was released 
into the vehicle. An additional simulation where the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) 
was shut off once the FFD reached 5 ppm of HCl showed that HCl stay ed in the atmosph ere considerably 
longer. Continuing the simulation with the ECLSS activated and after temperatures returned to their initial 
conditions, resulted in a rapid removal of HCL similar to that observed in the original HCl release scenario 
model. Finally, a simulation that used the heat release rate from a lithium-ion battery test to determine the 
effect it would have on a spacecraft was performed . This simulation used a heat addition rate that is 
considerably higher than what was determined from the burning of s olid fuels in the Saffire campaign and 
hence produced a non-trivial temperature increase in more locations within the vehicle.

Cp = specific heat 
ECLSS = Environmental Control and Life Support System

HEPA = High-Efficiency Particulate Air

k = conductive heat transfer coefficient 
LIB = Lithium Ion Battery 
lpm = liters per minute 
MFC = Mass Flow Controller 
MGR = Mass Generation Rate 
NG = Northrop Grumman 
NIST = National Institute of Standards and Technology 
PMMA = Polymethyl Methacrylate 
ppm = parts per million 
psig = pounds per square inch gauge 
RS = Remote Sensor

I. Introduction 
lanning effective responses to a fire on a spacecraft is o ne of the most impactful ways to reduce the risk to a 
spacecraft’s mission success and crew safety. Oxygen levels for planned missions will be elevated, only adding 
to this risk [1-3]. Increased oxygen reduces prebreathe time requirements and complexity for EVA operations, as well 
as decreases mass required for structural containment due to smaller pressure differentials between cabin and the 
vacuum of space [3]. Full-scale testing at the planned atmosphere, as implemented in previous space programs [4-6], 
are a way of quantifying the increased risk. This type of fire data was collected during the Saffire project in a 
microgravity environment [7-9]. Over six sets of orbital experiments, the Saffire payload burned thermally thick 
polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) and thin (cotton or solid inflammatory boundary at low -speed fabric (SIBAL)) 
fuels on Northrop Grumman’s (NG) Cygnus vehicle to study flame spread and fire effects on a space craft in a 
microgravity environment. These were carried out after Cygnus undocked from a resupply mission to the International 
Space Station (ISS). 
A computational model of Saffire VI was previously developed and validated against six remote sensors (RS) in 
Cygnus that measured temperature and CO2 during burn events in the Saffire campaign [ 10-13]. The model used the 
CO2 response or the six RS to validate that the trash and cargo placement in the model provided the appropriate flow 
paths, as well as the free volume matched the experimental value. The temperature response of the R S closest to the 
Saffire payload was used to calibrate an effective heat transfer coefficient of the cargo, and validate it against the other 
RS. The work described in this paper uses the validated computational model to predict other spacecraft fire scenarios 
not produced in the Saffire experiments . The first scenario being set of simulations explored acid gas transport with 
the objective of determining the effect flow had on the fate of acid gas in a spacecraft. The second set of simulations 
involved using experimental data from a lithi um-ion battery (LIB) fire, an increasingly relevant fire hazard, with the 
objective of simulating a more energetic fire than what was provided by the Saffire burn event. 
A fire in a spacecraft can create acid gases such as HCl from the burning of electronics, which stick to surfaces 
unlike other combustion products. In addition to the burn events in the Saffire VI experiments , a bottle of HCl was 
released to study the fate of acid gas in a spacecraft. While not measured at the RS locations, it was measured at the 
Far Field Device (FFD) in the zenith section of the cabin, which was representative of average cabin values. To 
complement the microgravity tests, small-scale ground testing was performed to determine the uptake of acid gas by 
typical spacecraft materials, predominantly treated aluminum [14,15]. This uptake rate was applied to the surfaces of 
the Saffire model and the transport to the FFD in the model was compared to the experiment. Once a reasonable 
comparison was observed, additional simulations were performed with the objective to determine the effect on cabin 
flow on the fate of acid gas. A typical recommendation during a fire in spacecraft is to turn off the flo w to prohibit 
oxygen transport to the flame to encourage extinction [ 5, 16 ]. Simulations were run where once HCl reached a 
threshold value, the environmental control and life support system (ECLSS) flow, as well as any flow associated with 
the Saffire Flow Unit (SFU) were shut off to see the effect on the fate of HCl. An additional simulation was run where 
the flow was turned back on once the temperature returned to the initial value. 
The last set simulation used the heat addition rate (HAR) produced from lithium-ion battery (LIB) tests with the 
objective of predicting a relevant fire hazard and a more energetic fire than that produced by the burning of SIBAL 
or PMMA would have on a spacecraft. The heat released into Cygnus from the burn events of Saffire proved to not 
increase the temperature in the vehicle significantly. The ground tests involving LIB fires provided a larger max HAR 
and more overall heat than the Saffire burn events, and hence a hotter cabin. 
II. Experiments 
A. Saffire Microgravity Experiments 
The Saffire campaign of experiments performed large-scale burn events to study the smoke plume and combustion 
product transport within an orbiting vehicl e [7-9]. All six of these set of experiments took place in between separate 
resupply mission s to the ISS and controlled burn up in the atmosphere, giving approximately three days of 
microgravity combustion experimentation and data downlink. Saffire VI, which is the focus of this paper, took place

contained the environmental control and life support system (ECLSS) for maintaining flow conditions, and various 
instrumentation for measuring temperature and combustion product concentrations throughout the vehicle. Figure 1 
gives a schematic of the Cygnus vehicle and Saffire experiments. 
Cargo and trash were placed in Cygnus to create channels to transport heat and combustion products from the 
outlet of Saffire in the nadir section to the zenith section of the spacecraft. This created four different channels, similar 
to the forward port standoff illustrated in Figure 1. Each channel had an RS that measured temperature and combustion 
products, such as CO 2. In order to apply heat and combustion products into the domain , or the gas volume of the 
model, a HAR and a mass generation rate (MGR) are applied to the 50 cm 2 SFU outlet that flows hot air into the 
Cygnus vehicle. 
 
Figure 1. Saffire VI experimental schematic. Dashed box area represents the Cygnus vehicle from the Nadir side 
for a view of the ECLSS outlet, RS1 and RS4 in the Aft Port standoff. Foam is removed in the Forward Port and Aft 
Port standoffs for visualization purposes. RS2 and RS5 are shown outside the foam for visualization purposes. 
 
Nine experimental events took place during the Saffire VI campaign, including four attempted burn events, two 
flow visualization tests, a gas release event, and two CO2 scrubs. The initial atmospheric conditions used in the model 
were the same used during the SIBAL burn of Saffire VI: 54.1 kPA, 31.0% oxygen, and a temperature of 24.3°C . 
More details of the experiment can be found in previous work [7-9].

Experiments to characterize the uptake of acid gas onto surfaces have taken place to support the Saffire project 
and help determine the fate of acid gases after a spacecraft fire . Specifically, HCl uptake onto treated aluminum 
surfaces has been measured in past studies [14, 15]. Figure 2 gives a schematic of the experimental setup. A bottle of 
dry air and a bottle of approximately 50 parts per million (ppm) of HCl balanced with nitrogen w ere used to flow a

gas stream through a cast acrylic test cell until it was saturated by HCl. An aluminum rod would then be inserted into 
the test cell, decreasing the response of the outlet HCl sensor. The air stream could be passed through a bubbler to 
control the humidity of the air stream. 
In mostly dry flow conditions, there is a finite capacity of aluminum to uptake HCl [ 14]. In the presence of the 
type of humidity you would find in a comfortable room or spacecraft (40 -60% humidity at approximately 20 °C), 
there is a near infinite capacity to uptake HCl. The graph in Figure 2 shows a typical response of the outlet HCl sensor 
when flowing 2 liters per minute ( lpm) of HCl into the reactor and 2 lpm of air through the bubbler, providing a 
humidity of approximately 50% , [17]. The difference between the inlet and outlet sensor was used to determine the 
rate of uptake by the sample inserted into the reactor. This rate of HCl uptake was applied to the cargo in the Saffire 
model. More information on the experimental setup and previous results can be found in earlier research [14, 17]. 
Saffire VI flew 1-liter HCl bottles at 100 pounds per square inch gauge (psig) pressure and 5% concentration balanced 
with N 2 producing a total HCl of 0. 59 g which was released from the bottle in the S FU at a rate of 2.68x10-3 kg-
HCl/m2-s. 
C. Lithium-Ion Battery Ground Testing 
An experiment was set up to determine the heat and product release of a LIB cell pack during thermal runaway. The 
apparatus included an outer enclosure that was connected to room ventilation air flow 2.29 m tall by 2.44 m in width 
and depth. Inside the outer enclosure was an inner enclosure where the battery cell pack was ignited with two hot 
plates. The inner enclosure connect ed to a measurement duct that was 76 mm in diameter and probed the air stream 
for O2, CO2, CO concentration and temperature. Figure 3 shows a schematic of the experimental apparatus. 
The data used to provide the HAR for the Saffire model was collected from the burning of a 97 Watt -hour, 6 LIB 
cell pack. The batteries were at their fully charged state. The cells were ignited with two 500 W strip heaters, each 
igniting three of the cells . The measurement duct was designed and built to allow for real -time calculation of mass 
flow rate, temperature, static pressure, and combustion products using ISO standard 5167. Two measurement devices, 
each with their own pump to draw in a sample of gas through the air stream, determined oxygen, CO 2 and CO 
concentrations. A HEPA filter and a cold trap filtered out particulates before concentration measurements. The flow 
through the measurement duct for the test used in the model was 1.99 m 3/min. The HAR that was used in the model 
was determined with oxygen consumption calorimetry, which used an energy release of 13.1 MJ/kg of O 2 consumed. 
More information on the development of the test cell, and oxygen consumption calorimetry measurements can be 
found in work performed by Easton et al. [18].

III. Modeling 
 A previously developed model of the Cygnus vehicle during the Saffire burn events was used to predict the effect 
of a fire inside a spacecraft. This model uses Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), which is a large-eddy turbulent code 
developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST ) [19]. Placement of cargo were discussed in 
previous work [ 13]. Table 1 gives the initial atmospheric conditions for all models, as well as the flow boundary 
conditions. 
 For the v alidated Saffire model, the HAR and M GR were calculated from the SFU inlet and outlet temperature 
and CO2 concentration experimental data, respectively [13]. The HCl MGR was also determined from experimental 
data. The LIB HAR was determined from oxygen consumption calorimetry [18]. The CO2 MGR for LIB tests w as 
calculated from CO 2 measurements in the measurement duct, but is not the focus of this paper. These values in the 
various simulations are applied to the outlet of the SFU, which is a thermally inert object that intakes cool cabin air

The first set of simulations focused on HCl transport in the vehicle. Since the SIBAL burn event in Saffire VI also 
released a bottle of HCl, concentration data was available in the FFD to compare to the simulation . The Saffire VI 
SIBAL simulations from previous work was re -simulated after adding the M GR of HCl from the SFU into Cygnus 
and applying the uptake rate at the cargo. The MGR of HCl into Cygnus from the SFU was 2.68x10-3 kg/m2-s applied 
to a 5 cm x 5 cm surface area for 90s. Integrating this gave a total mass of HCl of 0.59 g, which matched the calculated 
amount in the bottle, as well as the steady state value of the HCl concentration in a simulation that did not have any 
surface adsorption imposed . Tests were executed on anodized aluminum surfaces at 50% humidity as described in 
section II and were shown to have an approximate rate of uptake given by Eq. 1: [17]

International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
7 
 A strategy for extinguishing a fire in an enclosed pressure vessel in a microgravity environment is to turn off the 
flow in a vehicle in order to starve the fire of oxygen. While this can be effective, stagnation of flow can lead to 
pockets of high concen tration of hazardous combustion products. A simulation was run in which the ECLSS, SFU, 
and avionics flow w ere turned off once the FFD reached the 1-hour Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentration 
(SMAC) [20] of HCl, which was approximately 90 s for this s imulation. A subsequent simulation turned the flow 
back on once the temperature returned to initial values. 
 The last set of simulations focused on the effect that the increased HAR provided by the LIB had on the vehicl e. 
The temperature at the RS locations for the LIB simulation are compared to the temperatures of the Saffire VI SIBAL 
burn event. Additional simulations were completed that assigned material thermal properties to the cargo to see if the 
surfaces became hot enough to become hazardous. 
IV. Results and Discussion 
The concentration of HCl from the bottle release in Saffire VI SIBAL at the FFD is shown in Figure 6 against the 
model prediction. The peak concentration of 32 ppm and time to peak of 100 s m atch well with experimental results. 
This indicates that the bulk cabin flow and the release of the HCl bottle from the SFU in the simulation match the 
experiment. The drop in concentration happened significantly faster in the experiment than in the model. There are a 
couple reasons this discrepancy might exist. First, there was a lot of surface area in the FFD, as well as losses from 
the combustion product monitor that are not accounted for in the model which could add further decay. This is similar 
to the explanation of lower temperature in the FFD experiments compared to simulations during previous model 
development [10]. Second, the heat transfer coefficient that was calibrated during previous model development [11] 
is representative of an effective heat transfer coefficient to account for surfaces that are not perfec tly rectangular or 
smooth, but amorphous, rough, and porous, hence underestimating the real surface area participating in heat transfer , 
and likely mass transfer. This increased surface area, as well as mixed materials of the surface would lend itself to the 
same type of calibration of an effective uptake rate as the effective heat transfer coefficient if a more accurate 
prediction is needed. For this work, the simulation compares well enough with experimental data that it can be used 
to explore the effect of flow on the fate of acid gas. 
 
 
Figure 6. Prediction of HCl concentration at FFD against experiment during Saffire VI SIBAL burn. 
 
Next, the ECLSS, as well as the SFU and avionics flow in Saffire were turned off when the FFD reached 5ppm, 
which is the 1 hour SMAC for HCl. This event was triggered in the simulation at 90 s. With the flow turned off, the 
concentration reache d above 50 ppm and f ell much slower . Figure 7 shows the original prediction against the 
prediction where the flow is shut off. The next simulation turned all the flow systems back on after the temperature in 
the cabin reached its initial value, which was at 410 s . The concentration at the FFD immediately began to fall at an 
accelerated rate, indicating the importance of flow for the removal of hazardous products from the atmosphere. This 
could further be demonstrated by the mass of HCl in the domain across the three simulations, which is provided by

atmosphere, which is shown in gray in Figure 7. This proves to be a significant contribution and additional 
experimental HCl sensors at the outlet of the ECLSS would be needed to validate the assumption.

 Figure 9 and Figure 10 show the response of RS3 and RS6 , respectively for the three simulations. Concentration 
reached approximately 160 ppm at RS3 and 120 ppm for RS6 . For RS3, HCl returned to effectively 0 by 1000 s, 
compared to RS6 where the concentration was still decreasing in the case where the flow was shut off. RS3 is in a 
standoff where the volume to surface area was much higher, allowing for more uptake and hence more removal of 
HCl from the atmosphere. RS6 was located in a more open area, away from surfaces that uptake HCl. In that case, the 
HCl stayed in the atmosphere surrounding RS6 until the flow is turned back on.

The next set of simulations used the HAR of the LIB cell pack test in place of the H AR from the SIBAL test in 
Saffire VI. The HAR is derived from ground based (1 -g testing) and applied as an input in a 0 -g model. Despite not 
having 0-g data of a LIB fire and the differences that it would provide in the HAR curve (fire growth, entrainment, 
heat transfer, etc.), this still provides a good prediction of a fire with an order of magnitude more peak and total energy 
compared to the Saffire material burn events. The max heat release rate for the battery was 23.63 kW, compared to 
0.45 kW for the SIBAL burn. The total heat addition into the domain was 798 kJ vs. 124 kJ. Similar to the SIBAL 
test, the two remote sensors in the main flow path of Saffire (RS3 and RS6) produced the most noticeable temperature 
response, with RS2, RS4, and RS5 providing negligible response. RS1, which was near the ECLSS outlet on the nadir 
side of the vehicle, saw a brief 1 °C increase in the LIB case, compared to negligible response for the SIBAL case. 
Figure 11 shows the temperature at the exhaust of the SFU for the LIB case. The SFU outlet reached over 450 °C 
in the LIB simulation and returned to baseline at around 100 s. This is consistent with the profile of the HAR presented 
in Figure 4, as is expected with the surfaces of the SFU being adiabatic. The HAR for the SIBAL case was determined 
to effectively match the exhaust temperature of the SFU. This is why even though the flame spread end ed at 140 s,

of SIBAL and the heat from the surfaces that were released into the cabin. 
 Figures 12 and 13 give the temperature prediction for the LIB against the Saffire SIBAL case at RS3 and RS6 , 
respectively. While the increase in temperature for the SIBAL case was no more than 3 degrees, significant 
temperature increase c ould be seen in the LIB case. This increased atmospheric temperature poses a hazard to the

Figure 13. Prediction of temperature at RS6 for LIB against Saffire VI SIBAL case. 
 
To explore additional hazards in regard to increased surface temperature, additional simulations were run where 
surface thermal properties were also assigned to cargo in the channels. Steel and aluminum were first chosen as 
realistic metals , despite the bags of trash and cargo likely having multiple materials. Table 2 shows the material 
properties used. Figure 1 4 shows the surface temperature a t the surface directly below RS3. In comparing the two 
metals, the increased thermal diffusivity of the aluminum transport ed heat away from the surface and into the cool 
center, while heat stay ed longer at the surface of the steel. The increased thermal mass of the steel corresponds to a 
lower steady state temperature. In any case, the temperature d id not reach above 0.5 °C of the initial temperature, 
showing that surface temperature was not likely to be a critical hazard to the crew beyond surfaces directly in contact 
with a flame. This is also an indication that using an isothermal boundary condition at surfaces will in most cases 
provide a good prediction of the conditions of the atmosphere inside the vehicle. 
The material was then changed to foam to demonstrate how hot a material with a much lower thermal mass could 
become. Foam is present in Cygnus, as well as being an available material in the Pyrosim library. The surface reached 
45 °C but returned to its initial temperature by 200 s. Surface temperatures reaching 60 °C, as cited by ASTM standard 
C1055-03 [22], are often deemed hazardous. While the amount of heat added to the vehicle in these simulations did 
not produce surfaces hot enough to be hazardous, tests are planned to burn entire laptops and multiple battery packs . 
These tests could produce a larger and more sustained burn event, in which case the surface temperature could become 
a risk factor.

V. Conclusions 
 A previously validated model of the Cygnus vehicle during the burn events of the Saffire experimental campaign 
was used to simulate other fire scenarios of interest. First, a n HCl MGR was added to the Saffire VI SIBAL model 
that was provided experimentally and a n HCl uptake rate that was experimentally measured was implemented at the 
cargo of the vehicle. The simulated prediction of the HCl at the FFD matched the peak of the experimental data, with 
some deviations at the tail end of the response. Next, the flow in the vehicle was turned off once HCl reached 5 ppm 
at the FFD, which greatly reduced the rate of uptake and left high concentrations of HCl in the vehicle for extended 
periods of time. An additional simulation where the flow was turned back on after the temperature returned to baseline 
showed that the rate of uptake of HCl returned to the previous rate. The next set of simulations focused on the heat 
transfer from a LIB fire, and the results were compared to the previous SIBAL simulation. As expected, the increased 
HAR provided by the LIB produced higher temperatures for the remote sensors that were in the flow path of Saffire. 
Simulations where the material were changed from isothermal to either steel or aluminum and measured the surface 
temperature of the cargo provided an ins ignificant difference. Future experiments could provide heat and product 
release of multicell LIBs with entire laptops and battery fire bags burned that would provide even larger heat release 
for a sustained time. The burning of these LIBs, as well as other electronics, will create other acid gases that will need 
to be further investigated to determine their fate in a spacecraft. 
Acknowledgments 
The Saffire project was supported by NASA’s Advanced Exploration Systems Division. The authors would like 
to thank the international Saffire science team, with various agencies that include ESA, JAXA, CNES, RSA, DLR, 
the Russian Academy of Sciences and NASA. The authors are grateful for the efforts of ZIN Technologies, NG, and 
the on-orbit crew of the ISS on the Saffi re project, as well as Ryan Briggs and Mathieu Fradet from JPL for CPM 
development and testing.

distributed temperature measurements in the spacecraft and the pressure rise. Overall, the 
pressure rise and temperature change were small but the smoke particulate rose to substantial 
levels and the gaseous products also achieved hazardous levels. 
Acronyms and Nomenclature 
FFD = Far Field Diagnostics 
HRR = Heat Release Rate 
PMMA = polymethyl methacrylate 
SAFFIRE = Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project 
SFU = SAFFIRE Flow Unit 
SIBAL = Solid Inflammation Boundary at Low Speed 
SMAC = Spacecraft Maximum Allowed Concentration 
I. Introduction 
EVELOPMENT of systems and processes to ensure spacecraft fire safety requires an understanding of the 
behavior of fires in low -gravity and their impact on the habitability of the spacecraft. Prior to the SAFFIRE 
(Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project) experiment series, no tests of practical scale fires had been conducted 
in low gravity. The SAFFIRE series began in 2017 with SAFFIRE I through III occurring between 2017 and 2019 [1] 
[2]. This series focused primarily on observation of flame spread and growth for large samples of thin materials in 
flights I and III and a series of smaller samples for flight II [3]. The impact on the spacecraft was deliberately 
minimized. Subsequently, flights IV -VI studied large, thick, samples that were allowed to burn for longer durations, 
releasing heat and smoke into the spacecraft cabin. To evaluate the impact of the smoke and heat, a remote diagnostics 
and filtration system, referred to as the Far Field Diagnostics (FFD) was positioned at the other end of the spacecraft 
and 6 sensors were distributed across the open volume. Through these tests, it was possible to observe the growth rate 
of fires on large thick samples and to assess the impact of these fires on the spacecraft. The tests revealed important 
features of flame spread and growth on both thick [4] [5] and thin [6] materials. These results included delayed 
extinguishment and reignition of both thick and thin materials [6]; further evidence of the effect of the duct size on 
spread rate of thin materials; [6] the strong effect of surface structures (ribs) when aligned with the flow direction; [4] 
and concurrent flame spread on thick materials is suppressed at low flow rates due to the “oxygen shadow.” [6] 
Understanding the impact of the fire on the spacecraft habitability was a major objective of SAFFIRE IV-VI. The 
aerosol and gaseous species levels were measured for SAFFIRE IV -V [7] and their transport in the spacecraft was 
effectively modeled [8]. However, the fire heat release rate (HRR) was not successfully determined for SAFFIRE IV 
and V, so it was difficult to correlate the products with the fire size. For SAFFIRE VI, the HRR was successfully 
measured and preliminary analysis showed that, like terrestrial fires, the smoke products can be more hazardous than 
the heat produced by the fire [9]. This paper extends earlier analysis by considering the time to alarm for a smoke 
detector and the state of the spacecraft habitability when the alarm is triggered. The primary hazardous products from 
fires are heat, smoke, HCN, CO and CO 2. NASA requirements limit CO exposure in the Spacecraft Maximum 
Allowable Concentrations (SMAC) document [10]. For CO the 1-hour SMAC is 425 ppm, and the 24-hour SMAC is 
100 ppm. For CO 2, which is a metabolic product that is prevalent in crewed spacecraft, NASA -STD-3001 [11] 
establishes the limit based on the partial pressure to no more than 3 mm Hg for a 1- hour average. Planning fire 
response depends on understanding which are the most important hazards. This paper seeks to address that question 
by examining the CO and CO2 concentration changes caused by the fire events compared to NASA exposure standards 
at the time of alarm. These results demonstrate the importance of the hazard from fire smoke projects compared to 
the heat and pressure rise. 
II. Experimental Hardware and Operations 
The SAFFIRE flight hardware was installed in the Cygnus spacecraft before launch but was not supplied power 
until after the Cygnus had departed the International Space Station (ISS). As shown in Figure 1, the SAFFIRE Flow 
Unit (SFU) was located at the end cone (nadir). The FFD was installed at a middeck locker accommodation area near 
the hatch(zenith). The 6 remote sensors which measured CO2 and temperature were located with one in each standoff 
and one in the end cone (nadir) and one by the hatch (zenith). The vehicle was launched full of cargo which was 
removed by the ISS crew and replaced with material for disposal. Since the free volume in this configuration was

On each flight, the samples were installed on a single flat frame (Fig. 3) and were ignited individually in separate 
tests. The flames were imaged by 4 video cameras position to observe the top and edge of the samples. The back side 
was not imaged. During the burn sequence, the sample surface was briefly illuminated every 2 seconds for 
approximately 0.1 s by green LEDs. This enabled determination of the length of the pyrolysis zone. The parameters 
for each test were preprogramed but each test was triggered by ground command to assure continuous telemetry and 
free drift (not thruster firings) of the spacecraft. Once all of the tests were completed, the data download process began. 
Due to bandwidth limitations, the video data was compressed and only a reduced number of uncompressed images 
were downlinked. The spacecraft was initially at the pressure and oxygen concentration of the ISS but on each flight 
the Cygnus controllers vented the spacecraft to a predetermined pressure and the SFU released oxygen to bring the 
spacecraft to a targeted level. 
The FFD (Fig. 4) contained a series of gas sensors as described in more detail by Fortenberry et al. [7]. These 
included gas sensors to measure CO, CO2, and O2; an ionization sensor from a commercial smoke detector; and a TSI 
DustTrak DRX 8533 which uses light scattering to measure aerosol mass concentration. The location of the FFD was 
near the inlet of the Cygnus air circulation system so the FFD provided a good assessment of the habitability of the 
spacecraft, and it could be used to assess when a smoke detector would trigger as the air circulation system sweeps 
the air toward the intake. This is similar to the ISS where the smoke detectors are in front of air intakes [12]. 
The flames were tracked from the camera images using a thresholding analysis and using the average flame 
position over the central third of the flame (neglecting the edge effects). The images were adjusted for the automatic 
gain of the camera and averaged over 2 second intervals to reduce noise. In general, the trailing edge was very bright 
(soot) while the leading edge could be dim blue. The flame length was the difference between the average positions 
of the leading and trailing edges.

III. Results and Fire Impact on Habitability 
During SAFFIRE IV -VI, there were 4 flat PMMA samples successfully burned and three thin cotton- based 
samples (cotton t-shirt material and SIBAL fabric) [2]. The structured PMMA tests on SAFFIRE V are discussed in 
detail by Eigenbrod et al. [4]. The 1-sided PMMA sample for SAFFIRE IV shown in Figure 3 was not ignited due to 
excessive burning of the 2-sided sample [6]. The operational conditions for these tests along with summary results are 
presented in Table 1. The flame length of the PMMA samples versus time are shown in Figure 5. Since the ignition 
time for the one -sided samples was 120 seconds (twice the 2- sided samples) the time axis is referenced to when the 
ignitor was turned off. This adjustment was only done for this figure. The other figures reference to the experiment’s 
timeline start which is approximately 10 minutes before ignition. 
Unlike 1-g upward burning of thick materials such as PMMA, the flames did not spread but remained anchored at 
the leading edge and only spread as the material regressed. The PMMA samples all showed intervals of very linear 
flame growth for periods of several minutes. The slopes were generally similar ranging from 0.22 to 0.38 mm/s. This 
is significantly faster than the observations of the SAFFIRE II, 5 cm wide sample , [5] where the flame grew at less 
than 0.1 mm/s in air. The 2-sided samples are still growing at the end of the test ( around 500 seconds ) while the 1-
sided samples begin to plateau around 380 s for SAFFIRE V and 420 s for SAFFIRE VI. It is unknown if the 2-sided 
samples would eventually plateau, longer experiments would be helpful. A plausible explanation for the earlier plateau 
for the 1 -sided samples is the enhanced heat loss through the back side versus the zero -heat loss for the 2- sided 
samples. In the case of the SAFFIRE II samples, it is likely that heat losses at the edges of the much smaller samples 
led to the growth limitation. The SAFFIRE thin samples all showed linear flame spread [6]. In comparison, 
acceleratory flame growth is often seen in normal gravity for upward flame spread on thick fuels. [13] These results 
suggest that low-gravity flame spread, and growth can be expected to be linear or less and may reach a limiting size. 
Heat loss through the back side of a material is relevant in spacecraft applications, where isolated plates burning 
on both sides are uncommon. The 1- sided configuration simulates a panel or box cover with limited mass behind it. 
In the test configuration, the back side consisted of a 0.1 mm thick mica sheet (thermal diffusivity ~0.6 mm²/s) 
followed by a 0.8 mm thick aluminum card (thermal diffusivity ~97 mm²/s). Despite the large difference in diffusivity, 
the thinness of the mica layer and the high thermal conductivity of the aluminum mean that these back- side materials 
add less than 1% to the total thermal resistance of the assembly. However, the high diffusivity of aluminum will 
distribute heat laterally across the back side once the thermal wave has pen etrated through the material. 
The characteristic thermal penetration time for each layer can be estimated as τ = L²/α, where L is the thickness 
and α is the thermal diffusivity. This gives approximately 220 s for the 5 mm PMMA plate (α = 0.11 mm²/s), ~0.017 
s for the 0.1 mm mica sheet, and ~0.007 s for the 0.8 mm aluminum card. The combined characteristic time for the 
full assembly is therefore dominated by the PMMA layer at approximately 220 s, meaning the back-side materials do 
not meaningfully alter the thermal penetration timescale. For times greater than ~200 s, the thermal wave can be 
expected to have penetrated the full assembly thickness. The SAFFIRE VI flame growth rate results in Table 1 confirm 
that back -side heat loss had a significant effect on the growth rate. Since testing all possible configurations is

applications. 
 
This linear growth rate is an important finding as it suggests that even in high oxygen conditions, low -gravity 
flame spread and growth will not be acceleratory. Figure 6 shows very close agreement, in the later portion of the test, 
between the flame length and the radiometer signal for the 2-sided PMMA sample in SAFFIRE VI-3. Flame tracking 
was halted when the flow was reduced to 5 cm/s at 480 s, as the flame had weakened dramatically. The primary 
purpose of this low-flow interval was to cool the sample material and e nsure extinguishment upon flow termination, 
thereby avoiding the issues seen in SAFFIRE IV-2 [6]. Rather than dropping immediately, the radiometer 
measurements continued to rise steadily for an additional 50s. This behavior can be attributed to two simultaneous 
effects: the thermal expansion of the weakened flame at reduced flow, which shortened the distance between the flame 
front and the radiometers, and the accumulation of hot combustion products within the chamber resulting from the 
lower flow rate. 
Combined with the absence of spread discussed above, flame growth on thick materials in low -gravity is very 
different from normal-gravity. The growth rate trends for the 2-sided samples show a 73% increase in the spread rate 
from an oxygen concentration increase of 0.08 mol fraction despite the overall pressure decrease of 45%. For the 1 -
sided samples growth rate was unchanged for an oxygen increase of 0.03 mol fraction with a pressure decrease of 
27%.

fire is detected. Ideally, the fire detection threshold should be determined such that, for the expected possible fires in 
the spacecraft, the detection system will detect the fire in time for the crew to effectively respond to the fire. To

9 
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
examine this question, an alarm threshold of 2 mg/m 3 of total particulate matter detected by the TSI DustTrak DRX 
in the FFD was used as a reference point (see Fig. 7 for an example). The time to achieve this concentration is tabulated 
in Table 1 along with the increase in CO 2 and CO at that time interval. Also tabulated are the flame length and the 
HRR at detection. This detection threshold detected the fire before the SAFFIRE IV PMMA sample and SAFFIRE 
VI SIBAL sample reached hazardous CO levels however both PMMA samples from SAFFIRE VI exceeded the CO 
threshold with the 1-sided sample approaching the 1-hour SMAC. Notably the CO increase was worse for the 1-sided 
sample. The SAFFIRE VI results suggest that a lower threshold or additional detectors would be needed for this 
spacecraft configuration. 
IV. Conclusion 
Overall, the SAFFIRE IV-VI test series provided useful validation that flame growth rate for flat materials can be 
expected to exhibit linear growth without the acceleration seen in 1 -g. This fact is extremely significant when 
considering the timeline of the response to a spacecraft fire. In the case of the 1 -sided PMMA samples, th is growth 
reached a limiting size which is even more significant . It is possible that the 2-sided samples were not burned long 
enough to reach a limiting size. 
For this configuration spacecraft, a 2 mg/m3 detection threshold was not low enough to detect the fires before some 
cases exceeded the 24-hour SMAC for CO, however it only approached the 1-hour SMAC for one case. These results 
suggest that i mplementing smoke detection in this spacecraft for these design fires would require either a lower 
threshold or additional smoke detectors to reduce the transport time. Proper selection of fire detection and response 
systems depends on the ability to assess whether the smoke detector can identify a fire before the spacecr aft is 
uninhabitable. An assessment of this would require analysis specific to the spacecraft volume and flow conditions 
using heat and smoke production data such as this in a model of the planned spacecraft.

1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Extinction of solid diffusion flame in microgravity: 
details of quenching and blowoff processes 
 
Chengyao Lia, James S. T’iena,*, Paul V. Ferkulb, Sandra L. Olsonc, Michael 
C. Johnstonc 
 
aDepartment of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH, USA 
bUniversities Space Research Association, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
c NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
______________________________________________________________ 
 
Abstract 
 
Long duration microgravity experiments aboard the International Space Station determine diffusion flame 
extinction limits of PMMA spheres. Upon ignition from an electrically-heated coil, the 4-cm-diameter samples are 
exposed to forced flows ranging from 0.2 to 80 cm/s and an oxygen ranging from 13 to 28% in one atmosphere 
total pressure. Extinction is reached as oxygen concentration gradually decreases by natural depletion. Five 
extinction tests are presented at different flow velocities and oxygen concentrations. Quenching at low velocity is 
observed with the flame tip shrinking upstream and blowoff is observed when a hole forms in the flame at the 
forward flow st agnation point. However, these processes are not quasistatic. The quenching motion involves 
periodic flame tip pulsating toward downstream and shrinking upstream with a continually decreasing flame size 
at the end of each cycle. In blowoff, the flame base pulsates between the flame hole and the downstream location, 
although with far fewer cycles compared to quenching. The pulsations appear to be the result of a premixed flame 
front spreading into a combustible mixture. Two specific cases are discussed. In the first, at very low flow velocity 
(~ 0.4 cm/s) and elevated oxygen, self-sustained flame tip cyclic pulsations are observed for a lengthy period (~15 
minutes). In the second case with a higher flow velocity (50 cm/s), the diffusion flame is stabilized at the shoulder 
of the spherical sample after local stagnation point blowoff. With steady decrease in ambient oxygen due to 
depletion, spinning flamelets are formed. The long-duration microgravity environment makes it possible to observe 
these interesting and detailed extinction processes. 
 
 
Keywords: Flame quenching; Flame blowoff; Flame pulsation; Low stretch flame; Microgravity 
______________________________________________________________ 
 
 
*Corresponding author.

1. Introduction 1 
Extinction of diffusion flames is a classical topic 2 
with practical relevance to many combustion systems. 3 
Aerodynamic blowoff due to flow residence times can 4 
be interpreted using a critical small Damkohl er 5 
number concept [1,2] and is a flame stabilization 6 
problem. Aerodynamic quenching in slow flow (at 7 
long residence times) is the consequence of flame heat 8 
losses [3]. In slow flows, the combustion intensity is 9 
reduced and the ratio of heat loss (by radiat ion, for 10 
example) to heat generation is increased. The 11 
resulting reduced flame temperature leads to 12 
quenched extinction. Although blowoff experiments 13 
are common, aerodynamic quenching studies in an 14 
open-air environment (long residence time) are 15 
uncommon, e specially for solid fuels [4,5]. This is 16 
because the magnitude of the flow required for 17 
quenching is typically lower than that of the always 18 
present buoyancy -induced flow in normal Earth 19 
gravity. On Earth, low buoyant stretch stagnation -20 
point flames can on ly be obtained using very large 21 
diameter solid samples [6] or large radius burners 22 
[7,8]. To test a sample of a given size in low -speed 23 
flow, a microgravity environment is needed. In 24 
microgravity, the magnitude of the imposed (forced) 25 
flow can be independently controlled. 26 
Microgravity experiments are also important to 27 
spacecraft fire safety. Understanding extinction limits 28 
of solid materials is important to interpret the results 29 
of material screening tests performed on earth [9,10]. 30 
For thick solids with large solid -phase thermal 31 
response times, long -duration microgravity 32 
environments are needed. The present work is a part 33 
of the Growth and Extinction Experiment (GEL), 34 
which is the first of the five original experiments in 35 
the SoFIE ( Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) 36 
project. SoFIE is a NASA Biological and Physical 37 
Sciences (BPS) sponsored project on the International 38 
Space Station (ISS) on solid combustion [11]. The 39 
solid sample used in GEL is a 4-cm diameter PMMA 40 
(polymethylmethacrylate) sphere. The experimental 41 
findings of both quenching and blowoff processes are 42 
reported here, emphasizing the differences of their 43 
near-limit behaviors. 44 
 45 
2. Experiment setup 46 
 47 
The experiment is conducted using the SoFIE 48 
insert (main components shown in Fig.1) which is 49 
placed inside the Combustion Integrated Rig (CIR) 50 
aboard the ISS. CIR is equipped with a power supply, 51 
filters, lighting, gas cylinder intakes, radiometers, and 52 
oxygen, pressure, velocity and CO, CO 2 sensors. In 53 
this paper, oxygen percenta ge is reported from the 54 
sensor located at the flow duct entrance. The SoFIE 55 
insert has a square flow duct (13.3 cm x 13.3 cm cross-56 
section and 24.6 cm long). Forced flow ranging from 57 
0.2 - 80 cm/s is generated by two fan banks. A flow 58 
sensor at the upstream end of the flow duct provides a 59 
flow velocity reading. The spherical PMMA sample 60 
(4 cm diameter) used in GEL is supported by a long 61 
stainless-steel tube (6.35 mm diameter). Three 62 
samples are mounted 120  apart on an index system 63 
that can be rotated to install one sample at a time with 64 
the flow duct. 65 
Once the astronaut installs the samples and the 66 
oxidizer gas cylinders in the ISS, the rest of the 67 
experiment is controlled remotely from the NASA 68 
Glenn Research Center ISS Payload Operations 69 
Center (GIPOC). During the test, one sample is placed 70 
along the centerline of flow duct and about 1 cm from 71 
the duct exit for ignition. The igniter is an electrically 72 
heated coiled wire placed near the upstream 73 
stagnation point of the sphere. After ignition, the 74 
igniter is retracted. The sample can either stay at this 75 
location for the whole test or be translated into the 76 
duct. 77 
Four fixed cameras are used for flame 78 
visualization. Three Sony FCB-MA130 cameras with 79 
a 1400 x 1200 pixel array (named SoFIE Cam1,Cam2, 80 
and Cam3) are in orthogonal direction of a 1.4 81 
megapixel Allied Vision GC -1380CH ACME color 82 
camera assembly with a 1360 x 1024 pixel array. 83 
SoFIE Cam1 views the sample near the ignition 84 
location. SoFIE Cam2 and ACME are aligned and 85 
view the sample at the location af ter translating into 86 
the duct. SoFIE Cam3 is not activated in the cases 87 
presented in this paper. 88 
All the extinction cases in this paper are obtained 89 
using a natural and gradual oxygen depletion while 90 
the flow speed is held constant. In the sealed CIR 91 
chamber (free volume = 85.7 liter), oxygen is slowly 92 
consumed. This oxygen depletion method is the least 93 
intrusive (i.e., free of external disturbances), which is 94 
important both for determining accurate extinction 95 
limits and for observing spontaneous cyclical 96 
extinction dynamics [12,13,20]. Note that real time 97 
oxygen concentration measurement is made at the 98 
flow duct entrance upstream of the sample. 99 
 100 
Fig. 1. Diagram of the SoFIE flow duct with a 101 
thermocouple-instrumented GEL sphere sample. 102 
 103 
The PMMA sphere s amples are custom cast with 104 
five embedded thermocouples as illustrated in Fig. 1. 105 
Three thermocouples are placed along the center line 106 
close to the forward stagnation point. They are used 107 
to deduce the subsurface temperature gradient, which 108 
is a measure of the degree of solid sub -surface 109 
heating. More details on the preparation and 110

3 
 
fabrication of the samples and the method to compute 1 
the temperature gradient can be found in [14,15]. 2 
The 4-cm-diameter sphere was selected since it is 3 
a thick solid representa tive of many non -thin 4 
materials used in spacecraft. The spherical geometry 5 
has a richness of flame physics to study. When placed 6 
in an airflow stream, there are several distinct regions 7 
around the sphere, exhibiting different fluid 8 
mechanics characteristic s. In front of the sphere, 9 
stagnation point flow develops. Flames in this region 10 
are locally one-dimensional when the flame thickness 11 
is much smaller than the sphere radius, and 12 
experimental results can be compared with one -13 
dimensional models. This is also the flame 14 
stabilization region that controls the extinction 15 
characteristics of the envelope flame. The existence of 16 
the sphere shoulder and wake regions, on the other 17 
hand, can reveal additional multi -dimensional 18 
features of the extinction processes (to b e discussed 19 
later). PMMA spheres have also been employed in 20 
[16-18]. 21 
 22 
3. Experimental results 23 
 24 
Five tests are presented as listed in Table 1. Cases 25 
1 to 3 are representative of low-flow quenching, high-26 
flow blowoff, and intermediate -flow extinction, 27 
respectively. The differences between quenching and 28 
blowoff are highlighted in sections 3.1-3.3. In section 29 
3.4 and 3.5, a very low flow test (Case 4) and a higher 30 
flow test (Case 5) are shown. These last two tests 31 
reveal novel behavior and delineate the prominent 32 
features of the solid extinction phenomena. 33 
 34

 39 
3.1 A quenching sequence 40 
 41 
Figure 2 shows images of a representative 42 
quenching sequence from Case #1. During the 43 
extinction process (500 – 757.55 s), the flow velocity 44 
slightly varies between 4.46 – 4.92 cm/s, and oxygen 45 
depletes to extinction. There is a gradually increasing 46 
trend of the flow sensor reading in this time range. It 47 
is a result of flow resistance change, probably related 48 
to a slight decrease of chamber pressure during 49 
quenching due to the combustion products filtering. 50 
Figure 2(a) shows the flame tip is at around 100  51 
(measured from the front stagnation point). This is the 52 
furthest downstream that flame reaches as seen in the 53 
tracking of tip2 (red color) in Fig. 3. As oxygen slowly 54 
depletes, the flame tip slowly shrinks toward upstream 55 
(Fig 2(b)). As shown in Fig. 3, the flame tip begins to 56 
have small fluctuations later (also illustrated in Fig. 57 
2(c)). The fluctuations have varied amplitudes and 58 
time periods. Large amplitude cyclic flame tip 59 
pulsation and retreating starts much later at about 744 60 
s. With each pulsation cycle, the flame tip retrea ts 61 
more toward upstream and results in a shorter instant 62 
flame length until extinction occurred at 757.55 s. 63 
Figure 3 shows the flame tip tracking. Tracking is 64 
based on images in the orthogonal direction of that in 65 
Fig. 2. Flame tip position is represente d by the angle 66 
around the sphere with zero degrees at the forward 67 
stagnation point. Positive and negative angles are used 68 
to track the left and right tip position. Test telemetries 69 
of oxygen, pressure, and flow velocity are also plotted. 70 
The inset plot sho ws the zoom -in of the flame tip 71 
pulsations near extinction. Solid lines in the inset plot 72 
connect the data points to show pulsations. Black 73 
dotted line in the inset plot shows the decreasing trend 74 
with time of the lowest point in each cycle of tip2. 75 
Extinction occurred when tip2 shrinks past the 76 
stagnation region stabilization zone. The asymmetry 77 
between the two tips may be due to a slightly 78 
unsymmetric ignition or the intrinsic nature of the 79 
near-limit flames. 80 
Comparing the diffusion flame CH* luminosity 81 
near the stagnation point with the flame pulsation 82 
luminosity, the increased intensity of the flame during 83 
pulsating downstream seen in Fig. 2(e) suggests that 84 
this part is a premixed flame. The broaden flame 85 
image toward the back of the sphere suggests a 86 
widened reaction zone [19]. The hypothesis is that 87 
after flame tip retreat, fuel vapor can form a 88 
combustible mixture with varying fuel -air 89 
equivalence ratio distribution. The fuel vapor may 90 
come from two possible sources: leakage from the 91 
opening between the flame tip and the surface and 92 
pyrolysis from the newly exposed hot solid. The fact 93 
that the pulsating flame tip can reach far downstream 94 
to the rear of the sphere beyond the initial diffusion 95 
flame tip (see Fig. 3 inset and Fig 2(e)) supports the 96 
fuel leakage hypothesis. Additional discussion will be 97 
made in Sections 3.4. 98

speed is within the typical laminar premixed burning 1 
velocity range. After the two pulsation cycles, the 2 
flame shows azimuthal spinning (3D instability) for 3 
3.18 s with flame base anchored at the shoulder region 4 
of the sphere before complete blowoff extinction. 5 
 6 
3.3 Extinction at intermediate flow velocities 7 
and flow strain rates 8 
 9 
 In the previous sections we have shown how 10 
different the extinction processes for low -flow 11 
quenching and high -flow blowoff are. In quenching, 12 
the flame tip shrinks toward the upstream, in blowoff, 13 
the flame base retreats toward the downstream. In 14 
quenching, the flame tip pulsates while in blowoff, the 15 
flame base pulsates. One natural question is how does 16 
the flame go to extinction at intermediate flow 17 
velocities where the quenching and the blowoff 18 
boundaries meet? The meeting point of the two 19 
branches has been referred to as the fundamental limit 20 
where the oxygen limit is the lowest [3]. 21 
We have examined several test results in the 22 
intermediate flow range between 9.22 and 11.5 cm/s 23 
(strain rates 6.92 -8.23 s-1). They all exhibit the same 24 
description on the extinction processes as follows. As 25 
oxygen is depleted, flame tip shrinks but without any 26 
pulsation. Near extinction, the flame base color began 27 
to fade (a prelude to local blowoff or hole forming) 28 
but the fl ame goes out normally in one video frame 29 
without any base pulsation either. So, the transition 30 
from quench to blowoff is smooth along the extinction 31 
boundary. Case #3 in Table 1 is a representative 32 
intermediate case (see supplementary video S3). 33 
 34 
3.4 Self-sustained cyclic flame pulsation 35 
 36 
Case #4 is an ultra -low velocity case at relatively 37 
high oxygen atmosphere. As shown in Fig. 5(a), the 38 
flame tip pulsating downstream starts at 311 s, 39 
immediately after the nominal flow velocity is turned 40 
down to 0.4 cm/s at 309 s, and lasts until quenching at 41 
1237.88 s, for a total period of 927 s. In contrast, the 42 
near-limit pulsation in Case #1 only lasts for 18.84 s. 43 
In addition to flame tip position, test telemetries of 44 
oxygen, pressure, and flow velocity are also plotted in 45 
Fig. 5(a). It shows one side of the flame initiates the 46 
cyclic pulsation and the other side starts much later at 47 
around 1040 s. When the pulsation starts, oxygen 48 
concentration is at 26.25%. It gradually depletes to 49 
20.77% at quenched extinction . During most of the 50 
time, the pulsations are under elevated oxygen 51 
concentration. If the oxygen were not depleted, the 52 
pulsative cycles would have lasted even longer. So, 53 
we will refer this case as a “self -sustained” flame 54 
pulsation (i.e., limit cycle). During pulsations, though 55 
the nominal flow velocity is held constant at 0.2 cm/s 56 
(except the 0.4 cm/s set flow in the beginning 10 s), 57 
the flow sensor reading ranged from 0.16 to 0.5 cm/s. 58 
Similar to Case #1, there is a gradual increase of flow 59 
velocity dur ing the quenching process (Fig. 5(a)). 60 
Starting at around 880 s, there is also flow velocity 61 
oscillations in phase with the flame pulsation. Figure 62 
5(b) shows 10 s of the flame tip tracking and the flow 63 
sensor reading near extinction . The flow velocity 64 
fluctuation is thought to be the result of flame -flow 65 
interaction since the flow is very weak and these 66 
large-scale flame pulsations affect the flow resistance 67 
in the duct. 68 
 69 
Fig. 5. Flame tip tracking of (a) the whole cyclic pulsation 70 
period and (b) 10 s near extinction for Case #4 using SoFIE 71 
Cam1. 72 
 73 
The 30-fps frame rate gives very good resolution 74 
of the flame tracking in Fig. 5(b) within one cycle. 75 
The shape of the cycle shows that the flame tip spends 76 
much less time at the downstream position than at the 77 
upstream position. The trajectory of the tip is not 78 
sinusoidal or near-sinusoidal like typical oscillations. 79 
This is because the present cycle has two distinct time 80 
scales: the propagation time in a fuel -air mixture and 81 
the preparation time to form a new mixture after the 82 
flame passage. Figure 5(b) shows that the preparation 83 
time is the longer of the two although they are still 84 
within the same order of magnitude, close to the mass 85 
diffusion time, D/δ2, where δ is the flame standoff and 86 
D is the diffusion coefficient. In this low -flow case, 87 
escaping fuel vapor from the flame -tip-sphere 88 
opening might be the dominant source of fuel vapor 89 
to create a combustible mixture for pulsation, between 90 
the two sources discussed previously in Section 3.1. 91 
The pulsation frequency starts at 1.4 Hz, gradually 92 
decreases to 1 Hz, and is statistically constant in a 640 93 
s to 1200 s period. The frequency further drops to 0.8 94 
Hz before quenching at 1238 s. During this quasi -95 
steady period, the pulsation amplitude increases with 96

7(a) shows the asymmetry of flame tips before they 33

tracking at the stagnation point and the conductive 45 
heat loss into the solid interior during the cyclic 46 
quenching period. The average standoff starts at 7 mm 47

7 
 
Case #5 has the highest flow velocity among the 1 
five cases (50 cm/s) and the sample is located at the 2 
duct exit so the long flame tip can freely expand 3 
outward without wall constriction. Figure 9 shows its 4 
flame profiles. Before local blowoff at the stagna tion 5 
point, Fig. 9(a) shows an envelope flame with a very 6 
interesting structure. The flame tail spreads outward, 7 
but an inner weaker flame is also formed as indicated 8 
in the figure. This inner flame is connected to the 9 
downstream outer flame but extends ba ckward and 10 
ends close to the solid surface. This inner flame is 11 
attributed to the recirculation zone behind the sphere 12 
(Re ~ 1300) where the oxygen recirculates back to the 13 
rear of the sphere and reacts with the fuel vapors that 14 
may otherwise escape to the ambient. In Case #2, the 15 
sphere is inside the duct for extinction, and the 16 
recirculation zone is reduced due to the squeeze of the 17 
flame by the duct wall. The inner flame in this case is 18 
a weaker diffusion flame judging from its faint color 19 
compared with that at the stagnation point. This is 20 
expected from the lower velocity of the recirculating 21 
flow. This type of enveloping diffusion flame may be 22 
unique only for blunt -shape solids that have a flow 23 
separation region. 24 
 25 
Fig. 9. Side-stabilized flame and azimuthal spinning after 26 
local blowoff in a high-flow blowoff case (Case #5). 27 
 28 
Similar to Case #2, local blowoff occurs with a hole 29 
in the front stagnation region. The flame then 30 
stabilizes, and the flame base anchors at the shoulder 31 
of the sphere (Fig. 11(b )). The anchor flame base is 32 
indicated by the intense color due to high reactivity. 33 
In this test, the side -stabilized flame lasts for 40 s, 34 
around 35 s during which the flame is spinning. With 35 
continued oxygen depletion, the flame breaks into 36 
flamelets (Fig. 11(c) and (d)). The flamelet spins with 37 
frequencies ranging from 2 to 3.5 Hz. During 38 
spinning, the flamelets cover a shrinking surface area 39 
of the sphere due to oxygen depletion. With more and 40 
more area exposed, the solid surface cools down until 41 
the fu el vapor generated is not enough to sustain 42 
burning. This blowoff and flame spinning sequence is 43 
very dynamic (see supplementary video S5). 44 
 45 
4. Summary and discussions 46 
 47 
This is the first report on the experimental findings 48 
from a recent microgravity experiment aboard the 49 
International Space Station studying the burning of a 50 
4-cm diameter PMMA sphere. One of the main 51 
objectives of the experiment is to study solid diffusion 52 
flame extinction processes. Using an oxygen 53 
depletion method at specified flow velocities, both the 54 
transient details of the low-flow quenching and high-55 
flow blowoff processes are revealed. 56 
Quenching starts with the flame tip shrinking 57 
toward the stagnation region. Extinction occurs when 58 
the shrinking flame at the forward stagnation point 59 
becomes too small. An early quasi-steady model over 60 
a thin solid with surface radiative heat loss has 61 
predicted this trend [21]. The present experiment, 62 
however, shows t hat this trend of steady shrinking 63 
flame is only true for the average flame. The actual 64 
quenching process is very dynamic involving flame 65 
tip local fluctuation and downstream cyclic pulsations 66 
all the way to the back of the sphere over many cycles. 67 
In puls ations, flame tip spreads into partially 68 
premixed mixture next to the hot solid surface. The 69 
mixture is created by leakage of fuel vapor from the 70 
opening between the flame tip and the solid surface 71 
and solid pyrolysis from the still hot solid after the 72 
flame tip cyclic shrinking. In low stretch flames, this 73 
opening is large, which enhances the importance of 74 
fuel leakage contribution to the cyclic pulsations. In a 75 
higher oxygen atmosphere (>21%) and ultra-low flow 76 
velocity (< 1 cm/s), pulsative motion can last for more 77 
than 15 minutes. These implications for spacecraft 78 
safety need to be explored further. 79 
Blowoff starts with a hole opening at the stagnation 80 
region in front of the envelope diffusion flame. This 81 
is well known experimentally and studied in detai l in 82 
[20]. An early quasistatic numerical model on thin 83 
solid also predicted the local blowoff of the stagnation 84 
flame and the possibility of side stabilized diffusion 85 
flame with increasing flow velocity or decreasing 86 
Damkohler number [22]. Again, experime nts show 87 
that the extinction process is dynamic. Cyclic 88 
upstream pulsation and flame base retreat can proceed 89 
to the stabilization of the flame at the shoulder of the 90 
spherical sample. When the flame is weakened by 91 
reduced oxygen, flamelets form and azimuthally spin 92 
around the sphere. Other possible wake flame 93 
configurations have not been observed in the present 94 
setup possibly owing to the presence of the sample 95 
supporting rod. 96 
Regarding the near -limit flame extinction 97 
dynamics: while cyclic flame movement are observed 98 
both in quenching and in blowoff, there is a profound 99 
difference between the two cases. The pulsating part 100 
is the flame tip in quenching and the flame base in 101 
blowoff. The stagnation region is the flame 102 
stabilization zone whereas tip is not. However, both 103

cases are coupled with the hot solid surface which 1 
supplies the fuel vapor for the flame to pulsate. 2 
We note that blowoff and quench have been 3 
studied using a PMMA cylinder aligned with the 4 
flow[5, 20]. Using a large sphere, we have a better -5 
defined stagnation shoulder, and wake flow zones. 6 
The multiple embedded thermocouples enable us to 7 
characterize the sample preheat levels. The low -8 
velocity control also provides better resolved 9 
quenching limits. 10 
Also, regarding the scale effect of the samp le on 11 
quenching: low stretch flames can be established 12 
using large samples in higher velocity flows [6 -8] or 13 
using smaller sample in lower velocity flow such as in 14 
the present work. Although both can achieve the same 15 
low flame stretch rate, the near -limit behavior can 16 
differ in the details. In large sample, flame breaks into 17 
flamelets, strips or holes before the quenching of the 18 
complete flame. The flamelets are of the dimension of 19 
diffusion length. In the present work using smaller 20 
sample, there is pulsat ive motion but no flamelet 21 
formation during the quenching process. So, the 22 
detailed quenching and blowoff process can be multi-23 
dimensional in nature. They cannot be prescribed by 24 
the flow strain or flame stretch rate alone. An 25 
additional length scale may be required. 26 
One final remark on the diffusion flame extinction 27 
criterion. Even in the one-dimensional description of 28 
diffusion flames, one may wonder whether a single 29 
Damkohler number can be sufficient to describe both 30 
blowoff and quenching limits. Both are extinction 31 
processes and the concept of limiting ratio of chemical 32 
vs. flow times seems applicable. However, 33 
quantifying the chemical reaction rate will need 34 
accurate flame temperature information. The actual 35 
flame temperature will be affected by heat loss, so 36 
additional non -dimensional heat loss parameter(s) 37 
will be required. We believe that quenching and 38 
blowoff are distinct flame extinction modes having 39 
different characteristics. Blowoff at high speed is due 40 
to short flow residence time in the flame stabilization 41 
zone. Blowoff can occur even at adiabatic flame 42 
temperature (i.e., no heat loss) as demonstrated in 43 
classical theory. So, although heat loss may modify 44 
the blowoff boundary, its effect is modest (ratio of 45 
heat loss to heat generation is small ) and the flame 46 
temperature drop below the adiabatic value can be 47 
relatively small. On the other hand, at low stretch (low 48 
flow speed) with long flow residence time (or large 49 
flame standoff distance), aerodynamic quenching 50 
occurs when heat loss becomes a s ignificant fraction 51 
of the total heat release of the flame. This causes 52 
substantial flame temperature reduction and leads to 53 
extinction. We have demonstrated in the GEL 54 
experiment not only the existence of the two 55 
extinction branches but also describe thei r different 56 
mechanisms and transient responses. In addition, the 57 
flame behaviors when the two extinction boundaries 58 
merge have been clarified. 59

Executive Summary 
The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) program 
is a continuing set of experiments on droplet combus tion, 
performed employing the Multi -User Droplet Combustion 
Apparatus (MDCA), inside the chamber of the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR), which is located in the Destiny module 
of the International Space Station (ISS). This report describes 
the experimental hardware, the diagnostic equipment, the 
experimental procedures, and the methods of data analysis for 
FLEX. It also presents the results of the first 284 tests 
performed. The intent is not to interpret the experimental results 
but rather to make them available to the entire scientific 
community for possible future interpretations. 
The apparatus for the FLEX experiments was transported to 
the ISS and installed late in 2009. It includes canisters for fuel 
storage, two opposed-needle syringes for injecting fuel to form 
a droplet, two opposed hot -wire igniters for initiating combus-
tion, and a long, fine fiber that can be used to tether the droplet 
and move it at a programmable low velocity through the gas in 
the chamber. The combustion history is recorded photograph -
ically, with a visible -light color camera that views the entire 
field, a backlit camera that highlights the droplet to determine 
its diameter accurately as a function of time during burning, and 
a camera with a filter centered at 310 nm, intended to record 
emissions from excited hydroxyl radicals produced in the flame 
(Low Light Level Ultra -Violet, LLUV) , thereby providing a 
measure of the flame diameter . Although the ISS crew must 
change the fuel canisters and the gas bottles needed to establish 
the atmosphere in the combustion chamber, each droplet -
burning experiment is run remotely from the Telescience 
Support Center at the NASA Glenn Research Center i n
